overview: Immediately after the events of The Desolation of Smaug, Bilbo and the dwarves try to defend Erebor's mountain of treasure from others who claim it: the men of the ruined Laketown and the elves of Mirkwood. Meanwhile an army of Orcs led by Azog the Defiler is marching on Erebor, fueled by the rise of the dark lord Sauron. Dwarves, elves and men must unite, and the hope for Middle-Earth falls into Bilbo's hands.
tagline: Will you follow me... one last time?
review:
The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies wraps up Peter Jackson’s sprawling prequel trilogy with a sprawling, effects-heavy spectacle that feels like Lord of the Rings meets an all-out war movie on steroids. It’s a fitting if somewhat overstuffed finale that delivers on the promise of epic battles and emotional stakes, though it leans heavily on CGI carnage and bombastic set pieces over the quiet moments that made the earlier films sing. Fans of the franchise will appreciate the return of familiar faces like Ian McKellen’s Gandalf and Martin Freeman’s Bilbo, but this one’s really about the clash of armies and the fate of Middle-Earth.

What stands out here is the sheer scale of the conflict—the tag line “Will you follow me... one last time?” feels like a rallying cry amid the chaos. The film juggles multiple factions—dwarves, elves, men, and orcs—all vying for control of Erebor’s treasure, while the looming threat of Sauron adds a dark cloud over the proceedings. The writing, from Guillermo del Toro and company, tries to balance political intrigue with fantasy warfare, though at times the story gets lost in the spectacle. Visually, the battle sequences are ambitious and impressive, but the film’s pacing can drag in places, making some stretches feel like a long slog through CGI explosions.

For those sensitive to animal harm, be heavily warned: this film’s production reportedly involved animals being harmed, which is a serious consideration if you’re on the lookout for that trigger. Aside from that, the movie is less about jump scares or sexual violence and more about large-scale war violence and fantasy brutality, so keep that in mind before diving into Middle-Earth’s final showdown.
emailReview:
The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies delivers an epic, effects-packed finale filled with sprawling battles and the return of beloved characters, capturing the chaos and grandeur of Middle-Earth’s ultimate clash.

Be prepared for: on-screen animal harm during production, large-scale war violence, orc brutality, and intense fantasy combat sequences.

name: Shrek 2
overview: Happily ever after never seemed so far far away when a trip to meet the in-laws turns into a hilariously twisted adventure for Shrek and Fiona. tagline: What happens after happily ever after?

name: Ready Player One
overview: When the creator of a popular video game system dies, a virtual contest is created to compete for his fortune.
review:
Ready Player One is a neon-drenched, nostalgia-fueled sci-fi adventure that feels like Spielberg channeling the wild mash-up energy of The Wizard of Oz meets a high-stakes video game speedrun. It’s a visually dazzling plunge into a virtual contest where pop culture references collide with earnest coming-of-age beats. While it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, it’s a thrilling, if somewhat predictable, ride for anyone who grew up loving 80s and 90s geek culture—or just likes their action served with a side of pixelated whimsy.

What stands out most is the film’s ability to create a fully immersive digital world that’s both a playground and a battleground, anchored by Tye Sheridan’s likable Parzival and Olivia Cooke’s Art3mis. The tagline “A better reality awaits” hits on the film’s core theme—escapism versus reality—and the screenplay leans into that tension with some smart moments about identity and connection. Spielberg’s signature flair keeps the pace lively, though the story sometimes feels more like a checklist of fan-service Easter eggs than a fully fleshed narrative.

On the trigger front, be heavily warned if animal harm or death is something that unsettles you: this movie includes the deaths of multiple animals, including a dog, cat, horse, and even a dragon. There’s also a fair share of creepy crawlies—spiders, bugs, and snakes make appearances that might give arachnophobes or entomophobes pause. Plus, viewers sensitive to misgendering or gaslighting should approach with caution, as these elements are present in the story’s interpersonal conflicts.
emailReview:
Ready Player One is a neon-soaked, nostalgia-fueled thrill ride that plunges you into a dazzling digital playground where 80s and 90s pop culture collide with heartfelt coming-of-age moments.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, cat, horse, and dragon, creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes, plus scenes involving misgendering and gaslighting.

name: Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan
cleanName: borat cultural learnings america make benefit glorious nation kazakhstan
cleanNameArticles: borat cultural learnings of america for make benefit glorious nation of kazakhstan
overview: Kazakh journalist Borat Sagdiyev travels to America to make a documentary. As he zigzags across the nation, Borat meets real people in real situations with hysterical consequences. His backwards behavior generates strong reactions around him exposing prejudices and hypocrisies in American culture.
review:
Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan is a wildly irreverent mockumentary that rides the line between outrageous satire and social experiment. Sacha Baron Cohen’s infamous alter ego, Borat Sagdiyev, barrels through America with a clueless charm that exposes the worst and most ridiculous sides of American culture. Think of it as a sharp-tongued prank show crossed with a biting cultural critique—fans of Cohen’s later work will appreciate the roots of his shock-comedy style here, though this one’s arguably the most unfiltered and daring.

What really stands out is how the film uses Borat’s absurd behavior to pull genuine reactions from real people, making the comedy land with an uncomfortable yet hilarious punch. The tagline, “Come to Kazakhstan, it’s nice!” perfectly sums up the film’s tone: a mix of naivety and biting sarcasm. Directed by Larry Charles and co-written by Cohen, the film cleverly mingles scripted setups with real-world chaos, turning the documentary format on its head. The supporting cast, including Ken Davitian as Borat’s sidekick Azamat and surprise appearances like Pamela Anderson, add to the surreal atmosphere. The film is a wild ride into the bizarre fringes of American life, using offensive humor to hold up a mirror to cultural prejudices and hypocrisies.

That said, be heavily warned if animal harm or death triggers are on your list. The film features multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and other animals, which are more than just background details—they’re part of some of the film’s more uncomfortable moments. If the idea of animals suffering or dying on-screen is a deal-breaker, this one might sting.
emailReview:
Borat is a wildly irreverent mockumentary that blends outrageous satire with real-world chaos, delivering uncomfortable laughs through Sacha Baron Cohen’s clueless but sharp-tongued alter ego.

Be prepared for: multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse including dogs, cats, and horses, as well as unsettling real reactions from unsuspecting people.

writers: Derek Kolstad, Shay Hatten, Chris Collins, Marc Abrams
name: John Wick: Chapter 3 - Parabellum
overview: Super-assassin John Wick returns with a $14 million price tag on his head and an army of bounty-hunting killers on his trail. After killing a member of the shadowy international assassin’s guild, the High Table, John Wick is excommunicado, but the world’s most ruthless hit men and women await his every turn.
tagline: If you want peace, prepare for war.
review:
John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum cranks the franchise’s signature blend of sleek action and relentless world-building up to eleven. If you dug the first two films’ mix of stylish gun-fu and shadowy assassin politics, this one doubles down with even more inventive fight choreography and a sprawling, almost mythic take on the criminal underworld. It’s like John Wick meets an ultra-violent spy thriller — a wild ride that’s as much about slick style and kinetic energy as it is about the tired loner assassin trope. Keanu Reeves remains perfectly cast, embodying Wick’s quiet intensity with a cool that keeps this installment humming along.

What stands out is how director Chad Stahelski and his team push the boundaries of action cinema without losing sight of the story. The tagline “If you want peace, prepare for war” nails the film’s tone: every scene is a countdown to mayhem. The introduction of new characters like Halle Berry’s Sofia adds fresh energy, while familiar faces like Ian McShane’s Winston deepen the intrigue. The movie leans hard into its noir-ish assassin guild mythology, with a sharp visual style and a pulse-pounding score that keeps you on edge. It’s not just about the bodies piling up—there’s a strange elegance to the chaos, a kind of balletic brutality that’s rare in big-budget sequels.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to violence: this film is packed with intense gun violence, brutal hand-to-hand combat, and some pretty graphic mutilation moments that don’t pull punches. Animal lovers should note there’s no dog death despite the franchise’s history, but there is a horse death and various instances of animal harm, so tread carefully. If you’re into high-octane action and can handle the carnage, Parabellum delivers a relentless thrill.
emailReview:
John Wick: Chapter 3, Parabellum delivers sleek, balletic brutality with Keanu Reeves coolly guiding a mythic, ultra-violent world where every fight scene is a finely choreographed explosion of style and chaos.

Be prepared for: graphic hand-to-hand combat, intense gun violence, horse death, and vivid animal harm.

name: Lady Bird
overview: Lady Bird McPherson, a strong willed, deeply opinionated, artistic 17 year old comes of age in Sacramento. Her relationship with her mother and her upbringing are questioned and tested as she plans to head off to college.

writers: Ronald Bronstein, Josh Safdie, Benny Safdie
name: Uncut Gems
overview: A charismatic New York City jeweler always on the lookout for the next big score makes a series of high-stakes bets that could lead to the windfall of a lifetime. Howard must perform a precarious high-wire act, balancing business, family, and encroaching adversaries on all sides in his relentless pursuit of the ultimate win.
review:
Uncut Gems is a relentless, anxiety-drenched crime thriller that feels like a high-stakes rollercoaster ride through the chaotic underbelly of New York’s diamond district. Adam Sandler delivers a career-best turn as Howard Ratner, a fast-talking jeweler whose compulsive gambling and risky bets fuel a nerve-shredding plot. If you appreciate the Safdie brothers’ signature style—off-kilter camerawork and a pulse-pounding pace—this is their finest work yet. It’s not just a thriller; it’s an immersion into manic desperation, somewhere between Goodfellas and Requiem for a Dream, but with a unique urban grit and a pounding electronic score that keeps you on edge.

What stands out the most is how the film captures the chaos of Howard’s life, juggling business, family drama, and dangerous debts with a manic energy that’s almost overwhelming. The tagline, "This is how I win," perfectly captures his obsessive single-mindedness, even as everything threatens to collapse. The supporting cast, including LaKeith Stanfield and Julia Fox, add texture to this world, while real-life basketball star Kevin Garnett’s presence adds an unexpected but fitting layer. The Safdies’ direction keeps the tension taut without ever losing sight of the humanity beneath Howard’s frenetic exterior.

Be heavily warned if animal harm or death, especially involving pets or other animals, is on your list—there are multiple scenes that could be very upsetting. Also, this one doesn’t shy away from intense violence, screaming, and moments of severe emotional distress, so those sensitive to that should approach with caution. It’s a brutal ride that’s as exhausting as it is captivating.
emailReview:
Uncut Gems is a nerve-shredding crime thriller that plunges you into a chaotic, manic world fueled by Adam Sandler’s career-best performance and the Safdie brothers’ signature pulse-pounding style.

Be prepared for: multiple scenes of animal harm, intense violence, screaming, and severe emotional distress.

tagline: To save the future he must reshape the past.

primaryTitle: War for the Planet of the Apes
writers: Mark Bomback, Matt Reeves, Rick Jaffa, Amanda Silver, Pierre Boulle
Title_IMDb_Link: War for the Planet of the Apes
name: War for the Planet of the Apes

overview:
Caesar and his apes are forced into a deadly conflict with an army of humans led by a ruthless Colonel. After the apes suffer unimaginable losses, Caesar wrestles with his darker instincts and begins his own mythic quest to avenge his kind. 

As the journey finally brings them face to face, Caesar and the Colonel are pitted against each other in an epic battle that will determine the fate of both their species and the future of the planet.
tagline: For freedom. For family. For the planet.
review:
War for the Planet of the Apes wraps up the reboot trilogy with a grim, sometimes brutal tone that sets it apart from your average blockbuster sci-fi. It’s less about flashy action and more about heavy themes — family, revenge, and what it means to be human or animal. If you liked the thoughtful intensity of the first two films, this one will land well, though it leans darker and occasionally feels like a Western tragedy starring apes. Andy Serkis returns as Caesar with all the emotional heft he’s known for, and Woody Harrelson’s Colonel adds a chilling human villain to the mix.

The film’s standout is its ability to balance epic war spectacle with intimate moments of grief and moral conflict. The tagline “For freedom. For family. For the planet.” really nails the stakes here, and the story doesn’t shy away from the costs of that fight. Visually, Matt Reeves keeps the gritty realism strong, making the apes’ world feel lived-in and raw. The soundtrack supports the somber mood without ever overpowering Serkis’s nuanced performance or the weighty script. It’s a thoughtful capstone to a series that’s as much about identity and leadership as it is about survival.

Heads up: this movie features quite a bit of animal-related distress, including deaths of dogs, horses, and cats, plus some scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting. Those sensitive to animal harm should definitely tread carefully here. The presence of spiders, snakes, and bugs might also be unsettling if you’re on high alert for critters. It’s a war story, so expect some tough moments, but it’s especially heavy on the animal side of things.
emailReview:
War for the Planet of the Apes closes its trilogy with a grim, emotionally charged tone that blends epic war spectacle and intimate grief, anchored by Andy Serkis’s powerful Caesar and Woody Harrelson’s chilling villain.

Be prepared for: deaths of dogs, horses, and cats, scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, plus unsettling spiders, snakes, and bugs.

name: Me Before You
overview: A small town girl is caught between dead-end jobs. A high-profile, successful man becomes wheelchair bound following an accident. The man decides his life is not worth living until the girl is hired for six months to be his new caretaker. Worlds apart and trapped together by circumstance, the two get off to a rocky start. But the girl becomes determined to prove to the man that life is worth living and as they embark on a series of adventures together, each finds their world changing in ways neither of them could begin to imagine.
review:
Me Before You is a glossy, bittersweet romantic drama that’s a bit like The Fault in Our Stars meets The Intouchables—with a dash of small-town charm and big-city heartbreak. Emilia Clarke and Sam Claflin have decent chemistry as the mismatched duo thrown together by circumstance, but the film’s emotional punches sometimes feel carefully calibrated rather than fully earned. It’s a crowd-pleaser for fans of tearjerkers and love-against-the-odds stories, though it doesn’t quite transcend its genre’s familiar beats.

What stands out here is the way the movie leans into its “Live boldly” tagline, pushing Louisa to drag Will out of his self-imposed isolation and into a series of adventures that are as much about self-discovery as they are about romance. Thea Sharrock’s direction is straightforward, letting the performances and the bittersweet script by Jojo Moyes and team carry the weight. The film tackles themes of disability, autonomy, and quality of life with a sensitivity that’s commendable if occasionally clumsy, and the supporting cast, including Janet McTeer and Charles Dance, add some welcome gravitas.

Heads up for sensitive viewers: this one includes several animal-related triggers—dogs, horses, cats, and other animals die or are harmed, which might be a tough watch if you’re sensitive to animal harm or death. There are also bugs, spiders, and snakes on the menu, plus some emotional distress like gaslighting and vomiting. So if you’re scrolling through your triggers list, animal harm and death stand out as the big caution flags here.
emailReview:
Me Before You is a glossy, bittersweet romantic drama that blends small-town charm with big-city heartbreak, anchored by Emilia Clarke and Sam Claflin’s warm chemistry and a heartfelt push to live boldly despite life’s challenges.

Be prepared for: animal harm and death involving dogs, horses, and cats, plus unsettling scenes with bugs, spiders, and snakes, along with emotional distress like gaslighting and vomiting.

writers: Todd Komarnicki, Chesley Sullenberger, Jeffrey Zaslow
name: Sully
overview: On 15 January 2009, the world witnessed the 'Miracle on the Hudson' when Captain 'Sully' Sullenberger glided his disabled plane onto the frigid waters of the Hudson River, saving the lives of all 155 aboard. However, even as Sully was being heralded by the public and the media for his unprecedented feat of aviation skill, an investigation was unfolding that threatened to destroy his reputation and career.
tagline: The untold story behind the miracle on the Hudson.

name: The Lighthouse
overview: Two lighthouse keepers try to maintain their sanity while living on a remote and mysterious New England island in the 1890s.
tagline: There is enchantment in the light.
review:
The Lighthouse is a claustrophobic, psychosexual descent into madness wrapped in a black-and-white period-horror package. If you like your atmospheric dread served with a side of tortured performances, Robert Eggers’ 2019 film feels like a fever dream mashup of The Shining meets The Thing, with a nautical twist. Willem Dafoe and Robert Pattinson deliver powerhouse performances that anchor this unsettling tale of two lighthouse keepers unraveling on a remote island. It’s not just pretty standard horror — it’s a wild, immersive experience that oscillates between raw brutality and surreal myth.

What really stands out is how Eggers uses the cramped, decaying lighthouse as a pressure cooker for psychological torment. The tag “There is enchantment in the light” feels loaded with irony — the beacon is both a literal and figurative source of obsession and madness. The film’s writing and visuals lean heavily on maritime folklore and symbolism, with the mysterious mermaid and the eerie lighthouse lamp adding layers of haunting ambiguity. The soundtrack and sound design amplify the isolation and tension, building a suffocating atmosphere that never lets up. Themes of addiction, toxic masculinity, and mental illness swirl in a fog of violence and hallucination, pushing the characters to the brink in a story as much about internal demons as external ones.

Trigger-wise, this one is a minefield. Those sensitive to domestic violence, alcohol addiction, and intense psychological distress should be cautious. The film is relentlessly claustrophobic, with cramped interiors that contribute to the feeling of suffocation. Animal abuse and graphic gore, including eye mutilation and decapitation, appear in disturbing detail, and the ending is particularly brutal and bleak. There’s also sexual content and nudity, some of it tied into unsettling fantasies and power dynamics. Sudden loud noises and jump scares punctuate the tension, so if any of those are on your list, be warned. This is a dark, demanding watch that’s as mesmerizing as it is harrowing.
emailReview:
The Lighthouse is a claustrophobic psychosexual descent into madness with powerhouse performances from Willem Dafoe and Robert Pattinson, wrapped in a black-and-white nautical fever dream that blends surreal myth with raw brutality.

Be prepared for: eye mutilation, decapitation, animal abuse, intense psychological distress, and unsettling sexual content.

name: A Nightmare on Elm Street
overview: Teenagers in a small town are dropping like flies, apparently in the grip of mass hysteria causing their suicides. A cop's daughter, Nancy Thompson, traces the cause to child molester Fred Krueger, who was burned alive by angry parents many years before. Krueger has now come back in the dreams of his killers' children, claiming their lives as his revenge. Nancy and her boyfriend, Glen, must devise a plan to lure the monster out of the realm of nightmares and into the real world...
tagline: If Nancy doesn't wake up screaming, she won't wake up at all.

writers: John Wagner, Vince Locke, Josh Olson
name: A History of Violence
overview: An average family is thrust into the spotlight after the father commits a seemingly self-defense murder at his diner.
tagline: Tom Stall had the perfect life...until he became a hero.
review:
David Cronenberg’s *A History of Violence* is a taut crime thriller that sneaks up on you with its quiet intensity before delivering some seriously brutal punches. It’s not your typical action flick—more a slow burn that peels back the layers of a small-town family man’s dark past. Viggo Mortensen anchors the film with a magnetic performance, balancing the everyday Dad vibe with a simmering menace underneath. Fans of gritty, psychological crime dramas like *Mystic River* or *No Country for Old Men* will find plenty to appreciate here, though Cronenberg’s signature focus on identity and violence gives it a unique edge.

What really stands out is how the film explores the cost of violence on both the individual and the family. The tagline—“Tom Stall had the perfect life...until he became a hero”—perfectly captures the premise, as a seemingly ordinary man’s violent act throws his whole world into chaos. The screenplay by Josh Olson is sharp, with dialogue that feels real and moments that stick with you long after the credits roll. Plus, the film’s visuals and pacing let the tension build organically, making the violent scenes hit harder because they’re so rare and consequential.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: *A History of Violence* includes several instances of animal deaths and abuse, which are notably unsettling. The movie also features some spider and bug scenes that could trigger arachnophobia or entomophobia. If you’re wary of those topics, keep this in mind before diving in.
emailReview:
David Cronenberg’s *A History of Violence* is a slow-burning crime thriller anchored by Viggo Mortensen’s magnetic performance, blending quiet small-town life with a simmering, brutal menace.

Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths and abuse, unsettling spider and bug scenes, and tense, sudden bursts of violence.

name: The Talented Mr. Ripley
overview: Tom Ripley is a calculating young man who believes it's better to be a fake somebody than a real nobody. Opportunity knocks in the form of a wealthy U.S. shipbuilder who hires Tom to travel to Italy to bring back his playboy son, Dickie. Ripley worms his way into the idyllic lives of Dickie and his girlfriend, plunging into a daring scheme of duplicity, lies and murder.
tagline: How far would you go to become someone else.

name: Bram Stoker's Dracula
overview: In 19th century England, Count Dracula travels to London and meets Mina Harker, a young woman who appears as the reincarnation of his lost love.
review:
Francis Ford Coppola’s 1992 *Bram Stoker’s Dracula* is a lush, operatic take on the gothic vampire tale that leans heavily into romance and horror with equal passion. If you picture *Dracula* as *Interview with the Vampire* meets *Dangerous Liaisons*, you’re on the right track—this one’s all about doomed love wrapped in baroque visuals and moody atmosphere. Gary Oldman’s Dracula is mesmerizingly tragic, and Winona Ryder’s Mina is caught in a swirl of reincarnation and forbidden desire. It doesn’t quite reinvent the wheel but it spins the vampire myth with such style and emotional intensity that it remains a standout among its many adaptations.

What really grabs you here is the film’s commitment to extravagance: the ornate costumes and sumptuous sets feel like a painting come to life, and the score adds a haunting, almost hypnotic quality to the proceedings. The tagline, “Love never dies,” fits the film’s core—this is less about horror for horror’s sake and more about the fatal allure between Dracula and Mina, a love story stained with blood and centuries of longing. The narrative blends historical drama, supernatural terror, and psychological torment, peeling back layers of obsession and possession. Coppola’s direction doesn’t shy away from the darker, more disturbing aspects of the story, including scenes of possession, mind control, and brutal violence, all underscored by a persistent religious conflict that adds depth and tension.

Heads up: this movie carries some heavy trigger warnings. Those sensitive to sexual violence and assault, including non-consensual acts and sexualized possession, should be cautious. There’s also a significant amount of blood and gore, including decapitations and brutal attacks, along with scenes of torture and intense violence. Mental health themes appear in the form of a grim asylum setting with ableist behavior and restraint. Animal lovers beware—there’s some animal abuse and death, including distressing scenes involving horses and insects. The film also includes flashing lights and shaky cam effects that might unsettle some viewers. Lastly, the storyline involves cheating and large age gaps, woven into the complex emotional web of the characters. This is a visually stunning but intense ride that doesn’t pull punches.
emailReview:
Francis Ford Coppola’s *Bram Stoker’s Dracula* is a lush, operatic feast of gothic romance and horror, with Gary Oldman’s tragic vampire and Winona Ryder’s haunted Mina delivering unforgettable, emotionally charged performances.

Be prepared for: sexual violence and possession, brutal decapitations and torture, animal abuse involving horses and insects, and a grim asylum setting with ableist restraint.

name: The Evil Dead
overview: When a group of college students finds a mysterious book and recording in the old wilderness cabin they've rented for the weekend, they unwittingly unleash a demonic force from the surrounding forest.
tagline: The ultimate experience in gruelling terror.

writers: Chris Williams, Mark Dindal, David Reynolds, Stephen J. Anderson, Don Hall, John Norton, Roger Allers, Matthew Jacobs, Doug Frankel, Mark Kennedy, Mark Walton
name: The Emperors New Groove
overview: Kuzco is a self-centered emperor who summons Pacha from a village and to tell him that his home will be destroyed to make room for Kuzco's new summer home. Kuzco's advisor, Yzma, tries to poison Kuzco and accidentally turns him into a llama, who accidentally ends up in Pacha's village. Pacha offers to help Kuzco if he doesn't destroy his house, and so they form an unlikely partnership.

name: Lilo & Stitch
overview: As Stitch, a runaway genetic experiment from a faraway planet, wreaks havoc on the Hawaiian Islands, he becomes the mischievous adopted alien "puppy" of an independent little girl named Lilo and learns about loyalty, friendship, and 'ohana, the Hawaiian tradition of family.

name: Darkest Hour
overview: A thrilling and inspiring true story begins on the eve of World War II as, within days of becoming Prime Minister of Great Britain, Winston Churchill must face one of his most turbulent and defining trials: exploring a negotiated peace treaty with Nazi Germany, or standing firm to fight for the ideals, liberty and freedom of a nation. As the unstoppable Nazi forces roll across Western Europe and the threat of invasion is imminent, and with an unprepared public, a skeptical King, and his own party plotting against him, Churchill must withstand his darkest hour, rally a nation, and attempt to change the course of world history.
tagline: Never give up. Never give in.
review:
Darkest Hour is a gripping historical drama that leans hard into the weight of its moment, anchored by Gary Oldman’s transformative performance as Winston Churchill. If you’re into stirring wartime tales like Dunkirk or The King’s Speech, this one sits comfortably in that tradition—though it’s less about battlefield action and more about the high-stakes political chess game behind the scenes. It’s an intense, sometimes claustrophobic look at leadership under pressure, and Oldman really carries the film with a mix of grit and vulnerability that elevates the material.

What stands out here is the film’s focus on the moral and psychological turmoil Churchill faces as Britain teeters on the brink of defeat. The tagline, “Never give up. Never give in.” is a fitting mantra for the story’s relentless tension, with the writing by Anthony McCarten spotlighting the drama of choosing to fight or negotiate peace with Nazi Germany. Joe Wright’s direction keeps things visually tense without overwhelming the narrative, letting the sharp dialogue and finely tuned performances do the heavy lifting. The interplay between Churchill, King George VI, and the skeptical political elite adds layers to the story that go beyond typical war movie tropes.

Heads up for viewers sensitive to animal content: this film includes several distressing scenes involving the death and abuse of animals, including a dog and a cat, as well as other pet and horse deaths. If animal harm is a trigger for you, be prepared for moments that could be quite upsetting.
emailReview:
Gary Oldman’s transformative performance anchors this intense, claustrophobic look at Winston Churchill’s psychological and moral battles during Britain’s darkest hour.

Be prepared for: distressing scenes of dog and cat deaths, animal abuse, and multiple horse fatalities.

name: Garden State
overview: Andrew returns to his hometown for the funeral of his mother, a journey that reconnects him with past friends. The trip coincides with his decision to stop taking his powerful antidepressants. A chance meeting with Sam - a girl also suffering from various maladies - opens up the possibility of rekindling emotional attachments, confronting his psychologist father, and perhaps beginning a new life.

name: Beverly Hills Cop
overview: Fast-talking, quick-thinking Detroit street cop Axel Foley has bent more than a few rules and regs in his time, but when his best friend is murdered, he heads to sunny Beverly Hills to work the case like only he can.
tagline: He's been chased, thrown through a window and arrested. Eddie Murphy is a Detroit cop on vacation in Beverly Hills.
review:
Beverly Hills Cop is a classic 80s action-comedy that still holds up as a wild ride, thanks largely to Eddie Murphy’s magnetic turn as Axel Foley. It’s the perfect blend of street-smart Detroit grit crashing into sun-soaked, posh Beverly Hills, with Murphy’s quick wit and charm driving the whole thing. Fans of smart, snappy buddy-cop flicks will find this one a must-watch — it’s like Lethal Weapon meets Trading Places, with plenty of humor to keep it from tipping into straight-up crime drama.

What stands out here is the sharp contrast between Foley’s no-nonsense, rule-bending style and the stiff, buttoned-up Beverly Hills police force. The writing leans into that culture clash for laughs and tension, while the action sequences are satisfyingly energetic without overshadowing the comedy. Martin Brest’s direction keeps the pace brisk, and the supporting cast, including Judge Reinhold and John Ashton as the local cops, provide a nice foil to Murphy’s larger-than-life character. The tagline “He’s been chased, thrown through a window and arrested” perfectly captures the film’s mix of chaos and charm.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this movie includes multiple instances of animal death and abuse, including a dog, cat, and horse, among others. If you have those triggers, proceed with caution — it’s a bit rougher than you might expect from a comedy of this era.
emailReview:
Eddie Murphy’s electric performance powers Beverly Hills Cop, a smart and snappy 80s action-comedy that balances street grit with Beverly Hills glitz in a way that still feels fresh and fun.

Be prepared for: multiple instances of animal death and abuse including a dog, cat, and horse, plus some chaotic action scenes that bring the rough edges amid the laughs.

name: Carrie
overview: Carrie White, a shy and troubled teenage girl who is tormented by her high school peers and her fanatically religious mother, begins to use her powers of telekinesis to exact revenge upon them.
tagline: If you've got a taste for terror...Take Carrie to the prom!
review:
Brian De Palma’s 1976 Carrie is a classic blend of supernatural horror and high school drama that still packs a punch decades later. It’s a slow-burn terror tale about an outcast teen with telekinetic powers, and it’s probably the gold standard for Stephen King adaptations — think Carrie meets Heathers with a splash of Carrie’s own prom-night chaos. Sissy Spacek’s shy, unsettling performance as Carrie White is the heart of the film, while Piper Laurie’s portrayal of the fanatically religious mother adds a chilling layer of psychological torment. It’s not just a revenge story; it’s a deeply uncomfortable look at bullying, repression, and adolescent rage.

What really sticks is how the film leans into its horror roots with some iconic visuals — the infamous blood-soaked prom scene is practically etched into genre history. The tagline, “If you’ve got a taste for terror… take Carrie to the prom,” nails the film’s mix of teenage dread and supernatural horror perfectly. The soundtrack and the creepy atmosphere elevate what could have been a straightforward slasher flick into something far more unsettling. Plus, the supporting cast, including a young John Travolta and Amy Irving, bring some extra texture to the toxic high school environment.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: multiple triggers around animal death and abuse show up here, including the deaths of a dog, cat, and horse, though none of these are shown explicitly on screen. The film also features spiders, bugs, and snakes, which might unsettle some viewers. If animal harm or death is high on your list, be prepared for some unsettling moments.
emailReview:
Brian De Palma’s Carrie is a masterclass in creeping dread, anchored by Sissy Spacek’s haunting performance and a prom-night scene that still sends shivers decades later.

Be prepared for: off-screen dog, cat, and horse deaths, creepy spiders and snakes, plus moments of animal abuse.

name: Anora
overview: Anora, a young sex worker from Brooklyn, gets her chance at a Cinderella story when she meets and impulsively marries the son of an oligarch. Once the news reaches Russia, her fairytale is threatened as the parents set out for New York to get the marriage annulled.

writers: Nick Schenk, Bill Dubuque, David Dobkin
name: The Judge
overview: A successful lawyer returns to his hometown for his mother's funeral only to discover that his estranged father, the town's judge, is suspected of murder.

name: Conclave
overview: Cardinal Lawrence is tasked with leading one of the world's most secretive and ancient events, selecting a new Pope. Once the Catholic Church’s most powerful leaders have gathered from around the world and are locked together in the Vatican halls, Lawrence finds himself at the center of a conspiracy and discovers a secret that could shake the very foundation of The Church.
tagline: What happens behind these walls will change everything.
review:
Conclave is a tense, atmospheric thriller that feels like The West Wing meets The Borgias—if The West Wing were locked inside the Vatican and The Borgias had a newsroom’s sharp dialogue. Ralph Fiennes leads a powerhouse cast including Stanley Tucci and John Lithgow, delivering a cerebral spin on the classic secret society conspiracy genre. It’s not a light watch, but fans of political intrigue and religious drama will find plenty to chew on here, even if it doesn’t reinvent the genre.

What really stands out is how Conclave leans into the claustrophobia and weight of centuries-old tradition while unraveling a modern-day conspiracy that threatens to shake the Catholic Church to its core. The tagline, “What happens behind these walls will change everything,” perfectly captures the simmering tension and stakes. Director Edward Berger and writer Peter Straughan keep the pacing taut, with the Vatican’s shadowy halls serving almost as a character themselves. The film’s strength is its ability to balance quiet moments of reflection with sudden revelations that keep you guessing.

Heads up: this one carries a heavy load of animal-related triggers. If you’re sensitive to animal death or abuse—including dogs, cats, horses, or other creatures—you’ll want to be cautious. There are also bugs, snakes, and spiders lurking in the background, which may unsettle some viewers. So while the human drama is front and center, the animal elements demand a careful glance before diving in.
emailReview:
Conclave is a tense, atmospheric thriller where sharp dialogue and powerhouse performances turn Vatican intrigue into a gripping, claustrophobic chess match.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, unsettling scenes with snakes and spiders, and moments of intense animal abuse.

writers: Enrico Casarosa, Jesse Andrews, Simon Stephenson, Mike Jones, Julie Lynn, Randall Green
name: Luca
overview: Luca and his best friend Alberto experience an unforgettable summer on the Italian Riviera. But all the fun is threatened by a deeply-held secret: they are sea monsters from another world just below the water’s surface.

name: [REC]
overview: A television reporter and cameraman follow emergency workers into a dark apartment building and are quickly locked inside with something terrifying.

overview: Ash, a handsome, shotgun-toting, chainsaw-armed department store clerk, is time warped backwards into England's Dark Ages, where he romances a beauty and faces legions of the undead.
tagline: Trapped in time. Surrounded by evil. Low on gas.

name: Palm Springs
overview: When carefree Nyles and reluctant maid of honor Sarah have a chance encounter at a Palm Springs wedding, things get complicated as they are unable to escape the venue, themselves, or each other.

writers: Jerry Siegel, Joe Shuster, Mario Puzo, David Newman, Leslie Newman, Robert Benton, Tom Mankiewicz
name: Superman: The Movie
overview: Mild-mannered Clark Kent works as a reporter at the Daily Planet alongside his crush, Lois Lane. Clark must summon his superhero alter-ego when the nefarious Lex Luthor launches a plan to take over the world.
tagline: You'll believe a man can fly.

name: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
overview: When Sally hears that her grandfather's grave may have been vandalized, she and her paraplegic brother, Franklin, set out with their friends to investigate. After a detour to their family's old farmhouse, they discover a group of crazed, murderous outcasts living next door. As the group is attacked one by one by the chainsaw-wielding Leatherface, who wears a mask of human skin, the survivors must do everything they can to escape.
tagline: Who will survive and what will be left of them?
review:
The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is a foundational slice of 1970s horror that still packs a visceral punch. It’s gritty, raw, and unpolished in all the right ways, setting a template for slasher films that followed. Tobe Hooper’s debut feels like a grimy, more unsettling cousin to later, more polished horror franchises—fans of early horror and cult classics will appreciate its relentless tension and unflinching brutality. Marilyn Burns as Sally anchors the chaos with a performance that’s equal parts terrified and determined, making the film’s bleak tagline—“Who will survive and what will be left of them?”—hit hard.

What stands out is the film’s atmosphere: the oppressive Texas heat, the claustrophobic farmhouse, and the grotesque family of killers led by the iconic Leatherface, who wears a mask made of human skin. The narrative is straightforward but effective, with a creeping dread that builds as the group’s ill-fated investigation turns into a desperate fight for survival. The film leans heavily into body horror and the terror of isolation, stripping away any sense of safety. It’s less about jump scares and more about an unbearable feeling that something terrible is lurking just out of sight. The soundtrack is minimal but effective, amplifying the tension without overwhelming the senses.

Be heavily warned if animal harm, body horror, or sexual violence are on your list. The film includes distressing scenes involving animals and unsettling moments of assault, making it a tough watch for sensitive viewers. There’s also spitting, hate speech, and some pretty grim depictions of violence that don’t shy away from the grotesque, so it’s not for the faint of heart. If you’re in the mood for a horror movie that’s as much about atmosphere and dread as it is about gore, this one’s a classic—but it definitely earns its scars.
emailReview:
The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is a gritty and unpolished horror classic that builds relentless tension through its oppressive atmosphere and Marilyn Burns’ unforgettable performance as a terrified but determined survivor.

Be prepared for: animal harm, graphic body horror, sexual violence, spitting, and hate speech.

name: K-PAX

tagline: Change the way you look at the world.

name: Molly's Game
overview: Molly Bloom, a young skier and former Olympic hopeful becomes a successful entrepreneur (and a target of an FBI investigation) when she establishes a high-stakes, international poker game.

writers: Nick Hornby, D.V. DeVincentis, Steve Pink, John Cusack, Scott Rosenberg
name: High Fidelity
overview: When record store owner Rob Gordon gets dumped by his girlfriend, Laura, because he hasn't changed since they met, he revisits his top five breakups of all time in an attempt to figure out what went wrong. As Rob seeks out his former lovers to find out why they left, he keeps up his efforts to win Laura back.
tagline: A comedy about fear of commitment, hating your job, falling in love and other pop favorites.

name: Galaxy Quest
overview: The stars of a 1980s sci-fi show—now eking out a living through re-runs and sci-fi conventions—are beamed aboard an alien spacecraft. Believing the cast's heroic on-screen dramas are historical documents of real-life adventures, the band of aliens turn to the cast members for help in their quest to overcome the oppressive regime in their solar system.

writers: Dan Scanlon, Keith Bunin, Jason Headley
name: Onward
overview: In a suburban fantasy world, two teenage elf brothers embark on an extraordinary quest to discover if there is still a little magic left out there.
review:
Onward is a heartfelt animated adventure that blends suburban fantasy with a classic coming-of-age quest, starring the voices of Tom Holland and Chris Pratt as two elf brothers trying to reconnect with a bit of lost magic. It’s a warm, often funny ride that won’t exactly reinvent the wheel but delivers enough charm and emotional punches to stand out among other Pixar outings. Fans of films like Coco or The Good Dinosaur will appreciate its focus on family bonds and bittersweet themes, though it leans a bit more into the fantasy quest territory than those previous, more grounded tales.

What really elevates Onward is its blend of everyday suburban life with a whimsical fantasy world — think magic meets minivans — which creates some clever visual gags and relatable moments. The tagline, “Their quest beginneth,” nails the tongue-in-cheek tone, and the story’s heart is in the relationship between Ian and Barley Lightfoot, two brothers who balance each other out in both personalities and magical ability. The voice work from Holland and Pratt is solid, with some standout support from Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Octavia Spencer. The animation is bright and inventive, and the film doesn’t shy away from touching on loss and grief, giving it a surprising emotional depth for a family flick.

Heads up for those sensitive to loss and animal harm: the story involves the death of a parent and the sacrifice of a beloved animal companion, which are central to the plot and emotional stakes. There are also some jump scares, minor blood and scrapes, and a scene where someone is burned alive, so a cautious glance is warranted if those triggers are on your list. The film handles these moments gently but they’re definitely there.
emailReview:
Onward charms with its clever mix of suburban fantasy and heartfelt sibling dynamics, brought to life by a stellar voice cast and bright, inventive animation that balances humor with honest emotion.

Be prepared for: the death of a parent, the sacrifice of a beloved animal companion, a character burned alive, jump scares, and minor blood and scrapes.

name: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
overview: Sweethearts Brad and Janet, stuck with a flat tire during a storm, discover the eerie mansion of Dr. Frank-N-Furter, a transvestite scientist. As their innocence is lost, Brad and Janet meet a houseful of wild characters, including a rocking biker and a creepy butler. Through elaborate dances and rock songs, Frank-N-Furter unveils his latest creation: a muscular man named 'Rocky'.
review:
The Rocky Horror Picture Show is a campy, cult-classic musical horror-comedy that’s equal parts wild ride and time capsule. If you’re into the glam-rock energy of the ’70s mixed with a raunchy sci-fi B-movie vibe, this one’s a must-see—think of it as The Addams Family meets a midnight dance party, but with way more leather, fishnets, and questionable consent. Tim Curry’s Dr. Frank-N-Furter steals the show with his over-the-top, charismatic menace, setting the tone for an experience that’s as much about shocking and entertaining as it is about subversion. That said, it’s not as playful as modern queer cinema and definitely feels dated in its portrayal of gender and sexuality.

What really stands out is how the film blends musical numbers with horror and sci-fi tropes, creating an unsettling yet catchy atmosphere. The tagline, “A different set of jaws,” fits perfectly—this is a movie that bites with its bizarre characters and twisted narrative. The plot follows Brad and Janet’s descent from wholesome newlyweds to unwilling participants in Frank’s bizarre mansion of freaks, with memorable beats like the creation of Rocky, the “Time Warp” dance, and a dinner scene that’s as grotesque as it is iconic. The film breaks the fourth wall frequently, pulling the audience into its weird world, but the darker themes of manipulation, sexual assault, and violence lurk beneath the campy surface, complicating the experience.

Trigger-wise, be heavily warned if sexual assault, sexual objectification, and predatory behavior—especially tied to the portrayal of transgender characters—are on your list. There’s also quite a bit of blood and gore, gun violence, and disturbing scenes involving restraint and torture. The film’s treatment of minorities and gender identity is outdated and problematic. Flashing lights and sudden loud noises add to the sensory overload, so if you’re sensitive to those, proceed with caution. It’s a film that dazzles and disturbs in equal measure, and knowing what’s lurking beneath the sequins and strobe lights is essential.
emailReview:
The Rocky Horror Picture Show is a wild, campy cult classic that mixes glam-rock energy with raunchy sci-fi horror, anchored by Tim Curry’s unforgettable, larger-than-life performance.

Be prepared for: sexual assault, predatory behavior tied to transgender characters, graphic restraint and torture scenes, gun violence, and intense blood and gore.

name: Crimson Tide
overview: After the Cold War, a breakaway Russian republic with nuclear warheads becomes a possible worldwide threat. U.S. submarine Capt. Frank Ramsey signs on a relatively green but highly recommended Lt. Cmdr. Ron Hunter to the USS Alabama, which may be the only ship able to stop a possible Armageddon. When Ramsey insists that the Alabama must act aggressively, Hunter, fearing they will start rather than stop a disaster, leads a potential mutiny to stop him.

writers: Kim Wilson, Kelly Candaele, Lowell Ganz, Babaloo Mandel
name: A League of Their Own
overview: As America's stock of athletic young men is depleted during World War II, a professional all-female baseball league springs up in the Midwest, funded by publicity-hungry candy maker Walter Harvey (Garry Marshall). Competitive sisters Dottie Hinson (Geena Davis) and Kit Keller (Lori Petty) spar with each other, scout Ernie Capadino (Jon Lovitz) and grumpy has-been coach Jimmy Dugan (Tom Hanks) on their way to fame. Madonna and Rosie O'Donnell co-star as two of the sisters' teammates.
tagline: Once in a lifetime you get a chance to do something different.
review:
A League of Their Own is a spirited blend of sports drama and comedy that feels like a mix of classic baseball flicks with a feminist twist. Penny Marshall’s 1992 film is really beautiful in how it captures the energy and struggles of the all-female baseball league born out of World War II’s manpower shortage. It’s got that familiar underdog charm but elevated by strong performances—Tom Hanks as the grumpy, alcoholic coach Jimmy Dugan steals plenty of scenes, balancing his rough edges with unexpected warmth. Fans of heartfelt ensemble casts and period pieces will find plenty to enjoy here, even if some of the humor and attitudes haven’t quite aged gracefully.

What stands out is the way the film doesn’t shy away from the sexism and outright hostility these women faced, both on and off the field. The tagline “Once in a lifetime you get a chance to do something different” captures the spirit, but the players aren’t just cheered on—they’re heckled, objectified, and forced into “charm and beauty” classes, which the film plays with a wink but also acknowledges as real barriers. The dynamic between the competitive sisters Dottie and Kit adds emotional weight, while the supporting cast—including Madonna and Rosie O’Donnell—bring memorable, quirky energy. The film’s sunny visuals and vintage soundtrack contrast with some darker themes like addiction, harassment, and loss, giving it a layered tone that’s not just feel-good fluff.

Those who pin the sexual assault, sexual objectification, and alcohol abuse triggers should be cautious—Jimmy’s behavior includes unwanted advances and heavy drinking that’s integral to his character arc but can be uncomfortable. There’s also continuous sexist heckling, spitting, and some fat jokes sprinkled throughout. Be heavily warned if scenes of aggressive male hostility or emotional meltdowns might be upsetting, as those moments are part and parcel of the story’s depiction of the era’s challenges.
emailReview:
A League of Their Own blends classic sports movie charm with sharp feminist edges, buoyed by Tom Hanks’ scene-stealing grumpy coach and a spirited all-female cast facing real-world sexism and struggle.

Be prepared for: sexual assault, heavy alcohol abuse, relentless sexist heckling, spitting, and emotional meltdowns.

name: Jacobs Ladder
overview: After returning home from the Vietnam War, veteran Jacob Singer struggles to maintain his sanity. Plagued by hallucinations and flashbacks, Singer rapidly falls apart as the world and people around him morph and twist into disturbing images. His girlfriend, Jezzie, and ex-wife, Sarah, try to help, but to little avail. Even Singer's chiropractor friend, Louis, fails to reach him as he descends into madness.
tagline: The most frightening thing about Jacob Singer's nightmare is that he isn't dreaming.

name: Malèna
overview: On the day in 1940 that Italy enters the war, two things happen to the 12-year-old Renato: he gets his first bike, and he gets his first look at Malèna. writers: Sol Yurick, David Shaber, Walter Hill
name: The Warriors
overview: Prominent gang leader Cyrus calls a meeting of New York's gangs to set aside their turf wars and take over the city. At the meeting, a rival leader kills Cyrus, but a Coney Island gang called the Warriors is wrongly blamed for Cyrus' death. Before you know it, the cops and every gangbanger in town is hot on the Warriors' trail.
tagline: These are the armies of the night. They are 100,000 strong. They outnumber the cops five to one. They could run New York City. Tonight they're all out to get the Warriors.
review:
The Warriors is a gritty cult classic that feels like a pulpy, street-level thriller straight out of 1979 New York City—think Mad Max meets West Side Story, only with more leather jackets and gang tattoos. Walter Hill’s direction keeps the tension taut and the pace brisk as the titular gang tries to survive a city-wide manhunt after being framed for a murder they didn’t commit. It’s got that raw, neon-lit urban vibe that’s both stylish and brutal, though it’s not exactly subtle or deep. Fans of vintage crime dramas and ’70s action flicks will appreciate its iconic status, even if some of the dialogue and characters feel a bit dated.

What stands out is the film’s world-building: the gangs themselves are almost cartoonishly distinct tribes, giving the movie a tribal, almost mythic quality. The tagline—“They could run New York City. Tonight they’re all out to get the Warriors”—perfectly captures the paranoia and chaos that drives the plot. The score’s gritty synth and percussion underscore the relentless chase across the city’s underground and backstreets, while the cast, especially Michael Beck as Swan and David Patrick Kelly as the chilling antagonist Luther, bring a memorable intensity that keeps you hooked.

Heads up for animal lovers: The Warriors features multiple scenes involving animal harm and death, including dogs, cats, and horses. Those sensitive to animal abuse or distressing animal scenes should be cautious, as the film’s rough edges extend beyond human conflict. If you’re triggered by that kind of content, it might be tough to watch without bracing yourself.
emailReview:
The Warriors is a pulpy, neon-lit street thriller that blends ’70s grit with mythic gang clashes, anchored by memorable performances and a relentless, tense chase through New York’s underbelly.

Be prepared for: multiple scenes of animal harm including dogs, cats, and horses, intense gang violence, and a gritty urban atmosphere that spares no brutality.

writers: Billy Ray, Marie Brenner, Kent Alexander, Kevin Salwen
name: Richard Jewell
overview: Richard Jewell thinks quick, works fast, and saves hundreds, perhaps thousands, of lives after a domestic terrorist plants several pipe bombs and they explode during a concert, only to be falsely suspected of the crime by sloppy FBI work and sensational media coverage.
tagline: The world will know his name and the truth.
review:
Richard Jewell is a gripping true-crime drama that feels like a mix between a tense legal thriller and a character study of an unlikely hero caught in a maelstrom of media frenzy and bureaucratic missteps. Directed by Clint Eastwood and anchored by Paul Walter Hauser’s quietly powerful turn as Jewell, the film elevates a familiar “wrongly accused” narrative with a steady hand and a sharp eye for injustice. It’s not as flashy as some political thrillers, but it’s effective in its restraint—fans of films like *Spotlight* or *The Post* will appreciate the focus on institutional failure and media sensationalism.

What stands out here is the film’s commitment to portraying the emotional turmoil of its protagonist without slipping into melodrama. The tagline, “The world will know his name and the truth,” underscores the film’s thematic heartbeat: the struggle to clear one’s name amid overwhelming odds. The supporting cast, including Sam Rockwell and Olivia Wilde, adds depth, especially in scenes that highlight the invasive nature of press and law enforcement. Eastwood’s direction keeps the tone sober but compelling, letting the story’s real-life stakes breathe through meticulous pacing and a muted score that never overpowers the drama.

Be heavily warned if you’re sensitive to portrayals of animal harm—there are multiple instances of animals dying or being abused, which can be unexpectedly distressing given the film’s otherwise grounded tone. Additionally, the film includes scenes with gun violence and blood/gore, as well as moments of anxiety attacks and substance use, all of which contribute to the tense atmosphere but might be tough for some viewers.
emailReview:
Richard Jewell is a quietly powerful true-crime drama that combines a tense legal thriller with an intimate character study, anchored by Paul Walter Hauser’s standout performance and Clint Eastwood’s restrained direction.

Be prepared for: multiple scenes of animal harm, gun violence, blood and gore, anxiety attacks, and substance use.

name: The Wicker Man
overview: Police sergeant Neil Howie is called to an island village in search of a missing girl whom the locals claim never existed. Stranger still, however, are the rituals that take place there.
tagline: Flesh to touch...Flesh to burn! Don't keep the Wicker Man waiting!
review:
The Wicker Man is a cult classic that’s part folk horror, part mystery, and all unsettling atmosphere. It’s that peculiar beast where you expect a straightforward missing person story but instead get a slow-burn dive into pagan rituals and eerie island traditions. Fans of atmospheric horror like *The Witch* or *Midsommar* will appreciate how this 1973 film sets the template with its creeping dread and offbeat charm, though it’s less about jump scares and more about simmering tension and strange, haunting visuals. Edward Woodward’s earnest performance as Sergeant Neil Howie grounds the weirdness, while Christopher Lee’s turn as Lord Summerisle adds a charismatic but sinister edge.

What really stands out here is the way the film toys with themes of belief, isolation, and cultural clash, all wrapped in that unforgettable tagline: “Flesh to touch... Flesh to burn! Don’t keep the Wicker Man waiting!” Robin Hardy’s direction and Anthony Shaffer’s writing create a world that feels both quaint and menacing, with rituals and folk customs that seem bizarre yet almost plausible. The soundtrack adds to the eerie vibe, with traditional folk tunes that feel disarming until you realize how chilling they become in context. The film’s finale is infamous—and deservedly so—for delivering one of the most iconic, unsettling endings in horror cinema.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm: there are multiple instances involving animals, including deaths and distress that could hit hard. Also, if you’re on the lookout for unsettling insects or creepy crawlies, the film doesn’t shy away from spiders, snakes, and bugs. Finally, the story’s psychological manipulation and gaslighting moments mean viewers who are cautious about those themes should proceed carefully.
emailReview:
The Wicker Man is a slow-burning folk horror classic that blends eerie island rituals with a haunting atmosphere and standout performances from Edward Woodward and Christopher Lee.

Be prepared for: disturbing animal deaths, unsettling insect encounters with spiders and snakes, and intense psychological manipulation.

name: Notes On a Scandal
overview: A veteran high school teacher befriends a younger art teacher, who is having an affair with one of her 15-year-old students. However, her intentions with this new "friend" also go well beyond platonic friendship.

review:
Notes on a Scandal is a quietly intense psychological drama that hinges on the simmering toxicity between two teachers—a seasoned, sharp-edged Barbara (Judi Dench) and the vulnerable, secretive Sheba (Cate Blanchett). If you like your character studies with a side of moral dissection and simmering dread, this one fits snugly among films like *Fatal Attraction* or *The Children Act*, where personal flaws spiral into public catastrophe. It’s not exactly a thriller, but the tension is thick enough to keep you hooked, largely thanks to the powerhouse performances at its core.

What stands out here is the razor-sharp writing by Patrick Marber and Richard Eyre’s restrained direction that lets the characters do the heavy lifting. The tagline—“One woman’s mistake is another’s opportunity”—captures the bleak power dynamics at play, as Barbara’s obsession with Sheba turns the emotional imbalance into something darker and more manipulative. The film doesn’t sensationalize the scandalous affair itself; instead, it explores the corrosive effects of loneliness, jealousy, and betrayal in a claustrophobic school environment. Dench’s steely delivery, paired with Blanchett’s quietly crumbling facade, makes for a masterclass in simmering unease.

Trigger-wise, those who pin the “dead animal” category should be cautious, as there’s a mention of a deceased pet cat, though it’s handled off-screen and with subtlety. The film’s main emotional punches come from its human drama, so if you’re sensitive to themes of manipulation and emotional abuse, keep that in mind before diving in.
emailReview:
Notes on a Scandal is a quietly intense psychological drama that draws you in with powerhouse performances from Judi Dench and Cate Blanchett, simmering with tension and moral complexity in a claustrophobic school setting.

Be prepared for: emotional abuse, manipulation, and the subtle mention of a deceased pet cat.

review:
Nimona is a vibrant, genre-bending animated adventure that feels like Scott Pilgrim meets a medieval superhero origin story. It’s charming and scrappy, anchored by the voice talents of Chloë Grace Moretz and Riz Ahmed, who bring a lot of heart to their roles. The film juggles sharp humor with surprisingly heavy emotional beats, making it a cut above your typical animated fare. While it leans into fantasy tropes, it doesn’t shy away from subverting the usual “heroes vs. villains” narrative, which keeps things feeling fresh and unpredictable.

What really stands out is how Nimona’s shapeshifting powers aren’t just cool effects—they’re tied deeply to themes of identity and acceptance. The tagline, “A little anti. A little hero,” nails the tone perfectly, setting up a story that’s equal parts rebellious and earnest. The visuals pop with a colorful, kinetic energy, while the writing balances whimsical fun and a darker undercurrent that gives the story emotional weight. It’s an animated film that appeals to both kids and adults, thanks to its clever mix of humor, heart, and action.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: Nimona features multiple instances of animal death and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and mythical creatures like dragons. There are also bugs, snakes, and spiders present, so if those are on your list, prepare accordingly. The film doesn’t hold back on these darker elements, which might catch some viewers off guard amid the otherwise lively tone.

review:
Predator: Killer of Killers is a wild mash-up that throws history’s deadliest warriors—a Viking raider, a feudal Japanese ninja, and a WWII pilot—into the crosshairs of the ultimate extraterrestrial hunter. It’s like Predator meets a mash-up of historical action epics, with a pulse-pounding animated twist. Dan Trachtenberg’s direction keeps the pace brisk, and fans of the Predator franchise will appreciate the way it expands the mythos without feeling like a tired retread. It’s not just another monster flick; it leans into the brutal, primal instincts of its characters while mixing in some creative world-building.

What stands out here is the voice cast’s ability to bring these iconic archetypes to life, especially given the limited visual storytelling animation allows. The tagline, “The hunt begins,” nails the tone—this isn’t a slow-burn but a relentless chase that pits human skill against an almost mythic predator. The premise plays with genre conventions, blending historical drama with sci-fi horror, and the writing manages to balance the action with moments of tension and character grit. You get a sense that this predator really is the “killer of killers,” elevating the stakes beyond typical alien hunt scenarios.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this film features multiple instances of animal deaths, including dogs, cats, horses, and a dragon, as well as some harsh scenes involving bugs and spiders. There’s also body horror and a few moments of intense gore that might catch you off guard. If those kinds of triggers are on your list, this one might be a rough ride.

Having imagined a heroic version of his father during his absence, Boy comes face to face with the real version-an incompetent hoodlum who has returned to find a bag of money he buried years before. This is where the goat enters.

Armed with long-buried historical records of her incarceration, director Marc Rothemund expertly re-creates the last six days of Sophie Scholl's life.

name: Marty
overview: Marty, a butcher who lives in the Bronx with his mother is unmarried at 34. Good-natured but socially awkward he faces constant badgering from family and friends to get married but has reluctantly resigned himself to bachelorhood. Marty meets Clara, an unattractive school teacher, realising their emotional connection, he promises to call but family and friends try to convince him not to.

name: Remember
overview: Leaving home, a man gets a phone call. Answering it, his house is exploded. As if nothing has happened, he goes to work.
review:
Remember is a lean, unsettling thriller that wastes no time plunging you into its cold, detached nightmare. Directed by Shunsaku Hayashi, it’s a bit like if you crossed a minimalist art-house flick with a survival-horror intensity—think The Revenant stripped of nature’s beauty and replaced by a clinical, brutal atmosphere. The premise is simple but effective: a man’s home blows up during a phone call, yet he carries on as if nothing happened. This stark contrast between chaos and numb routine is what hooks you, though the film doesn’t bother with warm emotional beats or easy catharsis.

What really stands out is the film’s merciless exploration of trauma and disassociation. The silence and the man’s robotic behavior create a haunting tone, and the sparse storytelling leaves much to the imagination—sometimes for the better. The synopsis teases the surface, but the real shock comes from the brutal violence lurking beneath the calm facade. Hayashi doesn’t hold back on graphic and horrific imagery, which forces you to sit with discomfort instead of escaping into genre tropes. It’s not a crowd-pleaser but a disturbing puzzle that lingers.

Heads up for the intense physical horror: expect amputation, torture, eye and finger mutilation, and some truly grim scenes involving burning and blood. Those sensitive to graphic violence, gore, and extreme bodily harm should approach with caution. There’s also a heavy dose of psychological distress and trauma that might hit hard for viewers wary of those elements. This isn’t a casual watch—Remember drills down into the darkest corners with little mercy.
emailReview:
Remember is a stark, minimalist thriller that blends art-house cool with brutal survival-horror intensity, delivering a chilling atmosphere where trauma feels both clinical and suffocating.

Be prepared for: amputation, eye and finger mutilation, torture, burning scenes, and relentless psychological distress.

When he fails, he turns the gun on himself, and the two city-bred children must contend with harsh wilderness alone. They are saved by a chance encounter with an Aborigine boy who shows them how to survive, and in the process underscores the disharmony between nature and modern life.
tagline: A boy and girl face the challenge of the world's last frontier.

tagline: In a world of beasts, he found a family.

Aware that his days are numbered, the troubled man seeks solace and peace in a boarding house run by a widow and her son.However, it is not Brooks' fate to die in peace, as he becomes embroiled in one last valiant battle.

However, a series of bombings targets his empire on the very weekend the Americans are in town. Shand is convinced there is a traitor in his organization, and sets out to eliminate the rat in typically ruthless fashion.

name: Band of Outsiders
overview: Cinephile slackers Franz and Arthur spend their days mimicking the antiheroes of Hollywood noirs and Westerns while pursuing the lovely Odile. The misfit trio upends convention at every turn, be it through choreographed dances in cafés or frolicsome romps through the Louvre. Eventually, their romantic view of outlaws pushes them to plan their own heist, but their inexperience may send them out in a blaze of glory -- which could be just what they want.

name: Vera Drake

overview: Ricky and his family have been fighting an uphill struggle against debt since the 2008 financial crash. An opportunity to wrestle back some independence appears with a shiny new van and the chance to run a franchise as a self-employed delivery driver. It's hard work, and his wife's job as a carer is no easier. The family unit is strong but when both are pulled in different directions everything comes to breaking point.

writers: E.M. Forster, Kit Hesketh-Harvey, James Ivory

overview: After his lover rejects him, a young man trapped by the oppressiveness of Edwardian society tries to come to terms with and accept his sexuality.

writers: Jacques Lagrange, Jean L'Hôte, Jacques Tati
name: Mon Oncle
overview: Genial, bumbling Monsieur Hulot loves his top-floor apartment in a grimy corner of the city, and cannot fathom why his sister's family has moved to the suburbs. Their house is an ultra-modern nightmare, which Hulot only visits for the sake of stealing away his rambunctious young nephew. Hulot's sister, however, wants to win him over to her new way of life, and conspires to set him up with a wife and job.

writers: Joss Whedon, Stan Lee, Jack Kirby, Joe Simon, Jim Starlin
name: Avengers: Age of Ultron
overview: When Tony Stark tries to jumpstart a dormant peacekeeping program, things go awry and Earth’s Mightiest Heroes are put to the ultimate test as the fate of the planet hangs in the balance. As the villainous Ultron emerges, it is up to The Avengers to stop him from enacting his terrible plans, and soon uneasy alliances and unexpected action pave the way for an epic and unique global adventure.
review:
Avengers: Age of Ultron is a sprawling superhero spectacle that leans heavily into the “save the world” mode with a dash of existential dread—think Avengers-meets-Skynet, but with more quips from Robert Downey Jr.’s Tony Stark. It’s a solid follow-up that ups the ante in terms of stakes and action, though it occasionally gets bogged down in its own ambition. Fans of superhero team-ups will appreciate the dynamic between the core Avengers, even if the narrative sometimes feels like it’s juggling too many balls.

What stands out here is Joss Whedon’s signature blend of humor and heart, balanced by some genuinely tense moments as Ultron, the AI villain, threatens global catastrophe. The film’s tagline, “A new age has come,” is fitting, as it explores themes of technology run amok and uneasy alliances. The action sequences are big and bold, with the usual Marvel flair for spectacle, but there’s also a surprising emotional weight—especially when the team’s relationships are tested. The ensemble cast delivers strong performances, with Downey Jr. and Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner/Hulk offering some of the film’s best moments.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one is notorious for its animal-related content warnings. There are multiple instances of animals dying—including dogs, cats, and horses—and scenes involving animal abuse and dead animals. If those are triggers for you, be prepared and proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Avengers: Age of Ultron packs a hefty punch of superhero spectacle mixed with sharp humor and surprisingly emotional stakes, anchored by standout performances from Robert Downey Jr. and Mark Ruffalo.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, animal abuse, and unsettling scenes with dead animals.

name: Black Panther
