writers: S.S. Wilson, Brent Maddock, Ron Underwood
name: Tremors
overview: Val McKee and Earl Bassett are in a fight for their lives when they discover that their desolate town has been infested with gigantic, man-eating creatures that live below the ground.
tagline: They say there's nothing new under the sun. But under the ground…
review:
Tremors is a delightful mix of horror, comedy, and creature feature that’s aged like a fine wine since its 1990 release. If you like your monster movies with a side of witty banter and a bit of small-town charm, this one’s for you. Think of it as a lovechild between Jaws and The Thing, but with giant underground worms instead of sharks or alien parasites. Kevin Bacon and Fred Ward have solid chemistry as the reluctant heroes, and the film balances scares and laughs better than most in the genre. It’s not just another monster flick—it’s a fun, clever romp that still holds up as a cult classic.

The tagline, “They say there’s nothing new under the sun. But under the ground…” perfectly captures the film’s premise and tone. The story revolves around Val and Earl’s battle against the grabboids, giant subterranean predators that turn their sleepy desert town into a deathtrap. The movie leans into classic genre beats—jump scares, inventive kills, and plenty of gunfire—but mixes in some great character moments and practical effects that keep the tension alive without going over the top. It’s also worth noting how the film’s mix of humor and suspense gives it a unique voice, making it more than just a typical monster movie.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and intense gore: Tremors features several scenes where animals, including horses, are attacked and killed, and the creature violence isn’t shy about showing orange, slimy blood and body horror. There are multiple moments of people being buried alive, eaten, or stabbed by the creatures, accompanied by screaming and sudden loud noises that might catch you off guard. Gun violence is present throughout but is focused on the monsters rather than people. If jump scares and the sight (and sound) of gruesome monster attacks aren’t your thing, this one could be a tough watch.
emailReview:
Tremors is a clever blend of horror and comedy with standout chemistry between Kevin Bacon and Fred Ward, delivering a fun monster movie that balances scares and laughs with small-town charm.

Be prepared for: horses being attacked and killed, people buried alive by giant worms, slimy orange monster blood, intense body horror, and sudden loud jump scares.

name: They Live
overview: A lone drifter stumbles upon a unique pair of sunglasses that reveal aliens are systematically gaining control of the Earth by masquerading as humans and lulling the public into submission.
tagline: You see them on the street. You watch them on TV. You might even vote for one this fall. You think they're people just like you. You're wrong. Dead wrong.
review:
John Carpenter’s 1988 cult classic *They Live* is a wild ride of sci-fi paranoia wrapped in a B-movie package, with just the right mix of camp and social commentary to keep it endlessly quotable and surprisingly relevant. Think *Invasion of the Body Snatchers* meets 80s wrestling — thanks to Roddy Piper’s punchy lead performance as John Nada, a drifter who uncovers a hidden alien conspiracy through a very special pair of sunglasses. It’s not subtle, but that’s the point: Carpenter’s blunt critique of consumerism and control still hits hard decades later, even if the effects and dialogue lean into cheesiness on purpose.

What stands out is how the film uses its tagline — “You think they’re people just like you... You’re wrong. Dead wrong.” — as a lens to explore distrust and societal manipulation. The sunglasses reveal a grim truth: aliens disguised as humans are controlling the masses through subliminal messaging. The gritty, grainy visuals and pulsing synth score underscore this unsettling undercurrent, while Piper and Keith David’s chemistry adds a grounded edge amid the madness. It’s a genre mash-up that leans heavily into action and horror tropes but keeps a sharp satirical bite, making it more than just a cult curiosity.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and graphic violence: *They Live* includes several distressing scenes involving animals, including a dog and a horse dying, plus instances of eye mutilation and broken bones. There’s also sexual assault and suicide depicted, which adds a darker layer to the film’s already intense atmosphere. If those triggers are on your radar, be prepared for some rough content alongside the campy sci-fi thrills.
emailReview:
John Carpenter’s *They Live* is a cult classic cocktail of campy sci-fi paranoia and sharp social commentary, anchored by Roddy Piper’s unforgettable punchy lead and a gritty, synth-driven atmosphere.

Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths including a dog and a horse, eye mutilation, broken bones, sexual assault, and suicide.

directors: Brenda Chapman, Steve Hickner, Simon Wells
name: The Prince of Egypt
overview: The strong bond between two brothers is challenged when their chosen responsibilities set them at odds, with extraordinary consequences.
tagline: The power is real. The story is forever. The time is now.
review:
The Prince of Egypt stands out as a beautifully animated biblical epic that manages to balance grandeur with genuine emotional weight. This 1998 musical drama feels like a blend of traditional Disney-style storytelling and sweeping historical spectacle, with a voice cast including Val Kilmer and Ralph Fiennes bringing gravitas to the story of Moses and his brother Rameses. While it might not have the same lighthearted charm as some other animated classics, it’s elevated by its ambitious score and striking visuals, making it one of the more serious animated films tackling faith and family dynamics.

What really sticks with you here is the emotional core—the fraught brotherly bond tested by duty and destiny—and how the film interprets well-known biblical events with a fresh, if reverent, perspective. The tagline, “The power is real. The story is forever. The time is now,” captures the film’s tone perfectly, marrying epic themes with a timeless relevance. The animation style leans heavily into dramatic lighting and expressive character design, which helps sell the weighty themes like freedom, sacrifice, and leadership. Plus, the score and songs are memorable without feeling shoehorned in, punctuating the narrative moments instead of derailing them.

A heads-up for those sensitive to animal-related content: The film includes several scenes where animals appear in distress or death, including a lamb sacrifice that's shown briefly and other livestock depicted as dead. There are also insects and snakes present, which might be unsettling if you’re on the lookout for those triggers. While nothing gruesome is shown directly on screen, these elements are woven into the story’s backdrop and the harsh realities it portrays. So if animal harm or death is a key concern, approach with caution.
emailReview:
The Prince of Egypt dazzles with its stunning animation and powerful score, delivering a serious, emotionally rich take on a timeless biblical story that balances spectacle with heartfelt family drama.

Be prepared for: brief lamb sacrifice, dead livestock, unsettling insects, and snakes woven into the story’s intense backdrop.

name: Where the Crawdads Sing
overview: Abandoned by her family, Kya raises herself all alone in the marshes outside of her small town. When her former boyfriend is found dead, Kya is instantly branded by the local townspeople and law enforcement as the prime suspect for his murder.
tagline: Secrets are buried just beneath the surface.
review:
Where the Crawdads Sing is a moody Southern Gothic drama that blends coming-of-age with a murder mystery, anchored by Daisy Edgar-Jones’s quietly compelling performance as Kya Clark. It’s got that slow-burn, nature-imbued vibe reminiscent of a more restrained True Detective or The Secret Life of Bees, but filtered through a small-town American lens. While it doesn’t exactly reinvent the genre, it’s an engrossing watch for fans of atmospheric storytelling and character-driven suspense — just don’t expect a twist-heavy thriller.

What really stands out here is the way the marshland setting almost becomes a character itself. The tagline, “Secrets are buried just beneath the surface,” hits on both the literal and figurative layers of the story. The film leans into themes of isolation, prejudice, and resilience, with Kya’s abandonment and the town’s suspicion creating a tense social backdrop. Olivia Newman’s direction and Lucy Alibar’s writing deliver a meditative tone that lets the natural world’s beauty contrast with the darker human drama. Plus, the supporting cast adds texture, especially in how they reflect the community’s suspicion and complexity.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this one features multiple instances of animal death and abuse, including a dog, horse, and cat. There’s also unsettling scenes involving dog fighting and a range of creepy crawlies like spiders, snakes, and bugs. If you’re on the lookout for those triggers, be prepared before diving into the marsh.
emailReview:
Where the Crawdads Sing is a moody Southern Gothic drama that wraps a quietly compelling performance in a slow-burn, nature-soaked atmosphere, making the marshland feel like its own mysterious character.

Be prepared for: animal deaths including a dog, horse, and cat, dog fighting, and unsettling scenes with spiders, snakes, and bugs.

directors: Samuel Armstrong, Norman Ferguson, Wilfred Jackson, Jack Kinney, Bill Roberts, Ben Sharpsteen
writers: Joe Grant, Dick Huemer, Otto Englander, Bill Peet, Aurelius Battaglia, Joe Rinaldi, Vernon Stallings, Webb Smith, Helen Aberson, Harold Pearl
name: Dumbo
overview: Dumbo is a baby elephant born with over-sized ears and a supreme lack of confidence. But thanks to his even more diminutive buddy Timothy the Mouse,  the pint-sized pachyderm learns to surmount all obstacles.

name: Chasing Amy
overview: Holden and Banky are comic book artists. Everything is going good for them until they meet Alyssa, also a comic book artist. Holden falls for her, but his hopes are crushed when he finds out she's a lesbian.
tagline: It's not who you love. It's how.
review:
Kevin Smith’s *Chasing Amy* is a sharp, indie rom-com that feels like a clever mash-up of heartfelt relationship drama and comic book geek culture. It’s got that ‘90s slacker vibe but with a surprisingly earnest exploration of love and identity that still holds up. If you’re a fan of Smith’s View Askewniverse or movies like *Clerks* but want something a bit more emotionally nuanced, this one’s a solid pick. Ben Affleck and Joey Lauren Adams have a natural chemistry that carries the film’s mix of humor and awkward honesty, even if some of the dialogue can feel more clever than natural.

What really stands out is how *Chasing Amy* uses the comic book artist backdrop to explore complicated questions about sexuality, friendship, and jealousy without feeling preachy. The tagline, “It’s not who you love. It’s how,” nails the film’s central conflict—Holden’s struggle to accept Alyssa’s sexuality while dealing with his own desires and insecurities. The writing is sharp and witty, with Kevin Smith’s signature blend of pop culture references and real talk, but the story doesn’t shy away from messy emotions or uncomfortable conversations, which is what elevates it beyond a typical rom-com.

Heads up for animal-sensitive viewers: *Chasing Amy* is notable for several triggers related to animal harm. It includes mentions or depictions of animal deaths (dogs, cats, horses), and some scenes involve animals being abused or sad. If you’ve got a soft spot for pets or are cautious about animal-related content, this one could be a rough ride.
emailReview:
Kevin Smith’s *Chasing Amy* blends '90s slacker charm with sharp, witty dialogue and heartfelt explorations of love and identity, all set against a comic book artist backdrop that adds a unique edge.

Be prepared for: mentions of dog and cat deaths, horse suffering, and scenes of animal abuse that might tug at your heartstrings.

tagline: A world where heroes come in all sizes and adventure is the greatest magic of all.

Things get worse when Christine meets back up with her childhood acquaintance Raoul and the two fall in love

name: Friday
overview: Craig and Smokey are two guys in Los Angeles hanging out on their porch on a Friday afternoon, smoking and drinking, looking for something to do.
tagline: A lot can go down between Thursday and Saturday...
review:
Friday is a laid-back, iconic stoner comedy that feels like a perfect snapshot of 1990s LA neighborhood life, with Ice Cube and Chris Tucker’s chemistry driving the whole thing. It’s not trying to be high-concept—just two guys chilling on the porch, but it’s elevated by sharp writing and memorable characters like Deebo and Mr. Jones. If you like the vibe of other ’90s urban comedies or are a fan of Ice Cube’s early acting, this one’s a classic that still holds up, even if it’s not packed with plot twists.

What really stands out is how the film captures the small dramas and everyday humor of a Friday afternoon that somehow feels bigger than it is. The tagline, “A lot can go down between Thursday and Saturday...,” couldn’t be more true—there’s a nice balance between goofy moments and genuinely relatable scenes about friendship, responsibility, and community. F. Gary Gray’s direction keeps it moving at a chill pace without dragging, and the soundtrack underscores that easygoing West Coast mood perfectly.

Heads up: there are a surprising number of animal-related triggers here, from multiple animal deaths (dogs, cats, horses) to discussions about animal abuse and dog fighting, though most of the abuse talk is offscreen or exaggerated for dark humor. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or death, this might catch you off guard despite the film’s overall comedic tone. Also, some creepy crawlies (spiders, snakes, bugs) show up, so bug-phobes beware.
emailReview:
Friday is a laid-back stoner comedy that perfectly captures the easygoing vibe of 1990s LA with standout chemistry between Ice Cube and Chris Tucker and sharp, memorable characters.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, discussions of dog fighting and animal abuse, and appearances by spiders, snakes, and bugs.

directors: Ted Berman, Richard Rich, Art Stevens, David Hand, Wolfgang Reitherman
writers: Daniel P. Mannix, Larry Clemmons, Ted Berman, Dave Michener, Peter Young, Burny Mattinson, Steve Hulett, Earl Kress, Vance Gerry
name: The Fox And the Hound
overview: When a feisty little fox named Tod is adopted into a farm family, he quickly becomes friends with a fun and adorable hound puppy named Copper. Life is full of hilarious adventures until Copper is expected to take on his role as a hunting dog -- and the object of his search is his best friend!
tagline: A story of two friends who didn't know they were supposed to be enemies.
review:
The Fox and the Hound is a classic animated tearjerker that blends the charm of a childhood friendship story with the bittersweet realities of growing up and societal expectations. It’s the kind of film that sits comfortably alongside other Disney staples from the early ‘80s, balancing lighthearted mischief with surprisingly weighty themes. If you’re a fan of animated animal tales with heartfelt stakes—think Bambi meets Old Yeller—this one’s a must-watch, though it’s not shy about pulling at the heartstrings.

What really stands out here is the way the film handles the tension between friendship and natural instincts. Tod and Copper’s bond feels genuine and fun at first, capturing that innocent puppy-and-fox energy, but the tagline nails it: they don’t know they’re supposed to be enemies until life forces it. The voice work—Mickey Rooney and Kurt Russell as the leads—brings a surprising warmth, while the supporting cast, including Pearl Bailey’s Big Mama, adds humor and wisdom. The story’s emotional beats are bolstered by a gentle score and classic hand-drawn animation that gives the film a timeless feel. It’s largely a tale about loyalty and change, wrapped in the pastoral beauty of the farm and wild woods.

Those who pin the “animal is abandoned” trigger should be cautious here. While the film is tender overall, there are moments where the realities of animal life—separation, hunting roles, and the inevitable heartache—are front and center, which might sting for sensitive viewers.
emailReview:
A heartfelt classic that captures the bittersweet tug between friendship and nature with warm performances and timeless hand-drawn charm.

Be prepared for: animal abandonment, implied hunting violence, and emotional separation between animal friends.

name: Stuck In Love
overview: An acclaimed writer, his ex-wife, and their teenaged children come to terms with the complexities of love in all its forms over the course of one tumultuous year.
tagline: A story about first loves and second chances.

name: Five Feet Apart
overview: Seventeen-year-old Stella spends most of her time in the hospital as a cystic fibrosis patient. Her life is full of routines, boundaries and self-control — all of which get put to the test when she meets Will, an impossibly charming teen who has the same illness. There's an instant flirtation, though restrictions dictate that they must maintain a safe distance between them. As their connection intensifies, so does the temptation to throw the rules out the window and embrace that attraction.
tagline: When life keeps you apart, fight for every inch.
review:
Five Feet Apart is a romantic drama that plays like The Fault in Our Stars meets a hospital drama, with a heavy dose of teen angst and the tension of forbidden closeness. It’s earnest, occasionally a little saccharine, but Haley Lu Richardson and Cole Sprouse bring enough charm to keep you invested in their characters’ struggle to maintain distance while craving connection. If you’re into young adult romances that lean hard into the emotional stakes of illness and the rules that come with it, this one fits right in — though it doesn't quite reach the emotional heights of its peers.

What stands out here is the way the film makes the physical boundaries of cystic fibrosis a metaphor for the emotional walls people put up. The tagline, “When life keeps you apart, fight for every inch,” nails that tension perfectly. The writing leans into the routine and control that defines Stella’s life, and the visuals often emphasize the sterile hospital environment that confines them. Justin Baldoni’s direction keeps the story intimate, and the supporting cast — including Moisés Arias and Parminder Nagra — adds depth to the hospital world without overshadowing the leads. It’s a predictable ride, but there’s a sincerity to it that makes the emotional beats land.

Be heavily warned if animal deaths or the loss of young characters are on your list of tough triggers. The film includes the deaths of several animals and a kid, as well as the loss of an LGBT character, so those who pin those triggers should proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Five Feet Apart blends teen romance and hospital drama with earnest performances from Haley Lu Richardson and Cole Sprouse, capturing the bittersweet tension of forbidden closeness amid illness.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths, the loss of a young character, and the death of an LGBT character.

review:
Warfare is shaping up to be a gritty, memory-driven war drama that leans heavily into the psychological toll of combat, with a solid pedigree thanks to co-director and co-writer Alex Garland teaming up with ex-Navy Seal Ray Mendoza. While the exact premise is still under wraps, this feels like it could slot alongside films like American Sniper or The Hurt Locker, but with a more introspective, almost meditative tone suggested by the tagline “Everything is based on memory.” D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai as Ray anchors the cast, promising a personal and immersive take on Mendoza’s real-life experiences.

What’s most intriguing about Warfare is the promise of an authentic, firsthand account of the Iraq War, filtered through memory — which hints at an unreliable or fragmented narrative style. Garland’s involvement suggests the film won’t just be a straightforward war story but one that explores deeper themes of trauma and identity. Expect sharp writing and possibly some haunting visuals, given Garland’s track record. The ensemble cast, including Will Poulter and Kit Connor, rounds out a group that could bring a nuanced look at camaraderie and conflict.

Heads up: animal harm and death are significant triggers here, with multiple reports of dogs, cats, horses, and other animals dying or being abused. There are also mentions of spiders, snakes, and bugs, so anyone sensitive to animal suffering or creepy crawlies should proceed with caution. This is clearly a war story that doesn’t shy away from the harsh realities, animal-related or otherwise.
emailReview:
Warfare offers a haunting, memory-driven look at the psychological scars of combat, anchored by a compelling lead performance and a narrative that promises to be as introspective as it is intense.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, animal abuse, and unsettling scenes involving spiders, snakes, and bugs.

overview: When virtually all of the residents of Piedmont, New Mexico, are found dead after the return to Earth of a space satellite, the head of the US Air Force's Project Scoop declares an emergency. A group of eminent scientists led by Dr. Jeremy Stone scramble to a secure laboratory and try to first isolate the life form while determining why two people from Piedmont - an old alcoholic and a six-month-old baby - survived. The scientists methodically study the alien life form unaware that it has already mutated and presents a far greater danger in the lab, which is equipped with a nuclear self-destruct device designed to prevent the escape of dangerous biological agents..
tagline: The picture runs 130 minutes... The story covers 96 of the most critical hours in man's history... The suspense will last through your lifetime!
review:
The Andromeda Strain is a classic sci-fi thriller that feels like a slower, more methodical cousin to today’s fast-paced contagion dramas. Directed by Robert Wise and anchored by Arthur Hill’s steady turn as Dr. Jeremy Stone, it’s a tense, clinical dive into the dangers of extraterrestrial pathogens. It doesn’t have the flashy effects or nonstop action of modern fare, but its cold, procedural tone and the looming nuclear self-destruct protocol give it a uniquely eerie vibe that fans of vintage science fiction will appreciate.

What really stands out here is the blend of scientific rigor and mounting suspense. The tagline’s promise of “96 of the most critical hours in man’s history” feels justified as the film painstakingly tracks the team’s efforts to isolate the alien microbe and understand why two unlikely survivors remain. The sterile laboratory setting, the meticulous dialogue, and the slow mutation of the Andromeda organism build a creeping sense of dread that feels surprisingly fresh despite the film’s age. It’s a compelling reminder that sometimes the scariest threats are the invisible ones.

Those sensitive to animal harm should be cautious—this film is known to have involved animals in ways that may be upsetting. Otherwise, the film keeps its scares focused on the biological threat and tense human responses, so prepare for an unsettling but thoughtful sci-fi experience.
emailReview:
The Andromeda Strain is a chilling, methodical sci-fi thriller that trades flashy effects for cold scientific rigor and mounting dread, anchored by Arthur Hill’s steady performance and a haunting nuclear self-destruct countdown.

Be prepared for: animal harm, tense biological contamination, and slow, creeping mutation of an alien pathogen.

review:
An American Crime is a grim, unflinching true crime drama that dives into the horrific abuse suffered by Sylvia Likens, played with haunting vulnerability by Elliot Page. This 2007 film fits firmly in the tradition of harrowing, fact-based psychological thrillers like *The Girl Next Door* or *Martha Marcy May Marlene*, but with a 1960s Midwestern suburban backdrop that makes the darkness feel all the more unsettling. Catherine Keener’s portrayal of Gertrude Baniszewski, the housewife turned captor, is chillingly effective, elevating the film beyond a standard true crime retelling into something that feels deeply personal and suffocating.

What stands out most is the film’s commitment to showing the slow, creeping horror of captivity and neglect without resorting to sensationalism. The tagline, “The true story of a child's punishment that became a woman’s crime,” nails the tragic transformation at the story’s core. Director Tommy O’Haver and co-writer Irene Turner keep the tone cold and claustrophobic, managing to convey the oppressive atmosphere of the Indiana basement where Sylvia and her sister Jennie are imprisoned. The film’s visuals and pacing refuse to let viewers look away, which makes it a tough but necessary watch for those interested in stories about resilience under unimaginable cruelty.

Heads up: this film is heavy on child abuse, torture, and claustrophobic scenes. There’s also sexual assault, mutilation, and some extreme violence that makes it hard to stomach. If those triggers are on your list, be warned—this one doesn’t pull punches. There are also jump scares and flashing lights, adding to the tension in a way that might catch some off guard. The dog survives, but it’s clearly a sad and neglected presence throughout.

An American Crime is a chilling true crime drama anchored by Elliot Page’s haunting vulnerability and Catherine Keener’s coldly effective turn as a captor, creating a suffocating atmosphere that lingers long after the credits roll.

name: The 40-Year-Old Virgin
overview: Andy Stitzer has a pleasant life with a nice apartment and a job stamping invoices at an electronics store. But at age 40, there's one thing Andy hasn't done, and it's really bothering his sex-obsessed male co-workers: Andy is still a virgin. Determined to help Andy get laid, the guys make it their mission to de-virginize him. But it all seems hopeless until Andy meets small business owner Trish, a single mom.
review:
The 40-Year-Old Virgin is the quintessential mid-2000s Judd Apatow comedy, blending raunchy humor with a surprisingly sweet heart. Steve Carell’s awkward yet endearing performance as Andy Stitzer anchors a film that feels like a more relatable, less absurd take on classic coming-of-age comedies — think a buddy comedy meets romantic dramedy. While it leans heavily on crude jokes, it somehow manages to avoid feeling one-note, thanks largely to its genuine warmth and a strong supporting cast including Paul Rudd and Catherine Keener.

What stands out here is how the film balances its sex-obsessed workplace antics with a genuinely tender romance that subverts the typical “get the guy laid” trope. The tagline, “Better late than never,” sums up the film’s core message: it’s never too late to find connection or growth. The writing, co-penned by Carell and Apatow, walks the line between broad comedy and moments of real vulnerability, making Andy’s journey feel less like a punchline and more like a relatable human story. It’s a template that influenced a wave of awkward but heartfelt comedies that followed.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: the movie includes scenes involving the death and mistreatment of animals, which can be upsetting. There are also moments flagged for sexual assault and some pretty strong language around ableism and homophobia, so if those are on your radar, approach with caution. The humor often pushes boundaries, which is part of its charm for some and a red flag for others.
emailReview:
Steve Carell shines in this mid-2000s comedy that mixes raunchy laughs with a surprisingly tender look at late-blooming romance and awkward personal growth.

Be prepared for: animal death and mistreatment, sexual assault references, strong language involving ableism and homophobia.

writers: Stephen Sommers, Lloyd Fonvielle, Kevin Jarre, John L. Balderston, Nina Wilcox Putnam, Richard Schayer
name: The Mummy
overview: Dashing legionnaire Rick O'Connell stumbles upon the hidden ruins of Hamunaptra while in the midst of a battle to claim the area in 1920s Egypt. It has been over three thousand years since former High Priest Imhotep suffered a fate worse than death as a punishment for a forbidden love—along with a curse that guarantees eternal doom upon the world if he is ever awoken.
tagline: The sands will rise. The heavens will part. The power will be unleashed.
review:
The Mummy (1999) is that perfect blend of pulpy adventure and supernatural thrills that feels like Indiana Jones meets classic Hammer horror—only with a lot more CGI sandstorms and Brendan Fraser’s charming grin. It’s a solid, crowd-pleasing romp that doesn’t take itself too seriously, elevated by Rachel Weisz’s witty turn as the brainy Evelyn and Arnold Vosloo’s genuinely creepy Imhotep. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it’s a wild ride with enough humor and heart to stand out from the late-’90s action-adventure pack.

Stephen Sommers’ direction leans heavily into tone, mixing horror elements with swashbuckling heroics and some genuinely fun set pieces. The tagline—“The sands will rise. The heavens will part. The power will be unleashed.”—captures the film’s grandiose vibe, where ancient curses and forbidden love collide with 1920s Egypt’s dusty ruins. The chemistry between the leads and the brisk pacing keep things fresh, even if the plot hits a few familiar beats. The score and visuals do a solid job of evoking a pulpy, mythic atmosphere without going overboard.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and suspenseful situations: a horse dies on screen, and there’s a tense scene where someone struggles to breathe while hanged (though they get saved in time). The film also touches on some darker themes like being buried alive, and there’s a controversial moment involving antisemitism worth noting. So if any of those are on your watchlist, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
The Mummy (1999) is a rollicking blend of pulpy adventure and supernatural thrills that rides high on Brendan Fraser’s charm and Rachel Weisz’s sharp wit, all wrapped in a spooky, CGI-enhanced Egyptian atmosphere.

Be prepared for: an on-screen horse death, a hanging with a near-miss rescue, scenes of being buried alive, and a tense moment involving antisemitism.

overview: World-famous detective Benoit Blanc heads to Greece to peel back the layers of a mystery surrounding a tech billionaire and his eclectic crew of friends.

review:
Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery is a clever, stylish follow-up to the original that feels like Clue meets a tech billionaire’s yacht party—think sharp wit with a glossy, sun-soaked vibe. Daniel Craig returns as Benoit Blanc, and while this isn’t reinventing the detective genre, it’s a pretty delightful puzzle with a twisty plot and a cast that keeps things lively. If you enjoyed the first Knives Out, you’ll likely appreciate this one’s mix of satire and suspense, though it leans more into its ensemble comedy than pure whodunit tension.

What really stands out here is Rian Johnson’s knack for balancing sharp dialogue with playful social commentary. The setting—a sprawling Greek island retreat—adds a visually lush backdrop that contrasts nicely with the biting critiques of tech culture and wealth on display. The tagline, “When the game ends, the mystery begins,” feels fitting as the film peels back layers of deception and ego among the eccentric crew. Plus, the performances from Edward Norton and Janelle Monáe add some much-needed spice to the mix.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: there are multiple animal deaths and scenes involving animal abuse, including a dog and a horse. Also, bugs, spiders, and snakes appear, which might unsettle some viewers. If those are on your watchlist, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery serves up sharp wit and a glossy, sun-soaked setting that feels like Clue crashing a tech billionaire’s yacht party, with Edward Norton and Janelle Monáe adding lively spice to the mix.

writers: Justin Theroux, Ben Stiller, Etan Cohen
name: Tropic Thunder
overview: A group of self-absorbed actors set out to make the most expensive war film ever. After ballooning costs force the studio to cancel the movie, the frustrated director refuses to stop shooting, leading his cast into the jungles of Southeast Asia, where they encounter real bad guys.
review:
Tropic Thunder is a wild, R-rated satire of Hollywood action movies that manages to be both outrageously funny and sharp in its send-up of movie-making excess. Directed by and starring Ben Stiller, this 2008 flick feels like Apocalypse Now meets a dysfunctional buddy comedy, with a cast of egotistical actors lost in the jungle for a “realistic” war movie shoot gone off the rails. It’s not for everyone—some jokes land better than others—but it’s elevated by Robert Downey Jr.’s transformative performance and the way it gleefully skewers Hollywood vanity and the chaos behind the scenes.

What really stands out here is how the film flips the "actors stuck in danger" trope into something absurd and self-aware. The tagline “Get Some.” perfectly captures the brash, over-the-top tone. The story of a director losing control of his star-studded cast gets messier when the faux war zone turns into a real one, providing a clever meta-commentary on the blurred lines between performance and reality. Plus, the writing is packed with sharp one-liners and memorable beats, making the jungle setting as much a character as the titular “thunder” of the movie’s explosive humor.

That said, be heavily warned if animal harm triggers you—there’s quite a bit of dark humor involving animals, including a disturbing scene where a panda is stabbed repeatedly and worn as a costume, and another where a character eats a live bat. The film also includes multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse played for laughs, so those sensitive to animal-related content will want to proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Tropic Thunder is a wildly funny, sharp satire that blends Hollywood ego with jungle madness, elevated by Robert Downey Jr.’s standout performance and a brash, over-the-top tone that keeps the chaos rolling.

Be prepared for: repeated animal abuse played for laughs, a panda stabbed and worn as a costume, eating a live bat, and multiple instances of animal deaths.

overview: In the mystical Scottish Highlands, Merida is the princess of a kingdom ruled by King Fergus and Queen Elinor. name: Midsommar
overview: Several friends travel to Sweden to study as anthropologists a summer festival that is held every ninety years in the remote hometown of one of them. What begins as a dream vacation in a place where the sun never sets, gradually turns into a dark nightmare as the mysterious inhabitants invite them to participate in their disturbing festive activities.
review:
Midsommar is a sun-drenched descent into folk horror that flips the usual creepy-nighttime-cult trope on its head by setting everything in broad daylight during a never-ending Swedish summer festival. Ari Aster’s follow-up to Hereditary leans hard into unsettling vibes with a slow burn that’s equal parts mesmerizing and disturbing. Fans of unsettling psychological horror with a heavy dose of ritualistic dread will appreciate how this one blends the pastoral beauty of the setting with some truly grim, mind-bending moments. It’s not your typical jump-scare horror—think more subtle dread meets daylight nightmare.

What stands out most is the way the film uses its bright, almost pastoral visuals to mask the creeping horror beneath. Florence Pugh’s performance as Dani grounds the story emotionally, making the bizarre and brutal festival feel all the more personal and unsettling. The tagline “Let the festivities begin” feels almost sinister once you realize just how twisted these celebrations get. The film leans into anthropological curiosity gone wrong, and the slow unraveling of the group’s dynamic feels both natural and terrifying. Ari Aster’s writing and direction craft a world that’s as hypnotic and beautiful as it is horrifying, making the viewer question what they’d be willing to accept in the name of tradition and belonging.

Those sensitive to animal harm should be heavily warned here—yes, a dog dies, and it’s one of the more unsettling moments that sticks with you. The film’s unsettling atmosphere is punctuated by this and a handful of other disturbing events, so if you have a low tolerance for animal death or intense ritualistic violence, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Midsommar turns the typical horror formula inside out with its bright, sunlit setting and Florence Pugh’s deeply emotional performance, creating a slow-burning nightmare that lingers long after the credits roll.

Be prepared for: a disturbing dog death, graphic ritualistic violence, intense psychological dread, and unsettling scenes of human sacrifice.
