name: Booksmart
overview: Two academic teenage superstars realize, on the eve of their high school graduation, that they should have worked less and played more. Determined to never fall short of their peers, the girls set out on a mission to cram four years of fun into one night.
tagline: Getting straight A's. Giving zero F's.

writers: Yasmina Reza, Michael Katims, Roman Polanski
name: Carnage
overview: After 11-year-old Zachary Cowan strikes his classmate across the face with a stick after an argument, the victim's parents invite Zachary's parents to their Brooklyn apartment to deal with the incident in a civilized manner.
tagline: A new comedy of no manners.

name: Bone Tomahawk
overview: During a shootout in a saloon, Sheriff Hunt injures a suspicious stranger. One of the villagers takes care of him in prison. One day they both disappear – only the spear of a cannibal tribe is found. Hunt and a few of his men go in search of the prisoner and his nurse.

name: Let Me In
overview: A bullied young boy befriends a young female vampire who lives in secrecy with her guardian.  A remake of the movie “Let The Right One In” which was an adaptation of a book.

writers: Jason Hall, Zach Baylin, Alex Tse
name: Gran Turismo
overview: The ultimate wish-fulfillment tale of a teenage Gran Turismo player whose gaming skills won him a series of Nissan competitions to become an actual professional racecar driver.
review:
Gran Turismo is the kind of underdog sports biopic that feels like Ready Player One meets Rush, minus the sci-fi spectacle but with plenty of real-world grit. It’s a pretty straightforward wish-fulfillment story about a teenage gamer turned professional racecar driver, and while it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it’s elevated by solid performances—Archie Madekwe as Jann Mardenborough brings a believable mix of determination and vulnerability. If you’re into true-life inspirational tales or have a soft spot for high-octane racing drama, this one hits most of the right notes.

What stands out is how the film captures the crossover from virtual to real racing, leaning into the tagline “From gamer to racer” with an earnestness that avoids feeling gimmicky. Director Neill Blomkamp, better known for sci-fi, surprisingly keeps things grounded here, focusing on the emotional stakes rather than flashy visuals. The supporting cast, including David Harbour and Orlando Bloom, add some welcome texture, playing the mentors and rivals that shape Jann’s trajectory. The soundtrack and race sequences get the adrenaline pumping without feeling overly stylized, which gives the movie a more authentic vibe.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to certain intense content: Gran Turismo doesn’t shy away from the dangers of motorsport, including some pretty harrowing car crashes, and there’s a fair share of tragic deaths (including a kid and a dog), as well as jump scares and some harsh emotional beats. Those who pin the “car crashes,” “death of a child,” or “animal dies” triggers should proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Gran Turismo races past typical sports biopic beats with a grounded, emotionally charged story and standout performances that bring the gritty world of professional racing to life without flashy distractions.

Be prepared for: intense car crashes, death of a child, dog death, jump scares, and harsh emotional moments.

name: Heathers
overview: A girl who halfheartedly tries to be part of the "in crowd" of her school meets a rebel who teaches her a more devious way to play social politics: by killing the popular kids.
tagline: Best friends, social trends and occasional murder.
review:
Heathers is that cult-classic dark comedy from the late ’80s that still feels sharp and twisted today. It’s a high school satire with a deadly twist—think Clueless meets Heathers meets a gleefully grim black comedy about teenage cliques and chaos. Winona Ryder’s Veronica and Christian Slater’s J.D. make for a magnetic duo, balancing charm and menace as the story skews social politics through the lens of murder. It’s not just your typical teen drama; this one’s elevated by its biting wit and unapologetic dive into the darker side of popularity.

What really stands out is how the film blends sharp, quotable dialogue with a subversive look at the pressures and cruelty of high school life. The tagline—“Best friends, social trends and occasional murder”—perfectly sums up its twisted vibe. The writing leans into satire without letting up, and the cast, especially the trio of Heathers, nails a wickedly exaggerated version of teen royalty. Behind the slick 1989 aesthetic, there’s an undercurrent of sharp social commentary that still resonates, making it more than just a morbid teen flick.

Those who pin the eating disorder trigger should be cautious, as the film touches on this sensitive topic in its portrayal of high school pressures. While it’s not heavy-handed, it’s prominent enough to be a potential ambush for viewers sensitive to this content.
emailReview:
Heathers is a razor-sharp cult classic that mixes dark comedy with biting social satire, anchored by Winona Ryder and Christian Slater’s captivating clash of charm and menace.

Be prepared for: multiple teen deaths by gun and poison, suicide, and mentions of eating disorders.

writers: Tom Bleecker, Marc Rocco, Massy Tadjedin
name: The Jacket
overview: A military veteran goes on a journey into the future, where he can foresee his death and is left with questions that could save his life and those he loves.

name: Fast Times at Ridgemont High
overview:
Based on the real-life adventures chronicled by Cameron Crowe, Fast Times follows a group of high school students growing up in Southern California. 

Stacy Hamilton and Mark Ratner are looking for love, and are helped along by their older classmates, Linda Barrett and Mike Damone. Jeff Spicoli, a perpetually stoned surfer faces-off with the resolute teacher, Mr. Hand. Hilarity and heartbreak ensue.
tagline: At Ridgemont High, only the rules get busted!
review:
Fast Times at Ridgemont High is a quintessential early-80s teen comedy that still holds up as a vivid time capsule of Southern California adolescence — think John Hughes meets a laid-back surfer flick, with a sprinkle of Cameron Crowe’s signature observational wit. Amy Heckerling’s direction gives it a breezy, sometimes messy charm, and Sean Penn’s Jeff Spicoli is the kind of stoner character who’s become iconic, even if the film’s humor and tone feel a bit uneven by today’s standards. It’s not quite as sharp or self-aware as later teen classics, but it’s undeniably a wild ride through the awkward, messy, and sometimes heartwarming rites of passage.

What stands out here is how the film juggles multiple storylines with a mix of hilarity and genuine pathos, from young love and first heartbreak to stoner antics and schoolyard social dynamics. The tagline, “At Ridgemont High, only the rules get busted!” nails the film’s rebellious spirit — these teens are fumbling through growing up, guided by older classmates and a strict teacher who’s just as memorable as the kids. The soundtrack and setting perfectly evoke the era, and the cast delivers performances that range from goofy to surprisingly tender, making the highs and lows of adolescence feel both exaggerated and relatable.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to heavier moments: this one includes the death of a child and a dog, which can hit unexpectedly hard amid the comedy. There are also jump scares and some scenes involving burning and mutilation, so if you pin those triggers, tread carefully. The film mixes lighthearted teen hijinks with some darker beats that might catch you off guard.
emailReview:
Fast Times at Ridgemont High captures the messy, sun-soaked chaos of adolescence with a breezy charm and an iconic stoner performance from Sean Penn that’s equal parts goofy and tender.

Be prepared for: the death of a child, a dog dying, scenes of burning, mutilation, and sudden jump scares.

writers: Larry Clemmons, Vance Gerry, Ken Anderson, Frank Thomas, Eric Cleworth, Julius Svendsen, Ralph Wright, Tom McGowan, Tom Rowe
name: The Aristocats
overview: When Madame Adelaide Bonfamille leaves her fortune to Duchess and her children—Bonfamille’s beloved family of cats—the butler plots to steal the money and kidnaps the legatees, leaving them out on a country road. All seems lost until the wily Thomas O’Malley Cat and his jazz-playing alley cats come to the aristocats’ rescue.

name: Dogtooth
overview: Three teenagers are confined to an isolated country estate that could very well be on another planet. The trio spend their days listening to endless homemade tapes that teach them a whole new vocabulary. Any word that comes from beyond their family abode is instantly assigned a new meaning. Hence 'the sea' refers to a large armchair and 'zombies' are little yellow flowers. Having invented a brother whom they claim to have ostracized for his disobedience, the uber-controlling parents terrorize their offspring into submission.
review:
Dogtooth is a disturbingly brilliant dive into psychological horror and dark satire, the kind of film that lingers in your head long after the credits roll. Yorgos Lanthimos orchestrates a claustrophobic, surreal fable about control and language that feels like a twisted blend of The Village and The Stepford Wives, but with a uniquely Greek flavor of eerie absurdity. It’s not your typical horror or family drama — it’s an unsettling allegory disguised as a bizarre domestic nightmare, elevated by its deadpan performances and unsettling world-building.

What stands out most is the warped language system the family invents, turning everyday words into strange codewords, which highlights just how profoundly the parents manipulate their children’s reality. The isolation of the estate, which almost feels like another planet, adds to the film’s otherworldly vibe. The tape recordings the kids obsessively listen to create a weird, repetitive rhythm that feels both oppressive and hypnotic. The parents’ authoritarian control is chilling, and the invented “brother” subplot adds a layer of psychological terror that’s quietly devastating. It’s a film that’s as much about the power of language as it is about abuse and submission.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm or death — multiple types of animals, including dogs, cats, and horses, meet grim fates here, and there are scenes of animal abuse and abandonment. If bugs, spiders, or snakes set your teeth on edge, be warned those creepy crawlies also make an appearance. The film’s body horror elements and themes around control and abuse mean this isn’t a casual watch, but it’s a compelling, if unsettling, experience for those prepared for its darkness.
emailReview:
Dogtooth is a disturbingly brilliant psychological horror that blends surreal satire with eerie absurdity, anchored by deadpan performances and a claustrophobic, otherworldly atmosphere.

Be prepared for: animal death and abuse involving dogs, cats, and horses, creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes, and unsettling body horror scenes.

name: WarGames
overview: High School student David Lightman (Matthew Broderick) has a talent for hacking. But while trying to hack into a computer system to play unreleased video games, he unwittingly taps into the Defense Department's war computer and initiates a confrontation of global proportions! Together with his girlfriend (Ally Sheedy) and a wizardly computer genius (John Wood), David must race against time to outwit his opponent...and prevent a nuclear Armageddon.
tagline: Is it a game, or is it real?
review:
WarGames is a classic ‘80s techno-thriller that still feels surprisingly fresh in its portrayal of hacking and Cold War paranoia. Think of it as WarGames: “Hackers” meets “Dr. Strangelove”—a teen hacker accidentally triggering a nuclear crisis, with enough tension and humor to keep you hooked. Matthew Broderick’s likable turn as David Lightman anchors the film, while Ally Sheedy and John Wood round out a solid cast. It’s not just a relic of its time; it’s a clever, suspenseful ride that helped define the tech-thriller genre.

What really stands out is how the film blends youthful curiosity with high-stakes military drama. The tagline, “Is it a game, or is it real?” perfectly captures the film’s central tension—how the lines between digital play and devastating reality blur. The writing smartly balances the sci-fi elements with genuine suspense, and the early ‘80s tech aesthetic gives it a charming, nostalgic flavor without feeling dated. Plus, director John Badham keeps the pace brisk, making the countdown to potential Armageddon genuinely nail-biting.

Heads up to those sensitive to animal-related content: WarGames includes several instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, and horses. If that’s on your list, be cautious going in. The film’s tension isn’t just about nuclear war—it also involves some harsh animal moments that might catch you off guard.
emailReview:
WarGames is a sharp, suspenseful techno-thriller that mixes teenage hacking hijinks with Cold War dread, anchored by Matthew Broderick’s charming lead and a brisk, clever script.

Be prepared for: multiple scenes of animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, plus tense moments of animal abuse.

writers: John Grisham, Brian Koppelman, David Levien, Rick Cleveland, Matthew Chapman
name: Runaway Jury
overview: A juror on the inside and a woman on the outside manipulate a court trial involving a major gun manufacturer.
tagline: Trials are too important to be decided by juries.

name: Uncle Buck
overview: As an idle, good-natured bachelor, Uncle Buck is the last person you would think of to watch the kids. However, during a family crisis, he is suddenly left in charge of his nephew and nieces. Unaccustomed to suburban life, fun-loving Uncle Buck soon charms his younger relatives Miles and Maizy with his hefty cooking and his new way of doing the laundry. His carefree style does not impress everyone though - especially his rebellious teenage niece, Tia, and his impatient girlfriend, Chanice. With a little bit of luck and a lot of love, Uncle Buck manages to surprise everyone in this heartwarming family comedy.
tagline: He's crude. He's crass. He's family.

directors: Wolfgang Reitherman, Clyde Geronimi, David Hand
name: The Sword in the Stone
overview: Wart is a young boy who aspires to be a knight's squire. On a hunting trip he falls in on Merlin, a powerful but amnesiac wizard who has plans for him beyond mere squiredom. He starts by trying to give him an education, believing that once one has an education, one can go anywhere. Needless to say, it doesn't quite work out that way.
tagline: Tired of living in a Medieval mess... Merlin uses all his magic powers to change a scrawny little boy into a legendary hero!

name: A Real Pain
overview: Mismatched cousins David and Benji reunite for a tour through Poland to honor their beloved grandmother. The adventure takes a turn when the pair's old tensions resurface against the backdrop of their family history.
review:
A Real Pain is a family dramedy that leans into the messy, awkward dynamics of relatives forced to confront their past and each other. It’s a road trip movie with a twist of emotional baggage, anchored by Jesse Eisenberg pulling triple duty as writer, director, and lead. Fans of quirky sibling rivalry tales like The Royal Tenenbaums or The Skeleton Twins might find something to like here, though it doesn’t quite reach their sharpness or depth. Still, it’s a heartfelt if sometimes uneven exploration of family ties and unresolved tension.

What stands out most is the chemistry between Eisenberg’s David and Kieran Culkin’s Benji, whose bickering feels both real and occasionally stilted—a reflection of the film’s uneven tone. The Poland backdrop adds a moody, atmospheric layer to the journey, and the tagline “Join the family” hints at an invitation that’s as ironic as it is sincere. The film isn’t afraid to lean into uncomfortable moments, with its exploration of grief and familial conflict occasionally veering into darker emotional territory. It’s a modest, character-driven piece that’s more about the cracks than the shine.

Heads up for sensitive viewers: A Real Pain includes several tough triggers, notably the death and abuse of animals—including dogs, cats, and horses—which might be particularly hard to stomach. There’s also child abuse, domestic violence, and some heavy family loss, plus unsettling scenes involving bugs, spiders, snakes, and other creepy crawlies. The ending carries a sad tone, so if any of those are on your list, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
A Real Pain is a moody family dramedy anchored by Jesse Eisenberg and Kieran Culkin’s tense sibling chemistry, set against a somber Polish backdrop that adds weight to its awkward, heartfelt exploration of grief and family conflict.

Be prepared for: animal death and abuse involving dogs, cats, and horses, child abuse, domestic violence, and unsettling scenes with bugs, spiders, and snakes.

writers: Jim Jarmusch, Bill Raden, Sara Driver
name: Broken Flowers
overview: As the devoutly single Don Johnston is dumped by his latest girlfriend, he receives an anonymous pink letter informing him that he has a son who may be looking for him.

name: Concussion
overview: A dramatic thriller based on the incredible true David vs. Goliath story of American immigrant Dr. Bennet Omalu, the brilliant forensic neuropathologist who made the first discovery of CTE, a football-related brain trauma, in a pro player and fought for the truth to be known. Omalu's emotional quest puts him at dangerous odds with one of the most powerful institutions in the world.

name: West Side Story
overview: Two youngsters from rival New York City gangs fall in love, but tensions between their respective friends build toward tragedy.
tagline: A city divided. Their love will challenge everything.

name: Tommy Boy
overview: Party animal Tommy Callahan is a few cans short of a six-pack. But when the family business starts tanking, it's up to Tommy and number-cruncher Richard Hayden to save the day.
tagline: If at first you don't succeed, lower your standards.

name: Elephant
overview: Several ordinary high school students go through their daily routine as two others prepare for something more malevolent. The film chronicles the events surrounding a school shooting.
tagline: An ordinary high school day. Except that it's not.

name: The Frighteners
overview: Once an architect, Frank Bannister now passes himself off as an exorcist of evil spirits. To bolster his facade, he claims his "special" gift is the result of a car accident that killed his wife. But what he does not count on is more people dying in the small town where he lives. As he tries to piece together the supernatural mystery of these killings, he falls in love with the wife of one of the victims and deals with a crazy FBI agent.

writers: Jason Segel, Nicholas Stoller, Jim Henson
name: The Muppets
overview: When Kermit the Frog and the Muppets learn that their beloved theater is slated for demolition, a sympathetic human, Gary, and his puppet brother, Walter, swoop in to help the gang put on a show and raise the $10 million they need to save the day.

name: Half Nelson
overview: Despite his dedication to the junior-high students who fill his classroom, idealistic teacher Dan Dunne leads a secret life of addiction that the majority of his students will never know. But things change when a troubled student Drey makes a startling discovery of his secret life, causing a tenuous bond between the two that could either end disastrously or provide a catalyst of hope.

name: Cashback
overview: After a painful breakup, Ben develops insomnia. To kill time, he starts working the late night shift at the local supermarket, where his artistic imagination runs wild.

writers: Howard Ashman, Roger Corman, Charles B. Griffith
name: Little Shop of Horrors
overview: Seymour Krelborn is a nerdy orphan working at Mushnik's, a flower shop in urban Skid Row. He harbors a crush on fellow co-worker Audrey Fulquard, and is berated by Mr. Mushnik daily. One day as Seymour is seeking a new mysterious plant, he finds a very mysterious unidentified plant which he calls Audrey II. The plant seems to have a craving for blood and soon begins to sing for his supper.
tagline: A singing plant. A daring hero. A sweet girl. A demented dentist. It's the most outrageous musical comedy in years.
review:
Little Shop of Horrors is a wild, campy musical comedy that dances on the edge of horror and satire with a devilish grin. Directed by Frank Oz, it’s this oddball blend of 80s kitsch, catchy tunes, and dark humor that makes it stand out alongside other cult musicals—think The Rocky Horror Picture Show meets a twisted fairy tale. Rick Moranis as Seymour brings that lovable nerd energy, and Steve Martin’s sadistic dentist is memorably deranged, but it’s Levi Stubbs’ voice giving life to Audrey II, the bloodthirsty plant, that steals the show. It’s not exactly a lighthearted romp, but fans of bold, boundary-pushing musicals will appreciate its outrageousness and biting social commentary.

What really sticks with you here is the film’s sharp balance of whimsy and grit. The tagline—“A singing plant. A daring hero. A sweet girl. A demented dentist.”—barely scratches the surface of the darker themes lurking beneath all the catchy songs and campy visuals. The story sets its stage in a grimy Skid Row flower shop, where Seymour’s crush on Audrey unfolds amid emotional abuse, stalking, and a seriously unhinged dentist’s torture antics. The show also leans into classic musical tropes but subverts them with some heavy social issues—homelessness, domestic violence, and the cycle of abuse are all present, wrapped in a very 80s neon-soaked package. It’s equal parts unsettling and entertaining, which is a tough tightrope to walk.

Heads up for those sensitive to domestic violence, sexual assault, and psychological abuse—these elements are woven through the story and don’t shy away from uncomfortable portrayals. The movie also features blood and gore, disturbing dental torture scenes, as well as gun violence and death. The plant’s predatory behavior includes a sexual assault scene that’s hard to watch, and the frequent sudden loud noises and flashing lights might catch you off guard. If you’re triggered by stalking, animal abuse references, or intense emotional manipulation, approach with caution. This musical’s charm comes with a hefty dose of darkness beneath its catchy tunes.
emailReview:
Little Shop of Horrors mixes 80s kitsch, dark humor, and unforgettable performances into a campy musical that’s equal parts twisted fairy tale and biting satire.

Be prepared for: disturbing dental torture, sexual assault by a predatory plant, stalking, intense emotional abuse, and sudden blood and gore.

writers: Larry Beinhart, Hilary Henkin, David Mamet
name: Wag the Dog
overview: During the final weeks of a presidential race, the President is accused of sexual misconduct. To distract the public until the election, the President's adviser hires a Hollywood producer to help him stage a fake war.
tagline: A comedy about truth, justice and other special effects.

writers: Karen Blixen, Judith Thurman, Errol Trzebinski, Kurt Luedtke
name: Out of Africa
overview: Out of Africa tells the story of the life of Danish author Karen Blixen, who at the beginning of the 20th century moved to Africa to build a new life for herself. The film is based on the autobiographical novel by Karen Blixen from 1937.

name: The Kings of Summer
overview: Joe Toy, on the verge of adolescence, finds himself increasingly frustrated by his single father, Frank's attempts to manage his life. Declaring his freedom once and for all, he escapes to a clearing in the woods with his best friend, Patrick, and a strange kid named Biaggio. He announces that they are going to build a house there, free from responsibility and parents. Once their makeshift abode is finished, the three young men find themselves masters of their own destiny, alone in the woods.

name: In the Mouth of Madness
altName: john carpenter‘s in the mouth of madness
overview: With the disappearance of hack horror writer Sutter Cane, all Hell is breaking loose...literally! Insurance investigator John Trent is sent to investigate Cane's mysterious vanishing act and ends up in the sleepy little East Coast town of Hobb's End.

writers: Susannah Grant, Andy Tennant, Rick Parks, Charles Perrault
name: EverAfter
overview: A unique 16th century woman, Danielle possesses a love of books, and can easily quote from Sir Thomas More’s UTOPIA. An intriguing mix of tomboyish athleticism and physical beauty, she has more than enough charm to capture the heart of a prince ... after beaning him with an apple.

name: Blue Ruin
overview: When the quiet life of a beach bum is upended by dreadful news, he sets off for his childhood home to carry out an act of vengeance. However, he proves an inept assassin and finds himself in a brutal fight to protect his estranged family.

name: Brawl in Cell Block 99
overview: After working as a drug courier and getting into a brutal shootout with police, a former boxer finds himself at the mercy of his enemies as they force him to instigate violent acts that turn the prison he resides in into a battleground.

name: The Square
overview: A prestigious Stockholm museum's chief art curator finds himself in times of both professional and personal crisis as he attempts to set up a controversial new exhibit.

writers: Panna Rittikrai, Prachya Pinkaew, Suphachai Sittiaumponpan
name: Ong Bak: Muay Thai Warrior
overview: When the head of a statue sacred to a village is stolen, a young martial artist goes to the big city and finds himself taking on the underworld to retrieve it.

writers: Judd Apatow, Pete Davidson, Dave Sirus
name: The King of Staten Island
overview: A semi-autobiographical comedy-drama about Pete Davidson growing up in Staten Island, including losing his father during 9/11 and entering the world of stand up comedy.

name: Whatever Works
overview: Whatever Works explores the relationship between a crotchety misanthrope, Boris and a naïve, impressionable young runaway from the south, Melody. When Melody's uptight parents arrive in New York to rescue her, they are quickly drawn into wildly unexpected romantic entanglements. Everyone discovers that finding love is just a combination of lucky chance and appreciating the value of "whatever works."

name: Day of the Dead
overview: As the world is overrun by zombies, scientists and military personnel in an underground Florida bunker must decide on how they should deal with the undead.
tagline: The darkest day of horror the world has ever known!

writers: Alvin Sargent, Laura Ziskin, Tom Schulman
name: What About Bob
overview: Before going on vacation, self-involved psychiatrist Dr. Leo Marvin has the misfortune of taking on a new patient: Bob Wiley. An exemplar of neediness and a compendium of phobias, Bob follows Marvin to his family's country house. Dr. Marvin tries to get him to leave; the trouble is, everyone loves Bob. As his oblivious patient makes himself at home, Dr. Marvin loses his professional composure and, before long, may be ready for the loony bin himself.
tagline: Bob's a special kind of friend. The kind that drives you crazy.

name: That Thing You Do
overview: A Pennsylvania band scores a hit in 1964 and rides the star-making machinery as long as it can, with lots of help from its manager.

name: Tinder Swindler
overview: Documentary about an Israeli conman and his numerous female victims that he met through dating app Tinder

writers: H.P. Lovecraft, Dennis Paoli, William Norris, Stuart Gordon
name: Re-Animator
overview: A dedicated student at a medical college and his girlfriend become involved in bizarre experiments centering around the re-animation of dead tissue when an odd new student arrives on campus.
tagline: Herbert West has a good head on his shoulders...and another one on his desk.

name: The Dark Crystal
overview: On another planet in the distant past, a Gelfling embarks on a quest to find the missing shard of a magical crystal and restore order to his world, before the grotesque race of Skeksis find and use the crystal for evil.
tagline: Another world, another time... in the age of wonder.

name: Agora
overview: A historical drama set in Roman Egypt, concerning philosopher Hypatia of Alexandria and her relationship with her slave Davus, who is torn between his love for her and the possibility of gaining his freedom by joining the rising tide of Christianity.
tagline: Alexandria, Egypt. 391 A.D. The World Changed Forever.

writers: Stéphane Cabel, Christophe Gans, Canal Plus Ecriture
name: Brotherhood of the Wolf
overview: In 18th century France, the Chevalier de Fronsac and his Native American friend Mani are sent by the King to the Gevaudan province to investigate the killings of hundreds by a mysterious beast.
tagline: The year is 1766... The hunt for a killer has begun.

name: Soylent Green
overview: In an overpopulated futuristic Earth, a New York police detective finds himself marked for murder by government agents when he gets too close to a bizarre state secret involving the origins of a revolutionary and needed new foodstuff.
tagline: It's the year 2022. People are still the same. They'll do anything to get what they need. And they need Soylent Green.

name: God Bless America
overview: Fed up with the cruelty and stupidity of American culture, an unlikely duo goes on a killing spree, killing reality TV stars, bigots and others they find repugnant in this black comedy.
tagline: Taking out the trash, one jerk at a time.

name: Timecrimes
overview: A man accidentally gets into a time machine and travels back in time nearly an hour. Finding himself will be the first of a series of disasters of unforeseeable consequences.
tagline: A trip back in time from the present to...

name: A Tale of Two Sisters
overview: A recently released patient from a mental institution returns home with her sister, only to face disturbing events between her stepmother and the ghosts haunting their house- all of which are connected to a dark past in the family's history.
tagline: Our sorrow was conceived long before our birth.

name: Arthur Christmas
overview: Each Christmas, Santa and his vast army of highly trained elves produce gifts and distribute them around the world in one night. However, when one of 600 million children to receive a gift from Santa on Christmas Eve is missed, it is deemed ‘acceptable’ to all but one – Arthur. Arthur Claus is Santa’s misfit son who executes an unauthorized rookie mission to get the last present half way around the globe before dawn on Christmas morning.
tagline: Ever wonder how 2 Billion presents get delivered all in 1 night?

writers: Jeff Tremaine, Johnny Knoxville, Bam Margera, Steve-O, Chris Pontius, Ryan Dunn, Jason 'Wee Man' Acuña, Preston Lacy, Ehren McGhehey, Dave England, Spike Jonze, Loomis Fall, Barry Owen Smoler, The Dudesons, Dave Carnie, Mike Kassak, Madison Clapp, Knate Lee, Derek Freda, Trip Taylor, Sean Cliver, Dimitry Elyashkevich, J.P. Blackmon, Rick Kosick
name: Jackass 3D
overview: Johnny Knoxville, Bam Margera, Steve-O, Wee Man and the rest of their fearless and foolhardy friends take part in another round of outrageous pranks and stunts. In addition to standing in the path of a charging bull, launching themselves into the air and crashing through various objects, the guys perform in segments such as "Sweatsuit Cocktail," "Beehive Tetherball" and "Lamborghini Tooth Pull."
tagline: 3 Times the Laughs. 3 Times the Stupid. 3 Times the Pain.

writers: Aoi Hiiragi, Hayao Miyazaki, Reiko Yoshida
name: The Cat Returns
overview: Haru, a schoolgirl bored by her ordinary routine, saves the life of an unusual cat and suddenly her world is transformed beyond anything she ever imagined. The Cat King rewards her good deed with a flurry of presents, including a very shocking proposal of marriage to his son! Haru embarks on an unexpected journey to the Kingdom of Cats where her eyes are opened to a whole other world.
tagline: It's not so bad being a cat, now is it?

name: Coffee and Cigarettes
overview: Coffee And Cigarettes is a collection of eleven films from cult director Jim Jarmusch. Each film hosts star studded cast of extremely unique individuals who all share the common activities of conversing while drinking coffee and smoking cigarettes.

name: Chariots of Fire
overview: In the class-obsessed and religiously divided UK of the early 1920s, two determined young runners train for the 1924 Paris Olympics. Eric Liddell, a devout Christian born to Scottish missionaries in China, sees running as part of his worship of God's glory and refuses to train or compete on the Sabbath. Harold Abrahams overcomes anti-Semitism and class bias, but neglects his beloved sweetheart in his single-minded quest.

writers: Rosalie Ham, Jocelyn Moorhouse, P.J. Hogan
name: The Dressmaker
overview: In 1950s Australia, beautiful, talented dressmaker Tilly returns to her tiny hometown to right wrongs from her past. As she tries to reconcile with her mother, she starts to fall in love while transforming the fashion of the town.

writers: Debra Granik, Anne Rosellini, Peter Rock
name: Leave No Trace
overview: A father and daughter live a perfect but mysterious existence in Forest Park, a beautiful nature reserve near Portland, Oregon, rarely making contact with the world. But when a small mistake tips them off to authorities, they are sent on an increasingly erratic journey in search of a place to call their own.

name: Enough Said
overview: Eva is a divorced soon-to-be empty-nester wondering about her next act. Then she meets Marianne, the embodiment of her perfect self. Armed with a restored outlook on being middle-aged and single, Eva decides to take a chance on her new love interest Albert — a sweet, funny and like-minded man. But things get complicated when Eva discovers that Albert is in fact the dreaded ex–husband of Marianne...

writers: Piers Paul Read, John Patrick Shanley
name: Alive
overview: The amazing, true story of a Uruguayan rugby team's plane that crashed in the middle of the Andes mountains, and their immense will to survive and pull through alive, forced to do anything and everything they could to stay alive on meager rations and through the freezing cold.

writers: Jymn Magon, Chris Matheson, Brian Pimental, Curtis Armstrong, John Doolittle
name: A Goofy Movie
overview: Though Goofy always means well, his amiable cluelessness and klutzy pratfalls regularly embarrass his awkward adolescent son, Max. When Max's lighthearted prank on his high-school principal finally gets his longtime crush, Roxanne, to notice him, he asks her on a date. Max's trouble at school convinces Goofy that he and the boy need to bond over a cross-country fishing trip like the one he took with his dad when he was Max's age, which throws a kink in his son's plans to impress Roxanne.
tagline: It's hard to be cool when your Dad is Goofy.

writers: Jane Austen, Kevin Hood, Sarah Williams
name: Becoming Jane
overview: A biographical portrait of a pre-fame Jane Austen and her romance with a young Irishman.

writers: Steve Martin, Carl Gottlieb, Michael Elias
name: The Jerk
overview: After discovering he's not really black like the rest of his family, likable dimwit Navin Johnson runs off on a hilarious misadventure in this comedy classic that takes him from rags to riches and back to rags again. The slaphappy jerk strikes it rich, but life in the fast lane isn't all it's cracked up to be and, in the end, all that really matters to Johnson is his true love.
tagline: A rags to riches to rags story.
review:
Steve Martin’s The Jerk is a wild, goofy ride through late-70s absurdist comedy that’s equal parts slapstick and social satire. It’s a rags-to-riches-to-rags story that somehow feels both timeless and a little of its era, with a tone that’s zany and often self-aware. If you like your comedy a bit off-kilter and don’t mind some dated moments, this one’s a classic for fans of Martin’s unique brand of humor—think The Three Stooges meets a very weird fairy tale.

What stands out most is Martin’s performance as Navin Johnson, the lovable dimwit whose cluelessness drives the plot forward. The film leans heavily into the “fish out of water” trope, but what’s charming here is how it tackles identity and belonging with a goofy twist, especially with Navin’s discovery that he’s not actually black like his family. Carl Reiner’s direction keeps the pace brisk, and the cast—Bernadette Peters included—adds some solid support. The tagline, “A rags to riches to rags story,” nails the cyclical nature of Navin’s misadventures, which culminate in a surprisingly sweet note about the importance of love over money.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: this film includes multiple instances of animals dying or being harmed, including a dog, a horse, and a cat, plus some scenes involving bugs, snakes, and spiders that might be unnerving. There’s also some rougher language and mild instances of hate speech, as well as a gag involving vomiting. So if any of those are on your radar, be prepared for a handful of moments that might hit hard.
emailReview:
Steve Martin shines in this zany, off-kilter comedy that mixes slapstick with social satire for a timeless yet distinctly late-70s vibe.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, horse, and cat, unsettling scenes with bugs and snakes, plus rough language and a gag involving vomiting.

name: Breakdown
overview: When his SUV breaks down on a remote Southwestern road, Jeff Taylor lets his wife, Amy, hitch a ride with a trucker to get help. When she doesn't return, Jeff fixes his SUV and tracks down the trucker -- who tells the police he's never seen Amy. Johnathan Mostow's tense thriller then follows Jeff's desperate search for his wife, which eventually uncovers a small town's murderous secret.

writers: Daphne Du Maurier, Allan Scott, Chris Bryant
name: Don't Look Now
overview: While grieving a terrible loss, a married couple meet two mysterious sisters, one of whom gives them a message sent from the afterlife.

name: We Are Marshall
overview: When a plane crash claims the lives of members of the Marshall University football team and some of its fans, the team's new coach and his surviving players try to keep the football program alive.

name: An Officer and a Gentleman
overview: Zack Mayo is an aloof, taciturn man who aspires to be a navy pilot. Once he arrives at training camp for his 13-week officer's course, Mayo runs afoul of abrasive, no-nonsense drill Sergeant Emil Foley. Mayo is an excellent cadet, but a little cold around the heart, so Foley rides him mercilessly, sensing that the young man would be prime officer material if he weren't so self-involved. Zack's affair with a working girl is likewise compromised by his unwillingness to give of himself.

writers: Phil Alden Robinson, Lawrence Lasker, Walter F. Parkes
name: Sneakers
overview: When shadowy U.S. intelligence agents blackmail a reformed computer hacker and his eccentric team of security experts into stealing a code-breaking 'black box' from a Soviet-funded genius, they uncover a bigger conspiracy. Now, he and his 'sneakers' must save themselves and the world economy by retrieving the box from their blackmailers.
tagline: We could tell you what it's about. But then, of course, we'd have to kill you.

name: Benny & Joon
overview: A mentally ill young woman finds her love in an eccentric man who models himself after Buster Keaton.
tagline: A romance on the brink of reality.

writers: Chris Williams, Nell Benjamin, Sam Stratton, Mattson Tomlin
name: The Sea Beast
overview: When a young girl stows away on the ship of a legendary sea monster hunter, they launch an epic journey into uncharted waters — and make history to boot.

writers: Phil Hartman, Paul Reubens, Michael Varhol
name: Pee-wee's Big Adventure
overview: The eccentric and childish Pee-wee Herman embarks on a big adventure when his beloved bicycle is stolen. Armed with information from a fortune-teller and a relentless obsession with his prized possession, Pee-wee encounters a host of odd characters and bizarre situations as he treks across the country to recover his bike.
tagline: The story of a rebel and his bike.

name: The Apprentice
overview: A young Donald Trump, eager to make his name as a hungry scion of a wealthy family in 1970s New York, comes under the spell of Roy Cohn, the cutthroat attorney who would help create the Donald Trump we know today. Cohn sees in Trump the perfect protégé—someone with raw ambition, a hunger for success, and a willingness to do whatever it takes to win.

writers: Hal Needham, Robert L. Levy, James Lee Barrett, Charles Shyer, Alan Mandel
name: Smokey And the Bandit
overview: A race car driver tries to transport an illegal beer shipment from Texas to Atlanta in under 28 hours, picking up a reluctant bride-to-be on the way.
tagline: What we have here is a total lack of respect for the law!
review:
Smokey and the Bandit is a rollicking 1970s road comedy that feels like a high-octane mashup of classic car chase flicks and buddy comedies. Burt Reynolds’ charm as Bo “Bandit” Darville really anchors the film, bringing a cheeky swagger that makes the law-breaking escapades feel like a wild game rather than criminal acts. If you like your action with a side of Southern twang and a wink, this one’s a pretty iconic ride—though it’s not exactly subtle or deep, it’s got enough energy to stay entertaining.

What stands out is the effortless chemistry between Reynolds and Sally Field’s reluctant co-star, Carrie “Frog.” The plot—a race to haul an illegal beer shipment across state lines—leans hard into the outlaw spirit with plenty of car stunts and the inevitable bumbling sheriff pursuit, courtesy of Jackie Gleason’s over-the-top Sheriff Buford T. Justice. It’s classic Hal Needham directing, so expect some genuinely impressive driving sequences that still hold up as the film’s main draw. The tagline, “What we have here is a total lack of respect for the law!” nails the tone perfectly: irreverent, fast-paced, and unapologetically goofy.

Heads up for animal lovers: Smokey and the Bandit is heavily loaded with animal-related triggers. There’s a disturbing amount of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and other animals, plus some more unsettling mentions like dog fighting and animal harm during production. If you’re sensitive to animal cruelty or death, this one’s going to be rough. Beyond that, there are some creepy crawlies—spiders, snakes, bugs—so those with a bug phobia should stay cautious.
emailReview:
Smokey and the Bandit is a high-energy 1970s road comedy packed with Burt Reynolds’ trademark charm and some of the slickest car chases you’ll find outside a NASCAR race.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, dog fighting, on-set animal harm, and unsettling creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes.

name: We Live in Time
overview: An up-and-coming chef and a recent divorcée find their lives forever changed when a chance encounter brings them together, in a decade-spanning, deeply moving romance.
review:
We Live in Time is a quietly intense romance that leans into the bittersweet with a decade-spanning story about love and loss. If you’re into slow-burn dramas like Before Sunrise but with a more somber, reflective tone, this one might stick with you. Andrew Garfield and Florence Pugh bring a grounded vulnerability to their roles as Tobias and Almut, an up-and-coming chef and a recent divorcée whose lives intersect in ways that feel both inevitable and fragile. It’s not your typical romantic drama; it’s more meditative, less about grand gestures and more about the small, aching moments that define a relationship over time.

What really stands out here is the film’s patience—John Crowley’s direction gives the story room to breathe, letting the emotional weight unfold naturally rather than forcing it. The tagline, “Every minute counts,” isn’t just a throwaway line; the narrative structure plays with time in a way that underscores how fleeting and precious connection can be. The writing by Nick Payne is subtle but sharp, avoiding clichés while digging into themes of regret, healing, and the unpredictability of life’s intersections. Visually, the film is understated, which suits the intimate scale of the story, with just enough texture to keep it from feeling like a staged stage play.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related distress: the film features multiple triggers in that department, including the death of several animals like dogs, cats, horses, and even a non-human character. There’s also animal abuse and dog fighting depicted, plus unsettling appearances by bugs, spiders, and snakes. If animals are a big trigger for you, be prepared for some tough scenes here.
emailReview:
We Live in Time is a quietly intense romance that lingers on the fragile, small moments of love and loss, anchored by heartfelt performances from Andrew Garfield and Florence Pugh.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, plus unsettling insects, spiders, and snakes.

name: Lords of Dogtown
overview: "Lords of Dogtown" tells the radical true story behind three teenage surfers from Venice Beach, California, who took skateboarding to the extreme and changed the world of sports forever. Stacy Peralta (John Robinson, Elephant), Tony Alva (Victor Rasuk, Raising Victor Vargas) and Jay Adams (Emile Hirsch, The Girl Next Door) are the Z-Boys, a bunch of nobodies until they create a new style of skateboarding that becomes a worldwide phenomenon. But when their hobby becomes a business, the success shreds their friendship. Directed by Catherine Hardwicke (Thirteen) and written by Stacy Peralta, Lords of Dogtown is "...a dazzling daredevil ride." (Peter Travers, Rollng Stone)

writers: Casey McQuiston, Matthew López, Ted Malawer
name: Red White & Royal Blue
overview: Based on the Casey McQuiston Novel of the same name, this LGBTQ story focuses on Alex Claremont-Diaz, the First Son of the United States and his rivalry with the young Prince of Wales, Henry. After causing a major uproar at the older Prince's wedding, the two are forced to avoid a National incident by up-playing their non existent friendship with a goodwill visit to the UK. Their rivalry soon turns into a forced friendship and then blossoms into something even more. The two try to keep their relationship a secret despite their highly public lives amid his mother's re-election campaign as the first female President.
tagline: Love who you want. It's good foreign policy.

name: Grumpy Old Men
overview: For decades, next-door neighbors and former friends John and Max have feuded, trading insults and wicked pranks. When an attractive widow moves in nearby, their bad blood erupts into a high-stakes rivalry full of naughty jokes and adolescent hijinks. Will this love triangle destroy the two old grumps? Or will the geriatric odd couple overcome their differences and rediscover their friendship?
tagline: The best of enemies until something came between them.
review:
Grumpy Old Men is a quintessential ’90s comedy that leans hard into the grumpy-but-lovable buddy dynamic, with Jack Lemmon and Walter Matthau bringing their classic chemistry to a small-town feud that’s equal parts hilarious and heartwarming. It feels like a gentler, more nostalgic cousin to the rougher edges of the buddy-comedy genre, trading the usual high-octane antics for a slow-burn rivalry fueled by decades of snark and a surprising amount of charm. Fans of character-driven comedies with a dash of romantic rivalry will find themselves right at home here.

What stands out most is the way the film balances its mean-spirited pranks with genuinely sweet moments, especially as the two old-timers navigate the arrival of Ann-Margret’s spirited widow, Ariel. The tagline, “The best of enemies until something came between them,” nails the tone perfectly — it’s a story about friendship, grudges, and the messy middle ground in between. Donald Petrie’s direction keeps things light and breezy, while Mark Steven Johnson’s writing mixes sharp one-liners with a surprisingly tender look at aging and companionship. Plus, the supporting cast, especially Burgess Meredith and Kevin Pollak, add nice depth without stealing the spotlight.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one’s notorious on the trigger front. Multiple animals—dogs, cats, horses—don’t make it through unscathed, and there’s some rough stuff involving animals that might catch you off guard. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or death on screen, Grumpy Old Men isn’t the easiest watch in that department. Also, if creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes make you uneasy, they pop up here too. Otherwise, it’s a gentle comedy about cranky neighbors with a surprisingly soft core.
emailReview:
Grumpy Old Men charms with its slow-burn, grumpy-but-lovable buddy comedy vibe, anchored by Jack Lemmon and Walter Matthau’s timeless chemistry and a sweet look at aging and friendship.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths involving dogs, cats, and horses, unsettling scenes with spiders and snakes, and some rough animal harm that might catch you off guard.

review:
Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey is a heartwarming adventure that fits snugly into the tradition of feel-good family films from the early ’90s. It’s basically Lassie meets The Wizard of Oz, with Michael J. Fox, Sally Field, and Don Ameche lending their voices to a trio of pets on a cross-country trek to reunite with their owners. While it treads familiar ground, the mix of humor, earnestness, and a dash of peril keeps it engaging—though it’s not quite as sharp or funny as some other animal-led adventures of the era.

What stands out most here is the chemistry between the animals’ personalities: Chance’s goofy optimism, Sassy’s sarcastic sass, and Shadow’s dignified wisdom feel like a well-balanced trio. The film’s tagline about courage, adventure, and friendship truly rings true as the characters face various obstacles, both natural and manmade. The nostalgic Disney vibe is strong, with scenic outdoor shots and a score that gently underscores the emotional beats without overwhelming them. It’s an earnest story built on classic themes, leaning into the bond between pets and their humans without ever feeling too saccharine.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animals in distress: the film includes some upsetting moments with animal deaths and abuse, including the loss of a horse and a cat, as well as scenes of animals being sad or abandoned. There are also encounters with snakes and spiders that might be a tough watch for some. Those who pin the animal harm and death triggers should proceed with caution.

name: Black Christmas
overview: A sorority house is terrorized by a stranger who makes frightening phone calls and then murders the sorority sisters during Christmas break.
tagline: If this picture doesn't make your skin crawl... it's on TOO TIGHT.
review:
Black Christmas (1974) is a pioneer of the slasher genre that still manages to rattle nerves decades later. Think of it as the creepy, claustrophobic ancestor to Halloween and Friday the 13th, with a tense, voyeuristic vibe that lingers long after the credits roll. The film’s chilling tagline—“If this picture doesn’t make your skin crawl... it’s on TOO TIGHT”—is no joke. While it may not have the polished gore or jump scares of later slashers, its unsettling atmosphere and the slow-burn terror of an unseen menace stalking a sorority house during Christmas break make it a wild ride for horror buffs and a must-watch for those curious about the genre’s roots.

What really sets this one apart is its use of sound and silence to build dread, plus the eerie phone calls that kick off the nightmare. Olivia Hussey as Jess and Margot Kidder as Barb bring relatable vulnerability to their roles, making the terror feel personal. Bob Clark’s direction leans into the isolation of the setting and the paranoia creeping through the characters, turning a festive backdrop into a claustrophobic trap. The film subverts the cozy holiday mood with a raw, almost documentary-like feel that makes the horror hit harder. It’s a reminder that the real nightmare might be just a phone call away.

Heads up for those who are sensitive to animal-related triggers: this one includes multiple instances of animal harm and death, including dogs, cats, and horses, which might be tough to watch. Also, the film touches on themes of gaslighting and features some body horror elements. If you’re on the lookout for those triggers, be prepared for a rough ride—not just because of the human threat lurking around the sorority house.
emailReview: Black Christmas (1974) is a tense, claustrophobic pioneer of the slasher genre that uses sound and silence to build dread like few horror films can, with standout performances that make the terror feel deeply personal. review:
The Zookeeper’s Wife is a somber, quietly heroic World War II drama that blends historical biopic with the kind of human-and-animal compassion story that feels both earnest and necessary. Jessica Chastain anchors the film with a steady, heartfelt performance as Antonina Żabińska, whose courage and kindness shine amid the horrors of Nazi-occupied Warsaw. Fans of films like The Pianist or Defiance will find familiar ground here, but this one adds a unique angle by focusing on a zoo as a secret refuge, making it a bit of a genre hybrid that’s more moving than thrilling.

What stands out most is how the film balances its themes of resistance and survival with the poignant presence of animals—both as innocent bystanders and as quiet witnesses to humanity’s cruelty and bravery. The tagline, “They gave all they had to save all they could,” really sums up the spirit, and Niki Caro’s direction gives the story an intimate, grounded feel rather than epic bombast. It’s the kind of film that lingers because of its quiet moments—like the way the zoo itself becomes a symbol of sanctuary and loss. The writing leans into this duality well, though it doesn’t shy away from the brutal realities of war.

Heads-up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this film features multiple distressing scenes involving animals, including death and abuse, as well as dog fighting and bestiality. Those who pin the animal harm and death triggers should be cautious going in.

name: Nyad
overview: Athlete Diana Nyad sets out at 60 to achieve a nearly impossible lifelong dream: to swim from Cuba to Florida across more than 100 miles of open ocean.
review:
Nyad is a stirring sports biopic that joins the wave of true-life athletic triumph stories but stands out thanks to its focus on a 60-year-old woman chasing an almost mythic goal. Annette Bening carries the film with a quietly powerful performance as Diana Nyad, whose determination to swim from Cuba to Florida across 100-plus miles of open ocean feels both inspiring and humbling. It’s not your typical adrenaline-fueled sports flick; instead, it’s a reflective, character-driven drama that leans into the emotional and physical toll of chasing a lifelong dream.

Directed by documentary veterans Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, Nyad benefits from a keen eye for natural beauty and harrowing athletic feats, blending intimate moments with expansive ocean vistas. The tagline, “Witness the incredible true story,” nails it—this is a film about endurance, memory, and confronting the past as much as it is about the swim itself. The screenplay by Julia Cox balances the grueling physical challenge with the complex personal history behind Nyad’s journey, including the shadows from her youth that resurface during her quest. Jodie Foster’s presence as Bonnie Stoll adds a grounded emotional anchor, making the stakes feel more immediate.

Heads-up for anyone sensitive to themes of sexual trauma: the film addresses a disturbing episode from Nyad’s adolescence involving hebephilia and sexual assault, which is mentioned and depicted with care but no sugarcoating. Also, the ever-present sharks in the swim add an undercurrent of suspense, though the focus remains on the human story rather than horror. If those triggers are on your list, approach with caution.

Nyad is a quietly powerful sports drama anchored by Annette Bening’s stirring portrayal of a 60-year-old woman chasing an almost mythic swimming feat, blending breathtaking ocean vistas with intimate emotional depth.

Be prepared for: sexual assault and hebephilia themes, shark encounters during open-water swimming, and the physical toll of extreme endurance.

review:
Arthur the King is a heartfelt adventure drama that leans heavily into the feel-good territory of man-and-dog bonding stories, with a dash of endurance racing thrown in for good measure. If you’ve ever enjoyed films like *Eight Below* or *Hachi: A Dog’s Tale*, this one will hit similar emotional beats, though with a bit more grit and physical challenge thanks to the 435-mile race backdrop. Mark Wahlberg leads as Michael, the pro racer who finds an unexpected teammate in Arthur, a scrappy street dog. The story is pretty straightforward but elevated by the genuine warmth of their unlikely friendship.

What really stands out is the way the film balances the harsh realities of extreme endurance racing with the tender development of loyalty and companionship. The tagline—“An unexpected encounter. An unlikely bond. An unforgettable adventure.”—captures the heart of the story perfectly. The ten-day race pushes both man and dog to their limits, creating moments of tension and triumph that feel earned. The supporting cast, including Simu Liu and Bear Grylls playing himself, add texture without stealing the spotlight. Visually, the rugged landscapes serve as a powerful backdrop to the emotional journey, and the pacing keeps the story moving without dragging.

Heads up: this movie does contain some heavy triggers. Those who pin the “a dog dies” and “a kid dies” triggers should be cautious, as well as viewers sensitive to jump scares and intense scenes involving fire (someone is burned alive). There’s also some unsettling moments with spiders, flashing lights, and finger/toe mutilation, so tread carefully if those set off alarms for you. Despite these, the film wraps up on a genuinely uplifting note, with plenty of tail-wagging and happy endings for dog lovers.
emailReview:
Arthur the King delivers a gritty yet heartfelt adventure that shines through Mark Wahlberg’s sincere performance and the raw beauty of its rugged, race-toughened landscapes.

review:
The Innocents is a moody, Nordic supernatural drama that mixes the wonder of childhood discovery with unsettling darkness. It’s like if Stranger Things dialed down the spectacle and leaned more into eerie atmosphere and psychological tension. The film’s quiet, deliberate pacing and focus on the kids’ shifting friendships make it feel more intimate and unsettling than your typical young superpower story — it’s really less about the powers themselves and more about the loss of innocence that comes with them.

What stands out here is how the summer holiday setting, with its forests and playgrounds, becomes this almost claustrophobic playground for the children’s secret world. Eskil Vogt’s direction leans on subtle performances from the young cast — especially Rakel Lenora Fløttum as Ida — to build a slow-burning dread that creeps under your skin. The powers aren’t flashy; they’re mysterious and ambiguous, which fits with the film’s themes of childhood curiosity turning into something darker and more dangerous. It’s a quiet thriller that uses silence and natural sounds to amplify tension rather than a traditional score.

Heads up for animal lovers: The Innocents involves several upsetting moments involving animals, including deaths and abuse, which are woven into the story’s darker turns. If you have triggers around animal harm, pets dying, or even just unsettling scenes with bugs and spiders, be prepared. These elements are significant enough to shadow the film’s otherwise dreamlike quality, so it’s worth going in eyes open.

review:
Thor kicks off the Marvel Cinematic Universe with a solid blend of epic fantasy and superhero swagger, though it’s less a laugh riot than some later MCU entries and more a grand, Shakespearean soap opera with lightning bolts. Kenneth Branagh’s direction leans into the Nordic mythos with a stately seriousness that sets Thor apart from your typical comic book flick. Chris Hemsworth’s thunder god is brash but charming, and Tom Hiddleston’s Loki steals the show as the sly, scheming brother. Fans of myth-inspired superhero tales or the early MCU vibe will find plenty to enjoy here, even if it doesn’t quite hit the comedic highs of the franchise’s later outings.

What stands out most is the film’s ambition to blend two worlds—the celestial and the mundane—through Thor’s exile to Earth. The tagline “Courage is immortal” feels on point as the story explores humility and heroism beyond brute strength. Natalie Portman and Kat Dennings add a grounded, human touch that contrasts nicely with the Asgardian grandeur. The visuals are impressive for 2011, especially the otherworldly realms and the climactic battle that pits gods against dark forces. This origin story sets up not just a hero but a whole universe, with themes of family conflict and redemption woven through a classic “fall and rise” arc.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal harm: this movie includes multiple instances of animal deaths, including a dog, a horse, a cat, and a dragon, plus some scenes with bugs, spiders, and snakes. If those triggers are on your radar, be ready for a few moments that might sting.
emailReview:
Thor strikes a grand, Shakespearean tone with Chris Hemsworth’s brash charm and Tom Hiddleston’s scene-stealing Loki, all wrapped in Nordic myth and epic superhero swagger.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, horse, cat, and dragon, plus unsettling scenes with bugs, spiders, and snakes.

tagline: The question of whether or not we are alone in the universe has been answered.
review:
Independence Day is the quintessential ’90s alien invasion blockbuster—big, loud, and unapologetically patriotic. Roland Emmerich’s signature brand of disaster spectacle meets sci-fi here in a film that feels like Armageddon crashing headfirst into The X-Files. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it’s elevated by a charismatic cast, including Will Smith’s cocky fighter pilot and Bill Pullman’s surprisingly stirring presidential rally speech. If you like your thrills with a side of cheesy one-liners and massive explosions, this is a wild ride that still holds up as a crowd-pleaser.

What stands out is the film’s sheer scale and timing—the tagline, “The question of whether or not we are alone in the universe has been answered,” sets the tone for a story that escalates quickly from awe to all-out panic. The script taps into classic themes of survival and unity against overwhelming odds, with Jeff Goldblum’s tech whiz adding a dash of quirky intelligence. The destruction scenes still pack a punch, and the story’s pulse quickens as a ragtag group bands together for a last-ditch counterattack. It’s a perfect storm of ’90s CGI, patriotic fervor, and that “save the world” optimism that defines the era.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to intense violence and emotional hits: the film includes a range of difficult content, from multiple character deaths—including children and family members—to scenes of people being burned alive and significant jump scares. Animal lovers should brace themselves too, as a dog dies during the chaos. There’s also flashing lights throughout, which might be unsettling if you’re prone to seizures or sensory overload. This is a big, brash disaster movie, so expect the emotional and visual punches to land hard.
emailReview:
Independence Day is a loud, proud ’90s sci-fi spectacle packed with charismatic performances and explosive set pieces that still deliver a thrilling ride full of cheesy one-liners and patriotic punch.

writers: Jim Cash, Jack Epps Jr., Ehud Yonay
name: Top Gun
overview: For Lieutenant Pete 'Maverick' Mitchell and his friend and co-pilot Nick 'Goose' Bradshaw, being accepted into an elite training school for fighter pilots is a dream come true. But heavy competition, as well as personal demons, will threaten Pete's dreams of becoming an ace pilot.
tagline: Up there with the best of the best.

writers: Bob Fisher, Steve Faber, Sean Anders, John Morris
name: We're the Millers
overview: A veteran pot dealer creates a fake family as part of his plan to move a huge shipment of weed into the U.S. from Mexico.
review:
We’re the Millers is a stoner comedy that leans hard into its raunchy, road-trip hijinks, feeling like a mashup of Pineapple Express and a dysfunctional family sitcom. It’s got the usual suspects of awkward drug deals and fake-family antics, but the real draw is the cast’s chemistry, especially Jennifer Aniston’s sharp-edged mom figure and Jason Sudeikis’s hapless pot dealer. It’s not reinventing the genre, but it’s a reliably funny, if predictable, ride that hits the right beats for fans of 2010s comedies with a bit of heart beneath the chaos.

The movie’s tagline, “If anyone asks,” perfectly captures its sneaky charm and the characters’ attempts at keeping their lies straight while navigating absurd situations. The premise of assembling a fake family to smuggle weed might sound tired, but the screenplay tosses in enough awkward moments and character quirks to keep it fresh. Plus, Will Poulter’s awkward Kenny and Emma Roberts’s rebellious Casey add some nice layers to the otherwise broad humor. The soundtrack and pacing keep things breezy, making it an easy watch when you’re in the mood to laugh at some ridiculous, over-the-top scenarios.

Heads up on the triggers: this one is surprisingly heavy on animal-related distress, including the death of a dog, a horse, a cat, and other animals, as well as animal abuse, which could be a dealbreaker for sensitive viewers. There are also bugs, spiders, and snakes creeping around, and some gross-out moments like vomiting that might get under your skin. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or creepy crawlies, maybe bring your own popcorn and a strong will.
emailReview:
We’re the Millers charms with its sharp comedic chemistry and breezy road-trip chaos, led by Jennifer Aniston’s snappy mom and Jason Sudeikis’s hapless dealer in a familiar but fun stoner romp.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and a horse, animal abuse, creepy crawlies like bugs and snakes, and some gross-out vomiting moments.

name: The Devil Wears Prada
overview: Andy moves to New York to work in the fashion industry. Her boss is extremely demanding, cruel and won't let her succeed if she doesn't fit into the high class elegant look of their magazine.
tagline: Meet Andy Sachs. A million girls would kill to have her job. She's not one of them.
review:
The Devil Wears Prada is a sharp, stylish dramedy that feels like Sex and the City meets a high-fashion nightmare. It’s a glossy, sometimes biting look at the cutthroat world of fashion publishing, anchored by Meryl Streep’s iconic turn as the icy, imperious Miranda Priestly. Anne Hathaway’s Andy Sachs is the perfect wide-eyed foil, navigating a brutal workplace where style and cruelty go hand in hand. It’s not just a tale about fashion — it’s about how ambition, identity, and self-respect clash in a hyper-competitive environment. While it’s often funny and clever, it also leans into some darker, more uncomfortable territory that separates it from your typical workplace comedy.

The film’s standout quality is that wickedly precise script, which balances sharp wit with moments of genuine vulnerability. The tagline—“Meet Andy Sachs. A million girls would kill to have her job. She’s not one of them.”—perfectly captures that tension between desire and revulsion that runs throughout. The world of The Devil Wears Prada is glamorous but unforgiving, with visuals and soundtrack that keep you hooked, even as you cringe at the price the characters pay. Emily Blunt as Emily and Stanley Tucci as Nigel add fantastic texture to the office dynamics, while the film subtly explores themes around body image, self-worth, and the sacrifices demanded by the pursuit of success.

Heads up for those sensitive to body shaming, eating disorders, and coercive sexual encounters—there are fat jokes and comments around body dysmorphia that might sting, along with an ambiguous scene of sexual pressure involving Andy. There’s also a car accident that leads to a hospital scene and implied injury, plus frequent loud honking and flashing camera lights throughout. If those are on your radar, the film’s glamorous façade might come with some rough edges.
emailReview:
A sharp, stylish dramedy with iconic performances and a wickedly precise script, The Devil Wears Prada delivers a high-fashion nightmare where ambition clashes with identity in a glossy but unforgiving world.

Be prepared for: body shaming, comments on body dysmorphia, coercive sexual pressure, a car accident with implied injury, and frequent loud honking and flashing camera lights.

writers: Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Scott Rosenberg, Jeff Pinkner, Chris Van Allsburg, Greg Taylor, Jonathan Hensleigh, Jim Strain
name: Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle
overview: Four teenagers in detention discover an old video game console with a game they’ve never heard of. When they decide to play, they are immediately sucked into the jungle world of Jumanji in the bodies of their avatars. They’ll have to complete the adventure of their lives filled with fun, thrills and danger or be stuck in the game forever!
review:
Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle is a lively reboot that takes the classic board game concept and flips it into a video game adventure, blending action, comedy, and a bit of heartfelt buddy dynamics. It rides the wave of ’90s nostalgia updates but carves its own path with Dwayne Johnson and Kevin Hart’s banter-heavy chemistry leading the charge. It’s not quite a game-changer, but it’s a pretty solid jungle romp that fans of lighthearted action comedies will appreciate—think of it as a fun, less intense cousin to the original Jumanji, with a modern twist and more self-aware humor.

What stands out here is the cast’s charisma, especially Johnson’s confident, musclebound avatar and Jack Black’s delightfully nerdy gamer persona. The film leans into the “fish out of water” trope as the teens navigate their new in-game bodies, which adds some clever meta-commentary on identity and self-image. The jungle setting delivers the expected array of traps, snakes, and other perils, keeping things brisk and visually engaging. The tagline, “The game has evolved,” feels apt; it’s a playful nod to how this iteration embraces video game logic and mechanics, giving the story a fresh playground to explore.

Heads up for animal lovers: this movie is heavy on animal-related triggers. There are multiple instances of animal deaths (including dogs, cats, horses, and even a dragon-like creature), scenes with snakes and bugs, and some portrayals of animal abuse and dog fighting. If any of those are on your list, proceed with caution. The jungle adventure isn’t just perilous for the humans.
emailReview: Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle is a lively reboot packed with ’90s nostalgia, sharp humor, and standout performances from Dwayne Johnson and Jack Black that keep the jungle adventure fresh and fun. Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and a dragon-like creature, scenes with snakes and bugs, and portrayals of animal abuse and dog fighting.

name: Passengers
overview: A spacecraft traveling to a distant colony planet and transporting thousands of people has a malfunction in its sleep chambers. As a result, two passengers are awakened 90 years early.
tagline: There is a reason they woke up.

writers: Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Paul Rudd, Andrew Barrer, Gabriel Ferrari, Stan Lee, Larry Lieber, Jack Kirby
name: Ant-Man and the Wasp
overview: Just when his time under house arrest is about to end, Scott Lang once again puts his freedom at risk to help Hope van Dyne and Dr. Hank Pym dive into the quantum realm and try to accomplish, against time and any chance of success, a very dangerous rescue mission.

name: American Pie
overview: At a high-school party, four friends find that losing their collective virginity isn't as easy as they had thought. But they still believe that they need to do so before college. To motivate themselves, they enter a pact to all "score." by their senior prom.
tagline: There's nothing like your first piece.
review:
American Pie is the quintessential late-90s teen sex comedy that still holds up as a guilty pleasure, blending raunchy humor with surprisingly sweet moments of awkward adolescence. It’s the kind of film that launched a thousand “losing your virginity” jokes and set the template for the genre—think Porky’s meets a high school dance floor. While it’s not exactly subtle or groundbreaking, the charm of Jason Biggs’ painfully earnest Jim Levenstein and the ensemble’s chemistry elevates the familiar premise beyond just another party movie.

What stands out here is the film’s willingness to lean into the gross-out humor without losing sight of the characters’ real anxieties about growing up and fitting in. The tagline, “There’s nothing like your first piece,” perfectly captures that mix of desperation and hope that drives the plot. The pact among the four friends to lose their virginity before prom frames the narrative with a competitive yet endearing tone. Alyson Hannigan’s Michelle, with her deadpan delivery and unexpected sweetness, is a highlight, turning what could have been a throwaway role into a fan favorite.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to sexual content or awkward, cringe-inducing comedy: this movie is packed with both, including some shower scenes and plenty of vulgar jokes. Also, be cautious if you’re triggered by animal death or child death, as those heavier notes unexpectedly show up amid the laughs. It’s a wild ride through teenage awkwardness that doesn’t shy away from uncomfortable moments, even if it’s mostly aiming for laughs.
emailReview:
American Pie nails the late-90s teen comedy vibe with its mix of raunchy humor and surprisingly heartfelt awkwardness, anchored by Jason Biggs’ unforgettable performance and Alyson Hannigan’s deadpan charm.

Be prepared for: awkward sexual situations, shower scenes, animal death, child death, and cringe-worthy vulgar jokes.

writers: Michael Fallon, Mark Verheiden, Mike Werb
name: The Mask
overview: When timid bank clerk Stanley Ipkiss discovers a magical mask containing the spirit of the Norse god Loki, his entire life changes. While wearing the mask, Ipkiss becomes a supernatural playboy exuding charm and confidence which allows him to catch the eye of local nightclub singer Tina Carlyle. Unfortunately, under the mask's influence, Ipkiss also robs a bank, which angers junior crime lord Dorian Tyrell, whose goons get blamed for the heist.
review:
The Mask is a wild ride of ‘90s slapstick comedy meets supernatural chaos, anchored by Jim Carrey’s manic energy as Stanley Ipkiss. It’s the kind of movie that feels like Looney Tunes got a live-action reboot with a dash of Norse mythology thrown in for good measure. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it’s elevated by Carrey’s elastic expressions and the film’s gleefully over-the-top tone. Fans of energetic comedies with a touch of fantasy will appreciate this one, even if the plot occasionally leans on familiar tropes.

What stands out is how the film balances its zany visual effects—especially the cartoonish antics unleashed by the magical mask—with a surprisingly smooth narrative about transformation and confidence. The tagline, "From zero to hero," nails the core theme perfectly as timid Stanley morphs into an unstoppable charmer (and occasional bank robber). The mix of Jim Carrey’s physical comedy and the colorful, almost surreal visuals keeps the pace brisk and entertaining, while the undercurrent of crime drama with the junior crime lord Dorian Tyrell adds a bit of edge beneath the laughs.

Heads up for those sensitive to sudden shocks and darker moments: The Mask has jump scares, flashing lights, and some scenes involving burning and gun violence that might catch you off guard. Also, the film includes the death of a child and a dog, which are definitely worth noting for anyone who prefers to steer clear of those triggers.
emailReview:
Jim Carrey’s elastic antics turn this ‘90s slapstick comedy into a cartoonish whirlwind of supernatural mayhem and wild visual gags.

Be prepared for: the death of a child, the death of a dog, jump scares, gun violence, and scenes involving burning.

name: Cloverfield
overview: Five young New Yorkers throw their friend a going-away party the night that a monster the size of a skyscraper descends upon the city. Told from the point of view of their video camera, the film is a document of their attempt to survive the most surreal, horrifying event of their lives.
review:
Cloverfield feels like the original found-footage monster movie that kicked off a wave of shaky-cam chaos in the late 2000s. It’s a lean, relentless survival horror that trades big-budget spectacle for an intimate, frantic look at a city under siege—think Godzilla meets Blair Witch, but with more urban grit and less polish. The handheld camerawork is divisive, but it’s part of what gives the film its raw, immersive edge, even if it can get a bit nausea-inducing. It’s not the most original creature feature out there, but it’s one of the more effective ones at making you feel trapped and terrified alongside its characters.

What really stands out is how Cloverfield turns a simple going-away party into a nightmare of epic scale. The tagline, “Some thing has found us,” nails the eerie, unknowable menace lurking just offscreen. The cast of five young New Yorkers—played by the likes of Lizzy Caplan and Michael Stahl-David—never quite get the depth you might want, but their frantic attempts to survive the skyscraper-sized intruder keep the tension high. Matt Reeves’ direction leans into the chaos and confusion of a city under attack, making the monster’s presence feel both overwhelming and unknowable. The film’s sound design and sporadic glimpses of the creature add to the dread, making “Cloverfield” more about the experience of disaster than the monster itself.

Heads up for animal triggers: several animals die throughout the chaos, including a dog, a horse, and a cat, and there’s a particularly haunting moment involving an abandoned horse wandering the streets. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or death, be heavily warned. There are also bugs, spiders, and snakes to contend with, as well as some gross-out moments like vomiting. The film’s intensity and the handheld style mean if you’re wary of body horror or sudden scares, keep that in mind before diving in.
emailReview:
