Cloverfield delivers a raw, immersive monster movie experience with its gritty handheld camerawork and tense, chaotic atmosphere that traps you in a city under siege.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and horse, creepy bugs and spiders, and moments of intense nausea and vomiting.

name: Easy A
overview: Olive, an average high school student, sees her below-the-radar existence turn around overnight once she decides to use the school's gossip grapevine to advance her social standing. Now her classmates are turning against her and the school board is becoming concerned, including her favorite teacher and the distracted guidance counselor. With the support of her hilariously idiosyncratic parents and a little help from a long-time crush, Olive attempts to take on her notorious new identity and crush the rumor mill once and for all.
tagline: Let's not and say we did.
review:
Easy A is such a fun movie. Self-awareness, unapologetic humor, and a highly intelligent approach to a much-debated topic, make Easy A quite memorable in the crowded Coming-Of-Age genre. 

All the actors in the film bring their A-Level comedic chops, with standout work from pre-Oscar-winning Emma Stone proving she could carry a full film on her back. The scenes get stolen any time Stanley Tucci and Patricia Clarkson are on screen. The multi-time Emmy winners are so wholesome and wonderful, bringing the best kind of wit and sarcasm to their parts. 

This film treads the PG-13 rating line very closely, avoiding physicality and objectification with its sexual content, settling instead for a lot of vivid and graphic discussions about teen sex and virginity. So, prior to a viewing of the film, read up on some of the listed warnings and timestamps, especially if you pinned any of the Sexual-themes triggers.
emailReview:
Easy A shines with sharp wit and standout performances, especially from Emma Stone and the delightfully sarcastic Stanley Tucci and Patricia Clarkson, making it a clever and memorable take on teenage life.

Be prepared for: explicit sexual discussions, teen virginity themes, graphic language, and mature humor.

name: Fast & Furious 6
overview: Hobbs has Dominic and Brian reassemble their crew to take down a team of mercenaries: Dominic unexpectedly gets convoluted also facing his presumed deceased girlfriend, Letty.

writers: Michael Bacall, Oren Uziel, Rodney Rothman, Jonah Hill, Patrick Hasburgh, Stephen J. Cannell
name: 22 Jump Street
overview: After making their way through high school (twice), big changes are in store for officers Schmidt and Jenko when they go deep undercover at a local college. But when Jenko meets a kindred spirit on the football team, and Schmidt infiltrates the bohemian art major scene, they begin to question their partnership. Now they don't have to just crack the case - they have to figure out if they can have a mature relationship. If these two overgrown adolescents can grow from freshmen into real men, college might be the best thing that ever happened to them.

writers: Henry Gayden, Darren Lemke, Bill Parker, C.C. Beck
name: Shazam!
overview: A boy is given the ability to become an adult superhero in times of need with a single magic word.

writers: Troy Kennedy Martin, Donna Powers, Wayne Powers
name: The Italian Job
overview: Charlie Croker pulled off the crime of a lifetime. The one thing that he didn't plan on was being double-crossed. Along with a drop-dead gorgeous safecracker, Croker and his team take off to re-steal the loot and end up in a pulse-pounding, pedal-to-the-metal chase that careens up, down, above and below the streets of Los Angeles.
tagline: Get in. Get out. Get even.

writers: Jamie Delano, Garth Ennis, Kevin Brodbin, Frank A. Cappello
name: Constantine
overview: John Constantine has literally been to Hell and back. When he teams up with a policewoman to solve the mysterious suicide of her twin sister, their investigation takes them through the world of demons and angels that exists beneath the landscape of contemporary Los Angeles.
tagline: Hell wants him. Heaven won't take him. Earth needs him.
review:
Constantine is a dark urban fantasy that rides the line between supernatural thriller and neo-noir, anchored by Keanu Reeves in his signature brooding mode. It’s got that gritty, hell-and-back vibe reminiscent of Blade Runner’s rainy cityscapes mixed with a dash of Hellboy’s demon-slaying antics. While it’s not quite as sharp as some of the top-tier comic book adaptations, it carves out its own niche with a moody atmosphere and a plot that weaves angels, demons, and moral ambiguity into a Los Angeles underworld. Fans of occult mysteries and antihero leads will find plenty to chew on here.

What stands out is the blend of mythic elements with a procedural twist—the investigation into a twin sister’s suicide pulls the supernatural into the mundane, giving the story a grounded core amid the chaos. Rachel Weisz’s dual role as Angela and Isabel adds emotional weight, and the supporting cast, including Djimon Hounsou and Shia LaBeouf, bring some solid flavor to the mix. The tagline, “Hell wants him. Heaven won’t take him. Earth needs him,” nails the tone perfectly—John Constantine is caught in a no-man’s-land that feels both epic and personal. Director Francis Lawrence crafts a visually compelling world, with shadowy corners and fiery hellscapes that keep the tension simmering throughout.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to animal-related distress—Constantine includes multiple triggers around animal death and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and other creatures. There are also creepy-crawlies aplenty, with spiders, snakes, and bugs making appearances that might unnerve the arachnophobes and entomophobes out there. If you’re on the lookout for those triggers, this one’s definitely worth a cautious approach.
emailReview:
Constantine blends neo-noir grit with supernatural thrills, anchored by Keanu Reeves’ brooding charm and a visually striking world full of shadowy corners and fiery hellscapes.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths and abuse including dogs and horses, creepy-crawlies like spiders and snakes, and tense scenes of supernatural violence.

name: Wedding Crashers
overview: John and his buddy, Jeremy are emotional criminals who know how to use a woman's hopes and dreams for their own carnal gain. Their modus operandi: crashing weddings. Normally, they meet guests who want to toast the romantic day with a random hook-up. But when John meets Claire, he discovers what true love – and heartache – feels like.

name: Jack Reacher
overview: When a gunman takes five lives with six shots, all evidence points to the suspect in custody. On interrogation, the suspect offers up a single note: "Get Jack Reacher!" So begins an extraordinary chase for the truth, pitting Jack Reacher against an unexpected enemy, with a skill for violence and a secret to keep.
tagline: The law has limits. He does not.

name: Super 8
overview: In 1979 Ohio, several youngsters are making a zombie movie with a Super-8 camera. In the midst of filming, the friends witness a horrifying train derailment and are lucky to escape with their lives. They soon discover that the catastrophe was no accident, as a series of unexplained events and disappearances soon follows. Deputy Jackson Lamb, the father of one of the kids, searches for the terrifying truth behind the crash.

writers: Greg Glienna, Mary Ruth Clarke, Jim Herzfeld, John Hamburg
name: Meet the Parents
overview: Greg Focker is ready to marry his girlfriend, Pam, but before he pops the question, he must win over her formidable father, humorless former CIA agent Jack Byrnes, at the wedding of Pam's sister. As Greg bends over backward to make a good impression, his visit to the Byrnes home turns into a hilarious series of disasters, and everything that can go wrong does, all under Jack's critical, hawklike gaze.
tagline: First comes love. Then comes the interrogation.

name: Burn After Reading
overview: When a disc containing memoirs of a former CIA analyst falls into the hands of gym employees, Linda and Chad, they see a chance to make enough money for Linda to have life-changing cosmetic surgery. Predictably, events whirl out of control for the duo, and those in their orbit.

name: The Holiday
overview: Two women, one American and one British, swap homes at Christmastime following bad breakups. Each woman finds romance with a local man but realizes that the imminent return home may end the relationship.
tagline: It's Christmas Eve and we are going to go celebrate being young and being alive.
review:
The Holiday is a quintessential Nancy Meyers Christmas rom-com that leans hard into cozy, feel-good vibes with a dash of bittersweet reality. It’s the kind of movie that feels like Love Actually meets Sleepless in Seattle—familiar, warm, and sprinkled with those slightly quirky, heartfelt British-American cultural contrasts. Cameron Diaz and Kate Winslet anchor the film with charm, while Jude Law and Jack Black add that touch of swoon-worthy and comedic relief respectively. It’s not reinventing the genre, but it’s a pretty solid entry for anyone who loves their holiday cheer served with a side of romantic uncertainty.

What stands out most here is the film’s cozy atmosphere and the way it leans into the idea of second chances—not just in love, but in life. The tagline, “It’s Christmas Eve and we are going to go celebrate being young and being alive,” nails the bittersweet tone that runs through the story: new beginnings shadowed by the ticking clock of returning to reality. Meyers’ writing is warm and accessible, with a soundtrack and visuals that perfectly capture that magical Christmas glow. The house swap setup is a neat trick that allows for fresh perspectives, and the supporting cast, including Eli Wallach and Edward Burns, add layers of warmth and humor.

Heads up for animal lovers and those sensitive to animal-related content—this one carries quite a few heavy triggers involving the death of multiple animals, including pets, and some instances of animal abuse. If you’ve got those on your list, this might be a tougher watch than you’d expect from a holiday romance. There’s also some mild gross-out moments like vomiting and a few creepy-crawlies that might irk bug and spider watchers. Overall, if you can handle those, it’s a festive, if occasionally bittersweet, escape.
emailReview:
The Holiday wraps you in cozy Christmas charm with standout performances from Cameron Diaz and Kate Winslet, delivering a warm, bittersweet rom-com that feels like a festive hug with a side of romantic uncertainty.

Be prepared for: multiple pet deaths, animal abuse, vomiting, and unsettling creepy-crawlies.

name: The Witch
overview: In 1630s New England, William and Katherine lead a devout Christian life with five children, homesteading on the edge of an impassable wilderness, exiled from their settlement when William defies the local church. When their newborn son vanishes and crops mysteriously fail, the family turns on one another.

writers: Warren Ellis, Cully Hamner, Jon Hoeber, Erich Hoeber
name: RED
overview: When his peaceful life is threatened by a high-tech assassin, former black-ops agent, Frank Moses reassembles his old team in a last ditch effort to survive and uncover his assailants.
tagline: Still armed. Still dangerous. Still got it.
review:
RED is that rare breed of action-comedy where a cast full of seasoned pros actually makes the whole thing feel like a blast rather than a tired riff on spy tropes. Think Die Hard meets The Expendables, but with a sharper sense of humor and a surprisingly warm heart. Bruce Willis leads a stellar ensemble including John Malkovich and Helen Mirren, all of whom bring a cheeky charm to their retired black-ops personas. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but it’s a well-oiled, pretty enjoyable thrill ride.

The film’s tagline, “Still armed. Still dangerous. Still got it.” nails the tone perfectly—this is a movie comfortably leaning into its premise of older spies pulling off high-stakes action with a wink. The writing balances slick one-liners with moments that let the characters’ histories and quirks shine through, making it more than just an excuse for explosions. Robert Schwentke’s direction keeps things brisk, and the chemistry among the players elevates what might otherwise be a generic shoot-’em-up into something that’s actually fun to watch.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to animal-related content—this one features a surprising number of animal deaths and some scenes of animal abuse, including dogs, cats, and horses. Those who pin the animal harm trigger should definitely be cautious here, as it’s woven into the story enough to be unsettling rather than incidental. If you prefer your action without furry casualties, this might sting a bit.
emailReview:
RED delivers a surprisingly warm and witty action-comedy experience, with Bruce Willis, John Malkovich, and Helen Mirren bringing charm and cheek to their retired spy roles.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, scenes of animal abuse, and a steady undercurrent of furry casualties woven into the action.

name: Death Proof
overview: Austin's hottest DJ, Jungle Julia, sets out into the night to unwind with her two friends Shanna and Arlene. Covertly tracking their moves is Stuntman Mike, a scarred rebel leering from behind the wheel of his muscle car, revving just feet away.
review:
Death Proof is Quentin Tarantino’s adrenaline-fueled homage to grindhouse cinema—a slick, pulpy thriller that’s equal parts creepy stalker tale and explosive revenge fantasy. It rides shotgun with cult classics like Duel and Death Race 2000, but with Tarantino’s signature snappy dialogue and cool, retro style. While it’s not as dialogue-heavy or sprawling as some of his other work, it’s a wild ride elevated by Kurt Russell’s menacing turn as Stuntman Mike and a standout cast of badass women who flip the script on the typical victim role.

The film’s tagline, "A crash course in revenge," perfectly encapsulates its two distinct halves: first, a slow-burn stalking sequence that builds tension with eerie precision, then a turbo-charged finale where the tables turn in brutal, satisfying fashion. The soundtrack pulses with vintage rock that propels the night scenes, while the visuals lean into that grindhouse grain and gritty 1970s vibe. Tarantino even plays with the audience directly—Stuntman Mike’s chilling fourth-wall breaks add an unsettling, almost predatory edge that lingers beyond the scenes. Plus, Zoë Bell’s real-life stunt skills bring authenticity and visceral thrills to the action.

If you’re sensitive to stalking, car crashes, or animal harm, be heavily warned. The movie features several intense vehicle collisions as well as the unsettling deaths of animals including a dog, cat, and horse. Shaky cam and some graphic physical damage also add to the rough-and-tumble feel of the film’s more violent moments. This isn’t a quiet thriller—it’s a full-throttle, grindhouse-style blood rush that’s as stylish as it is savage.
emailReview:
Death Proof is a gritty, retro-fueled thrill ride that blends creepy stalker vibes with explosive revenge, anchored by Kurt Russell’s menacing charm and a cast of fierce women who rewrite the rules.

Be prepared for: intense car crashes, the unsettling deaths of a dog, cat, and horse, stalking, and gritty, graphic violence.

name: Rush Hour
overview: When Hong Kong Inspector Lee is summoned to Los Angeles to investigate a kidnapping, the FBI doesn't want any outside help and assigns cocky LAPD Detective James Carter to distract Lee from the case. Not content to watch the action from the sidelines, Lee and Carter form an unlikely partnership and investigate the case themselves.
tagline: The fastest hands in the East meet the biggest mouth in the West.

name: The Platform
overview: A mysterious place, an indescribable prison, a deep hole. An unknown number of levels. Two inmates living on each level. A descending platform containing food for all of them. An inhuman fight for survival, but also an opportunity for solidarity…
tagline: There are 3 kinds of people; the ones above, the ones below, and the ones who fall.

writers: Peter Baynham, Robert Smigel, Todd Durham, Dan Hageman, Kevin Hageman
name: Hotel Transylvania
overview: Welcome to Hotel Transylvania, Dracula's lavish five-stake resort, where monsters and their families can live it up and no humans are allowed. One special weekend, Dracula has invited all his best friends to celebrate his beloved daughter Mavis's 118th birthday. For Dracula catering to all of these legendary monsters is no problem but the party really starts when one ordinary guy stumbles into the hotel and changes everything!
tagline: Where monsters go to get away from it all.

writers: Kevin Grevioux, Len Wiseman, Danny McBride
name: Underworld
overview: Vampires and werewolves have waged a nocturnal war against each other for centuries. But all bets are off when a female vampire warrior named Selene, who's famous for her strength and werewolf-hunting prowess, becomes smitten with a peace-loving male werewolf, Michael, who wants to end the war.
review:
Underworld is the 2003 vampire-versus-werewolf flick that jumpstarted a whole wave of moody, action-heavy supernatural franchises in the early 2000s. Starring Kate Beckinsale as Selene, a fierce vampire warrior, it’s a glossy, gothic romp that feels like Blade meets Twilight but with more leather and brooding stares. It’s not exactly high art, but it’s a wild ride elevated by Beckinsale’s steely presence and Len Wiseman’s stylish direction. If you’re here for sexy immortal grudges and a dash of star-crossed romance, it delivers—and then some.

What really stands out is the world-building: centuries-old feuds, secret histories, and the classic “love across enemy lines” trope. Selene’s conflict with the werewolves, especially the peace-seeking Michael, adds a surprisingly heartfelt layer to what could easily have been a straightforward monster mash. The tagline “An immortal battle for supremacy” nails the tone—this is a relentless, dark struggle with plenty of slick fight scenes and brooding atmosphere. Plus, the supporting cast, including Bill Nighy as the vampire elder Viktor and Michael Sheen as the werewolf leader Lucian, bring a gravitas that keeps the supernatural politics engaging.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: there are multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dog and horse deaths, as well as some uncomfortable scenes involving insects and spiders. Sexual violence is also present, so if that trigger’s on your radar, proceed with caution. Underworld isn’t shy about its darker, grittier moments, which are integral to its grim, gothic vibe.
emailReview:
Underworld is a slick, gothic vampire-versus-werewolf thriller that pairs Kate Beckinsale’s fierce performance with stylish direction and brooding supernatural politics.

Be prepared for: dog and horse deaths, insect and spider abuse, and sexual violence.

name: Hellboy II: the Golden Army
overview: An evil elf breaks an ancient pact between humans and creatures, and is on a mission to release 'The Golden Army', a deadly group of fighting machines that can destroy the human race. As Hell on Earth is ready to erupt, Hellboy and his crew set out to defeat prince and his army.
tagline: Believe it or not... He's the good guy.

name: Happy Gilmore
overview: Failed hockey player-turned-golf whiz Happy Gilmore -- whose unconventional approach and antics on the grass courts the ire of rival Shooter McGavin -- is determined to win a PGA tournament so he can save his granny's house with the prize money. Meanwhile, an attractive tour publicist tries to soften Happy's image.
tagline: He doesn't play golf... he destroys it.
review:
Happy Gilmore is classic Adam Sandler at his irreverent best—a sports comedy that feels like a mashup of Rocky and a frat party, with golf clubs instead of boxing gloves. The film leans hard into goofy, over-the-top humor, with Sandler’s brash, underdog hockey player-turned-golf-phenom shaking up the stuffy world of PGA tournaments. It’s not highbrow, but it’s a wild ride packed with memorable one-liners and absurd antics that have aged surprisingly well for a ’90s comedy. Fans of Sandler’s early work or anyone who likes their sports movies with a heavy dose of slapstick will find plenty to enjoy here.

What really stands out is the way Happy’s unorthodox style flips golf’s usual prim-and-proper image on its head. The tagline, “He doesn’t play golf… he destroys it,” nails the tone perfectly. Christopher McDonald’s Shooter McGavin is a perfect foil, oozing smugness that makes every showdown satisfying. Julie Bowen’s publicist character adds a nice balance, trying to polish Happy’s rough edges without dulling the comedy. The film’s heart is in its earnest, if absurd, effort to save Grandma’s house, which gives the chaos a surprisingly sweet emotional core.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: there’s a dog death that’s pivotal to the plot’s emotional weight. Also, be prepared for some jump scares and scenes involving spiders—not the usual suspects in a comedy, but they’re there. If any of that is on your list, approach with caution.
emailReview:
Happy Gilmore is a riotous blend of sports and slapstick comedy where Adam Sandler’s wild energy turns golf into a hilarious battleground of absurd antics and memorable one-liners.

Be prepared for: a dog death with emotional weight, jump scares, and unexpected spider scenes.

name: The Northman
overview: Prince Amleth is on the verge of becoming a man when his father is brutally murdered by his uncle, who kidnaps the boy's mother. Two decades later, Amleth is now a Viking who's on a mission to save his mother, kill his uncle and avenge his father.

name: The Adjustment Bureau
overview: A man glimpses the future Fate has planned for him – and chooses to fight for his own destiny. Battling the powerful Adjustment Bureau across, under and through the streets of New York, he risks his destined greatness to be with the only woman he's ever loved.

directors: Aaron Horvath, Michael Jelenic, Pierre Leduc, Fabien Polack
name: The Super Mario Bros. Movie
overview: While working underground to fix a water main, Brooklyn plumbers—and brothers—Mario and Luigi are transported down a mysterious pipe and wander into a magical new world. But when the brothers are separated, Mario embarks on an epic quest to find Luigi.
tagline: Not all heroes wear capes. Some wear overalls.

name: Chronicle
overview: Three high school students make an incredible discovery, leading to their developing uncanny powers beyond their understanding. As they learn to control their abilities and use them to their advantage, their lives start to spin out of control, and their darker sides begin to take over.

name: Orphan
overview: After losing their baby, a married couple adopt 9-year old Esther, who may not be as innocent as she seems.

name: Spy
overview: A desk-bound CIA analyst volunteers to go undercover to infiltrate the world of a deadly arms dealer, and prevent diabolical global disaster.
tagline: She's a risk they had to take.

primaryTitle: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
Title_IMDb_Link: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
name: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
cleanNameArticles: austin powers international man of mystery
overview:
As a swingin' fashion photographer by day and a groovy British superagent by night, Austin Powers is the '60s' most shagadelic spy, baby! 

But can he stop megalomaniac Dr. Evil after the bald villain freezes himself and unthaws in the '90s? With the help of sexy sidekick Vanessa Kensington, he just might.
review:
Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery is a cheeky, irreverent romp that firmly stakes its claim in the spy spoof hall of fame. Mike Myers doubles down on his knack for broad, self-aware comedy, playing both the flamboyant ’60s superagent and his nefarious nemesis Dr. Evil with equal parts charm and absurdity. It’s the kind of movie that feels like a swinging ’60s James Bond pastiche meets Saturday Night Live silliness—a wild ride that’s not always subtle but rarely boring. Fans of tongue-in-cheek parodies and Myers’ brand of goofy humor will find this a pretty delightful blast from the past.

What stands out here is the film’s commitment to its campy, retro vibe, highlighted by Elizabeth Hurley’s no-nonsense Vanessa Kensington as a perfect foil to Austin’s outlandish antics. The tagline—“Debonair. Defiant. Defrosted.”—sums it up nicely: it’s all about a fish-out-of-water spy trying to navigate the ’90s with ’60s flair. The writing leans heavily on pop culture callbacks and exaggerated stereotypes, but that’s part of the charm. The soundtrack and visuals lean into the psychedelic, making it feel like a colorful fever dream of spy clichés and groovy dance moves.

Heads up for animal lovers: there’s a fair amount of animal deaths and distress, including dogs, cats, and horses, which might catch some off guard. If the idea of animals in peril hits close to home, be cautious here. Otherwise, prepare for a spy flick that’s more silly than sinister—but with a few darker moments hiding beneath all the velvet and paisley.
emailReview:
Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery is a colorful, campy spy spoof that blends groovy ’60s vibes with Mike Myers’ signature goofy charm and sharp parody.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, some scenes of animal distress, and a quirky mix of silly violence and darker moments beneath the retro fun.

writers: Simon Pegg, Doug Jung, Gene Roddenberry, Roberto Orci, Patrick McKay, John D. Payne
name: Star Trek Beyond
overview: The USS Enterprise crew explores the furthest reaches of uncharted space, where they encounter a mysterious new enemy who puts them and everything the Federation stands for to the test.

writers: Jim Wheat, Ken Wheat, David Twohy
name: Pitch Black
overview: When their ship crash-lands on a remote planet, the marooned passengers soon learn that escaped convict Riddick isn't the only thing they have to fear. Deadly creatures lurk in the shadows, waiting to attack in the dark, and the planet is rapidly plunging into the utter blackness of a total eclipse. With the body count rising, the doomed survivors are forced to turn to Riddick with his eerie eyes to guide them through the darkness to safety. With time running out, there's only one rule: Stay in the light.
tagline: Don't be afraid of the dark. Be afraid of what's in the dark.
review:
Pitch Black is a lean, lean sci-fi thriller that feels like Alien meets The Descent, but with Vin Diesel’s Riddick casting a long shadow over the usual “stranded on a hostile planet” trope. It’s a tight, gritty survival story elevated by Diesel’s brooding antihero and the relentless menace of creatures that thrive in utter darkness. While it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, it’s a wild ride for fans of claustrophobic, creature-feature horror with a space twist — and it kicks off a franchise that leans into Riddick’s mysterious, badass vibe.

What stands out here is how the film uses light and darkness as almost a character unto itself—“Don’t be afraid of the dark. Be afraid of what’s in the dark” isn’t just a tagline, it’s the core mechanic of the tension. The total eclipse ramping up the stakes is a clever touch, forcing characters to scramble for safety as shadows close in. The mix of jump scares and creepy critters (yes, including spiders and other bugs) keeps you on edge, while the writing doesn’t shy away from the grim realities of survival. Riddick’s glowing eyes and moral ambiguity add a nice twist to the typical space castaway story, especially when the other passengers are too busy turning on each other to notice the real threat.

Heads up: this one is heavy on animal deaths (dogs, cats, horses), and there’s some pretty intense jump-scary moments along with creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes. If you’re sensitive to loss of pets or unexpected creature horrors, be warned—Pitch Black doesn’t pull punches when it comes to the darker side of its survival scenario.
emailReview:
Pitch Black is a gritty sci-fi thriller that thrives on darkness as a living, breathing threat, with Vin Diesel’s brooding Riddick stealing the show amid claustrophobic terror and creepy crawlies.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, jump scares, spiders, snakes, and intense moments of survival horror.

writers: Art Monterastelli, Sylvester Stallone, David Morrell
name: Rambo
overview: When governments fail to act on behalf of captive missionaries, ex-Green Beret John James Rambo sets aside his peaceful existence along the Salween River in a war-torn region of Thailand to take action.  Although he's still haunted by violent memories of his time as a U.S. soldier during the Vietnam War, Rambo can hardly turn his back on the aid workers who so desperately need his help.
tagline: Live for nothing, or die for something.
review:
Rambo (2008) is a grim, no-frills action thriller that leans hard into its reputation as a violent, unflinching war movie. Sylvester Stallone returns as the iconic John Rambo, this time trading the jungles of Vietnam for the brutal conflicts in Thailand’s borderlands. If you’re coming in expecting the slick, almost campy action of the '80s originals, prepare for something much darker and more visceral—think Rambo meets a gritty humanitarian crisis documentary. It’s not subtle, but it’s effective in showing a man who can’t escape the ghosts of his violent past while trying to do some good.

What stands out here is Stallone’s dual role as director and star, which brings a personal intensity to the film’s tone. The tagline, “Live for nothing, or die for something,” perfectly captures the film’s bleak worldview and Rambo’s tortured moral code. The movie doesn’t shy away from the horror of war, especially the plight of captive missionaries, and it’s that grim authenticity that elevates it above your average action flick. The supporting cast, including Julie Benz as Sarah, fill out the story, but it’s really Stallone’s brooding presence and the harsh, unforgiving setting that leave the strongest impression.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal harm: the film notably includes a dog death, so those who pin that trigger should be cautious. It’s one of the more emotionally jarring moments in an otherwise relentless and brutal story.
emailReview:
Rambo (2008) strips away the camp for a grim, unflinching war thriller that feels more like a gritty humanitarian crisis than an action flick, with Stallone’s brooding intensity driving every brutal moment.

Be prepared for: a dog death, graphic violence against captives, intense war brutality, and a relentless atmosphere of moral despair.

writers: Court Crandall, Todd Phillips, Scot Armstrong
name: Old School
overview: Three friends attempt to recapture their glory days by opening up a fraternity near their alma mater.
tagline: All the fun of college. None of the education.
review:
Old School is a raunchy early-2000s comedy that tries to bottle the chaotic spirit of college days through the misadventures of three grown men opening a new fraternity near their alma mater. Directed by Todd Phillips and anchored by Luke Wilson, Will Ferrell, and Vince Vaughn, it’s a wild ride that feels like Animal House meets The Hangover—though it leans harder into slapstick and gross-out humor than sharp wit. Not as clever as some of its peers but definitely a goofy, spirited romp fueled by Ferrell’s over-the-top antics.

What makes Old School stand out is how it captures the absurd lengths grown-ups will go to in order to relive their youth, with a tagline that nails the tone: “All the fun of college. None of the education.” The chemistry among the leads sells the ridiculous premise, and the film’s writing often dips into outrageous set pieces—think wild parties and cringe-worthy scenarios—that push genre conventions without trying to reinvent the wheel. It’s less about clever commentary and more about delivering a steady stream of lowbrow laughs and memorable character moments.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to certain content: this one includes a handful of heavy triggers like a dog dying, a kid dying, and even someone being burned alive, which feels jarring amid the comedy. There are also jump scares, flashing lights, and some pretty graphic stuff sprinkled throughout. So if any of those hit your list hard, maybe brace yourself before diving into this frat-house chaos.
emailReview:
Old School is a raunchy, slapstick college comedy fueled by Will Ferrell’s wild antics and a goofy, spirited vibe that channels Animal House with a nudge toward gross-out humor.

Be prepared for: a dog dying, a kid dying, someone burned alive, jump scares, and flashing lights.

name: Saltburn
overview: Struggling to find his place at Oxford University, student Oliver Quick finds himself drawn into the world of the charming and aristocratic Felix Catton, who invites him to Saltburn, his eccentric family's sprawling estate, for a summer never to be forgotten.
tagline: We're all about to lose our minds.
review:
Saltburn is a darkly intoxicating blend of psychological thriller and twisted social satire, helmed by Emerald Fennell, who clearly has a flair for turning privilege and obsession into something deliciously unsettling. Think Oxford-set aristocratic decadence meets the slow-burn menace of something like *Rebecca* or *The Talented Mr. Ripley*. Barry Keoghan’s Oliver is the perfect outsider, drawn into the web of Jacob Elordi’s charismatic but enigmatic Felix, and the claustrophobic atmosphere of the Catton family estate only deepens the sense that things are about to spiral spectacularly out of control.

What really sticks is how the film plays with its tagline—*“We’re all about to lose our minds.”* The creeping tension is amplified by a lush score and eerie visuals that make the sprawling estate feel like a character itself. Fennell’s writing leans into themes of class, identity, and the intoxicating dangers of playing with fire in elite circles. The Catton family’s eccentricities and dark secrets provide plenty of memorable beats, while the slow reveal keeps you guessing about just who’s really in control—and who’s being manipulated.

Heads up for animal lovers: Saltburn doesn’t shy away from some pretty heavy animal-related content. There are multiple animal deaths, including a dog, a cat, and a horse, plus scenes involving animal abuse and dog fighting. Also, bugs, spiders, and snakes make unsettling appearances, adding to the overall creepy vibe. If those triggers hit close to home, be prepared for a rough ride.
emailReview:
Saltburn is a darkly intoxicating psychological thriller wrapped in twisted social satire, with Barry Keoghan and Jacob Elordi delivering magnetic performances against the eerie backdrop of an aristocratic estate that feels alive with menace.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, cat, and horse, scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, plus unsettling appearances by bugs, spiders, and snakes.

name: Civil War
overview: In the near future, a group of war journalists attempt to survive while reporting the truth as the United States stands on the brink of civil war.
review:
Civil War is a grim, near-future dystopian thriller that feels like Alex Garland’s take on frontline journalism meets a political powder keg. The film’s tense atmosphere and apocalyptic undertone set it apart from your usual war dramas, leaning heavily into the chaos of a nation on the brink. It’s not your feel-good flick; rather, it’s a raw, unsettling look at truth and survival, anchored by a strong ensemble including Kirsten Dunst and Wagner Moura. Fans of gritty, realistic conflict stories like *The Report* or *Beasts of No Nation* will find something here, though it’s darker and more harrowing than most.

What stands out is Garland’s signature sharp writing and claustrophobic direction, which really put you in the middle of the frontline with these war journalists. The tagline, “Welcome to the frontline,” isn’t just a slogan—it’s an invitation to witness the brutal reality of a country unraveling from the inside. The film doesn’t shy away from the horrors that come with reporting in a civil war, laying bare the physical and psychological toll. The cast delivers solid performances, especially Dunst as Lee, whose perspective feels both vulnerable and steely amid the chaos. The visuals and sound design amplify the tension, with moments that linger long after the credits roll.

That said, be heavily warned if animal harm or death triggers you—there’s a distressing amount of it here, including dogs, cats, and horses. Sexual assault and intense violence like burning alive also feature prominently, alongside other tough content like body horror and abuse. This isn’t a film for the faint of heart, especially if you’re sensitive to graphic depictions of suffering, both human and animal. Those who pin these triggers should approach with caution.
emailReview:
Civil War plunges you into a grim, claustrophobic frontline experience, where Kirsten Dunst’s steely performance cuts through the chaos of a nation unraveling in brutal, unflinching detail.

Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, sexual assault, burning alive, intense violence, and body horror.

name: Body of Lies
overview: The CIA’s hunt is on for the mastermind of a wave of terrorist attacks. Roger Ferris is the agency’s man on the ground, moving from place to place, scrambling to stay ahead of ever-shifting events. An eye in the sky – a satellite link – watches Ferris.  At the other end of that real-time link is the CIA’s Ed Hoffman, strategizing events from thousands of miles away. And as Ferris nears the target, he discovers trust can be just as dangerous as it is necessary for survival.

writers: Gil Kenan, Jason Reitman, Ivan Reitman, Dan Aykroyd, Harold Ramis
name: Ghostbusters: Afterlife
overview: When single mom Callie and her two kids Trevor and Phoebe arrive in a small Oklahoma town, they begin to discover their connection to the original Ghostbusters and the secret legacy their grandfather left behind.
tagline: Discover the past. Save the future.

name: Barbarian
overview: In town for a job interview, a young woman arrives at her Airbnb late at night only to find that it has been mistakenly double-booked and a strange man is already staying there. Against her better judgement, she decides to stay the night anyway, but soon discovers that there is much more to be afraid of in the house than the other house guest.
tagline: Some stay for a night. Some stay for a week. Some never leave.
review:
Barbarian is a lean, unsettling horror-thriller that leans hard into atmosphere and creeping dread. It feels like a mash-up of classic creepy-house horror and a twisty indie thriller, with a touch of the uncanny that sets it apart from your usual haunted Airbnb story. If you like your scares with a side of mystery and some sharp performances, especially from Georgina Campbell and Bill Skarsgård, this one hits the mark. It’s not a comedy or a gore-fest, but it keeps you on edge in a way that horror fans who appreciate slow-building tension will respect.

What really sticks with you here is how the film plays with expectations—starting with a simple double-booked Airbnb premise but quickly turning into something far more sinister. The tagline, "Some stay for a night. Some stay for a week. Some never leave," nails that creeping sense of doom perfectly. The writing and direction by Zach Cregger manage to keep the tension tight without over-explaining, and the house itself almost becomes a character, its secrets unfolding in unexpected ways. The cast does solid work grounding the eerie setup in believable interactions before the horror kicks in.

Those sensitive to animal harm should be cautious, as both a dog and a horse die on screen. Also, there are some flashing lights early on that might bother viewers prone to seizures or migraines. If those are on your list, definitely approach with care.
emailReview:
Barbarian is a quietly unsettling horror-thriller that builds tension with sharp performances and an uncanny atmosphere that turns a familiar haunted Airbnb tale inside out.

Be prepared for: on-screen deaths of a dog and a horse, intense creeping dread, and flashing lights that might affect sensitive viewers.

name: Planet Terror
overview: Two doctors find their graveyard shift inundated with townspeople ravaged by sores. Among the wounded is Cherry Darling, a dancer whose leg was ripped from her body. As the invalids quickly become enraged aggressors, Cherry and her ex-boyfriend El Wray lead a team of accidental warriors into the night.
tagline: Humanity's last hope… rests on a high power machine gun!

writers: Richard LaGravenese, Steven Rogers, Cecelia Ahern
name: P.S. I Love You
overview: A young widow discovers that her late husband has left her 10 messages intended to help ease her pain and start a new life.
tagline: His life ended. Now, a new one will begin.

name: I Love You, Man
overview: Peter Klaven is a successful real estate agent who, upon getting engaged to the woman of his dreams, Zooey, discovers, to his dismay and chagrin, that he has no male friend close enough to serve as his Best Man. Peter immediately sets out to rectify the situation, embarking on a series of bizarre and awkward "man-dates."
tagline: Are you man enough to say it?

writers: John le Carré, Bridget O'Connor, Peter Straughan
name: Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy
overview: In the bleak days of the Cold War, espionage veteran George Smiley is forced from semi-retirement to uncover a Soviet mole within his former colleagues at the heart of MI6.
tagline: How do you find an enemy who is hidden right before your eyes?

name: Jarhead
overview: Jarhead is a film about a US Marine Anthony Swofford’s experience in the Gulf War. After putting up with an arduous boot camp, Swofford and his unit are sent to the Persian Gulf where they are eager to fight, but are forced to stay back from the action. Swofford struggles with the possibility of his girlfriend cheating on him, and as his mental state deteriorates, his desire to kill increases.
review:
Jarhead is a gritty, introspective war drama that trades the usual battlefield carnage for a simmering, psychological stew—think Full Metal Jacket meets The Hurt Locker, but with a sharper focus on boredom and mental unraveling rather than action. Directed by Sam Mendes and anchored by Jake Gyllenhaal’s quietly intense performance as Marine Anthony Swofford, it’s a film about the frustration of waiting to fight and the corrosive effects that anticipation can have on a soldier’s mind. It’s not your typical war movie, and fans of the genre who expect nonstop combat might find it frustratingly subdued, but that’s kind of the point.

What stands out in Jarhead is how it captures the monotony and claustrophobia of deployment, peeling back the glamorized mythology of war to reveal the psychological cost beneath. The tagline "Welcome to the suck" perfectly sums up the tone—this is about enduring the grind, not glory. The film explores Swofford’s internal struggles, including paranoia about his girlfriend’s fidelity and a growing, unsettling desire for violence, which builds tension in a way that’s less about explosions and more about mental decay. The supporting cast, including Jamie Foxx and Peter Sarsgaard, adds depth to the unit’s dynamic, while William Broyles Jr.’s script and Mendes’ direction keep the mood taut and simmering.

Heads up for those sensitive to bestiality and animal death triggers—Jarhead includes both, which might catch some viewers off guard given the military backdrop. If those are on your list, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Jarhead is a tense, introspective war drama that swaps battlefield chaos for a slow-burning look at boredom and mental strain, anchored by Jake Gyllenhaal’s quietly powerful performance and Sam Mendes’ sharp direction.

Be prepared for: animal death, bestiality, intense psychological unraveling, and simmering paranoia.

name: Stargate
overview: An interstellar teleportation device, found in Egypt, leads to a planet with humans resembling ancient Egyptians who worship the god Ra.
tagline: It will take you a million light years from home. But will it bring you back?
review:
Stargate is a ’90s sci-fi adventure that feels like Indiana Jones meets Star Trek—Roland Emmerich’s signature blend of action and spectacle with a dash of ancient mythology. It’s not exactly subtle, but it’s a lot of fun if you’re in the mood for a throwback cosmic romp with some earnest world-building. James Spader and Kurt Russell make a solid team, with Spader’s nerdy archaeologist and Russell’s no-nonsense military man playing off each other nicely. While it’s not as polished as later sci-fi epics, Stargate stands out for its clever premise and early-’90s charm.

The film’s standout is definitely its concept: an interstellar portal discovered in Egypt that leads to a planet with humans modeled after ancient Egyptians worshipping Ra as a god. The mix of mythology and sci-fi gives the story a unique flavor, and the visuals—especially the design of the Stargate itself—hold up as iconic. The tagline, “It will take you a million light years from home. But will it bring you back?” nails that sense of wonder and danger. The pacing is brisk, with enough twists and desert-set action to keep things moving, even if some elements feel a bit dated now.

Heads up for animal lovers: Stargate’s content warnings include multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and more. There’s also mention of spiders, snakes, bugs, and a few unsettling moments involving animals, so those sensitive to animal harm or creepy crawlies should proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Stargate is a spirited ’90s sci-fi adventure mixing ancient mythology with cosmic action, boosted by the engaging chemistry of James Spader and Kurt Russell and a genuinely iconic portal design.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, scenes of animal abuse, and creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes.

name: A Knight's Tale
overview: William Thatcher, a peasant, is sent to apprentice with a Knight named Hector as a young boy. Urged by his father to "change his Stars", he assumes Sir Hector's place in a tournament when Hector dies in the middle of it. He wins. With the other apprentices, he trains and assumes the title of Sir Ulrich von Lichtenstein.

primaryTitle: Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle
Title_IMDb_Link: Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle
name: Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle
cleanNameArticles: harold and kumar go to white castle
overview: Nerdy accountant Harold and his irrepressible friend, Kumar, get stoned watching television and find themselves utterly bewitched by a commercial for White Castle. Convinced there must be one nearby, the two set out on a late-night odyssey that takes them deep into New Jersey. Somehow, the boys manage to run afoul of rednecks, cops and even a car-stealing Neil Patrick Harris before getting anywhere near their beloved sliders.
review:
Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle is a stoner comedy classic that feels like Dazed and Confused meets an all-night road trip fueled by fast food cravings and absurd mishaps. It’s a wild, goofy ride that helped define early-2000s buddy comedies with a fresh twist—two likable leads navigating a maze of ridiculous obstacles in pursuit of some sliders. John Cho and Kal Penn have great chemistry, and Neil Patrick Harris steals scenes as a wildly over-the-top version of himself, making the film way more memorable than your average munchies-fueled quest.

What stands out is the film’s knack for blending lowbrow humor with surprisingly sharp cultural observations, from racial stereotypes to the quirks of suburban New Jersey life. The tagline, “Fast food. High times.” perfectly sums up the vibe: lighthearted and silly, but with enough heart to keep it from being a total stoner cliché. The chaotic encounters with rednecks, cops, and a car-stealing Harris add layers of escalating absurdity, and the writing by Hayden Schlossberg and Jon Hurwitz keeps the energy high without overstaying its welcome.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content—this one features multiple animal deaths, including a dog, cat, and horse, along with scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting. If those are on your radar, be cautious. Spiders, bugs, and snakes also make appearances, so it’s not just your typical harmless comedy when it comes to critters.
emailReview:
Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle is a stoner comedy classic with sharp cultural wit and unforgettable performances, especially Neil Patrick Harris as a wildly over-the-top version of himself.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, cat, and horse, scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, plus appearances by spiders, bugs, and snakes.

primaryTitle: The Killing of a Sacred Deer
Title_IMDb_Link: The Killing of a Sacred Deer
name: The Killing of a Sacred Deer
overview: Dr. Steven Murphy is a renowned cardiovascular surgeon who presides over a spotless household with his wife and two children. Lurking at the margins of his idyllic suburban existence is Martin, a fatherless teen who insinuates himself into the doctor's life in gradually unsettling ways.
review:
The Killing of a Sacred Deer is a grim, unsettling psychological thriller that feels like Yorgos Lanthimos’ signature brand of dark absurdism meets a Greek tragedy. It’s meticulously controlled and chillingly deadpan, with Colin Farrell and Nicole Kidman anchoring the sterile suburban nightmare. If you appreciate films that lean into discomfort and moral ambiguity—think The Lobster but with higher stakes and a far heavier dose of dread—this one’s for you. It’s not exactly crowd-pleasing, but it’s haunting and memorable in a way that sticks long after the credits roll.

What stands out here is the film’s eerie tone and the way it subverts typical family drama by injecting supernatural menace through Martin, the enigmatic teen who insinuates himself into the Murphy family’s life. The writing by Lanthimos and Efthimis Filippou is sharp and unsettling, blending clinical dialogue with moments of surreal horror. The storyline’s slow burn tension and the film’s clinical visuals create a disquieting atmosphere where the idyllic veneer of suburban life cracks in the most disturbing ways imaginable.

Be heavily warned if animal deaths or harm are on your list—this movie features several, including a dog, horse, cat, and other animals. There’s also body horror and unsettling imagery involving insects and spiders, which might catch some viewers off guard. Fans of psychological unease and stark, weird horror should proceed with caution here.
emailReview:
Yorgos Lanthimos delivers a grim, deadpan psychological thriller that turns suburban family drama into a chilling Greek tragedy, anchored by haunting performances from Colin Farrell and Nicole Kidman.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dog and horse, unsettling body horror, and creepy insect and spider imagery.

writers: Phil Johnston, Pamela Ribon, Rich Moore, Jim Reardon, Josie Trinidad
name: Ralph Breaks the Internet
overview: Video game bad guy Ralph and fellow misfit Vanellope von Schweetz must risk it all by traveling to the World Wide Web in search of a replacement part to save Vanellope's video game, Sugar Rush. In way over their heads, Ralph and Vanellope rely on the citizens of the internet — the netizens — to help navigate their way, including an entrepreneur named Yesss, who is the head algorithm and the heart and soul of trend-making site BuzzzTube.

name: Last Night in Soho
overview: A young girl, passionate in fashion design, is mysteriously able to enter the 1960's where she encounters her idol, a dazzling wannabe singer. But 1960's London is not what it seems, and time seems to be falling apart with shady consequences.
tagline: A murder in the past. A mystery in the future.

writers: Charles Addams, Caroline Thompson, Larry Wilson
name: The Addams Family
overview: When a man claiming to be long-lost Uncle Fester reappears after 25 years lost, the family plans a celebration to wake the dead. But the kids barely have time to warm up the electric chair before Morticia begins to suspect Fester is fraud when he can't recall any of the details of Fester's life.
review:
The Addams Family (1991) is a delightfully macabre comedy that manages to feel both timeless and fresh, thanks to its campy charm and sharp wit. It’s like if Tim Burton’s gothic sensibilities met a quirky family sitcom, with Raúl Juliá and Anjelica Huston bringing warmth to their monstrously odd roles. Christopher Lloyd’s Uncle Fester is a particular standout, balancing weirdness with heartfelt sincerity. This film leans into the weirdness with gusto, celebrating the idea that “weird is relative” in a way that’s both funny and oddly comforting.

What really makes this movie memorable is how it subverts the “fish out of water” trope by throwing in a fake Fester who somehow fits right in with the bizarre Addams clan. The writing cleverly plays with the idea of family loyalty and identity while keeping the tone light and playful. Barry Sonnenfeld’s direction gives the film a gothic flair without becoming too dark for a wider audience, and the quirky score and kooky visuals only add to the offbeat atmosphere. The film rides the line between spooky and silly in a way that’s genuinely fun.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal harm: The film features multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, and even a horse. There’s also a fair share of creepy-crawly critters like spiders, snakes, and bugs, plus some body horror and a bit of vomiting thrown in for good measure. If those kinds of triggers are high on your list, you’ll want to approach with caution.
emailReview: The Addams Family (1991) is a campy gothic comedy that mixes quirky charm with sharp wit, anchored by standout performances from Raúl Juliá, Anjelica Huston, and a heartfelt Christopher Lloyd. Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, creepy-crawly creatures, body horror, and some unsettling vomiting scenes.

writers: Roald Dahl, Nicholas Kazan, Robin Swicord
name: Matilda
overview: An extraordinarily intelligent young girl from a cruel and uncaring family discovers she possesses telekinetic powers and is sent off to a school headed by a tyrannical principal.
tagline: Somewhere inside all of us is the power to change the world.
review:
Matilda is a charming blend of dark comedy and family fantasy that still holds up as a beloved classic from the '90s. Directed by Danny DeVito, who also voices the narrator and stars as Matilda’s neglectful dad, it’s like Roald Dahl’s mischievous spirit meets a kid-friendly superhero origin story. Mara Wilson’s performance as the whip-smart, telekinetic Matilda anchors the film with just the right mix of sweetness and sass. Fans of quirky children’s tales with a bit of bite—think *Coraline* or *The Witches*—will find plenty to enjoy here, even if the whimsical tone occasionally veers into the ominous.

What stands out most is how the film balances its fantastical elements with some truly memorable characters: the tyrannical Miss Trunchbull, played with gleeful menace by Pam Ferris, and the gentle Miss Honey, who offers a warm counterpoint to the cruelty around her. The tagline, “Somewhere inside all of us is the power to change the world,” feels earned as Matilda uses her powers to challenge injustice and find her own voice. The writing leans into classic Dahl themes of empowerment and resilience, while the visuals—bright and slightly stylized—keep the tone playful even during darker moments.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: several animal deaths and scenes involving animal distress are featured, including those involving dogs, cats, horses, and other creatures. Additionally, there are creepy-crawly triggers like spiders, snakes, and other bugs, as well as some scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting. If those are on your watchlist, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Matilda is a delightfully dark family fantasy where Mara Wilson’s sharp-witted heroine and Pam Ferris’s gleefully terrifying Miss Trunchbull create a world that’s both playful and a little bit menacing.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, scenes of animal abuse, dog fighting, and creepy-crawly triggers like spiders and snakes.

writers: Tab Murphy, Victor Hugo, Irene Mecchi, Bob Tzudiker, Noni White, Jonathan Roberts, Kevin Harkey, Gaëtan Brizzi, Paul Brizzi, Ed Gombert, Brenda Chapman, Jeff Snow, Jim Capobianco, Denis Rich, Burny Mattinson, John Sanford, Kelly Wightman, James Fujii, Geefwee Boedoe, Floyd Norman, Francis Glebas, Kirk Hanson, Christine Blum, Sue C. Nichols, Will Finn
name: The Hunchback of Notre Dame
overview: Isolated bell-ringer Quasimodo wishes to leave Notre Dame tower against the wishes of Judge Claude Frollo, his stern guardian and Paris' strait-laced Minister of Justice. His first venture to the outside world finds him Esmeralda, a kind-hearted and fearless Romani woman who openly stands up to Frollo's tyranny.
tagline: He dared to dream, he dared to love. This is the tale of a man… and a monster.

writers: Mike Myers, Bonnie Turner, Terry Turner
name: Wayne's World
overview: When a sleazy TV exec offers Wayne and Garth a fat contract to tape their late-night public access show at his network, they can't believe their good fortune. But they soon discover the road from basement to big-time is a gnarly one, fraught with danger, temptation and ragin' party opportunities.
tagline: You'll laugh. You'll cry. You'll hurl.

name: Heretic
overview: Two Mormon missionaries attempt to convert a man who turns out to be far more dangerous than they could have anticipated.
review:
Heretic is a tense psychological thriller that leans into its unsettling premise with a slow-burning dread reminiscent of “The Invitation” meets “Get Out.” The film’s tagline, “Question everything,” sets the stage for a story where nothing is quite as it seems—two Mormon missionaries encounter a man whose danger lurks beneath a calm exterior. While the setup feels familiar, the execution is elevated by a cast that includes Hugh Grant, who plays Mr. Reed with a chilling subtlety that keeps you guessing. Fans of atmospheric, character-driven horror will find plenty to appreciate here, though it’s not quite the nerve-shredder some might expect.

What stands out is how the film uses its modest premise to explore themes of belief, control, and manipulation without ever feeling preachy. Directors Scott Beck and Bryan Woods craft an unnerving mood, aided by a minimalist score that quietly ratchets up the tension. The interactions between the missionaries—Sophie Thatcher and Chloe East especially—feel authentic, which makes the slow unraveling all the more effective. The film toys with genre conventions, blending psychological horror with a touch of religious thriller, and manages to keep the audience off-balance without resorting to cheap scares.

Be heavily warned if animal harm or death is a trigger for you, as the film includes multiple instances of animals dying and being abused, including a dog, cat, horse, and other pets. There’s also some unsettling imagery involving spiders, snakes, and dog fighting, which contributes to the overall disturbing atmosphere. Those sensitive to gaslighting or manipulative behavior will want to brace themselves as well, since psychological torment is a core part of the story. If any of these are on your list, proceed with caution.
emailReview: Heretic is a slow-burning psychological thriller that blends atmospheric dread with chilling performances, especially Hugh Grant’s subtly sinister turn as Mr. Reed, keeping you guessing long after the credits roll. Be prepared for: multiple instances of animal death and abuse including dogs and horses, graphic dog fighting, unsettling spider and snake imagery, and intense psychological manipulation.

writers: Guillermo del Toro, Kim Morgan, William Lindsay Gresham
name: Nightmare Alley
overview: An ambitious carnival man with a talent for manipulating people with a few well-chosen words hooks up with a female psychologist who is even more dangerous than he is.
review:
Nightmare Alley is a dark, stylish dive into noir territory with Guillermo del Toro’s signature flair for the grotesque and the beautiful. It’s a twisted carnival ride of manipulation and ambition, anchored by Bradley Cooper’s slick but slippery Stanton Carlisle and Cate Blanchett’s icy, calculating psychologist, Dr. Lilith Ritter. Think old-school film noir meets a carnival sideshow—if you like your crime dramas with a side of psychological cat-and-mouse games, this one’s a rich, moody treat.

What really stands out is how del Toro and co-writer Kim Morgan layer the story with themes of deception and power, all wrapped in a visual palette that’s both grimy and eerily mesmerizing. The carnival setting isn’t just window dressing; it feeds into the film’s exploration of man versus beast, both literally and metaphorically, as the tagline “Man or beast” suggests. The supporting cast, including Toni Collette and Willem Dafoe, add textured performances that keep the tension simmering beneath the surface, making this more than just a slick thriller.

Those sensitive to animal harm should proceed with caution. Nightmare Alley features multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse—including dogs, cats, and horses—and even dog fighting, making it a tough watch for animal lovers. There’s also some gaslighting in the mix, so if emotional manipulation is a trigger for you, it’s worth being aware. The dark, unsettling atmosphere is a big part of the film’s power, but it’s not for the faint of heart.
emailReview:
Nightmare Alley is a grimy, beautifully twisted noir carnival ride where psychological manipulation meets Guillermo del Toro’s flair for the grotesque, anchored by standout performances from Bradley Cooper and Cate Blanchett.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, dog fighting, and intense emotional gaslighting.

name: One Day
overview: A romantic comedy centered on Dexter and Emma, who first meet during their graduation in 1988 and proceed to keep in touch regularly. The film follows what they do on July 15 annually, usually doing something together.

name: Buried
overview: Paul is a U.S. truck driver working in Iraq. After an attack by a group of Iraqis he wakes to find he is buried alive inside a coffin. With only a lighter and a cell phone it's a race against time to escape this claustrophobic death trap.
tagline: 170,000 sq miles of desert. 90 minutes of oxygen. No way out.

name: Logan Lucky
overview: Trying to reverse a family curse, brothers Jimmy and Clyde Logan set out to execute an elaborate robbery during the legendary Coca-Cola 600 race at the Charlotte Motor Speedway.
tagline: See how the other half steals.

writers: Scott Frank, Don Roos, John Grogan
name: Marley & Me
overview: A newly married couple who, in the process of starting a family, learn many of life's important lessons from their trouble-loving retriever, Marley. Packed with plenty of laughs to lighten the load, the film explores the highs and lows of marriage, maturity and confronting one's own mortality, as seen through the lens of family life with a dog.
review:
Marley & Me is that classic tearjerker-family-comedy hybrid that’s equal parts heartwarming and chaotic, riding the wave of pet-centric life lessons with a style that feels like a mashup of Homeward Bound meets a bittersweet sitcom about growing up and growing old. Owen Wilson and Jennifer Aniston bring solid charm as the newlyweds navigating marriage and parenthood, but it’s really Marley—the gloriously unruly retriever—that steals the show, turning typical pet-movie tropes into something a bit more grounded and relatable.

What stands out here is how the film balances laughter and life’s tougher realities without feeling preachy. The tagline “Heel the love” nails it: this is about the messy, imperfect love that carries a family through ups and downs. There’s plenty of humor in Marley’s mischief, but the story doesn’t shy away from mortality and change, making it more than just a fluffy pet flick. The writing leans on familiar beats but gives them enough warmth and sincerity to keep you invested. Director David Frankel keeps things comfortably paced, letting the emotional moments breathe without dragging the comedy down.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to pet loss: Marley & Me does not shy away from the fact that “the dog dies,” and it hits with a sadness that’s earned but still tough to watch. Those who pin the “a dog dies” and “the ending is sad” triggers should be cautious going in. There’s also some mild bug-related content (spiders and general bugs), but nothing too intense. Overall, a heartfelt romp that’s as much about family life as it is about the dog.
emailReview:
Marley & Me is a heartwarming yet chaotic family comedy that captures the messy, imperfect love of marriage and parenthood through the gloriously unruly Marley, whose mischief brings both laughs and real emotional weight.

Be prepared for: a dog dying, a sad ending, spiders, and general bug-related content.

name: Hard Candy
overview: Hayley’s a smart, charming teenage girl. Jeff’s a handsome, smooth fashion photographer. An Internet chat, a coffee shop meet-up, an impromptu fashion shoot back at Jeff’s place. Jeff thinks it’s his lucky night. He’s in for a surprise.
tagline: Strangers shouldn't talk to little girls.

name: The Drop
overview: Bob Saginowski finds himself at the center of a robbery gone awry and entwined in an investigation that digs deep into the neighborhood's past where friends, families, and foes all work together to make a living - no matter the cost.

writers: Scott Neustadter, Michael H. Weber, Tim Tharp
name: The Spectacular Now
overview: Sutter, a popular party animal unexpectedly meets the introverted Aimee after waking up on a stranger's lawn. As Sutter deals with the problems in his life and Aimee plans for her future beyond school, an unexpected romance blossoms between them.
tagline: Hits You Like A Shot In The Heart.

writers: Joe Russo, Ande Parks, Anthony Russo
name: Extraction 2
overview: The sequel to Netflix's 2020 huge hit.
tagline: Prepare for the ride of your life.

name: The Mule
overview: Earl Stone, a man in his eighties, is broke, alone, and facing foreclosure of his business when he is offered a job that simply requires him to drive. Easy enough, but, unbeknownst to Earl, he's just signed on as a drug courier for a Mexican cartel. He does so well that his cargo increases exponentially, and Earl hit the radar of hard-charging DEA agent Colin Bates.

name: Challengers
overview: Tennis player turned coach Tashi has taken her husband, Art, and transformed him into a world-famous Grand Slam champion. To jolt him out of his recent losing streak, she signs him up for a "Challenger" event — close to the lowest level of pro tournament — where he finds himself standing across the net from his former best friend and Tashi's former boyfriend.
review:
Challengers is a sleek, character-driven sports drama that feels like a mash-up of intense tennis rivalry and tangled romantic history — think Battle of the Sexes meets a messy love triangle. Zendaya leads as Tashi, a fiercely determined coach who’s as much in control of the game off-court as she is on it, flipping the usual sports movie script where men hog the spotlight. The film’s sharp tension comes from the triangle between Tashi, her husband Art, and his former best friend (and Tashi’s ex) Patrick, giving it more emotional layers than your average underdog story.

What stands out is Luca Guadagnino’s trademark stylish direction, which elevates the tennis scenes into something almost balletic, combined with a simmering, intimate look at ambition and jealousy. The tagline “Her game. Her rules.” nails the tone perfectly — this isn’t just about tennis, it’s about power dynamics and personal reinvention. The writing keeps things tight, with just enough backstory to make the characters’ conflicts feel real without bogging down the pace. Zendaya’s performance anchors it all, balancing vulnerability with steely resolve.

Heads up for viewers sensitive to animal harm triggers: the movie includes the deaths of multiple animals, including a dog, cat, and horse, plus some scenes that could be unsettling if you’re triggered by blood or gore. There are also jump scares and some creepy bug and spider moments that might catch you off guard. If these are on your watchlist, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Challengers serves up a stylish, emotionally charged sports drama with Zendaya commanding the spotlight in a tangled love triangle that flips the usual game-day script.

Be prepared for: the deaths of a dog, cat, and horse, unsettling blood and gore, jump scares, and creepy bug and spider scenes.

name: Bad Santa
overview: A miserable conman and his partner pose as Santa and his Little Helper to rob department stores on Christmas Eve. But they run into problems when the conman befriends a troubled kid, and the security boss discovers the plot.
tagline: He doesn't care if you're naughty or nice.

writers: Aline Brosh McKenna, Cameron Crowe, Benjamin Mee
name: We Bought a Zoo
overview: Benjamin has lost his wife and, in a bid to start his life over, purchases a large house that has a zoo – welcome news for his daughter, but his son is not happy about it. The zoo is in need of renovation and Benjamin sets about the work with the head keeper and the rest of the staff, but, the zoo soon runs into financial trouble.

name: A Serious Man
overview: It is 1967, and Larry Gopnik, a physics professor at a quiet Midwestern university, has just been informed by his wife Judith that she is leaving him. She has fallen in love with one of his more pompous acquaintances Sy Ableman.

writers: Gregory Widen, Peter Bellwood, Larry Ferguson
name: Highlander
overview: He fought his first battle on the Scottish Highlands in 1536. He will fight his greatest battle on the streets of New York City in 1986. His name is Connor MacLeod. He is immortal.
review:
Highlander is a cult classic that blends fantasy, action, and a dash of ’80s neon noir into a tale of immortals battling across centuries. It’s got that “there can be only one” tagline that’s as memorable as the flick itself, and while it sometimes leans into camp, the film’s mix of flashbacks to 16th-century Scotland and gritty New York City showdowns keeps it feeling unique among sword-and-sorcery fare. Think of it as a predecessor to modern supernatural epics—fans of shows like *The Witcher* or movies like *The Matrix* might appreciate how it handles immortal rivals with style, even if the dialogue occasionally feels a little dated.

What sticks with you is the world-building and the mythos around Connor MacLeod’s immortal journey. The film doesn’t just throw swords and fights at you; it spends time weaving in themes of loneliness, destiny, and the burden of living through centuries. The casting is strong, with Christopher Lambert bringing a brooding charisma to the Highlander and Sean Connery popping in as a mentor with a dry wit that adds gravitas. The score, a mix of synth and rock, perfectly captures that ’80s vibe and elevates the sword clashes to something almost operatic. It’s a bit of a genre mashup—historical drama meets urban fantasy—that still holds up well for fans of vintage cult hits.

Heads up for animal lovers: Highlander features multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and other creatures, which might be quite upsetting. Those sensitive to animal harm or death should definitely be cautious going in, as these moments are woven into the story and not just fleeting background details. On the bug front, spiders, snakes, and other critters also make appearances, so if those are triggers for you, consider yourself warned.
emailReview:
Highlander is a cult classic that mixes ’80s neon noir style with timeless sword fights and a haunting mythos about immortality, all brought to life by Christopher Lambert’s brooding charisma and Sean Connery’s dry wit.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, scenes of animal abuse, and unsettling appearances by spiders and snakes.

writers: John Hoberg, Kat Likkel, Brenda Hsueh, Peter Sohn
name: Elemental
overview: In a city where fire, water, land and air residents live together, a fiery young woman and a go-with-the-flow guy will discover something elemental: how much they have in common.

writers: Pamela Pettler, Shane Acker, Ben Gluck
overview: When 9 first comes to life, he finds himself in a post-apocalyptic world. All humans are gone, and it is only by chance that he discovers a small community of others like him taking refuge from fearsome machines that roam the earth intent on their extinction. Despite being the neophyte of the group, 9 convinces the others that hiding will do them no good.
tagline: When our world ended, their mission began.

name: Foxcatcher
overview: The greatest Olympic Wrestling Champion brother team joins Team Foxcatcher led by multimillionaire sponsor John E. du Pont as they train for the 1988 games in Seoul - a union that leads to unlikely circumstances.

name: Green Room
overview: A punk rock band becomes trapped in a secluded venue after finding a scene of violence. For what they saw, the band themselves become targets of violence from a gang of white power skinheads, who want to eliminate all evidence of the crime.
tagline: One way in. No way out.

name: Den of Thieves
overview: A gritty crime saga which follows the lives of an elite unit of the LA County Sheriff's Dept. and the state's most successful bank robbery crew as the outlaws plan a seemingly impossible heist on the Federal Reserve Bank.
tagline: Cops without limits. Thieves without fear.
review:
Den of Thieves is a gritty, no-nonsense crime thriller that leans hard into the LA heist genre with a swagger that fans of Heat or The Town might appreciate. It’s not reinventing the wheel by any means, but Gerard Butler’s tough, world-weary cop and Pablo Schreiber’s calculating bank robber give it enough punch to stand out in a crowded field. The tagline—“Cops without limits. Thieves without fear.”—pretty much sums up the film’s relentless, balls-to-the-wall tone. If you’re here for a wild ride through the cat-and-mouse game between law enforcement and criminals, this one delivers, though it’s a bit heavier on grit than on nuance.

What’s worth talking about is how the film balances its dual focus on the elite sheriff’s unit and the bank robbery crew, making each side feel fleshed out enough to care about the stakes. Christian Gudegast’s direction keeps the pace taut, and the script doesn’t shy away from the brutal realities of crime—no sugarcoating here. The Federal Reserve heist lends a high-stakes centerpiece that’s both thrilling and tense, and the supporting cast, including O’Shea Jackson Jr. and 50 Cent, add some flavorful texture to the mix. The atmosphere is dank and dirty, perfectly capturing the underbelly of LA without trying to glamorize it.

Heads up: this one’s loaded with heavy triggers. There’s plenty of gun violence, blood and gore, and scenes of torture. Animal lovers should be warned—there’s a dog death that’s hard to stomach. On top of that, the movie doesn’t hold back on jump scares or flashing lights, so sensitive viewers should brace themselves. There’s also a fair amount of death, including the loss of children and parents, and some brutal mutilation moments. If you’re on the lookout for a polished crime drama with a lot of edge, Den of Thieves fits the bill—but it’s definitely not light viewing.
emailReview:
Den of Thieves delivers a gritty, no-nonsense heist thriller with Gerard Butler and Pablo Schreiber bringing enough firepower to make this tough LA crime saga stand out in a crowded genre.

Be prepared for: a gut-wrenching dog death, intense scenes of torture, brutal mutilation, heavy gun violence, and the loss of children and parents.

name: Pearl
overview: Trapped on her family’s isolated farm, Pearl must tend to her ailing father under the bitter and overbearing watch of her devout mother. Lusting for a glamorous life like she’s seen in the movies, Pearl’s ambitions, temptations, and repressions collide.
review:
Pearl is a dark and stylish origin story that carves out a niche in the psychological horror genre, feeling like a twisted blend of classic gothic drama and a mid-century Hollywood nightmare. Mia Goth, who also co-wrote the film with director Ti West, delivers a performance that’s both unsettling and oddly sympathetic as Pearl, a woman suffocating under her mother’s rigid control while dreaming of a glamorous escape. It’s not your typical slasher or scream-fest, but rather a slow-burn character study elevated by its period detail and Goth’s intense presence.

What stands out most is the film’s claustrophobic atmosphere and how it uses its isolated farm setting as a pressure cooker for Pearl’s spiraling desires and frustrations. The tagline, “An X-traordinary origin story,” hints at Pearl’s transformation, and the film leans into that with a mix of surreal visuals and a simmering tension that builds toward moments of shocking release. Ti West’s direction is meticulous, balancing eerie quiet with bursts of violence, while the supporting cast adds texture without stealing focus from Pearl’s unraveling. It’s a unique take on ambition and repression that fans of slow-burning horror with a psychological edge will appreciate.

The film is free from real animal harm, so if that’s a hard line for you, you can watch with peace of mind. However, be warned that Pearl’s journey involves intense psychological distress and some disturbing violence, so those sensitive to graphic content or emotional cruelty might want to proceed with caution.
emailReview: Pearl is a haunting psychological horror that blends gothic drama with mid-century Hollywood unease, anchored by Mia Goth’s mesmerizing and deeply unsettling performance. Be prepared for: intense psychological cruelty, graphic violence, and a claustrophobic atmosphere that tightens like a noose.

writers: Brock Norman Brock, Nicolas Winding Refn
name: Bronson
overview: A young man who was sentenced to 7 years in prison for robbing a post office ends up spending 30 years in solitary confinement. During this time, his own personality is supplanted by his alter ego, Charles Bronson.
tagline: The Man. The Myth. The Celebrity.

name: The Kids Are All Right
overview: Two women, Nic and Jules, brought a son and daughter into the world through artificial insemination. When one of their children reaches age, both kids go behind their mothers' backs to meet with the donor. Life becomes so much more interesting when the father, two mothers and children start to become attached to each other.

name: The Kingdom
