overview: A team of U.S. government agents is sent to investigate the bombing of an American facility in the Middle East.

primaryTitle: To All the Boys I've Loved Before
Title_IMDb_Link: To All the Boys I've Loved Before
name: To All the Boys I've Loved Before
cleanNameArticles: all the boys ive loved before
overview: Lara Jean's love life goes from imaginary to out of control when her secret letters to every boy she's ever fallen for are mysteriously mailed out.
review:
To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before is a sweet, breezy teen rom-com that leans fully into the charm of its premise: what happens when your secret love letters get unexpectedly mailed out? Lana Condor’s Lara Jean feels like the relatable heart of this whole thing, caught between awkwardness and earnestness in a way that’s more genuine than your average high school rom-com. Think Clueless meets a modern-day Jane Austen, with a dash of Netflix’s signature cozy vibe. It’s not groundbreaking, but it’s undeniably endearing and elevated by a cast that’s comfortable in their roles.

What stands out here is how the film balances the typical rom-com beats with moments of genuine warmth and family dynamics, especially with Lara Jean’s protective older sister Margot and her mischievous little sister Kitty. The “letters are out” tagline perfectly captures that mix of chaos and tenderness, with the story exploring the messy, confusing emotions of young love without getting too sappy or cynical. The writing by Sofia Alvarez keeps things light but with enough heart to avoid feeling disposable, and Susan Johnson’s direction favors a colorful, inviting look that suits the story’s uplifting tone.

Heads up for animal-sensitive viewers: this one features quite a few triggers around animals, including multiple pet deaths and some distressing moments involving bugs and spiders. If you’re particularly wary of animal harm or loss, this movie might hit a little harder than expected. Otherwise, it’s a mostly gentle ride through teenage crushes and growing up.
emailReview:
A sweet and breezy teen rom-com with a cozy, colorful vibe and a cast that nails the awkward earnestness of young love.

Be prepared for: multiple pet deaths, distressing bug and spider scenes, and moments of animal harm.

writers: Nora Ephron, Julie Powell, Julia Child, Alex Prud'homme
name: Julie & Julia
overview: Julia Child and Julie Powell – both of whom wrote memoirs – find their lives intertwined. Though separated by time and space, both women are at loose ends... until they discover that with the right combination of passion, fearlessness and butter, anything is possible.

name: Sixteen Candles
overview: A teenage girl deals with her parents forgetting her birthday and a crush on her high school's heartthrob.
tagline: Turning sixteen isn't easy, when you've fallen in love... for the first time.

name: Mallrats
overview: Both dumped by their girlfriends, two best friends seek refuge in the local mall.
tagline: They're not there to shop. They're not there to work. They're just there.
review:
Mallrats is a quintessential ’90s Kevin Smith comedy that feels like Clerks’ laid-back cousin who just wants to hang out and riff endlessly about pop culture while wandering a suburban mall. It’s not as sharp or tightly written as some of Smith’s later work, but there’s a goofy charm here anchored by Jason Lee and Jeremy London as two guys aimlessly nursing their heartbreaks. Fans of stoner comedies or ’90s nostalgia trips will find plenty to enjoy, though it’s definitely a product of its time—flippant, a bit indulgent, and very much about vibe over plot.

What stands out most is the way the mall itself becomes a character, a sprawling playground for awkward encounters and quirky side plots. The tagline “They’re not there to shop. They’re not there to work. They’re just there.” nails the aimlessness that defines the film’s tone, which leans into that low-stakes, slice-of-life comedy with a cultish affection for pop references and offbeat humor. The cast, including Ben Affleck and Shannen Doherty in fun supporting roles, rounds out a colorful ensemble that makes wandering the mall feel like an oddly comforting experience.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: Mallrats includes multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, and even a horse. Those who have these triggers should proceed with caution, especially since the film doesn’t shy away from showing some of these moments, which feel jarring compared to the otherwise lighthearted tone. There are also bugs, spiders, and snakes lurking in the background for anyone who’s uneasy about creepy crawlies.
emailReview:
Mallrats is a goofy ’90s stoner comedy that turns a suburban mall into a quirky playground for pop culture riffs and aimless hangouts, anchored by Jason Lee’s laid-back charm.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and a horse, scenes of animal abuse, and unsettling appearances of bugs, spiders, and snakes.

name: The Foreigner
overview: Quan is a humble London businessman whose long-buried past erupts in a revenge-fueled vendetta when the only person left for him to love dies in a senseless act of politically-motivated terrorism.
tagline: Never push a good man too far.

name: Greyhound
overview: A first-time captain leads a convoy of allied ships carrying thousands of soldiers across the treacherous waters of the “Black Pit” to the front lines of WW2. With no air cover protection for 5 days, the captain and his convoy must battle the surrounding enemy Nazi U-boats in order to give the allies a chance to win the war.

writers: Mitch Glazer, Michael O'Donoghue, Charles Dickens
name: Scrooged
overview: In this modern take on Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol," Frank Cross (Bill Murray) is a wildly successful television executive whose cold ambition and curmudgeonly nature has driven away the love of his life, Claire Phillips (Karen Allen). But after firing a staff member, Eliot Loudermilk (Bobcat Goldthwait), on Christmas Eve, Frank is visited by a series of ghosts who give him a chance to re-evaluate his actions and right the wrongs of his past.
tagline: The spirits will move you in odd and hysterical ways.

name: Maverick
overview: Bret Maverick is a gambler who would rather con someone than fight them, and needs an additional $3k in order to enter a winner-takes-all poker game beginning in a few days. He joins forces with a woman with a marvelous Southern accent, and the two try and enter the game.

writers: Leonard Ripps, Tim Burton, John August
name: Frankenweenie
overview: When a car hits young Victor's pet dog Sparky, Victor decides to bring him back to life the only way he knows how. But when the bolt-necked "monster" wreaks havoc and terror in the hearts of Victor's neighbors, he has to convince them that Sparky's still the good, loyal friend he was.

name: Water for Elephants
overview: In this captivating Depression-era melodrama, impetuous veterinary student Jacob Jankowski joins a celebrated circus as an animal caretaker but faces a wrenching dilemma when he's transfixed by angelic married performer Marlena.

writers: Christopher Wood, Richard Maibaum, Ian Fleming
name: The Spy Who Loved Me
overview: Russian and British submarines with nuclear missiles on board both vanish from sight without a trace. England and Russia both blame each other as James Bond tries to solve the riddle of the disappearing ships. But the KGB also has an agent on the case.
tagline: It's the BIGGEST. It's the BEST. It's BOND. And B-E-Y-O-N-D.

name: A Scanner Darkly
overview: An undercover cop in a not-too-distant future becomes involved with a dangerous new drug and begins to lose his own identity as a result.
tagline: Everything is not going to be OK.

name: Filth
overview: A bigoted junkie cop suffering from bipolar disorder and drug addiction manipulates and hallucinates his way through the festive season in a bid to secure promotion and win back his wife and daughter.
tagline: It's a filthy job getting to the top, but someone's got to do it.

name: Trance
overview: A violent gang enlists the help of a hypnotherapist in an attempt to locate a painting which somehow vanished in the middle of a heist.

writers: Lynn Siefert, Michael Ritchie, Tommy Swerdlow, Michael Goldberg
name: Cool Runnings
overview: When a Jamaican sprinter is disqualified from the Olympic Games, he enlists the help of a dishonored coach to start the first Jamaican Bobsled Team.
tagline: One dream. Four Jamaicans. Twenty below zero.

name: What Dreams May Come
overview: Chris Neilson dies to find himself in a heaven more amazing than he could have ever dreamed of. There is one thing missing: his wife. After he dies, his wife, Annie killed herself and went to hell. Chris decides to risk eternity in hades for the small chance that he will be able to bring her back to heaven.
tagline: After life there is more. The end is just the beginning.

name: The Last Boy Scout
overview: When the girl that detective Joe Hallenback is protecting gets murdered, the boyfriend of the murdered girl attempts to investigate and solve the case. What they discover is that there is deep seated corruption going on between a crooked politician and the owner of a pro football team.
tagline: Everyone had counted them out. But they're about to get back in the game.

writers: Jay Chandrasekhar, Kevin Heffernan, Steve Lemme, Paul Soter, Erik Stolhanske
name: Super Troopers
overview: Five bored, occasionally high and always ineffective Vermont state troopers must prove their worth to the governor or lose their jobs. After stumbling on a drug ring, they plan to make a bust, but a rival police force is out to steal the glory.
tagline: In their town, you don't screw with the law, the law screws with you.
review:
Super Troopers is a cult classic comedy that rides the line between stoner slapstick and absurd buddy cop antics. If you’re a fan of the Broken Lizard troupe’s irreverent humor, this one’s a wild ride full of goofy pranks, quotable lines, and just enough police procedural nonsense to keep things moving. It’s like if Reno 911! and The Hangover had a Vermont-born lovechild—sometimes lowbrow, often silly, but with a surprisingly endearing core of camaraderie. It’s not high art, but it’s a reliably fun watch for those who enjoy their comedy with a side of ridiculousness.

What stands out here is how the film leans into its oddball charm, anchored by Jay Chandrasekhar’s direction and the ensemble’s chemistry—Kevin Heffernan’s Farva is an especially memorable goofball. The premise is simple: a bunch of bored state troopers trying to prove their worth, which sets the stage for a string of absurd gags and escalating chaos. The tagline, “In their town, you don’t screw with the law, the law screws with you,” perfectly captures the film’s playful subversion of authority and small-town police clichés. The drug ring subplot adds a thin thread of structure but mostly serves as a backdrop for the characters’ antics.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one is notorious on the trigger front. There are multiple instances involving animals dying, including a dog, cat, and horse, along with scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting. If any of those top your list, consider yourself warned—Super Troopers doesn’t shy away from its darker, more uncomfortable humor moments involving animals. Also, spiders and snakes make appearances, so those with arachnophobia or ophidiophobia might want to proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Super Troopers delivers goofy, stoner-infused buddy cop chaos with a sharp ensemble cast and a playful poke at small-town law enforcement that keeps the laughs coming.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, cat, and horse, scenes of animal abuse, dog fighting, and appearances by spiders and snakes.

directors: Bibo Bergeron, Don Paul, Jeffrey Katzenberg
writers: Ted Elliott, Terry Rossio, Karey Kirkpatrick, Philip LaZebnik
name: The Road to El Dorado
overview: After a failed swindle, two con-men end up with a map to El Dorado, the fabled "city of gold," and an unintended trip to the New World.  Much to their surprise, the map does lead the pair to the mythical city, where the startled inhabitants promptly begin to worship them as gods.  The only question is, do they take the worshipful natives for all they're worth, or is there a bit more to El Dorado than riches?
tagline: They came for the gold. They stayed for the adventure.
review:
The Road to El Dorado is a cheeky, fast-paced animated adventure that feels like Indiana Jones meets DreamWorks’ early 2000s charm. It’s not quite as sharp or clever as some of its contemporaries, but the dynamic between the two con-men leads—voiced by Kevin Kline and Kenneth Branagh—keeps things lively enough. The film trades on classic treasure-hunting tropes but adds a lighthearted, irreverent spin that makes it a fun ride, especially for fans who enjoy a bit of swashbuckling with their laughs.

What stands out most is the vibrant animation and catchy score that capture the spirit of the mythical city of gold. The tagline, “They came for the gold. They stayed for the adventure,” nails the film’s tone perfectly—it’s all about the unexpected journey rather than the destination. While it sometimes leans into broad humor (including a few fat jokes and “man in a dress” jabs), the story also manages to poke at themes of identity and deception with a wink rather than a scowl. Rosie Perez’s Chel adds much-needed sass and helps keep the plot from feeling too predictable.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and death: the movie features multiple instances of animal deaths, including a seagull, a horse, and even a dog. There’s also a shark scene played for laughs, but it might still be unsettling for some. Sexual content and objectification pop up sporadically, and the film includes some outdated minority representations and jokes that haven’t aged well. If these are on your radar, it’s worth keeping an eye out.
emailReview:
The Road to El Dorado is a cheeky, fast-paced animated adventure with lively voice work and a catchy score that captures the spirit of a mythical city of gold.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and a seagull, a shark scene played for laughs, and some outdated minority jokes.

name: ParaNorman
overview: In the town of Blithe Hollow, Norman Babcock can speak to the dead, but no one other than his eccentric new friend believes his ability is real. One day, Norman's eccentric uncle tells him of a ritual he must perform to protect the town from a curse cast by a witch centuries ago.
tagline: It's all fun and games until someone raises the dead.

writers: Tom Clancy, Donald E. Stewart, Steven Zaillian, John Milius
name: Clear And Present Danger
overview: CIA Analyst Jack Ryan is drawn into an illegal war fought by the US government against a Colombian drug cartel.

name: Cop Land
overview: Freddy Heflin is the sheriff of a place everyone calls “Cop Land” — a small and seemingly peaceful town populated by the big city police officers he’s long admired. Yet something ugly is taking place behind the town’s peaceful facade. And when Freddy uncovers a massive, deadly conspiracy among these local residents, he is forced to take action and make a dangerous choice between protecting his idols and upholding the law.

name: Unleashed
overview: Raised as a slave, Danny is used to fighting for his survival. In fact, his "master," Bart, thinks of him as a pet and goes as far as leashing him with a collar so they can make money in fight clubs, where Danny is the main contender. When Bart's crew is in a car accident, Danny escapes and meets a blind, kindhearted piano tuner who takes him in and uses music to free the fighter's long-buried heart.

name: Juror #2
overview: A juror on a murder trial realizes that he may have caused the victim's death and must grapple with the dilemma of whether to manipulate the jury to save himself or reveal the truth and turn himself in.
tagline: Justice is blind. Guilt sees everything.

name: Alpha Dog
overview: Johnny Truelove likes to see himself as tough. He's the son of an underworld figure and a drug dealer. Johnny also likes to get tough when things don't go his way. When Jake Mazursky fails to pay up for Johnny, things get worse for the Mazursky family, as Johnny and his 'gang' kidnap Jake's 15 year old brother and holds him hostage. Problem now is what to do with 'stolen boy?'
tagline: One crime. 38 witnesses. No way back.

name: Romancing the Stone
overview: Though she can spin wild tales of passionate romance, novelist Joan Wilder has no life of her own. Then one day adventure comes her way in the form of a mysterious package. It turns out that the parcel is the ransom she'll need to free her abducted sister, so Joan flies to South America to hand it over. But she gets on the wrong bus and winds up hopelessly stranded in the jungle.
tagline: She's a girl from the big city. He's a reckless soldier of fortune. For a fabulous treasure, they share an adventure no one could imagine... or survive.

name: Fatal Attraction
overview: A married man's one-night stand comes back to haunt him when that lover begins to stalk him and his family.
tagline: A look that led to an evening. A mistake he'll regret... FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE.
review:
Fatal Attraction is the quintessential ’80s psychological thriller that still manages to feel tense and relevant decades later. It rides that razor’s edge between domestic drama and outright horror, with Michael Douglas as the hapless husband and Glenn Close delivering one of the most unforgettable performances of obsessive menace in film history. If you like your thrillers with a side of simmering dread and moral chaos, think Fatal Attraction as Fatal Attraction meets a cautionary tale about temptation gone nuclear. It’s not just a wild ride—it’s a slow burn that sticks with you.

What really sets this film apart is how it leans into its tagline: "A look that led to an evening. A mistake he'll regret... FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE." The writing smartly explores the fallout of infidelity with a laser focus on escalating consequences, while Adrian Lyne’s direction ensures every scene drips with anxiety and dread. The psychological unraveling of Alex Forrest (Close) is chilling, and the way the film balances her unpredictability against Dan’s growing panic is a masterclass in tension-building. Plus, the score and moody visuals perfectly capture that late ’80s corporate and suburban malaise, making the story feel both intimate and uncomfortably universal.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and violence—Fatal Attraction isn’t shy about showing the nastier side of obsession. There are multiple instances involving the death and abuse of animals, including pets, as well as some intense moments of domestic violence and stalking that can be pretty unsettling. Also, spiders and other creepy crawlies make appearances, so if bugs are on your trigger list, tread carefully. The ending is grim too, so be prepared for a heavy conclusion.
emailReview:
Fatal Attraction is the ultimate ’80s thriller that combines simmering dread with a masterclass in obsessive menace, anchored by Glenn Close’s unforgettable performance and a mood that’s equal parts corporate malaise and domestic horror.

Be prepared for: pet death and abuse, intense domestic violence, stalking, creepy spiders, and a grim ending.

name: Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close
overview: A year after his father's death, Oskar, a troubled young boy, discovers a mysterious key he believes was left for him by his father and embarks on a scavenger hunt to find the matching lock.

name: Holes
overview: Stanley's family is cursed with bad luck. Unfairly sentenced to months of detention at Camp Green Lake, he and his campmates are forced by the warden to dig holes in order to build character. What they don't know is that they are digging holes in order to search for a lost treasure hidden somewhere in the camp.
tagline: Some secrets are too big to keep hidden.

name: The Outsiders
overview: In 1960s Tulsa, class divisions ignite a violent rivalry between the working-class Greasers and the privileged Socs. When a deadly encounter forces two Greasers, Ponyboy and Johnny, to flee, their struggle for survival and redemption exposes the fragile innocence and enduring bonds of youth on the wrong side of town.
tagline: They grew up on the outside of society. They weren't looking for a fight. They were looking to belong.

writers: Erin Cressida Wilson, Mary Gaitskill, Steven Shainberg
name: Secretary
overview: A young woman, recently released from a mental hospital, gets a job as a secretary to a demanding lawyer, where their employer-employee relationship turns into a sexual, sadomasochistic one.

writers: Alan Trustman, Leslie Dixon, Kurt Wimmer
name: The Thomas Crown Affair
overview: A very rich and successful playboy amuses himself by stealing artwork, but may have met his match in a seductive detective.
tagline: How do you get the man who has everything?

name: Out of Sight
overview: Meet Jack Foley, a smooth criminal who bends the law and is determined to make one last heist. Karen Sisco is a federal marshal who chooses all the right moves … and all the wrong guys. Now they're willing to risk it all to find out if there's more between them than just the law.

name: Big Eyes
overview: The story of the awakening of painter, Margaret Keane, her phenomenal success in the 1950s, and the subsequent legal difficulties she had with her husband, who claimed credit for her works in the 1960s.
tagline: She created it. He sold it. And everyone bought it.

name: Another Earth
overview: On the night of the discovery of a duplicate Earth in the Solar system, an ambitious young student and an accomplished composer cross paths in a tragic accident.

name: Pig
overview: A truffle hunter who lives alone in the Oregon wilderness must visit Portland to find the mysterious person who stole his beloved foraging pig.
tagline: We don't get a lot of things to really care about.
review:
Pig is a quietly intense character study that flips the revenge thriller on its head, anchored by a surprisingly restrained Nicolas Cage. Far from the usual Hollywood frenzy, this indie drama leans into melancholy and introspection, with a tone that’s more contemplative than cathartic. Fans of films like *Leave No Trace* or *The Rider* will appreciate its slow-burn approach and the way it meditates on loss and connection through the unusual lens of a truffle hunter whose prized pig goes missing.

What really stands out is how the film uses its sparse Oregon wilderness setting against the grittier, more impersonal backdrop of Portland. The tagline, “We don’t get a lot of things to really care about,” feels like a thematic throughline, with the story quietly unpacking grief and human fragility without resorting to melodrama. The writing and performances work hand-in-hand to create a mood that’s far more about emotional subtlety than spectacle, and the relationship between Rob Feld and his pig—more than just a pet—carries a surprising emotional heft.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: this one carries multiple triggers involving animal deaths and abuse, including pets and wildlife, plus some unsettling bugs and spiders. If those kinds of things are on your list, be cautious going in.
emailReview:
Pig is a quietly intense indie drama that subverts the revenge thriller with a slow, contemplative mood and a restrained, heartfelt performance from Nicolas Cage.

Be prepared for: animal deaths and abuse involving pets and wildlife, unsettling bugs, spiders, and a deeply emotional bond tested by loss.

name: Sisu
overview: When an ex-soldier who discovers gold in the Lapland wilderness tries to take the loot into the city, German soldiers led by a brutal SS officer battle him.
review:
Sisu is a lean, brutal revenge thriller that feels like a wild mashup of John Wick’s relentless grit and the rugged Nordic wilderness vibe of The Revenant. Jalmari Helander’s film zeroes in on Aatami, an ex-soldier turned treasure hunter, whose discovery of gold in the Lapland wilderness quickly turns into a violent showdown with Nazi soldiers led by a ruthless SS officer. It’s a pulse-pounding, no-frills action flick, elevated by Jorma Tommila’s fierce physicality and a raw, unforgiving tone that sets it apart from your average war movie.

What makes Sisu stand out isn’t just the high-stakes chase but how it leans into the harshness of its environment—the icy desolation of Lapland becomes almost a character itself, amplifying the film’s themes of survival and unyielding determination (or “sisu,” if you will). The tagline “Vengeance is golden” nails the mix of gritty action and mythic heroism, while the battle scenes are brutal and unflinching, leaning heavily into classic revenge tropes without feeling tired. The sparse dialogue and intense visuals keep the story tight and focused, making it a solid pick for fans of minimalist but intense war thrillers.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to animal-related content: Sisu includes the deaths of a dog, a horse, and a cat, along with other animal harm and abuse, which might be distressing. Also, watch out for bugs and spiders appearing in the wilderness setting. If any of that is on your list, this isn’t a gentle ride.
emailReview:
Sisu is a lean, brutal revenge thriller that combines John Wick’s relentless grit with the icy, unforgiving wilderness of Lapland, brought to life by Jorma Tommila’s fierce physicality and a raw, minimalist style.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, horse, and cat, graphic animal harm, tense wilderness survival scenes with bugs and spiders, and relentless Nazi brutality.

name: Fallen
overview: Homicide detective John Hobbes witnesses the execution of serial killer Edgar Reese. Soon after the execution the killings start again, and they are very similar to Reese's style.
tagline: Detective John Hobbes is searching for a criminal he's already met... already caught... and already killed.

name: Monster's Ball
overview: Set in the southern USA, a racist white man, Hank, falls in love with a black woman named Leticia. Ironically, Hank is a prison guard working on Death Row who executed Leticia's husband. Hank and Leticia's inter-racial affair leads to confusion and new ideas for the two unlikely lovers.

name: Get Shorty
overview: Chili Palmer is a Miami mobster who gets sent by his boss, the psychopathic "Bones" Barboni, to collect a bad debt from Harry Zimm, a Hollywood producer who specializes in cheesy horror films. When Chili meets Harry's leading lady, the romantic sparks fly. After pitching his own life story as a movie idea, Chili learns that being a mobster and being a Hollywood producer really aren't all that different.

name: My Girl
overview: Vada Sultenfuss is obsessed with death. Her mother is dead, and her father runs a funeral parlor. She is also in love with her English teacher, and joins a poetry class over the summer just to impress him. Thomas J., her best friend, sticks with Vada despite her hangups. When Vada's father hires Shelly, and begins to fall for her, things take a turn.
tagline: When your Dad's an undertaker, your Mom's in heaven, and your Grandma's got a screw loose...it's good to have a friend who understands you. Even if he is a boy.
review:
My Girl is that bittersweet coming-of-age dramedy from the early ’90s that flirts with the macabre without ever losing its heart. It’s like a more grounded, less chaotic cousin to movies like *Ghost World* or *The Virgin Suicides*—a tender snapshot of childhood grappling with loss and first love, anchored by Anna Chlumsky’s quietly compelling performance as Vada. Macaulay Culkin’s Thomas J. is the perfect foil, a loyal friend who balances Vada’s morbid curiosity with boyish charm. It’s not exactly a laugh riot, but it’s a surprisingly warm and wistful look at growing up surrounded by death.

What really stands out is the way the film handles its heavy themes with a light touch, leaning into the awkwardness and innocence of youth. The tagline nails it: Vada’s world is shaped by death and dysfunction, but the story is really about connection—whether it’s with her best friend, her grieving father, or that summer poetry class crush. The performances are sincere, and there’s a nostalgic early-’90s vibe that’s hard to resist, especially with Jamie Lee Curtis showing up to shake things up as Shelly. The movie’s tone is a delicate blend of melancholy and humor, with moments of genuine tenderness that keep it from feeling too bleak.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one’s a bit rough on the furry and hoofed side. Multiple animals die, including a dog, a cat, and even a horse, and there’s some dog fighting depicted as well. If those kinds of scenes hit a nerve, be warned—it’s a recurring motif tied into the film’s meditation on mortality and innocence lost.
emailReview:
My Girl is a tender, bittersweet coming-of-age dramedy that balances melancholy and humor with quietly compelling performances from Anna Chlumsky and Macaulay Culkin, wrapped in a nostalgic early-’90s vibe.

Be prepared for: the deaths of a dog, a cat, and a horse, scenes of dog fighting, and a recurring focus on mortality that shapes the story’s emotional core.

name: Grave
overview: In Justine’s family everyone is a vet and a vegetarian. At 16, she’s a gifted teen ready to take on her first year in vet school, where her older sister also studies. There, she gets no time to settle: hazing starts right away. Justine is forced to eat raw meat for the first time in her life. Unexpected consequences emerge as her true self begins to form.

name: Confessions of a Dangerous Mind
overview: Television made him famous, but his biggest hits happened off screen. Television producer by day, CIA assassin by night, Chuck Barris was recruited by the CIA at the height of his TV career and trained to become a covert operative. Or so Barris said.

name: The Longest Ride
overview: The lives of a young couple intertwine with a much older man as he reflects back on a lost love while he's trapped in an automobile crash.

name: Sorry to Bother You
overview: In an alternate present-day version of Oakland, black telemarketer Cassius Green discovers a magical key to professional success – which propels him into a macabre universe.

name: Fighting With My Family
overview: Born into a tight-knit wrestling family, Paige and her brother Zak are ecstatic when they get the once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to try out for the WWE. But when only Paige earns a spot in the competitive training program, she must leave her loved ones behind and face this new cutthroat world alone. Paige's journey pushes her to dig deep and ultimately prove to the world that what makes her different is the very thing that can make her a star.
tagline: The hilarious true story of a British girl who fights a little differently.

writers: Barry Wernick, Allen Covert, Nick Swardson
name: Grandma's Boy
overview: Even though he's 35, Alex acts more like he's 13, spending his days as the world's oldest video game tester and his evenings developing the next big Xbox game. But he gets kicked out of his apartment and is forced to move in with his grandmother.
tagline: A movie that proves you're never too old to come of age.

name: Stir of Echoes
overview: After being hypnotized by his sister-in-law, Tom Witzky begins seeing haunting visions of a girl's ghost and a mystery begins to unfold around her.
tagline: In every mind there is a door that should never be opened.
review:
Stir of Echoes is a late-90s supernatural thriller that rides the line between eerie mystery and psychological horror, anchored by Kevin Bacon’s reliably grounded performance as Tom Witzky. It feels like a more restrained cousin to The Sixth Sense, with its ghostly visions and haunted pasts, but leans into hypnotic mind games rather than jump scares. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, the film’s moody atmosphere and creeping sense of dread make it a solid pick for fans of paranormal suspense who appreciate a slow burn over outright terror.

What stands out here is how the movie uses hypnosis as a gateway to unraveling a chilling mystery, playing with the idea that some doors in the mind are better left closed—the tagline nails the mood. The writing by David Koepp and Andrew Kevin Walker keeps the story tight, weaving spectral hauntings with a grounded family drama, all wrapped in a late-90s aesthetic that’s more unsettling than flashy. The supporting cast, including Kathryn Erbe and Illeana Douglas, rounds out the tension well, though it’s Bacon’s everyman vibe that keeps the film feeling relatable amidst the supernatural.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: this one contains multiple distressing moments involving animals—several pets and other creatures meet grim fates, and there’s some animal abuse depicted. If you’re wary of animal harm or death in your horror, be heavily warned here.
emailReview:
Stir of Echoes blends a moody late-90s vibe with hypnotic mind games and a grounded performance from Kevin Bacon, crafting a slow-burn supernatural thriller that’s more eerie mystery than outright horror.

Be prepared for: multiple distressing animal deaths, animal abuse, and unsettling scenes involving pets.

name: My Week with Marilyn
overview: Sir Laurence Olivier is making a movie in London. Young Colin Clark, an eager film student, wants to be involved and he navigates himself a job on the set. When film star Marilyn Monroe arrives for the start of shooting, all of London is excited to see the blonde bombshell, while Olivier is struggling to meet her many demands and acting ineptness, and Colin is intrigued by her. Colin's intrigue is met when Marilyn invites him into her inner world where she struggles with her fame, her beauty and her desire to be a great actress.

writers: Roger Spottiswoode, Walter Hill, Larry Gross, Steven E. de Souza
name: 48 Hrs.
overview: A hard-nosed cop reluctantly teams up with a wise-cracking criminal temporarily paroled to him, in order to track down a killer.

primaryTitle: Legend of the Guardians: The Owls of Ga'Hoole
writers: John Orloff, Emil Stern, Kathryn Lasky

name: Legend of the Guardians: the Owls of GaHoole

overview: Soren, a young barn owl, is kidnapped by owls of St. Aggie's, ostensibly an orphanage, where owlets are brainwashed into becoming soldiers. He and his new friends escape to the island of Ga'Hoole, to assist its noble, wise owls who fight the army being created by the wicked rulers of St. Aggie's. The film is based on the first three books in the series.
tagline: On his way to finding a legend...he will become one.

name: The Christmas Chronicles
overview: Siblings Kate and Teddy try to prove Santa Claus is real, but when they accidentally cause his sleigh to crash, they have to save Christmas.

writers: Jeffrey Hatcher, Anders Thomas Jensen, Saul Dibb, Amanda Foreman
name: The Duchess
overview: A chronicle of the life of 18th century aristocrat Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, who was reviled for her extravagant political and personal life.

name: Kids
overview: A group of bored, disaffected New York City teenagers spend a day skating, smoking, drinking, partying, deflowering virgins, and getting into fights.
tagline: Shocking. Depraved. Sickening. And they're only Kids.

name: Bottle Rocket
overview: Upon his release from a mental hospital following a nervous breakdown, the directionless Anthony joins his friend Dignan, who seems far less sane than the former. Dignan has hatched a hair-brained scheme for an as-yet-unspecified crime spree that somehow involves his former boss, the (supposedly) legendary Mr. Henry.
tagline: They're not really criminals, but everyone's got to have a dream.

name: Climax
overview: When a dance troupe is lured to an empty school, a bowl of drug-laced sangria causes their jubilant rehearsal to descend into a dark and explosive nightmare as they try to survive the night—and find who's responsible—before it's too late.
tagline: Birth and death are extraordinary experiences. Life is a fleeting pleasure.

name: All Is Lost
overview: During a solo voyage in the Indian Ocean, a veteran mariner awakes to find his vessel taking on water after a collision with a stray shipping container. With his radio and navigation equipment disabled, he sails unknowingly into a violent storm and barely escapes with his life. With any luck, the ocean currents may carry him into a shipping lane -- but, with supplies dwindling and the sharks circling, the sailor is forced to face his own mortality.

writers: Bathsheba Doran, David Mackenzie, James MacInnes, David Harrower, Mark Bomback
name: Outlaw
overview: Forced into exile by the English after being crowned King of Scotland, legendary warrior Robert the Bruce fights to reclaim the throne.
tagline: Based on the untold true story

name: Fright Night
overview: Nobody believes teenager Charley Brewster when he discovers that his suave new neighbor, Jerry Dandrige, is a vampire. So when the bloodsucker starts stalking Charley, he turns to has-been actor Peter Vincent, famed for portraying a ghoul hunter. Unfortunately for the would-be vampire slayers, Dandrige has set his sights on Charley's girlfriend.
tagline: There are some very good reasons to be afraid of the dark.
review:
Fright Night is a cult classic 80s horror-comedy that blends genuine scares with a self-aware wink, landing somewhere between the camp of Buffy and the vampire menace of Salem’s Lot. It’s not just your typical teen-vampire flick — thanks to Tom Holland’s tight direction and a strong cast led by Chris Sarandon’s charismatic vampire Jerry Dandrige, it feels elevated above the usual genre fare. The dynamic between the clueless but determined Charley Brewster and washed-up horror host Peter Vincent adds a fun, meta layer that keeps the tone light even when the stakes get dark.

What really stands out here is the balance of thrills and humor, with some memorable practical effects that have aged like a fine vintage. The tagline, “There are some very good reasons to be afraid of the dark,” nails the vibe — the film leans into classic vampire tropes with a knowing twist, and the tension ramps up nicely as Jerry’s predatory focus shifts to Charley’s girlfriend. Roddy McDowall’s Peter Vincent is a highlight, providing both comic relief and a surprisingly earnest hero in this story about disbelief and danger lurking right next door.

Heads up for animal lovers and those sensitive to animal-related content: Fright Night is heavy on that front, with multiple instances of animal deaths and harm that are upsetting and definitely not glossed over. If the idea of pets or other animals suffering is a red flag, this one deserves caution before diving in.
emailReview:
Fright Night is a cult 80s horror-comedy that perfectly blends genuine scares with cheeky humor, anchored by Chris Sarandon’s magnetic vampire and a witty dynamic that keeps things fun even when the tension climbs.

Be prepared for: multiple graphic animal deaths, pets harmed on screen, and unsettling predator-prey scenes that add a dark edge beneath the campy exterior.

name: Nineteen Eighty-Four
overview: George Orwell's novel of a totalitarian future society in which a man whose daily work is rewriting history tries to rebel by falling in love.

name: Girl With a Pearl Earring
overview: This film, adapted from a work of fiction by author Tracy Chevalier, tells a story about the events surrounding the creation of the painting "Girl With A Pearl Earring" by 17th century Dutch master Johannes Vermeer. A young peasant maid working in the house of painter Johannes Vermeer becomes his talented assistant and the model for one of his most famous works.

name: Ballerina
altName: from the world of john wick ballerina
overview: Taking place during the events of John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum, Eve Macarro begins her training in the assassin traditions of the Ruska Roma.
review:
Ballerina carves out its own niche within the John Wick universe, delivering a slick, stylized assassin origin story that fans of high-octane action won’t want to miss. It’s got that signature blend of relentless fight choreography and neon-lit grit but shifts focus onto Ana de Armas as Eve, whose training within the Ruska Roma traditions adds cultural depth and a fresh perspective to the franchise’s mythology. Think John Wick meets a dark ballet—there’s elegance in the violence, but it’s not as emotionally searing as the main series.

What stands out here is the way the film leans into its tagline, “Vengeance has a new face,” by highlighting Eve’s transformation and immersion into a shadowy world with its own rules and codes. The writing by Shay Hatten strikes a balance between terse action beats and moments that hint at a larger, more personal story behind Eve’s quest. Len Wiseman’s direction keeps the pace tight and visually arresting, though it occasionally leans too heavily on genre tropes. You’ll appreciate the supporting cast’s gravitas—Ian McShane and Anjelica Huston bring an old-school assassin vibe that grounds the madness, even if the emotional stakes don’t quite hit as hard as you’d hope.

Heads up: this one is a minefield for animal lovers. The film features multiple instances of animal deaths—including dogs, cats, horses, and more—and animal abuse is a recurring element. There are also creepy-crawly moments with spiders, snakes, and bugs. Those who are sensitive to animal harm or distressing animal scenes should definitely approach with caution.
emailReview:
Ballerina spins a stylized assassin origin story with sleek fight scenes and Ana de Armas bringing a fresh, culturally rich edge to the John Wick universe’s neon-lit chaos.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, animal abuse, and unsettling scenes with spiders and snakes.

overview: A young wannabe musician discovers he has bitten off more than he can chew when he joins an eccentric pop band led by the mysterious and enigmatic Frank.

name: The Edge

Together with the two other passengers, photographer Robert and assistant Stephen, Charles devises a plan to help them reach civilization. However, his biggest obstacle might not be the elements, or even the Kodiak bear stalking them -- it could be Robert, whom Charles suspects is having an affair with his wife and would not mind seeing him dead.
tagline: They were fighting over a woman when the plane went down. Now, their only chance for survival is each other.

overview: In Los Angeles, a wealthy man, known as Mr. Fuller, discovers a shocking secret about the world he lives in. Fearing for his life, he leaves a desperate message for a friend of his in the most unexpected place.

The story follows Nanisca (Davis), general of the all-female military unit, and her daughter Nawi, who together fought the French and neighboring tribes who violated their honor, enslaved their people and threatened to destroy everything they’ve lived for.

writers: Jared Stern, John Whittington, Jerry Siegel, Joe Shuster, Bob Kane, Bill Finger, William Moulton Marston
name: DC League of Super-Pets
overview: When Superman and the rest of the Justice League are kidnapped, Krypto the Super-Dog must convince a rag-tag shelter pack - Ace the hound, PB the potbellied pig, Merton the turtle and Chip the squirrel - to master their own newfound powers and help him rescue the superheroes.

name: Bringing Out the Dead
overview: 48 hours in the life of a burnt-out paramedic. Once called Father Frank for his efforts to rescue lives, Frank sees the ghosts of those he failed to save around every turn. He has tried everything he can to get fired, calling in sick, delaying taking calls where he might have to face one more victim he couldn't help, yet cannot quit the job on his own.
tagline: Any call can be murder, any stop can be suicide, any night can be the last.

writers: Jacques Audiard, Thomas Bidegain, Patrick DeWitt
name: The Sisters Brothers
overview: Oregon, 1851. Hermann Kermit Warm, a chemist and aspiring gold prospector, keeps a profitable secret that the Commodore wants to know, so he sends the Sisters brothers, two notorious assassins, to capture him on his way to California.
tagline: Make a killing. Make a living.
review:
The Sisters Brothers is a darkly comic Western that feels like a mashup of Coen brothers’ dry wit and a classic revenge road trip. John C. Reilly and Joaquin Phoenix as the titular brothers give a bruised but oddly tender spin on the outlaw duo trope, while Riz Ahmed’s chemist character adds an intellectual edge to the dusty chase. It’s not your typical shoot-’em-up frontier flick—it’s moodier, more reflective, and oddly funny, with Jacques Audiard’s direction giving it a European arthouse polish that sets it apart from standard Western fare.

What really sticks is how the movie balances grim violence with moments of absurdity and melancholy. The tagline, “Make a killing. Make a living,” nails the film’s mix of grim business and human survival. The chemistry between the brothers—especially Eli’s more sensitive outlook clashing with Charlie’s ruthless streak—provides the emotional core. And Jake Gyllenhaal’s John Morris, a bounty hunter of sorts, rounds out this unlikely trio with an air of mystique. The film’s tone and pacing lean into the existential weariness of the Old West, making it less about gunfights and more about the cost of violence on the soul.

Heads up for those sensitive to deeply unsettling content: the film features bestiality, which is a rare and jarring narrative element that some viewers will definitely want to know about in advance. Also, if creepy insects make your skin crawl, there are bugs present that might set off those triggers. The violence is more implied than glorified, so it’s not a bloodbath but the weirdness factor here is definitely higher than your average Western.
emailReview:
The Sisters Brothers blends Coen brothers-style dry wit with a moody, arthouse Western vibe, anchored by bruised yet tender performances from John C. Reilly and Joaquin Phoenix.

Be prepared for: bestiality, creepy insects, implied violence, and a strange, unsettling atmosphere that lingers beyond the dusty frontier.

overview: Young history buff Kevin can scarcely believe it when six dwarfs emerge from his closet one night. Former employees of the Supreme Being, they've purloined a map charting all of the holes in the fabric of time and are using it to steal treasures from different historical eras. Taking Kevin with them, they variously drop in on Napoleon, Robin Hood and King Agamemnon before the Supreme Being catches up with them.
tagline: …they didn’t make history, they stole it!

name: Whip It
overview: In Bodeen, Texas, Land Of The Dragon, an indie-rock loving misfit finds a way of dealing with her small-town misery after she discovers a roller derby league in nearby Austin.

tagline: Good is no fun at all.

overview: Sonic, Knuckles, and Tails reunite against a powerful new adversary, Shadow, a mysterious villain with powers unlike anything they have faced before. With their abilities outmatched in every way, Team Sonic must seek out an unlikely alliance in hopes of stopping Shadow and protecting the planet.

name: Black Snake Moan
overview: A God-fearing bluesman takes to a wild young woman who, as a victim of childhood sexual abuse, is looking everywhere for love, but never quite finding it.

name: Free State of Jones
overview: In 1863, Mississippi farmer Newt Knight serves as a medic for the Confederate Army. Opposed to slavery, Knight would rather help the wounded than fight the Union. After his nephew dies in battle, Newt returns home to Jones County to safeguard his family but is soon branded an outlaw deserter. Forced to flee, he finds refuge with a group of runaway slaves hiding out in the swamps. Forging an alliance with the slaves and other farmers, Knight leads a rebellion that would forever change history.
tagline: For justice. For pride. For freedom.

Together, the two travel from Portland, Oregon to Idaho and finally to the coast of Italy in a quest to find Mike's estranged mother. Along the way they turn tricks for money and drugs, eventually attracting the attention of a wealthy benefactor and sexual deviant.

Unaware of Fletch's true identity, businessman Alan Stanwyk offers Fletch $50,000 to kill him. Intrigued, Fletch decides to unearth the full story behind the offer.

With Cooper's help and her own natural instincts, Gia quickly shoots to the top of the modeling world. When Cooper dies of lung cancer, however, Gia turns to drugs – and both she and her career begin to spiral out of control.
tagline: Too beautiful to die. Too wild to live.

name: Bubba Ho-Tep
overview: Bubba Ho-tep tells the "true" story of what really did become of Elvis Presley. We find Elvis as an elderly resident in an East Texas rest home, who switched identities with an Elvis impersonator years before his "death," then missed his chance to switch back. He must team up with JFK and fight an ancient Egyptian mummy for the souls of their fellow residents.

overview: After his wife is murdered by street punks, a pacifistic New York City architect becomes a one-man vigilante squad, prowling the streets for would-be muggers after dark.

name: Women Talking
overview: Follows a group of women in an isolated Mennonite religious colony in Bolivia as they struggle to reconcile their faith with a series of sexual assaults committed by the colony’s men.

name: King of New York
overview: A former drug lord returns from prison determined to wipe out all his competition and distribute the profits of his operations to New York's poor and lower classes in this stylish and ultra violent modern twist on Robin Hood.

name: The Half of It
overview: Shy, straight-A student Ellie is hired by sweet but inarticulate jock Paul, who needs help wooing the most popular girl in school. But their new and unlikely friendship gets tricky when Ellie discovers she has feelings for the same girl.
tagline: A different kind of love story.
review:
The Half of It is a quietly charming coming-of-age rom-com that flips the usual high school love triangle on its head. It’s less about the chase and more about the awkward, tender messiness of figuring out who you are and what you want. Think of it as a thoughtful, modern update to classic teen fare like *Love, Simon* or *10 Things I Hate About You*—but with a sharper, more introspective voice thanks to Alice Wu’s writing and direction. Leah Lewis as Ellie brings a subtle vulnerability that anchors the film’s delicate emotional beats.

What really stands out is how the story uses the familiar trope of a tutoring-turned-crush scenario to explore identity and friendship in a nuanced way. Ellie’s internal conflict, caught between helping Paul and her own feelings for Aster, is handled with a refreshing honesty and no cheap drama. The film’s tagline, “A different kind of love story,” holds true—the romance is less about fireworks and more about quiet yearning and connection. Plus, the supporting cast, especially Daniel Diemer’s sweet, if somewhat clueless, Paul, adds a nice dimension to the dynamic.

Those sensitive to homophobic language should be aware that the film includes homophobic slurs, which might be uncomfortable or triggering. Aside from that, the tone remains gentle and thoughtful throughout.
emailReview:
The Half of It charms with its tender, introspective take on teenage love and identity, anchored by Leah Lewis’s quietly vulnerable performance.

Be prepared for: homophobic slurs, emotional awkwardness, and the gentle but real sting of unspoken feelings.

name: Radio
overview: High school football coach, Harold Jones befriends Radio, a mentally-challenged man who becomes a student at T.L. Hanna High School in Anderson, South Carolina. Their friendship extends over several decades, where Radio transforms from a shy, tormented man into an inspiration to his community.

name: Trust
overview: A suburban family is torn apart when fourteen-year-old Annie meets her first boyfriend online. After months of communicating via online chat and phone, Annie discovers her friend is not who he originally claimed to be. Shocked into disbelief, her parents are shattered by their daughter's actions and struggle to support her as she comes to terms with what has happened to her once innocent life.

name: Boy Erased
overview: Jared, the son of a Baptist pastor in a small American town, is outed to his parents at age 19. Jared is faced with an ultimatum: attend a gay conversion therapy program – or be permanently exiled and shunned by his family, friends, and faith.
review:
Boy Erased is a tough, emotionally charged drama that joins the wave of recent films shining a harsh light on the cruel reality of gay conversion therapy. It’s a sober, grounded portrait that feels like The Miseducation of Cameron Post meets a quieter, less sensationalized Take Me to Church. Lucas Hedges anchors the film with a quietly powerful performance as Jared, a young man caught between his identity and the rigid expectations of his evangelical family. The presence of heavy hitters like Nicole Kidman and Russell Crowe adds weight, but it’s Joel Edgerton’s direction and script that keep the story intimate and focused rather than melodramatic.

What stands out here is the film’s commitment to portraying the complexity of faith, family loyalty, and self-acceptance without resorting to simplistic good-versus-evil storytelling. The tagline, "The truth cannot be converted," nails the core theme: the brutal futility of trying to erase who someone truly is. The narrative’s quiet moments—like Jared’s internal struggles and the subtle but searing interactions with fellow program participants—linger long after the credits roll. It’s not an easy watch, but it’s elevated by its honesty and the refusal to sugarcoat the psychological damage inflicted by these programs.

Heads up for those sensitive to sexual violence and animal harm—Boy Erased includes some difficult content in both areas. The film also features scenes of restraint and general emotional trauma that are very much part of the story’s unflinching look at its subject. If any of those triggers are on your list, be prepared for a heavy dose here.
emailReview:
Boy Erased delivers a quietly powerful look at the devastating impact of gay conversion therapy, anchored by Lucas Hedges' compelling performance and Joel Edgerton’s intimate direction that avoids melodrama.

Be prepared for: sexual violence, animal harm, emotional trauma, and scenes of restraint.

name: Ravenous
overview: Upon receiving reports of missing persons at Fort Spencer, a remote Army outpost on the Western frontier, Capt. John Boyd investigates. After arriving at his new post, Boyd and his regiment aid a wounded frontiersman who recounts a horrifying tale of a wagon train murdered by its supposed guide -- a vicious U.S. Army colonel gone rogue. Fearing the worst, the regiment heads out into the wilderness to verify the gruesome claims.

name: My Old Ass
overview: Described as a “modern coming-of-age comedy”.

writers: Jean-Claude Carrière, Louise Kugelberg, Julian Schnabel
name: At Eternity's Gate
overview: Famed but tormented artist Vincent van Gogh spends his final years in Arles, France, painting masterworks of the natural world that surrounds him.

name: Up In Smoke
overview: An unemployed pot-smoking slacker and amateur drummer, Anthony Stoner ditches his strict parents and hits the road, eventually meeting kindred spirit Pedro de Pacas. While the drug-ingesting duo is soon arrested for possession of marijuana, Anthony and Pedro get released on a technicality, allowing them to continue their many misadventures and ultimately compete in a rock band contest, where they perform the raucous tune "Earache My Eye."
tagline: It will make you feel VERY funny!
review:
Up In Smoke is the stoner comedy that launched a whole wave of laid-back, dopey humor—think Cheech and Chong’s signature brand of goofy counterculture antics wrapped up in a ’70s road movie. It’s pretty much the blueprint for buddy stoner flicks to come, with its loose plot about two potheads on the run, culminating in a wild rock band contest. While it’s not the sharpest or most polished comedy, it’s undeniably funny in that slow-burning, irreverent way that fans of stoner culture will appreciate.

What stands out is the chemistry between Cheech Marin and Tommy Chong, who also co-wrote the film, giving it that authentic, lived-in vibe. The tagline “It will make you feel VERY funny!” is a cheeky promise they mostly deliver on with a mix of absurd scenarios and memorable musical moments—like the infamous “Earache My Eye” performance—which adds a raucous energy to the laid-back tone. The film leans heavily into stoner stereotypes but with a playful charm rather than mean-spiritedness, making it a cult classic that’s more about the vibe than any tightly crafted narrative.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related distress: the film includes scenes where an animal dies and features bestiality content that might catch some viewers off guard. If those triggers are on your list, approach with caution.
emailReview:
Up In Smoke is a laid-back stoner comedy that set the tone for decades of goofy counterculture humor, fueled by the undeniable chemistry of Cheech Marin and Tommy Chong and punctuated by absurd, memorable musical moments.

Be prepared for: animal death, bestiality content, and plenty of offbeat hijinks.

overview: In 1978, a Kiss concert was an epoch-making event. For the three teen fans in Detroit Rock City getting tickets to the sold-out show becomes the focal point of their existence. They'll do anything for tickets -- compete in a strip club's amateur-night contest, take on religious protesters, even rob a convenience store!

writers: Jim Schutze, David McKenna, Roger Pullis
name: Bully
overview: After finding himself at the constant abuse of his best friend Bobby, Marty has become fed up with his friend's twisted ways. His girlfriend, a victim of Bobby's often cruel ways, couldn't agree more and they strategize murdering Bobby.
tagline: It's 4 a.m... do you know where your kids are?

name: Nine to Five
overview: Frank Hart is a pig. He takes advantage in the grossest manner of the women who work with him. When his three assistants manage to trap him in his own house they assume control of his department and productivity leaps, but just how long can they keep Hart tied up?

tagline: Arthur Miller's timeless tale of truth on trial.

name: Shin Godzilla
overview: When a massive, gilled monster emerges from the deep and tears through the city, the government scrambles to save its citizens. tagline: A god incarnate. A city doomed.
review:
Shin Godzilla is a fresh, intense reboot of the classic kaiju genre that blends political thriller with monster mayhem in a way that feels both timely and uniquely Japanese. Directed by Shinji Higuchi and Hideaki Anno, it’s less about giant monster spectacle for spectacle’s sake and more about the bureaucratic chaos and human drama unfolding as a city—and a government—scrambles to respond to an evolving, terrifying force of nature. If you like your monster movies with a heavy dose of dry wit and procedural detail, this one’s a wild ride that stands apart from the usual Godzilla fare.

What really stands out here is the film’s layered approach to disaster. The tagline, “A god incarnate. A city doomed,” nails the looming dread, but the story’s strength lies in the rag-tag team navigating red tape and political inertia to find a way to stop the creature. The visuals are grim and striking, capturing the destructive scale without losing sight of the human cost. The cast, including Hiroki Hasegawa and Satomi Ishihara, ground the story in credible urgency, while the direction and writing by Anno give the monster a chilling, almost biological evolution that’s genuinely unsettling.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this one includes multiple animal deaths (dog, cat, horse) and some scenes of animal abuse that might hit hard. If things like bugs, spiders, or snakes freak you out, be aware they pop up here too, woven into the unsettling atmosphere. It’s a dense, intense film that doesn’t shy away from showing the collateral damage of Godzilla’s rampage—human and animal alike.

Upon arrival, Wilson goes to task battling Valentine and an army of L.A.'s toughest criminals, hoping to find clues and piece together what happened. After surviving a near-death beating, getting thrown from a building and being chased down a dangerous mountain road, the Englishman decides to dole out some bodily harm of his own.
review:
The Limey is a coolly stylish revenge thriller that feels like a British noir meets L.A. crime saga, with Terence Stamp delivering a quietly intense performance as Wilson, the grizzled ex-con on a mission. Steven Soderbergh’s direction keeps things lean and gritty, avoiding the usual over-the-top vengeance tropes in favor of a more measured, almost meditative tone. If you’re into crime dramas with a bit of art-house flair—think Point Blank with a dash of Soderbergh’s signature visual polish—this one’s worth a look.

What stands out is the film’s economy of storytelling and its sharp, almost elliptical editing that pieces together Wilson’s quest like a puzzle. The tagline, “Tell him I’m coming,” perfectly captures that simmering, relentless drive behind the plot. The action scenes are brutal but grounded, especially the mountain-road chase and the gritty beatings, which feel raw rather than cartoonish. The supporting cast, including Luis Guzmán and Nicky Katt, add texture without stealing focus from Stamp’s stoic lead. It’s a film that wears its revenge story on its sleeve but still manages to keep you guessing about the true cost of Wilson’s journey.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one includes several triggers related to animal harm and death, including dogs, cats, and horses, as well as some unsettling bugs and spiders. If those are on your no-go list, you’ll want to proceed carefully.

review:
UHF is a cult classic comedy that’s basically a sketch show disguised as a movie, led by “Weird Al” Yankovic’s delightfully quirky charm. It’s a goofy, low-budget love letter to the weirdness of local TV stations, filled with absurd characters and off-the-wall humor. Think of it as the wild, anarchic cousin to other ’80s comedies that celebrate underdog misfits—fans of Airplane! or The Naked Gun might appreciate its same kind of offbeat silliness, though it’s definitely less polished and more niche.

What stands out is how the film embraces its own ridiculousness, with Yankovic’s George Newman trying to save a failing UHF station by throwing every bizarre idea at the wall—from bizarre game shows to oddball sketches. Michael Richards as the endlessly enthusiastic janitor Stanley Spadowski is a particular highlight, bringing genuinely goofy heart to the chaos. The tagline, “A lot of TV stations have forgotten what ‘quality’ means, but not Channel 62. They NEVER knew what it meant,” nails the film’s self-aware, irreverent tone perfectly.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: UHF includes a surprising number of triggers involving animals—everything from pet and horse deaths to animal abuse and even dog fighting. Those who pin the animal harm or death triggers should definitely be cautious going in, as it’s a weird and sometimes uncomfortable mix in an otherwise silly comedy.

review:
Captain America: The First Avenger feels like the perfect origin story to kick off the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s Phase One—equal parts earnest wartime drama and old-school superhero spectacle. Chris Evans nails the transformation from scrawny Steve Rogers to the iconic super-soldier, making this feel less like a comic book movie and more like a classic adventure wrapped in a cape. Fans of World War II epics with a comic twist will appreciate the blend of period detail and larger-than-life heroics, though it doesn’t quite reach the emotional heights or sharp wit of later Marvel entries.

What stands out most is how the film balances its patriotic tone with genuine character moments, especially between Steve and Peggy Carter, who isn’t just a love interest but a formidable presence in her own right. The villain, Red Skull, played by Hugo Weaving, is suitably menacing, leaning hard into the campy yet chilling vibe that fits this era’s pulp sensibilities. The tagline, “The one who never gives up awakens,” sums up the film’s relentless optimism, even as it leans on familiar tropes like secret weapons and shadowy organizations. Joe Johnston’s direction keeps the pacing brisk, and the period-appropriate score adds a nice touch of nostalgic grandeur.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one’s heavy on animal-related triggers. There are multiple instances of animals dying, including a dog and a horse, and scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, so be cautious if those are on your list. Plus, if bugs, spiders, or snakes set off alarms for you, this movie doesn’t shy away from unsettling critters either. It’s a classic superhero tale, but it’s not without its darker and more unsettling moments when it comes to our furry and scaly friends.

writers: Justin Theroux, Stan Lee, Don Heck, Larry Lieber, Jack Kirby
name: Iron Man 2
overview: With the world now aware of his dual life as the armored superhero Iron Man, billionaire inventor Tony Stark faces pressure from the government, the press and the public to share his technology with the military. Unwilling to let go of his invention, Stark, with Pepper Potts and James 'Rhodey' Rhodes at his side, must forge new alliances – and confront powerful enemies.
tagline: It's not the armor that makes the hero, but the man inside.
review:
Iron Man 2 is classic Marvel popcorn fare—slick, action-packed, and buoyed by Robert Downey Jr.’s signature charisma as the genius billionaire Tony Stark. It doesn’t quite reach the fresh heights of the original, but it’s an entertaining follow-up that doubles down on the government-versus-hero tension and introduces some memorable villains, like Mickey Rourke’s brooding Ivan Vanko. If you liked the first Iron Man’s mix of smart tech and snark, you’ll find plenty here, though the story occasionally buckles under the weight of setting up the larger MCU.

What stands out here is the interplay between Stark, Pepper Potts, and Rhodey, who now gets a proper upgrade to War Machine thanks to Don Cheadle stepping in. Scarlett Johansson’s Natasha Romanoff adds a layer of intrigue, teasing the spy thriller vibe beneath the superhero capes. The film’s tagline, "It’s not the armor that makes the hero, but the man inside," sums up its core theme—Tony’s struggle isn’t just external threats but his own identity and legacy. Jon Favreau’s direction keeps the tone glossy and fast-moving, with some solid action sequences and a techno-thriller edge courtesy of Justin Theroux’s script.

Heads up for animal lovers: Iron Man 2 features multiple instances of animal deaths and distress, including dogs, cats, and horses, as well as some scenes involving animal abuse and abandonment (a pet parrot is notably left behind). If those triggers are on your list, this one might sting a bit more than your average superhero blockbuster.
emailReview:
Iron Man 2 serves up classic Marvel swagger with Robert Downey Jr.’s charm front and center, mixing slick action and a splash of spy thriller intrigue thanks to Scarlett Johansson.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths and distress involving dogs, cats, horses, as well as scenes of animal abuse and abandonment including a pet parrot.

writers: James Vanderbilt, Alvin Sargent, Steve Kloves, Stan Lee, Steve Ditko
name: The Amazing Spider-Man
overview: Peter Parker is an outcast high schooler abandoned by his parents as a boy, leaving him to be raised by his Uncle Ben and Aunt May. Like most teenagers, Peter is trying to figure out who he is and how he got to be the person he is today. As Peter discovers a mysterious briefcase that belonged to his father, he begins a quest to understand his parents' disappearance – leading him directly to Oscorp and the lab of Dr. Curt Connors, his father's former partner. As Spider-Man is set on a collision course with Connors' alter ego, The Lizard, Peter will make life-altering choices to use his powers and shape his destiny to become a hero.
review:
The Amazing Spider-Man offers a fresh spin on the classic superhero origin story, blending teen angst with science-fiction thrills. Andrew Garfield brings a brooding intensity to Peter Parker that sets this apart from the more lighthearted takes, while the film’s moodier tone and Marc Webb’s direction give it a slightly more grounded, emotional edge than your typical comic book flick. It’s not quite the game-changer some hoped for, but fans of origin stories with a bit more heart and mystery—think Spider-Man meets The Social Network—will find plenty to enjoy.

What stands out here is the film’s focus on Peter’s personal quest to understand his parents' disappearance, which adds a layer of intrigue beyond the usual “bitten by a spider” setup. The Oscorp lab scenes, with their creepy spider experiments and unsettling animal specimens, give the story a darker, almost gothic vibe. Rhys Ifans as the Lizard/Dr. Curt Connors delivers a suitably tragic villain, while the mix of science, family drama, and superhero action keeps things engaging. The tagline “The untold story begins” feels fitting, as the film leans into Peter’s identity struggles and moral choices more than just flashy set pieces.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content—there are plenty of spiders on display, some of which are shown in distress or dead, as well as lab animals undergoing genetic experiments. The movie also contains intense moments of gun violence, blood/gore, and character deaths, including a particularly emotional loss that shapes Peter’s journey. Physical restraint and scenes of choking and stabbing add to the tension, so if you’re queasy about violence or animal treatment, it’s worth approaching with caution.
emailReview:
The Amazing Spider-Man gives the classic origin story a darker, more emotional spin, with Andrew Garfield’s brooding Peter Parker and eerie lab scenes adding a gothic edge to the usual superhero thrills.

Be prepared for: distressed and dead spiders, genetic experiments on lab animals, intense gun violence, choking and stabbing, and emotional character deaths.

Jurassic World is a flashy, action-packed reboot that leans heavily into the spectacle Jurassic Park fans expect, but with a modern blockbuster sheen. It’s basically Jurassic Park meets a theme park ad campaign, with Chris Pratt’s Owen as the rugged dino-whisperer and Bryce Dallas Howard’s Claire running the business side of things. While it doesn’t quite capture the wonder and suspense of the original, it delivers enough thrills and a few nods to the past to keep dinosaur enthusiasts entertained.

What stands out here is the film’s confident embrace of spectacle over subtlety. The tagline—“The park is open”—feels both inviting and ominous, perfectly setting the tone for a story about human hubris and genetic experimentation gone awry. The visuals are impressive, especially the CGI dinosaurs, though the plot occasionally stumbles into familiar blockbuster clichés. The dynamic between Owen and Claire offers some charm, and the themes of control versus chaos are riffed on with varying degrees of success.

Heads up: Jurassic World is not light on animal-related triggers. There are multiple animal deaths, including a dog, cat, and horse, as well as scenes of animal abuse and dead animals shown on screen. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or the distress of pets and other creatures, this one could be a rough ride. The presence of bugs, spiders, snakes, and even some bestiality-related triggers also make it a notable caution for those viewers.
emailReview:
Jurassic World dazzles with blockbuster spectacle and a rugged charm from Chris Pratt, delivering enough dino thrills to satisfy fans despite its glossy theme park vibe.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and horse, on-screen animal abuse, bugs and spiders, snakes, and unsettling bestiality implications.

The standout here is how the movie uses its tagline, “Enter a new dimension of Strange,” to full effect. The multiverse concept isn’t just window dressing—it’s a playground for mind-bending visuals and narrative twists that occasionally veer into genuinely creepy territory. Elizabeth Olsen’s Scarlet Witch is a compelling and terrifying presence, elevating the stakes beyond the usual hero-villain dynamic. The supporting cast, including newcomer Xochitl Gomez as America Chavez, adds fresh energy, and the mystical battles are as inventive as they are intense. Raimi’s horror background brings in unexpected scares, making this MCU installment feel less like a standard blockbuster and more like a genre hybrid.

Heads up to those sensitive to animal-related content: this one is heavy on animal harm and death, featuring the demise of multiple creatures including pets and mythical beasts. If you’re on the lookout for animal harm or creepy critters, this film leans into both in ways that could be tough to watch.
emailReview:
Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness mixes Marvel spectacle with Sam Raimi’s cult horror flair, delivering a visually lush, unsettling journey full of mind-bending twists and a terrifying Scarlet Witch.

tagline: The beloved masterpiece comes to life.
review:
The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe is a pretty classic entry in the fantasy adventure genre, capturing that magical, timeless vibe that fans of The Lord of the Rings or Harry Potter will recognize and appreciate. It’s a solid adaptation of C.S. Lewis’s beloved book, full of wonder and chills, anchored by the iconic presence of Aslan and the icy menace of the White Witch. While it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, it’s elevated by Tilda Swinton’s chilling performance and Liam Neeson’s majestic voice work, making it more than just your average kids’ fantasy flick.

What stands out here is the blend of rich, wintry visuals and a stirring score that really sell the epic battle between good and evil. The story leans heavily into classic fantasy tropes—children-turned-heroes, talking animals, and an eternal winter that needs breaking—but it never feels stale thanks to the earnest performances and the palpable sense of stakes. The tagline, “The beloved masterpiece comes to life,” rings true, as the film captures the heart of the novel’s themes about courage, sacrifice, and redemption without getting bogged down.

That said, be heavily warned if animal death or harm is on your list—multiple animals, including a dog, cat, horse, and even a dragon, meet unfortunate ends. There’s also blood and gore, jump scares, and plenty of creepy critters like spiders and snakes lurking in the shadows. If you’re sensitive to scenes with animals in distress or sudden scares, this one can pack an emotional punch beyond just the fantasy adventure.
emailReview:
The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe enchants with its timeless fantasy atmosphere, elevated by Tilda Swinton’s icy menace and Liam Neeson’s majestic narration that bring C.S. Lewis’s world vividly to life.

overview: Instead of flying to Florida with his folks, Kevin ends up alone in New York, where he gets a hotel room with his dad's credit card—despite problems from a clerk and meddling bellboy. review:
Home Alone 2: Lost in New York cranks up the holiday mischief with Kevin McCallister navigating the Big Apple solo, wielding his dad’s credit card like a pint-sized kingpin. This sequel sticks close to the original’s slapstick blueprint—think Home Alone meets a city slicker’s Christmas—and while it’s not quite as fresh or funny as the first, it still delivers plenty of goofy traps and memorable one-liners. Fans of ’90s family comedies and the original will find familiar comfort here, though it’s hard to shake the feeling that the magic dims just a bit without the cozy Chicago backdrop.

What stands out this time is the setting: New York City itself practically becomes a character, from the Plaza Hotel to Central Park, giving Kevin’s antics a bigger, bolder stage. The Wet Bandits are back, and Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern reprise their roles with gleeful villainy, though their schemes feel more cartoonish than threatening. The screenplay by John Hughes plays it safe with heartwarming notes and the classic underdog vibe, while Chris Columbus’s direction keeps the pace brisk. The inclusion of the Pigeon Lady adds a surprisingly sweet layer to the story, offering a touch of genuine warmth amid the chaos.

Heads up for animal triggers: this movie has a surprising number of scenes involving animals that might rattle sensitive viewers—there’s a dog, a cat, even a horse, and some scenes where animals are abused or sad. If you find animal distress upsetting, you’ll want to approach with caution here.
emailReview: Home Alone 2: Lost in New York turns the Big Apple into a slapstick playground where Kevin McCallister reigns supreme with clever traps and classic ’90s charm, while Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern bring the Wet Bandits back with gleeful, cartoonish villainy. review:
28 Weeks Later is a grim and relentless follow-up to the original 28 Days Later, doubling down on the post-apocalyptic horror with more chaos and visceral intensity. It’s a pulse-pounding mix of zombie outbreak and military thriller, where the temporary calm after the storm proves dangerously deceptive. Fans of fast-moving infection tales like Train to Busan or the original Dawn of the Dead might appreciate how this one layers in family drama and moral ambiguity amidst the carnage, though it doesn’t quite hit the emotional highs of its predecessor.

What stands out here is the bleak atmosphere and the way director Juan Carlos Fresnadillo ratchets up tension with claustrophobic settings and sudden bursts of violence. The tagline “When days turn to weeks…” nails the creeping dread of a world still far from safe, even months after the worst seems to have passed. Robert Carlyle delivers a standout performance as Donald Harris, grappling with the personal cost of the outbreak, while Rose Byrne and Jeremy Renner anchor the gritty survival story. The film leans hard into genre conventions—infected hordes, government cover-ups—but also adds a layer of tragic inevitability that lingers after the credits roll.

Be heavily warned if animal harm is a major trigger for you—this one doesn’t shy away from distressing scenes involving dogs, cats, horses, and other animals. Subscribing to the “animal death” and “animal abuse” alerts is a smart move here, as the film’s raw portrayal of survival extends beyond human suffering. Also worth noting: the presence of spiders, bugs, and snakes adds to the overall sense of unease for those sensitive to creepy crawlies.
emailReview:
28 Weeks Later delivers a grim and relentless post-apocalyptic horror experience, with a claustrophobic atmosphere and standout performances that keep the tension ratcheted sky-high.
