overview: Times are changing for Manny the moody mammoth, Sid the motor mouthed sloth and Diego the crafty saber-toothed tiger. Life heats up for our heroes when they meet some new and none-too-friendly neighbors – the mighty dinosaurs.

overview: For the past 60 years, a space-traveling smart-ass named Paul has been locked up in a top-secret military base, advising world leaders about his kind. review:
Paul is a cheeky sci-fi comedy that feels like Shaun of the Dead meets E.T. if E.T. had a potty mouth and a penchant for wisecracks. Simon Pegg and Nick Frost bring their familiar nerdy charm as two sci-fi geeks who get way more than they bargained for when they pick up an alien hitchhiker voiced by Seth Rogen. The film rides that sweet spot between affectionate genre parody and outright silliness, making it a solid pick for anyone who enjoys their extraterrestrials with a side of raunchy humor.

What really stands out is the script, co-written by Pegg and Frost themselves, packed with sharp dialogue and a bunch of pop-culture nods that fans of geek culture will eat up. Paul’s sarcastic personality and the dynamic between the three leads keep the pace lively, while Greg Mottola’s direction balances the absurd moments with surprisingly heartfelt beats. It’s not just about the laughs; the film sneaks in some commentary on government secrecy and friendship, all wrapped up in a road trip adventure that’s more endearing than you’d expect.

That said, heads up—this one comes with a pretty unique trigger: bestiality. It’s not exactly a common warning, but it’s there. So if that’s a sensitive area for you, proceed with caution. Otherwise, Paul delivers a fun, offbeat ride for sci-fi fans who don’t mind their aliens a bit irreverent.

Crank is a high-octane action flick that feels like a caffeine shot to the heart—Jason Statham’s Chev Chelios has to keep his adrenaline pumping or die. It’s a wild ride of hyperkinetic energy, equal parts absurd and thrilling, sliding easily into the “so-bad-it’s-good” cult category alongside movies like Crank’s own sequel or Transporter if it’d been directed by a madman with a GoPro. Fans of relentless pacing and no-breathing-room storytelling will appreciate the sheer commitment to chaos here.

What really stands out about Crank is its refusal to slow down—not just in plot, but in style. The tagline promises a thousand ways to raise your adrenaline, and the film delivers with inventive set pieces, frantic camerawork, and a pulsing electronic score that matches Chev’s frantic heartbeat. The poison premise adds a neat twist to the standard assassin revenge story, turning the ticking clock into a throttle rather than a countdown. Amy Smart’s Eve provides a grounding presence, but this is very much Statham’s manic playground, with a supporting cast that adds color but rarely steals the spotlight.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one leans heavily into animal harm triggers. A dog, a cat, a horse, and even a pet bird meet unfortunate ends, some played for dark humor but all pretty blunt. If seeing animals in distress or dying on screen is a nonstarter, be heavily warned here.

Crank is a relentless adrenaline rush of chaotic energy and wild style, with Jason Statham delivering a manic performance that keeps the momentum at breakneck speed.

name: Clueless
overview: Shallow, rich and socially successful Cher is at the top of her Beverly Hills high school's pecking scale. Seeing herself as a matchmaker, Cher first coaxes two teachers into dating each other. Emboldened by her success, she decides to give hopelessly klutzy new student Tai a makeover. When Tai becomes more popular than she is, Cher realizes that her disapproving ex-stepbrother was right about how misguided she was -- and falls for him.
tagline: Sex. Clothes. Popularity. Is there a problem here?

writers: Carlos Saldanha, Earl Richey Jones, Todd R. Jones, Don Rhymer, Joshua Sternin, Jennifer Ventimilia, Sam Harper
name: Rio
overview: Captured by smugglers when he was just a hatchling, a macaw named Blu never learned to fly and lives a happily domesticated life in Minnesota with his human friend, Linda. Blu is thought to be the last of his kind, but when word comes that Jewel, a lone female, lives in Rio de Janeiro, Blu and Linda go to meet her. Animal smugglers kidnap Blu and Jewel, but the pair soon escape and begin a perilous adventure back to freedom -- and Linda.
tagline: 1 out of every 8 Americans is afraid of flying. Most of them don't have feathers.
review:
Rio is a colorful, upbeat animated adventure that mixes the charm of a fish-out-of-water story with a tropical samba soundtrack—and a dash of environmental awareness. It’s the kind of family-friendly romp that leans heavily on its starry voice cast, including Jesse Eisenberg as the neurotic Blu and Anne Hathaway as the feisty Jewel. If you like your animated films with a side of romance and a splash of Brazilian flair, think of this as a lighter, bird-centric cousin to movies like Madagascar or Happy Feet.

What stands out here is the vibrant depiction of Rio de Janeiro, which practically dances off the screen, and the way Blu’s journey tackles themes of freedom, friendship, and overcoming fears. The tagline—“1 out of every 8 Americans is afraid of flying. Most of them don’t have feathers.”—sums up the film’s playful tone nicely. The story’s heart comes from Blu’s struggle to find his wings (literally), set against the backdrop of some surprisingly tense moments involving animal smugglers that keep the stakes from feeling too fluffy.

That said, heads up to anyone sensitive to animal harm or death—there are multiple instances where animals are hurt, abandoned, or die, including pets and wildlife. The presence of spiders, snakes, and bugs might also make some squirm. While the movie keeps things mostly lighthearted, those triggers are definitely woven through the adventure, so approach with caution if those themes hit close to home.
emailReview:
Rio bursts with vibrant colors, catchy samba tunes, and a charismatic voice cast that brings a playful bird-centric adventure to life with charm and heart.

Be prepared for: animal smuggling violence, multiple animal deaths and abandonment, spiders, snakes, and bug encounters.

name: The Hitman's Bodyguard
overview: The world top bodyguard gets a new client, a hit man who must testify at the International Court of Justice. They must put their differences aside and work together to make it to the trial on time.
tagline: Everyone's out to get them... If they don't kill each other first.

writers: Akira Kurosawa, Shinobu Hashimoto, Hideo Oguni, Nic Pizzolatto, Richard Wenk
name: The Magnificent Seven
overview: Looking to mine for gold, greedy industrialist Bartholomew Bogue seizes control of the Old West town of Rose Creek. With their lives in jeopardy, Emma Cullen and other desperate residents turn to bounty hunter Sam Chisolm for help. Chisolm recruits an eclectic group of gunslingers to take on Bogue and his ruthless henchmen. With a deadly showdown on the horizon, the seven mercenaries soon find themselves fighting for more than just money once the bullets start to fly.

name: Rocky IV
overview: After iron man Drago, a highly intimidating 6-foot-5, 261-pound Soviet athlete, kills Apollo Creed in an exhibition match, Rocky comes to the heart of Russia for 15 pile-driving boxing rounds of revenge.
tagline: He's facing the ultimate challenge. And fighting for his life.

name: Enemy
overview: A mild-mannered college professor discovers a look-alike actor and delves into the other man's private affairs.
review:
Enemy is a haunting psychological thriller that feels like David Lynch’s surrealism meets a Kafkaesque identity crisis, with Jake Gyllenhaal delivering a quietly intense dual performance as Adam and Anthony. Directed by Denis Villeneuve before he became a sci-fi heavyweight, this 2013 film stands out for its eerie atmosphere and unsettling ambiguity rather than straightforward scares or twists. It’s less about plot and more about mood, making it a slow burn that fans of cerebral, unsettling cinema will appreciate — though it’s not for those wanting clear answers or a conventional narrative.

What really sticks with you is the film’s relentless exploration of doubling and internal conflict, wrapped in a grim, almost monochromatic palette that mirrors the murky psychological terrain. The tagline, "You can’t escape yourself," nails the existential dread that permeates every scene. The writing is sparse but loaded with symbolism, supported by a brooding score that amplifies the tension without ever overwhelming. Mélanie Laurent and Sarah Gadon add depth to the tangled relationships, but it’s Gyllenhaal’s twin roles that anchor the film’s eerie, dreamlike quality.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm triggers: Enemy features several distressing scenes involving animals, including a dog, a cat, and a horse dying, as well as animal abuse and even dog fighting. There are also unsettling insect and spider appearances, plus some harsh moments like vomiting and someone getting hit by a car. If any of those are on your watchlist, it’s definitely a film where you’ll want to stay alert.
emailReview:
Enemy is a haunting psychological thriller where Jake Gyllenhaal’s dual performance anchors a surreal, dreamlike atmosphere thick with existential dread and eerie symbolism.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, cat, and horse, scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, unsettling insects and spiders, vomiting, and a hit-and-run incident.

name: Rocky III
overview: Now the world champion, Rocky Balboa is living in luxury and only fighting opponents who pose no threat to him in the ring, until Clubber Lang challenges him to a bout. After taking a pounding from Lang, the humbled champ turns to former bitter rival Apollo Creed for a rematch with Lang.

name: Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves
overview: When the dastardly Sheriff of Nottingham murders Robin's father, the legendary archer vows vengeance. To accomplish his mission, Robin joins forces with a band of exiled villagers (and comely Maid Marian), and together they battle to end the evil sheriff's reign of terror.

name: Legend
overview: Suave, charming and volatile, Reggie Kray and his unstable twin brother Ronnie start to leave their mark on the London underworld in the 1960s. Using violence to get what they want, the siblings orchestrate robberies and murders while running nightclubs and protection rackets. With police Detective Leonard "Nipper" Read hot on their heels, the brothers continue their rapid rise to power and achieve tabloid notoriety.
tagline: Love, fight, live, rule like a legend.

name: Crazy Rich Asians
overview: An American-born Chinese economics professor accompanies her boyfriend to Singapore for his best friend's wedding, only to get thrust into the lives of Asia's rich and famous.
tagline: The only thing crazier than love is family.

name: Cinderella
overview: When her father unexpectedly passes away, young Ella finds herself at the mercy of her cruel stepmother and her daughters. Never one to give up hope, Ella's fortunes begin to change after meeting a dashing stranger in the woods.

name: Yesterday
overview: Jack Malik is a struggling singer-songwriter in an English seaside town whose dreams of fame are rapidly fading, despite the fierce devotion and support of his childhood best friend, Ellie. After a freak bus accident during a mysterious global blackout, Jack wakes up to discover that he's the only person on Earth who can remember The Beatles.
tagline: Everyone in the world has forgotten The Beatles. Everyone except Jack…

name: Adventureland
overview: In the summer of 1987, a college graduate takes a 'nowhere' job at his local amusement park, only to find it's the perfect course to get him prepared for the real world.
tagline: It was the worst job they ever imagined… and the best time of their lives.

name: The Wedding Singer
overview: Robbie, a local rock star turned wedding singer, is dumped on the day of his wedding. Meanwhile, waitress Julia finally sets a wedding date with her fiancée Glenn. When Julia and Robbie meet and hit it off, they find that things are more complicated than anybody thought.

writers: Robert E. Howard, John Milius, Oliver Stone, Edward Summer
name: Conan the Barbarian
overview: A horde of rampaging warriors massacre the parents of young Conan and enslave the young child for years on The Wheel of Pain. As the sole survivor of the childhood massacre, Conan is released from slavery and taught the ancient arts of fighting. Transforming himself into a killing machine, Conan travels into the wilderness to seek vengeance on Thulsa Doom, the man responsible for killing his family. In the wilderness, Conan takes up with the thieves Valeria and Subotai. The group comes upon King Osric, who wants the trio of warriors to help rescue his daughter who has joined Doom in the hills.
review:
Conan the Barbarian is a classic sword-and-sorcery epic that’s as much about muscle-bound myth-making as it is about brutal revenge. This 1982 film, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger in his breakout role, feels like Conan meets a gritty spaghetti western—savage, mythic, and unapologetically macho. While it’s not exactly subtle or nuanced, it’s elevated by John Milius’s direction and the iconic presence of James Earl Jones as the villainous Thulsa Doom. Fans of old-school fantasy with a heavy dose of ‘80s action will find a lot to chew on here, even if the pacing can drag and the dialogue sometimes leans into camp.

What stands out most is the blend of raw physicality and almost operatic storytelling. The tagline—“Thief. Warrior. Gladiator. King.”—perfectly captures Conan’s journey from enslaved child to unstoppable force. The film’s themes of vengeance and survival are straightforward but effective, and the supporting characters, especially Valeria and Subotai, add some much-needed depth and camaraderie. The score and visuals lean heavily into that grim, barbaric world, with memorable scenes that have stuck in the pop culture imagination ever since. It’s a fantasy tale that doesn’t shy away from blood and grit, making the mythology feel lived-in and dangerous.

Trigger-wise, this film is a wild ride for anyone sensitive to animal harm. There are multiple instances of animals dying or being abused, including horses and dogs, and the behind-the-scenes reports about real-life mistreatment during the making add a heavy weight. If you’re on the lookout for animal-related triggers, especially those involving death or abuse, Conan the Barbarian should be approached with caution. Additionally, the presence of snakes and bugs might unsettle some viewers.
emailReview:
Conan the Barbarian is a savage, mythic sword-and-sorcery epic that pairs Arnold Schwarzenegger’s raw physicality with a grim, operatic tale of vengeance and survival.

Be prepared for: multiple scenes of animal death and abuse including horses and dogs, snake attacks, and unsettling insect encounters.

writers: Domee Shi, Julia Cho, Sarah Streicher
name: Turning Red
overview: Thirteen-year-old Mei is experiencing the awkwardness of being a teenager with a twist – when she gets too excited, she transforms into a giant red panda.

writers: David Kirschner, Mick Garris, Neil Cuthbert
name: Hocus Pocus
overview: After 300 years of slumber, three sister witches are accidentally resurrected in Salem on Halloween night, and it is up to three kids and their newfound feline friend to put an end to the witches' reign of terror once and for all.
tagline: It's just a bunch of Hocus Pocus.
review:
Hocus Pocus is the quintessential '90s Halloween romp that’s become a cult classic for a reason. It’s a breezy blend of family-friendly fantasy, slapstick comedy, and just the right amount of spooky, with Bette Midler leading the charge as the delightfully wicked Winifred Sanderson. If you’re into movies that feel like a candy-coated mash-up of classic witches-meet-kids adventure and nostalgic seasonal fun, this one fits right in—though it’s not exactly high art, it’s undeniably charming and full of memorable moments.

What really sticks is the trio of sister witches, each bringing a distinct flavor of mischief and mayhem that keeps the story lively. The tagline, “It’s just a bunch of Hocus Pocus,” nails the film’s playful tone—there’s no pretense here, just lighthearted fun with a sprinkle of Halloween magic. The kids and their feline sidekick add a nice dynamic, making the witches’ resurrection feel like a spirited, if predictable, race against time. Kenny Ortega’s direction keeps the pace snappy, and the cast delivers with enough energy to carry the film through its campy twists and turns.

Heads up for animal lovers: the film features multiple upsetting moments involving animals, including the death of pets and other creatures, which might be hard to watch. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or death, this one could be a rough ride despite its otherwise playful vibe. Also, expect creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes to show up, adding to the Halloween atmosphere but potentially triggering for some.
emailReview:
Hocus Pocus is a charming '90s Halloween classic that mixes slapstick comedy with a playful witches-meet-kids adventure, led by Bette Midler’s delightfully wicked performance.

Be prepared for: pet deaths, animal harm, spiders, snakes, and spooky creepy crawlies.

overview: Four adopted brothers return to their Detroit hometown when their mother is murdered and vow to exact revenge on the killers.
tagline: They came home to bury mom... and her killer

primaryTitle: Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
writers: Josh Friedman, Rick Jaffa, Amanda Silver
Title_IMDb_Link: Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
name: Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
cleanNameArticles: kingdom of the planet of the apes
overview: Several generations in the future following Caesar's reign, apes are now the dominant species and live harmoniously while humans have been reduced to living in the shadows. As a new tyrannical ape leader builds his empire, one young ape undertakes a harrowing journey that will cause him to question all that he has known about the past and to make choices that will define a future for apes and humans alike.
tagline: No one can stop the reign.
review:
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes feels like a darker, more sprawling continuation of the franchise’s legacy, leaning hard into its dystopian sci-fi roots while adding a new generational saga to the mix. Wes Ball directs with a clear eye for epic scope, and the story’s focus on a young ape’s rebellion against a tyrannical leader fits snugly among recent wave of post-apocalyptic tales with a political edge. It’s not quite as groundbreaking as the original Caesar trilogy, but it’s a solid, ambitious entry that fans of the series and thoughtful sci-fi will appreciate.

What stands out here is the layering of ape society mythology with themes of power, legacy, and identity. The tagline, "No one can stop the reign," hints at a grim inevitability that the film leans into, exploring how power corrupts even in a supposedly harmonious world. The cast, including Owen Teague and Kevin Durand, brings some grit to their roles, although the real star remains the world-building and visual effects that capture this post-human landscape. The film doesn’t shy away from harsh realities, forcing its protagonist to question everything he’s been taught—which makes for some genuinely tense and thought-provoking moments.

On the trigger front, be heavily warned if animal harm or death is a concern. Multiple animals—dogs, cats, horses, and other creatures—die on screen or are depicted in distressing situations, including some scenes of abuse and dog fighting. Spiders, snakes, bugs, and other critters appear as well, which might unsettle sensitive viewers. If you’re sensitive to animal-related content, this one’s a tough watch in that department.
emailReview:
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes delivers a dark, sprawling saga with impressive world-building and a gritty look at power and legacy in a post-apocalyptic ape society.

Be prepared for: multiple on-screen deaths of dogs, cats, and horses, scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, as well as unsettling appearances by spiders, snakes, and bugs.

name: The Firm
overview: Mitch McDeere is a young man with a promising future in Law. About to sit his Bar exam, he is approached by 'The Firm' and made an offer he doesn't refuse. The FBI contact him, asking him for information and suddenly his life is ruined. He has a choice - work with the FBI, or stay with the Firm. Either way he will lose his life as he knows it. Mitch figures the only way out is to follow his own plan...
tagline: Power can be murder to resist.

name: The Autopsy of Jane Doe
overview: Father and son coroners receive a mysterious unidentified corpse with no apparent cause of death. As they attempt to examine the beautiful young "Jane Doe," they discover increasingly bizarre clues that hold the key to her terrifying secrets.
review:
The Autopsy of Jane Doe is a lean, claustrophobic horror thriller that sneaks up on you with a slow boil rather than cheap jump scares. It’s part procedural mystery, part supernatural puzzle, evoking vibes of The Ring’s creeping dread and the eerie intimacy of a morgue-set thriller. While it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, director André Øvredal crafts a tense, smartly paced descent into horror that fans of atmospheric chills will appreciate more than those looking for gore-heavy frights.

What stands out is the film’s tight focus on the father-son coroners, played with solid gravitas by Brian Cox and Emile Hirsch, whose dynamic adds weight to the increasingly bizarre and unsettling discoveries about the enigmatic Jane Doe. The tagline, “Every body has a secret,” hits home as the autopsy reveals uncanny clues that escalate the tension and mystery. The writing leans into body horror without going overboard, and the confined setting amps up the claustrophobia, making the weird, otherworldly elements land with a satisfying creepiness.

Be heavily warned if animal deaths are sensitive for you—there’s a series of upsetting scenes involving various animals, including a dog, cat, and horse. Also, viewers wary of body horror or creepy crawlies (bugs, spiders, snakes) should proceed with caution. The film doesn’t shy away from unsettling imagery and some grim moments that could catch you off guard if you’re not prepared.
emailReview:
The Autopsy of Jane Doe is a claustrophobic horror gem that builds tension through a slow-burning mystery and the compelling chemistry of its lead coroners, creating a chilling atmosphere that lingers long after the credits.

Be prepared for: unsettling animal deaths including a dog, cat, and horse, intense body horror, and creepy crawlies like bugs, spiders, and snakes.

tagline: Horton hears more than anyone believes.

writers: Richard Wenk, Michael Sloan, Richard Lindheim
name: The Equalizer 3
overview: Third film in The Equalizer franchise.
review:
The Equalizer 3 rounds out the franchise with more of the same: Denzel Washington’s Robert McCall doling out vigilante justice with steely calm and brutal precision. It’s classic Antoine Fuqua directing — gritty, no-nonsense action that hits the familiar beats fans expect but doesn’t stray far from the formula. If you liked the first two, this will feel like a solid if predictable continuation; if you’re new, it’s basically John Wick meets a modern-day Western with a moral compass. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but Washington’s presence still elevates the material above run-of-the-mill action flicks.

What stands out here is the tagline, “Justice knows no borders,” which hints at a broader scope, and the cast adds some interesting flavor with Dakota Fanning and Eugenio Mastrandrea joining the fray. The story stays firmly in McCall’s wheelhouse — a man who takes down bad guys with a mix of brains and brawn — but the film leans into themes of loyalty, sacrifice, and the cost of vengeance. Fuqua’s direction keeps things taut, and the writing by Richard Wenk delivers the tough-guy dialogue and set-piece violence that the series is known for, though it doesn’t break new ground.

Heads up for sensitive viewers: this one is heavy on animal-related triggers — dogs, cats, horses, and other animals die or are abused — which is unusual for an action film but very much present here. There are also deaths involving children and some unsettling insect and snake appearances. If any of those are on your list, this installment demands caution.
emailReview:
Denzel Washington returns with steely calm and brutal precision in this gritty, no-nonsense finale that blends John Wick energy with a modern Western moral code.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths and abuse including dogs, cats, and horses, child fatalities, and unsettling scenes involving insects and snakes.

tagline: Demon to some. Angel to others.

With the use of Rufus' time machine, Bill and Ted travel to various points in history, returning with important figures to help them complete their final history presentation.

name: Swiss Army Man
overview: Alone on a tiny deserted island, Hank has given up all hope of ever making it home again. But one day everything changes when a dead body washes ashore, and he soon realizes it may be his last opportunity to escape certain death. Armed with his new “friend” and an unusual bag of tricks, the duo go on an epic adventure to bring Hank back to the woman of his dreams.
tagline: We all need some body to lean on.

name: One Hour Photo
overview: Sy Parrish has lovingly developed photographs for the Yorkin family since their son was a baby. But as the Yorkins' lives become fuller, Sy's only seems lonelier, until he eventually convinces himself he's part of their family. When Sy's picture-perfect fantasy collides with an ugly dose of reality, a bizarre and thrilling confrontation ensues.
tagline: The things that we fear the most have already happened to us...

name: A Christmas Carol
overview: Miser Ebenezer Scrooge is awakened on Christmas Eve by spirits who reveal to him his own miserable existence, what opportunities he wasted in his youth, his current cruelties, and the dire fate that awaits him if he does not change his ways. Scrooge is faced with his own story of growing bitterness and meanness, and must decide what his own future will hold: death or redemption.
tagline: It only takes one night to change your life.
review:
Robert Zemeckis’s 2009 take on *A Christmas Carol* is a visually ambitious retelling of the Dickens classic, blending moody CGI with a star-studded cast led by Jim Carrey in multiple voice roles. It’s a familiar story about redemption and the spirit of Christmas, delivered with a kind of spooky, almost haunted vibe that feels like *The Polar Express* meets *The Nightmare Before Christmas*—a bit dark for a holiday tale but fitting for Scrooge’s grim journey. While it’s not the warmest or most heartfelt version out there, Carrey’s energetic vocal performances keep things lively enough to hold your attention.

What stands out here is the film’s immersive atmosphere and the way the animation accentuates the bleakness of Scrooge’s world. The tagline, “It only takes one night to change your life,” sums up the emotional thrust, as Scrooge is forced to confront his past, present, and future in a nightmarish parade of regret and possibility. The voices of Gary Oldman and Colin Firth add a nice touch of gravitas, especially as Scrooge’s family and victims. The visuals lean into the ghostly and unforgiving nature of Dickens’s tale, with some chilling moments that emphasize the cost of Scrooge’s bitterness.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal distress: there’s a brief but unsettling scene where a rat is chased and threatened with a fire poker, though it’s left ambiguous whether it survives. Also, the film features the sight of dead poultry being carried and shown in a few scenes, which might be a turn-off for some. If those kinds of moments are on your no-go list, you’ll want to be cautious.
emailReview:
Robert Zemeckis’s *A Christmas Carol* is a visually moody retelling with Jim Carrey’s lively voice work bringing energy to a ghostly, almost haunted holiday tale that’s more spooky than sweet.

Be prepared for: a rat threatened with a fire poker, the sight of dead poultry, and an overall bleak, unsettling atmosphere.

name: Nymphomaniac: Vol. I
overview: A man named Seligman finds a fainted wounded woman in an alley and he brings her home. She tells him that her name is Joe and that she is nymphomaniac. Joe tells her life and sexual experiences with hundreds of men since she was a young teenager while Seligman tells about his hobbies, such as fly fishing, reading about Fibonacci numbers or listening to organ music.

name: Safety Not Guaranteed
overview: Three magazine employees head out on an assignment to interview a guy who placed a classified ad seeking a companion for time travel.
tagline: What would you go back for?

name: Bombshell
overview: Bombshell is a revealing look inside the most powerful and controversial media empire of all time; and the explosive story of the women who brought down the infamous man who created it.

writers: Richard Maibaum, John Hopkins, Jack Whittingham, Kevin McClory, Ian Fleming
name: Thunderball
overview: A criminal organization has obtained two nuclear bombs and are asking for a 100 million pound ransom in the form of diamonds in seven days or they will use the weapons. The secret service sends James Bond to the Bahamas to once again save the world.
tagline: Look up! Look down! Look out! Here comes the biggest Bond of all!
review:
Thunderball is classic 1960s Bond at its most lavish and bombastic—a sun-soaked spy thriller where Sean Connery’s suave secret agent is up against a nuclear ransom demand in the Bahamas. It’s the kind of globe-trotting, gadget-fueled escapism that defined the early Bond era, sitting comfortably alongside Goldfinger and From Russia with Love, though it leans harder into underwater spectacle and extended action set pieces. Fans of Connery’s Bond will appreciate the familiar charm, even if the pacing sometimes feels like it’s stretching to fill the runtime.

What really stands out here is the underwater cinematography, which was groundbreaking at the time and remains a highlight—there’s a certain campy thrill in watching Bond scuba dive through explosions and shootouts. The supporting cast, including Claudine Auger as Domino and Luciana Paluzzi as the sultry Fiona Volpe, bring that 60s Bond mix of glamour and danger. The tagline “Look up! Look down! Look out!” perfectly captures the film’s kinetic energy, though the story itself is pretty straightforward: save the world before it blows up. Terence Young’s direction keeps things stylish, even when the plot feels like a checklist of spy tropes.

That said, a serious warning for animal lovers: Thunderball’s production involved real harm to marine life, with footage showing sharks being harpooned and killed. It’s gruesome and deeply unsettling, especially knowing these scenes aren’t just special effects but actual animal cruelty. Anyone sensitive to animal harm should be heavily warned before watching.
emailReview:
Thunderball delivers classic 1960s Bond charm with Sean Connery’s suave performance and groundbreaking underwater action that still dazzles decades later.

Be prepared for: real shark killings, harpooning, animal cruelty, and tense underwater violence.

overview: Bumbling cop Frank Drebin is out to foil the big boys in the energy industry, who intend to suppress technology that will put them out of business.
tagline: If you see only one movie this year... you ought to get out more often.
review:
The Naked Gun 2½: The Smell of Fear is classic Leslie Nielsen slapstick at its goofiest and most relentless. This 1991 sequel leans hard into the franchise’s signature blend of absurdity and deadpan delivery, with Nielsen’s bumbling Lt. Frank Drebin once again stumbling through a convoluted plot about sabotaging shady energy tycoons. It’s pretty much what you’d expect if you like your comedy with a side of surreal one-liners and physical gags—think Airplane! meets a police procedural that forgot to be serious. Not as fresh as the original but still a wild ride for fans of goofy police spoofs.

What really sticks out here is the way the film parodies corporate greed and conspiracy theory staples without ever losing its silly tone. The tagline, “If you see only one movie this year… you ought to get out more often,” nails the self-aware, jokey vibe perfectly. The cast, including Priscilla Presley and George Kennedy, rounds out a quirky ensemble that plays their parts straight enough to let the comedy land. Plus, David Zucker’s direction keeps the pacing brisk, with plenty of slapstick moments and ridiculous set pieces that keep the laughs coming even when the plot meanders.

Heads up: this one is heavy on animal-related triggers. Expect some upsetting scenes involving dead animals (including a dog and a horse), animal abuse, and even dog fighting. There are also bugs, spiders, and snakes making appearances, plus a mention of sexual assault. If those are on your list, brace yourself—this comedy isn’t shy about tossing in some uncomfortable moments alongside the laughs.
emailReview:
Leslie Nielsen’s slapstick charm shines through in this absurdly goofy sequel, blending surreal one-liners with relentless physical comedy that keeps the laughs coming even when the plot wanders.

Be prepared for: dead dog, horse death, animal abuse, dog fighting, and unsettling mentions of sexual assault.

tagline: A story about love at second sight.

name: Addams Family Values
overview: Siblings Wednesday and Pugsley Addams will stop at nothing to get rid of Pubert, the new baby boy adored by parents Gomez and Morticia. Things go from bad to worse when the new "black widow" nanny, Debbie Jellinsky, launches her plan to add Fester to her collection of dead husbands.
tagline: The family just got a little stranger.
review:
Addams Family Values leans hard into dark comedy territory with that trademark offbeat charm that made the original Addams Family movie a cult classic. It’s a wild, twisted sibling rivalry sitcom-meets-murder-mystery, with Christina Ricci’s Wednesday Addams stealing the show as usual. The film rides the wave of ’90s quirky comedies but spices things up with genuinely sharp wit and a delightfully macabre tone. Joan Cusack’s Debbie Jellinsky is a scene-stealer as the “black widow” nanny, adding a deliciously sinister edge to the family’s already off-kilter dynamic.

What really stands out is how the film balances its gothic aesthetic with a clever script by Paul Rudnick and Barry Sonnenfeld’s direction, which keeps the weirdness both visually engaging and tonally consistent. The tagline, “The family just got a little stranger,” perfectly sums up the chaos that ensues when the new baby, Pubert, arrives and the kids plot to get rid of him. Meanwhile, Debbie’s dark plan to nab Uncle Fester adds a layer of murderous farce that feels both campy and wickedly funny. The supporting cast, including Anjelica Huston and Raúl Juliá, bring a warmth that contrasts nicely with the morbid humor.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content—this one’s loaded. The film features several animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and even a dragon (sort of), as well as creepy-crawly bugs and spiders. If you’re queasy about animal harm or death, this might not be the lighthearted spooky romp you’re expecting. There’s also some body horror and a fair share of gross-out moments (hello, vomiting), plus a bit of gaslighting. If those trigger categories are on your radar, you’ll want to tread carefully here.
emailReview:
Addams Family Values doubles down on quirky ’90s dark comedy with Christina Ricci’s Wednesday shining in a twisted sibling rivalry full of sharp wit and delightfully macabre moments.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and cats, creepy bugs and spiders, body horror, vomiting, and some gaslighting.

name: Final Destination: Bloodlines
overview:
Sixth film in the Final Destination franchise.

Plagued by a violent recurring nightmare, college student Stefanie heads home to track down the one person who might be able to break the cycle and save her family from the grisly demise that inevitably awaits them all.
review:
Final Destination: Bloodlines sticks to the franchise’s well-worn formula of death’s inevitability with a dash of family drama, but it’s got enough fresh blood to keep fans engaged. This sixth installment leans into the nightmare-fueled horror angle, blending the usual inventive death traps with a more personal story about Stefanie Reyes trying to break a deadly family curse. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but it’s a solid addition that feels like Final Destination meets a supernatural family thriller. If you’ve enjoyed previous entries, especially those with a tighter emotional core, this one will hit the right notes.

What stands out here is the focus on Stefanie’s recurring nightmare and its impact on her family, which adds a layer of psychological tension to the usual body count. The tagline “Death runs in the family” isn’t just clever marketing—it reflects the film’s theme of inherited fate and the struggle to escape it. Directors Zach Lipovsky and Adam B. Stein keep the pacing brisk, and the cast, led by Kaitlyn Santa Juana, brings enough sincerity to sell the stakes. The movie leans heavily on jump scares and visceral moments, typical of the series, but the nightmare sequences and the search for a “cure” add some atmospheric flair.

Heads up for those sensitive to graphic violence and distressing themes: this film doesn’t shy away from blood and gore, mutilations, and some truly unsettling deaths—including someone burned alive. Animal lovers should brace themselves, as there’s the death of a dog and other animal harm. Plus, jump scares and flashing lights are frequent, so those triggers are definitely in play. This one’s a wild ride for horror fans but not for the faint of heart.
emailReview:
Final Destination: Bloodlines mixes the franchise’s signature inventive death traps with a fresh psychological edge, turning nightmares and family curses into a tense supernatural thriller.

Be prepared for: graphic mutilations, a dog death, a character burned alive, jump scares, and flashing lights.

writers: Gillian Flynn, Steve McQueen, Lynda La Plante
name: Widows
overview: A police shootout leaves four thieves dead during an explosive armed robbery attempt in Chicago. Their widows have nothing in common except a debt left behind by their spouses' criminal activities. Hoping to forge a future on their own terms, they join forces to pull off a heist.
tagline: Left with nothing. Capable of anything.
review:
Widows is a slick, tense heist thriller with a sharp social edge, blending the gritty crime drama vibes of something like *The Town* with the fierce, female-driven power of *Ocean’s 8*—only way darker and smarter. Steve McQueen’s direction, paired with Gillian Flynn’s writing, keeps the stakes high and the characters complex, anchored by Viola Davis’s commanding turn as Veronica Rawlings. It’s not just about the heist mechanics; it’s a story about survival, power, and what it means to pick up the pieces after trauma, which elevates it above your average caper flick.

What stands out most is how the film weaves political tension and personal struggle into the narrative. The widows’ attempt to rewrite their destinies is underscored by a Chicago setting that feels as much a character as the cast, with class conflict and corruption simmering beneath the surface. The ensemble cast, including Michelle Rodriguez, Elizabeth Debicki, and Cynthia Erivo, bring a mix of raw grit and layered vulnerability that keeps you invested beyond the explosions and gunfire. The tagline, "Left with nothing. Capable of anything," really nails the spirit of desperate empowerment driving the plot.

Be heavily warned if animal harm is a sensitive topic for you. The film features multiple instances where animals die or are abused, including dogs, cats, horses, and even a dragon (yes, a dragon), plus scenes involving dog fighting. These moments are tough and unflinching, so if that’s on your list, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Widows is a smart, gritty heist thriller powered by Viola Davis’s fierce performance and a Chicago backdrop thick with political tension and raw emotion.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, horses, a dragon, and intense scenes of dog fighting.

name: Thirteen
overview: Tracy is a normal 13-year-old trying to make it in school. After befriending the most popular girl at school, Evie, Tracy's world is turned upside down when Evie introduces her to a world of sex, drugs and cash. But it isn't long before Tracy's new world and attitude finally takes a toll on her, her family, and old friends.
review:
Thirteen is a raw, unflinching coming-of-age drama that feels like a grittier, more unsettling counterpart to the usual teen rebellion stories. Directed by Catherine Hardwicke and co-written by Nikki Reed, who also stars as the dangerously magnetic Evie, it captures the whirlwind descent of 13-year-old Tracy (Evan Rachel Wood) into a chaotic world of sex, drugs, and cash. It’s not pretty, and it doesn’t sugarcoat the toll this lifestyle takes, making it a standout among early 2000s indie dramas about adolescence gone awry.

What really sticks with you is the film’s kinetic energy—the tagline “It’s happening so fast” nails it. The writing and performances, especially from Wood and Reed, feel authentically troubled without tipping into melodrama. Hardwicke’s direction leans into the chaos of adolescence with a raw, almost documentary-like edge that pulls you into Tracy’s spiraling reality. The family dynamics, particularly with Holly Hunter as Tracy’s mom, add a weighty emotional core amid the reckless behavior. This isn’t your average teen movie; it’s a sobering look at how quickly everything can unravel when you’re so young and lost.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm: multiple animals die on-screen, including a dog, horse, and cat, and there’s a heavy dose of animal-related distress. If you’re wary of that kind of content, be prepared. There’s also some bodily distress and gaslighting, so it’s not a light watch by any stretch.
emailReview:
Thirteen is a raw and unflinching coming-of-age drama that grabs you with its kinetic energy and painfully authentic performances, especially from Evan Rachel Wood and Nikki Reed.

Be prepared for: multiple on-screen animal deaths including a dog and horse, intense animal distress, bodily harm, and emotional gaslighting.

name: Dream Scenario
overview: A schlubby professor who never made it becomes an overnight celebrity after appearing in every person on Earth’s dream.
tagline: Meet the man of your dreams.
review:
Dream Scenario is a quirky blend of surreal comedy and subtle social satire, anchored by a typically intense Nicolas Cage as Paul Matthews, a down-on-his-luck professor who suddenly becomes a global phenomenon after he starts appearing in everyone’s dreams. It feels like a mash-up of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and Being John Malkovich — a concept that’s as weird and intriguing as it sounds, with a loose, offbeat tone that keeps you guessing. While it doesn’t fully lean into the absurdity, the film’s charm lies in Cage’s unpredictable presence and the way it pokes at our obsession with fame and the subconscious.

What stands out here is Kristoffer Borgli’s direction and writing, which balance the bizarre premise with surprisingly grounded human moments. The tagline, “Meet the man of your dreams,” nails the ironic twist at the heart of the story: Paul is nobody’s dream guy in real life, yet he’s plastered across the collective unconscious. The supporting cast, including Julianne Nicholson and Michael Cera, add subtle layers to the story’s exploration of identity and connection. The film doesn’t shy away from some dark, unsettling imagery, which contrasts nicely with its comedic beats, making it more than just a straightforward comedy.

That said, heads-up to anyone sensitive to animal content—Dream Scenario features multiple instances of animal harm and death, including a dog, cat, horse, and even a dragon. There are also scenes with bugs, spiders, and snakes that might creep out those who aren’t fans of creepy crawlies. If you’re triggered by animal abuse or death in media, this one could be a rough ride.
emailReview:
Nicolas Cage delivers his trademark intensity in this surreal comedy that plays like Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind meets Being John Malkovich, blending offbeat humor with sharp social satire about fame and the subconscious.

Be prepared for: multiple instances of animal harm and death including a dog, cat, horse, and dragon, as well as unsettling scenes with bugs, spiders, and snakes.

name: Young Guns
overview: A group of young gunmen, led by Billy the Kid, become deputies to avenge the murder of the rancher who became their benefactor. But when Billy takes their authority too far, they become the hunted.
tagline: Six reasons why the west was wild.
review:
Young Guns rides into the late ’80s with a youthful swagger, blending classic Western grit with a rebellious teen-movie vibe. It’s basically The Outsiders meets Tombstone—an ensemble of fresh-faced actors like Emilio Estevez as Billy the Kid, Kiefer Sutherland, and Lou Diamond Phillips delivering a spirited take on the mythic Old West. While it doesn’t quite reinvent the genre, it’s a lively, fast-paced shootout fest elevated by its charismatic cast and a script that leans into camaraderie and recklessness more than dusty moralizing.

What stands out is how the film frames its outlaw posse as both heroes and antiheroes, caught between loyalty and lawlessness. The tagline, “Six reasons why the west was wild,” nails the chaotic energy that drives the story—a group of young men given authority and then spiraling out of control. Christopher Cain’s direction keeps things moving briskly, and the score punctuates moments of tension and youthful bravado without overstaying its welcome. It’s not a philosophical deep dive, but it captures a certain restless spirit that makes the western frontier feel alive and dangerous.

Heads up for sensitive viewers: this one doesn’t shy away from animal death, including horses, which might be tough if you’re sensitive to that. Plus, there’s a troubling bestiality element that will definitely catch some off guard. If those triggers are on your list, proceed with caution.
emailReview: Young Guns charges in with a rebellious teen-movie energy wrapped in classic Western grit, anchored by a charismatic cast that keeps the action lively and the tension high. Be prepared for: horse deaths, animal cruelty, bestiality, and intense gun violence.

name: Draft Day
overview: At the NFL Draft, general manager Sonny Weaver has the opportunity to rebuild his team when he trades for the number one pick. He must decide what he's willing to sacrifice on a life-changing day for a few hundred young men with NFL dreams.

name: Storks
overview: Storks deliver babies…or at least they used to. Now they deliver packages for a global internet retail giant. Junior, the company’s top delivery stork, is about to be promoted when he accidentally activates the Baby Making Machine, producing an adorable and wholly unauthorized baby girl...

writers: Mitch Cullin, Jeffrey Hatcher, Arthur Conan Doyle
name: Mr. Holmes
overview: The story is set in 1947, following a long-retired Holmes living in a Sussex village with his housekeeper and rising detective son. But then he finds himself haunted by an unsolved 50-year old case. Holmes' memory isn't what it used to be, so he only remembers fragments of the case: a confrontation with an angry husband, a secret bond with his beautiful but unstable wife.

name: Dog Soldiers
overview: A squad of British soldiers on training in the lonesome Scottish wilderness find a wounded Special Forces captain and the remains of his team. As they encounter zoologist Megan, it turns out that werewolves are active in the region. They have to prepare for some action as the there will be a full moon tonight...
tagline: Six men. Full moon. No chance.

name: The Ghost and the Darkness
overview: A bridge engineer and an experienced old hunter begin a hunt for two lions after they start attacking local construction workers.

name: Bones and All
overview: Abandoned by her father, a young woman embarks on a thousand-mile odyssey through the backroads of America where she meets a disenfranchised drifter. But despite their best efforts, all roads lead back to their terrifying pasts and to a final stand that will determine whether their love can survive their otherness.
tagline: You can’t run from who you are.
review:
Bones and All is a haunting blend of coming-of-age romance and dark horror that feels like a cross between a road trip movie and a grim fairy tale — think Call Me By Your Name meets The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, but with a poetic sadness that lingers. Luca Guadagnino’s direction gives it a lush, atmospheric quality, while Taylor Russell and Timothée Chalamet bring a raw vulnerability to their roles as two outcasts bound by a terrifying secret. It’s not your typical love story, and that’s what makes it stand out: a beautiful yet unsettling exploration of otherness and survival.

What really sticks with you is the film’s commitment to its tagline, "You can’t run from who you are." The journey across America’s backroads isn’t just physical but deeply emotional, with a script that balances quiet moments of tenderness against spine-chilling body horror. The score and visuals work in tandem to amplify this eerie, almost mythic vibe. It’s a slow burn that rewards patience, with themes of abandonment, identity, and the monstrous parts of ourselves that we try to hide. Mark Rylance adds a grizzled, enigmatic presence that grounds the story in a world that’s both familiar and unsettling.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content — this one’s heavy on animal deaths and harm, including dogs, cats, horses, and more. Body horror elements are prominent, so if that’s a dealbreaker, be prepared. Plus, there are some difficult moments involving gaslighting and general emotional trauma. If those triggers are on your radar, approach with caution.
emailReview:
Bones and All blends a haunting coming-of-age romance with dark, poetic horror, anchored by raw performances from Taylor Russell and Timothée Chalamet that linger long after the credits roll.

Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths (dogs, cats, horses), intense body horror, gaslighting, and emotional trauma.

name: Innerspace
overview: Test pilot Tuck Pendleton volunteers to test a special vessel for a miniaturization experiment. Accidentally injected into a neurotic hypochondriac, Jack Putter, Tuck must convince Jack to find his ex-girlfriend, Lydia Maxwell, to help him extract Tuck and his ship and re-enlarge them before his oxygen runs out.

writers: Ron Bass, Jen Smolka, Chris Shafer, Paul Vicknair
name: Before We Go
overview: Brussels, La Monnaie Opera House. Three people near the end of their lives meet with choreographers, actors and musicians. They take part in a unique experience which involves music, dance and silence. Their journey becomes a tribute to the fragility of the human condition, between reality and representation, tragedy of the body and freedom of the spirit. Together they question their own relationship with death.

name: Inland Empire
overview: An actress's perception of reality becomes increasingly distorted as she finds herself falling for her co-star in a remake of an unfinished Polish production that was supposedly cursed.

name: City Slickers
overview: Three New York businessmen decide to take a "Wild West" vacation that turns out not to be the relaxing vacation they had envisioned.
tagline: Yesterday they were businessmen. Today they're cowboys. Tomorrow they'll be walking funny.
review:
City Slickers is a classic early ’90s comedy that mixes fish-out-of-water antics with a surprisingly heartfelt look at friendship and midlife crises. It’s like The Three Amigos meets a cattle drive, with Billy Crystal leading the charge as Mitch Robbins, one of three New York businessmen who trade skyscrapers for saddles on a rugged Wild West vacation. The tagline—“Yesterday they were businessmen. Today they’re cowboys. Tomorrow they’ll be walking funny”—perfectly captures the goofy, self-aware tone that sets it apart from more straightforward comedies of the era. It’s not just laughs; there’s a genuine warmth here that elevates it beyond your typical buddy flick.

What really stands out is how the film balances humor with some surprisingly grounded themes. The city slickers’ trip quickly turns into a real challenge, forcing them to confront their own insecurities and life choices. The dialogue, penned by Lowell Ganz and Babaloo Mandel, zings with sharp wit but also lets moments breathe, especially in the quieter beats involving Mitch’s connection with a newborn calf named Norman. The visuals lean into classic Western tropes but with a modern, comedic spin—the dusty landscapes juxtaposed against these out-of-place businessmen make for memorable scenes. Plus, the supporting cast, including Daniel Stern and Bruno Kirby, rounds out the trio with great chemistry.

Heads up for animal lovers: this movie is heavy on animal-related content, including the deaths of several animals such as a dog, cat, horse, and other livestock. There’s also some animal abuse, abandonment, and sad animals shown, which might hit hard if you’re sensitive to that. On top of that, there are bugs, spiders, and snakes lurking in the background, plus a car crash and some vomiting. If any of those are on your “no thanks” list, be prepared before saddling up for the ride.
emailReview:
City Slickers blends sharp wit and heartfelt moments with a goofy, self-aware take on a Wild West adventure led by Billy Crystal and his mismatched crew of city slickers.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, cat, and horse, animal abuse and abandonment, plus bugs, snakes, and a car crash.

overview: In small-town Texas, affable and popular mortician Bernie Tiede strikes up a friendship with Marjorie Nugent, a wealthy widow well known for her sour attitude. When she becomes controlling and abusive, Bernie goes to great lengths to remove himself from her grasp.
tagline: A story so unbelievable it must be true.

When her classy, but villainous boss breaks a leg skiing, Tess takes over her office, her apartment and even her wardrobe. She creates a deal with a handsome investment banker that will either take her to the top, or finish her off for good.
tagline: For anyone who's ever won. For anyone who's ever lost. And for everyone who's still in there trying.

overview: New York City, 1957. Lionel Essrog, a private detective living with Tourette syndrome, tries to solve the murder of his mentor and best friend, armed only with vague clues and the strength of his obsessive mind…

writers: David Zelag Goodman, William F. Nolan, George Clayton Johnson
name: Logan's Run
overview: In the 23rd century, inhabitants of a domed city freely experience all of life's pleasures- but no one is allowed to live past 30. Citizens can try for a chance at being 'renewed' in a civic ceremony on their 30th birthday. Escape is the only other option.
tagline: Welcome to the 23rd century. The perfect world of total pleasure...there's just one catch.
review:
Logan’s Run is a 1976 sci-fi cult classic that feels like a hall-of-mirrors reflection of utopian dystopias from its era, sitting comfortably alongside films like THX 1138 or Rollerball. Its bright, glossy future conceals a grim catch: no one lives past 30, and the threat of “renewal” hangs over every citizen. Michael York’s Logan makes for a good reluctant hero, and Jenny Agutter’s Jessica brings a grounded presence to the shiny, hedonistic world. It’s not the most subtle or deep dystopia, but it’s a wild ride fueled by its striking visuals and a sense of creeping paranoia.

What stands out most here is the world-building—Michael Anderson’s direction leans hard into the sleek, almost campy design of the domed city, which feels both inviting and claustrophobic. The tagline “Welcome to the 23rd century. The perfect world of total pleasure...there’s just one catch,” nails that tension perfectly. The story’s central idea—escaping a society that mandates your death at 30—still hits some emotional notes about youth, freedom, and conformity, even if the plot sometimes stumbles over its own ambition. The supporting cast adds flavor, with Roscoe Lee Browne’s Box providing a memorable oddity amid the sterile environment.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related triggers—Logan’s Run includes multiple instances of animal death and abandonment, which might be jarring given the sci-fi context. There’s also bestiality flagged, which is pretty unusual and certainly a curveball for a film of this type and era. If bugs, snakes, sharks, or spiders set off alarms for you, be prepared—they show up in ways that lean into the unsettling side of this “perfect” world unraveling.
emailReview:
Logan’s Run glows with glossy, campy sci-fi style and a paranoid edge that makes its utopian dystopia feel both inviting and claustrophobic, anchored by Michael York’s reluctant hero and Jenny Agutter’s grounded presence.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths and abandonment, bestiality, unsettling appearances of bugs, snakes, sharks, and spiders.

name: Lilo & Stitch
overview: The story is about the bond formed between a lonely human girl named Lilo and a dog-like alien named Stitch, who is engineered to be a force of destruction.
review:
Lilo & Stitch (2025) is a fresh take on the beloved story of an unlikely friendship between a lonely girl and a mischievous alien, blending heartfelt family drama with sci-fi whimsy. This version leans into the tropical vibe with its “Hold on to your coconuts” tagline and stays true to the original’s charm while adding a bit more emotional depth. If you’re a fan of character-driven stories like E.T. or even the original animated classic, this one’s a sweet, if sometimes uneven, ride. The voice work—especially Chris Sanders as Stitch and Maia Kealoha as Lilo—really helps ground the film’s more fantastical elements.

What stands out here is the dynamic between Lilo and Stitch, which feels earnest and well-rounded thanks to the writing team of Chris Kekaniokalani Bright and Mike Van Waes. Director Dean Fleischer Camp brings a warm, intimate feel to the Hawaiian setting, making the island almost a character itself. The supporting cast, including Sydney Agudong as Nani and Zach Galifianakis as Jumba, add light humor and heart without overshadowing the core relationship. The story does lean into some familiar tropes—alien-as-pet, mischievous creature learns to care—but it’s elevated by genuine emotion and a strong sense of place.

Heads up: this film packs a surprising punch for animal lovers. There are multiple instances of animal deaths, including a dog, a horse, and even a cat, as well as scenes depicting animal abuse and dog fighting. If those are on your watchlist, be heavily warned. There’s also a fair share of creepy crawlies like spiders, snakes, and bedbugs, which might ruffle some feathers. This isn’t your typical feel-good family movie when it comes to animal content—so tread carefully if you’re sensitive on that front.
emailReview:
Lilo & Stitch (2025) brings a warm, intimate Hawaiian setting to the classic tale, with standout voice work that grounds its heartfelt sci-fi whimsy and family drama.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and a horse, scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting, and unsettling creepy crawlies like spiders and bedbugs.

name: Martha Marcy May Marlene
overview: After several years of living with a cult, Martha finally escapes and calls her estranged sister, Lucy, for help. Martha finds herself at the quiet Connecticut home Lucy shares with her new husband, Ted, but the memories of what she experienced in the cult make peace hard to find. As flashbacks continue to torment her, Martha fails to shake a terrible sense of dread, especially in regard to the cult's manipulative leader.
tagline: You can get away, but you can never escape.
review:
Martha Marcy May Marlene is a haunting psychological thriller that lingers long after the credits roll. Elizabeth Olsen delivers a quietly devastating performance as Martha, a young woman struggling to reclaim her identity after escaping a cult. The film’s tone is unsettling and slow-burning, more about mood and memory than outright scares, making it feel like a cross between The Invitation’s cult unease and Black Swan’s psychological unraveling. It’s an intense character study that rewards patience, though it’s not exactly a crowd-pleaser for those wanting a tidy resolution.

What really stands out here is Sean Durkin’s direction and writing, which craft a disorienting narrative blending past and present so seamlessly that you almost feel trapped alongside Martha. The quiet Connecticut setting contrasts sharply with the dark, oppressive flashbacks of cult life, underscoring the tagline: “You can get away, but you can never escape.” The film doesn’t spell everything out, instead relying on subtle cues and Elizabeth Olsen’s expressive performance to convey trauma’s persistent grip. It’s a film that leans heavily on atmosphere and psychological tension rather than traditional thriller beats.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content—there are several instances of animal harm, including a dog and a horse dying, which might be tough for some viewers. Plus, if bugs or spiders set off alarms for you, those are present too. The film also deals with psychological manipulation and gaslighting, so if those themes hit close to home, prepare accordingly.
emailReview:
Martha Marcy May Marlene is a haunting, slow-burning psychological thriller anchored by Elizabeth Olsen’s quietly devastating performance and a disorienting narrative that traps you in the shadows of cult trauma.

Be prepared for: dog and horse deaths, spider and bug encounters, psychological manipulation, and gaslighting.

name: Rent

In the year that follows, the group deals with love, loss, HIV/AIDS, and modern day life.

name: To Die For
overview: Suzanne Stone wants to be a world-famous news anchor and she is willing to do anything to get what she wants. What she lacks in intelligence, she makes up for in cold determination and diabolical wiles. As she pursues her goal with relentless focus, she is forced to destroy anything and anyone that may stand in her way, regardless of the ultimate cost or means necessary.
tagline: All she wanted was a little attention.
review:
To Die For is a pitch-black satirical drama from the mid-90s that feels like a twisted blend of biting social commentary and dark comedy. Nicole Kidman’s icy portrayal of Suzanne Stone, a woman who’s ruthless in her quest for fame, really drives the film’s sharp edge. If you’re into stories about ambition gone off the rails with a side of murder and media critique, this one’s a cult classic worth revisiting—think Fatal Attraction meets Network, but with a more sardonic, off-kilter vibe courtesy of Gus Van Sant’s direction.

What stands out here is how the film skewers the American obsession with celebrity and media spotlight, painting Suzanne as a disturbingly relatable antiheroine. The tagline, “All she wanted was a little attention,” nails the core obsession that fuels her diabolical schemes. The writing by Buck Henry layers the narrative with dark humor and irony, while the supporting cast—including a pre-fame Joaquin Phoenix and Casey Affleck—adds texture to the world of manipulation and moral decay. The film’s tone is both unsettling and oddly playful, making it linger long after the credits roll.

Be heavily warned if animal harm or death is a sensitive subject for you. The film includes multiple distressing scenes involving animals—dogs, cats, horses—and there are even elements of animal abuse and dog fighting. Those who pin the “animal harm” or “pet dies” triggers should approach with caution, as these moments are not only present but integral to the unsettling atmosphere.
emailReview:
To Die For is a pitch-black satirical drama fueled by Nicole Kidman’s icy performance and a sardonic take on fame’s dark underbelly, blending dark comedy with sharp social critique.

Be prepared for: graphic animal abuse including dog fighting, multiple pet deaths (dogs, cats, horses), and unsettling scenes of animal harm.

name: Bottoms
overview: Unpopular best friends PJ and Josie start a high school self-defense club to meet girls and lose their virginity. They soon find themselves in over their heads when the most popular students start beating each other up in the name of self-defense.
tagline: A movie about empowering women (the hot ones).
review:
Bottoms is a sharp, raunchy teen comedy that rides the wave of awkward coming-of-age stories but amps up the chaos with an all-girls self-defense club that quickly spirals into high school mayhem. If you’ve enjoyed the biting humor of films like Booksmart or the irreverent edge of Eighth Grade, this one will hit a similar groove — though it’s distinctly livelier and messier. Rachel Sennott and Ayo Edebiri bring a fierce, neurotic energy to their roles as PJ and Josie, two best friends who just want to lose their virginity but end up entangled in a bizarre turf war of popularity and punches.

What stands out here is how Bottoms manages to blend genuine teen insecurity with absurdist comedy, leaning hard into the “empowering women (the hot ones)” tagline with a wink and a nudge. The writing, co-penned by Sennott and director Emma Seligman, keeps the jokes rapid-fire and the stakes surprisingly emotional beneath the surface of slapstick fights and awkward hookups. The high school self-defense club setup is a clever twist on the genre, turning expected tropes on their heads while poking fun at the social hierarchies and sexual politics of adolescence.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal harm: Bottoms features multiple scenes involving animals dying or being abused, including pets, which could be upsetting. There’s also some body horror and gaslighting moments sprinkled in, so if those are on your mental no-go list, proceed with caution. And yes, there are spiders and bugs—because why not add a dash of creepy crawlies to the chaos?
emailReview:
Bottoms is a wildly entertaining teen comedy that mixes sharp wit with messy high school chaos, led by Rachel Sennott and Ayo Edebiri’s fierce, neurotic performances as two best friends caught in a bizarre self-defense club turf war.

Be prepared for: multiple scenes of animal deaths and abuse, unsettling body horror moments, gaslighting, and creepy crawly spiders and bugs.

overview: Wife and mother Valerie Plame (Naomi Watts) has a double life as a CIA operative, hiding her vocation from family and friends. Her husband, Joseph Wilson (Sean Penn), writes a controversial article in The New York Times, refuting stories about the sale of enriched uranium to Iraq, Then Valerie's secret work and identity is leaked to the press. With her cover blown and other people endangered, Valerie's career and personal life begin to unravel.

writers: Maneesh Sharma, Habib Faisal, Sharat Katariya
name: Fan
overview: A man who bears a striking resemblance to a renowned movie star becomes an obsessive fan, but when his fierce love is spurned by the star, he decides to destroy the star's life and reputation.

writers: Harry Julian Fink, Rita M. Fink, Stirling Silliphant, Dean Riesner, Gail Morgan Hickman, S.W. Schurr
name: The Enforcer
overview: Dirty Harry Callahan returns again, this time saddled with a rookie female partner. Together, they must stop a terrorist group consisting of angry Vietnam veterans.
tagline: The dirtiest Harry of them all.
