tagline: The past is not what it seems.

writers: Arturo Pérez-Reverte, John Brownjohn, Enrique Urbizu, Roman Polanski
name: The Ninth Gate
overview: An all-expenses-paid international search for a rare copy of the book, 'The Nine Gates of the Kingdom  Of Shadows' brings an unscrupulous book dealer deep into a world of murder, double-dealing and satanic worship.
tagline: Every book has a life of its own.

writers: Johnston McCulley, Ted Elliott, Terry Rossio, Randall Jahnson, John Eskow
name: The Mask of Zorro
overview: It has been twenty years since Don Diego de la Vega fought Spanish oppression in Alta California as the legendary romantic hero, Zorro. Having escaped from prison he transforms troubled bandit Alejandro into his successor, in order to foil the plans of the tyrannical Don Rafael Montero who robbed him of his freedom, his wife and his precious daughter.
tagline: No one has seen his face... but everyone... knows this mark.
review:
The Mask of Zorro is a swashbuckling throwback that mixes classic adventure with a bit of ’90s charm, landing somewhere between The Three Musketeers and a romantic action flick. Antonio Banderas steps into the iconic mask with admirable swagger, while Anthony Hopkins brings a dignified gravitas as the original Zorro passing the torch. It’s a pretty solid mix of swordplay, romance, and revenge that still holds up as a crowd-pleaser, even if it doesn’t reinvent the genre.

What makes this one worth revisiting is the chemistry among the leads and the way it leans into that old-school heroism with a modern sheen. The story of legacy and redemption—Don Diego training Alejandro to take down the villainous Don Rafael Montero—feels like a classic tale with a fresh coat of paint. Plus, Catherine Zeta-Jones adds a spark as the daughter caught in the crossfire, balancing the film’s action with some emotional stakes. Director Martin Campbell keeps the pace brisk, and the fight choreography is sharp and fun, making the “no one has seen his face…” tagline feel earned.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this one’s heavy on animal triggers, including several animal deaths and abuse, plus some dog fighting. There are also spiders, snakes, and other creepy crawlies making appearances, so if you’re on edge about bugs or animals being harmed, tread carefully here.
emailReview:
The Mask of Zorro delivers classic swashbuckling fun with Antonio Banderas’ charming swagger and Anthony Hopkins’ dignified gravitas, wrapped in a lively blend of swordplay, romance, and old-school heroism.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths, dog fighting, animal abuse, spiders, and snakes.

tagline: The future isn't big enough for the both of them.

name: The Power of the Dog
overview: A domineering but charismatic rancher wages a war of intimidation on his brother's new wife and her teen son, until long-hidden secrets come to light.
review:
Jane Campion’s *The Power of the Dog* is a slow-burn western drama that leans heavily into psychological tension and simmering menace. Benedict Cumberbatch’s Phil Burbank is a fascinating mix of charm and cruelty, turning what could be a straightforward family feud into a layered exploration of power, repression, and vulnerability. Fans of character-driven stories like *There Will Be Blood* or *No Country for Old Men* will appreciate the film’s careful pacing and atmospheric dread, though it’s less about action and more about the quiet unraveling beneath the surface.

What really stands out here is the way Campion uses the sprawling ranch setting almost as a character itself — vast, isolating, and harsh, mirroring the emotional terrain the characters navigate. The performances are quietly intense, especially Kodi Smit-McPhee’s portrayal of Peter, whose secret quietly flips the power dynamics. The film’s writing is subtle but sharp, unraveling emotional wounds and family secrets with a kind of poetic cruelty that lingers long after the credits roll.

Heads up: this one includes the death of a horse, which is a significant moment that might catch sensitive viewers off guard. If the idea of animal harm is tough for you, be prepared.
emailReview:
Jane Campion’s *The Power of the Dog* is a slow-burning western that wraps psychological tension and simmering menace in a hauntingly vast and isolating ranch setting, anchored by Benedict Cumberbatch’s quietly cruel performance.

Be prepared for: the death of a horse, emotional cruelty, family violence, and moments of intense psychological manipulation.

Yet Annie ends up with more than just a story in this popular romantic comedy.
tagline: What if someone you never met, someone you never saw, someone you never knew was the only someone for you?

tagline: Right now, this serial killer could be looking at his next victim.

Jack finds himself a lost soul in the modern world, seeking answers to the origins and meaning of life while questioning the existence of faith.

name: A Simple Favor
overview: Stephanie, a dedicated mother and popular vlogger, befriends Emily, a mysterious upper-class woman whose son Nicky attends the same school as Miles, Stephanie's son. When Emily asks her to pick Nicky up from school and then disappears, Stephanie undertakes an investigation that will dive deep into Emily's cloudy past.

writers: Jeffrey Boam, Robert Mark Kamen, Shane Black

name: Mickey 17
overview: Unlikely hero Mickey Barnes finds himself in the extraordinary circumstance of working for an employer who demands the ultimate commitment to the job… to die, for a living.
review:
Mickey 17 is Bong Joon Ho’s latest sci-fi outing, and it’s a sharp, darkly funny meditation on sacrifice and identity that feels like The Matrix meets Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind—but with a much weirder employment contract. Robert Pattinson leads the charge as Mickey Barnes, a man whose job literally requires him to die repeatedly for the greater good. It’s a wild concept that Bong uses to explore what it means to live a meaningful life when your existence is disposable. Fans of his genre-bending style will appreciate the blend of humor, horror, and existential dread.

What stands out here is how Bong layers his signature social commentary under a sleek sci-fi veneer. The tagline, “He’s dying to save mankind,” nails the film’s grim irony while hinting at a larger-than-life plot packed with philosophical questions. The supporting cast, including Naomi Ackie and Steven Yeun, adds depth and nuance, making this more than just a high-concept thriller. Visually, it’s a moody, immersive experience that balances the bleakness of Mickey’s situation with moments of genuine tenderness and absurdity. It’s not just about the sci-fi spectacle; it’s about the human cost behind it all.

Heads up: this one is heavy on animal-related triggers. If you’re sensitive to animal deaths or abuse, including pets and wild creatures like horses and dogs, be cautious. There are also unsettling bugs and spiders that might creep out some viewers. Those who prefer to avoid animal harm or distressing scenes involving animals should definitely take note before diving in.
emailReview:
Mickey 17 is a darkly funny, mind-bending sci-fi that blends existential dread with sharp social commentary and standout performances from Robert Pattinson and a stellar supporting cast.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including horses and dogs, unsettling insect scenes, and persistent themes of sacrifice and bodily harm.

With the help of a feisty stewardess and an old friend, Matrix has only a few hours to overcome his greatest challenge: finding his daughter before she's killed.
tagline: Somewhere, somehow, someone's going to pay.

tagline: Twice the Fun, Double the Trouble.

tagline: Don't fear the end of the world. Fear what happens next.

overview: Monsters under the bed are scary enough, but what happens when an entire house is out to get you? Three teens aim to find out when they go up against a decrepit neighboring home and unlock its frightening secrets.

name: The Rundown
overview: When Travis, the mouthy son of a criminal, disappears in the Amazon in search of a treasured artifact, his father sends in Beck, who becomes Travis's rival for the affections of Mariana, a mysterious Brazilian woman. With his steely disposition, Beck is a man of few words -- but it takes him all the discipline he can muster to work with Travis to nab a tyrant who's after the same treasure.
tagline: Bulls, guns, whips, gold and one sacred cat.

name: The Exorcism of Emily Rose
overview: When a younger girl called Emily Rose dies, everyone puts blame on the exorcism which was performed on her by Father Moore prior to her death. The priest is arrested on suspicion of murder. The trial begins with lawyer Erin Bruner representing Moore, but it is not going to be easy, as no one wants to believe what Father Moore says is true.
tagline: One person's story of faith and possession.

writers: Neal Israel, Pat Proft, Hugh Wilson, Paul Maslansky
name: Police Academy
overview: New rules enforced by the Lady Mayoress mean that sex, weight, height and intelligence need no longer be a factor for joining the Police Force. This opens the floodgates for all and sundry to enter the Police Academy, much to the chagrin of the instructors. Not everyone is there through choice, though.
tagline: The new police recruits. Call them slobs. Call them jerks. Call them gross. Just don't call them when you're in trouble.
review:
Police Academy is the kind of broad 1980s comedy that tries to wring laughs out of every oddball character and slapstick scenario imaginable. It’s a goofy, irreverent take on the police procedural, leaning into the chaos of an all-comers police force with zero filter or finesse. Think Animal House meets Lethal Weapon’s rookie cop side, but way sillier and way more lowbrow. It’s not exactly refined humor, but it has a goofy charm that some fans of classic ‘80s dumb comedies will appreciate.

The core of Police Academy’s gag is the premise itself—the new rules that let anyone join the force regardless of sex, weight, height, or intelligence—which opens the door for a motley crew of recruits who are as much a headache to their instructors as they are to criminals. Steve Guttenberg’s Mahoney leads a cast of misfits, including Kim Cattrall and Bubba Smith, who bring memorable quirks to the table. The tagline, “Call them slobs. Call them jerks. Call them gross. Just don’t call them when you’re in trouble,” perfectly captures the movie’s tone: messy, unpolished, and self-awarely ridiculous. The writing leans heavily into physical comedy and stereotypes, and while it’s dated in some spots, the film’s energy and Hugh Wilson’s direction keep things moving.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one’s loaded with animal-related triggers, including several instances where animals die and some animal abuse, plus bugs, spiders, snakes, and other critters make appearances that might unsettle sensitive viewers. If you’re uneasy about animal harm or death in media, proceed with caution here.
emailReview:
Police Academy is a raucous 1980s comedy that thrives on its chaotic cast of misfit recruits and slapstick humor, delivering a goofy charm that fans of classic dumb comedies will enjoy.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths, animal abuse, bugs, spiders, and snakes.

name: Death Becomes Her
overview: Madeline is married to Ernest, who was once arch-rival Helen's fiance. After recovering from a mental breakdown, Helen vows to kill Madeline and steal back Ernest. Unfortunately for everyone, the introduction of a magic potion causes things to be a great deal more complicated than a mere murder plot.
tagline: In one small bottle... The fountain of youth. The secret of eternal life. The power of an ancient potion. Sometimes it works... sometimes it doesn't.
review:
Death Becomes Her is a darkly comic fantasy that feels like a campy mashup of Heathers meets The Addams Family, with a splash of early ’90s Hollywood vanity thrown in. Directed by Robert Zemeckis, this cult classic leans hard into its satirical take on eternal youth and toxic relationships, anchored by the deliciously over-the-top performances of Meryl Streep, Goldie Hawn, and Bruce Willis. It’s not just a quirky romp — it’s a wild ride through obsession and immortality that’s way more fun than it has any right to be, even if the special effects can’t totally escape their era.

What really sticks is the premise itself: a magical potion promising eternal life that complicates what starts as a straightforward love triangle turned murder plot. The tagline—“Sometimes it works... sometimes it doesn’t”—perfectly captures the film’s gleeful embrace of chaos and dark humor. The writing by David Koepp and Martin Donovan strikes a sharp balance between biting wit and absurdity, while the visual quirks and body horror moments keep the tone delightfully off-kilter. Plus, the way the film skewers vanity and desperation feels surprisingly fresh, even decades later.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and body horror — this one packs in a surprising number of upsetting moments involving pets and creatures, alongside some really grotesque physical transformations. If you’re on the fence about bugs, snakes, or the more grotesque elements, be warned that this film isn’t shy about leaning into those triggers either. It’s campy, it’s creepy, and it’s definitely not for everyone, but if you like your dark comedy with a side of immortal mischief, this one’s worth the trip.
emailReview:
Death Becomes Her is a gleefully campy cult classic that mashes up sharp satire on vanity with delightfully grotesque body horror, all brought to life by over-the-top performances from Meryl Streep and Goldie Hawn.

Be prepared for: disturbing pet deaths, grotesque physical transformations, bug and snake harm, and a wild ride of darkly comic chaos.

writers: Cyril Hume, Richard Maibaum, Richard Price, Alexander Ignon

writers: Brian Fee, Ben Queen, Eyal Podell, Jonathon E. Stewart, Kiel Murray, Bob Peterson, Mike Rich
name: Cars 3
overview: Blindsided by a new generation of blazing-fast racers, the legendary Lightning McQueen is suddenly pushed out of the sport he loves. tagline: From this moment, everything will change.

name: The Gorge
overview: Two elite snipers are assigned a mysterious mission to guard either side of a deep, impenetrable gorge, without knowing what actually lies beneath them.
tagline: The world's most dangerous secret lies between them.
review:
The Gorge is a tense, atmospheric thriller that feels like a stripped-down hybrid of Enemy and 1917—two elite snipers locked in a mysterious mission, separated by a shadowy chasm that seems to hold more secrets than either knows. Scott Derrickson’s direction keeps the suspense taut, while Miles Teller and Anya Taylor-Joy bring a quiet intensity to their roles as Levi and Drasa. It’s not your typical action flick; instead, it leans into psychological unease and the burden of duty, making it a slow burn that fans of cerebral thrillers will appreciate.

What stands out here is the film’s commitment to claustrophobic tension despite the open setting. The deep gorge is almost a character itself, a looming presence that amplifies the characters’ isolation and paranoia. The tagline, “The world’s most dangerous secret lies between them,” is spot-on, as the narrative slowly peels back layers of mystery with minimal exposition. Zach Dean’s writing smartly avoids over-explaining, letting the eerie silence and subtle exchanges carry much of the weight. Plus, with a supporting cast that includes Sigourney Weaver and Ṣọpẹ́ Dìrísù, the stakes feel grounded even amidst the enigma.

Be warned if you’re sensitive to animal harm, as the film notably includes scenes where rabbits are harmed—something that might catch viewers off guard given the otherwise human-centered story. If that’s a trigger for you, it’s worth keeping in mind before diving into this moody, deliberate thriller.
emailReview:
The Gorge is a taut, atmospheric thriller that turns a vast, shadowy chasm into a claustrophobic stage for two elite snipers locked in a slow-burning psychological duel, anchored by intense performances from Miles Teller and Anya Taylor-Joy.

Be prepared for: rabbit harm, intense sniper standoffs, and the creeping unease of isolation.

name: Tron
overview: When brilliant video game maker Flynn hacks the mainframe of his ex-employer, he is beamed inside an astonishing digital world and becomes part of the very game he is designing. In his mission through cyberspace, Flynn matches wits with a maniacal Master Control Program and teams up with Tron, a security measure created to bring balance to the digital environment.
tagline: A world inside the computer where man has never been. Never before now.
review:
Tron is a pioneering sci-fi adventure that feels like an early mash-up of The Matrix and a neon-lit arcade game. Steven Lisberger’s 1982 film dives headfirst into the digital frontier with Jeff Bridges as Kevin Flynn, who literally gets sucked into the computer world he helped create. It’s a wild mix of live-action and early CGI that still holds a certain retro charm—fans of vintage tech aesthetics and video game culture will find a lot to appreciate here. While the story can feel a bit dated and the acting occasionally stiff, Tron’s ambition and visual inventiveness set it apart from other ’80s sci-fi fare.

What really stands out is the film’s imaginative take on “a world inside the computer,” complete with glowing grids, light cycles, and an iconic showdown against the tyrannical Master Control Program. The tagline promises a place “where man has never been,” and for 1982, this digital realm was fresh and mind-bending. Jeff Bridges plays dual roles as Flynn and his digital alter ego Clu, while Bruce Boxleitner’s Tron serves as the heroic program fighting for balance. The blend of practical effects and early computer graphics creates a unique, immersive vibe that’s equal parts thrilling and cheesy in the best way.

Heads up for those sensitive to intense imagery: Tron includes jump scares and flashing lights that could be tough for some viewers. name: Smile 2
overview: About to embark on a new world tour, global pop sensation Skye Riley begins experiencing increasingly terrifying and inexplicable events. Overwhelmed by the escalating horrors and the pressures of fame, Skye is forced to face her dark past to regain control of her life before it spirals out of control.
tagline: It's the last thing you'll see.
review:
Smile 2 doubles down on the psychological horror and body horror that made the original a tense, unsettling experience, but this sequel cranks everything up to an almost exhausting level of gore and trauma. Naomi Scott’s portrayal of Skye Riley—pop star under siege by a supernatural force—is compelling, and the film leans heavily into the pressures of fame as a breeding ground for real horror. It feels like The Ring meets a brutal descent into addiction and PTSD, with Parker Finn’s signature Monstrosity ratcheting up the nightmare fuel. It’s not for the faint of heart, but horror fans looking for a visceral, relentless ride will find plenty to chew on here.

What stands out most is how the film blends supernatural stalking with very raw, human struggles: addiction, emotional abuse, and the crushing weight of tragedy. The Monstrosity’s shapeshifting and reality-warping powers make for some truly disorienting sequences, and the shaky cam and sudden loud noises keep you on edge. The tagline, “It’s the last thing you’ll see,” takes on gruesome layers by the end, especially as the finale unspools in a shocking, theatrical death that feels both inevitable and devastating. The interplay between Skye’s dark past and the escalating horrors makes this more than just a jump-scare fest, even if those scares come thick and fast.

If blood, gore, and body horror set off alarms for you, Smile 2 is a hard pass—or at least come prepared. There’s abundant graphic violence, including stabbing, mutilation, and self-harm, as well as intense possession and psychological torment. The film also deals heavily with addiction, emotional abuse, and PTSD, with Skye’s mental state deteriorating amid relentless supernatural assault. Sudden loud noises, jump scares, and flashing lights are constant, and the final act is especially brutal with some truly harrowing imagery and a tragic ending. Those sensitive to stalking, gaslighting, or depictions of suicide and assault should tread carefully.
emailReview: Smile 2 cranks up the tension with Naomi Scott’s gripping turn as a pop star haunted by a relentless supernatural force, blending psychological horror with brutal body horror for a visceral, almost exhausting experience. Be prepared for: graphic mutilation, intense possession, self-harm, suicide depiction, and relentless psychological torment.

review:
Violent Night is a coal-dark holiday thriller that leans hard into the “Santa as badass” subgenre, with David Harbour leading the charge as a very non-traditional Claus. If you’re into genre mashups like Die Hard meets bad Santa, this one’s a wild ride—gritty, violent, and unapologetically over the top. It’s not trying to be a warm, fuzzy Christmas movie, and that’s exactly why it stands out among the usual holiday fare. The tagline, “You better watch out,” sets the tone perfectly: this ain’t your grandma’s Christmas special.

What really sticks is how the film embraces its grim tone without losing sight of the fun. The writing from Patrick Casey and Josh Miller leans into clever, brutal set pieces that keep the momentum snapping along, while Tommy Wirkola’s direction doesn’t shy away from the messier, bloodier bits. The cast, especially Harbour’s gruff Santa, manages to straddle the line between tough guy and darkly comic hero. The synopsis’s hint that you should “always bet on red” feels like a nod to the film’s gleeful indulgence in chaos and carnage. There’s a definite edge here—this isn’t just a holiday flick but a holiday thriller that knows how to entertain the darker side of Christmas.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm: Violent Night features multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including a dog, cat, horse, and other animals, which are central enough to warrant caution. Alongside that, there’s body horror and scenes involving spiders, snakes, and bugs that might unsettle some viewers. If you’re on the lookout for triggers like animal harm or unsettling creature appearances, this one comes heavily flagged.
emailReview:
Violent Night throws tradition out the window with a gritty, blood-soaked Santa who’s equal parts lethal and darkly hilarious, making this holiday thriller a chaotic blast for fans of violent genre mashups.

name: Where the Wild Things Are
overview: Max imagines running away from his mom and sailing to a far-off land where large talking beasts -- Ira, Carol, Douglas, the Bull, Judith and Alexander -- crown him as their king, play rumpus, build forts and discover secret hideaways.

review:
Spike Jonze’s *Where the Wild Things Are* is a moody, whimsical dive into childhood imagination that feels like *Coraline* meets a more somber *Peter Pan*. It’s not your typical kids’ movie—there’s a bittersweet undercurrent that makes it linger long after the credits roll. Max Records carries the film with a quiet intensity, and the voice cast—featuring James Gandolfini and Forest Whitaker—brings a surprising depth to the creatures of Max’s fantasy world. Fans of storybook adaptations with an offbeat edge will appreciate this one, though it leans more toward reflective than raucous fun.

What really stands out is how the film captures the messy emotions of growing up: loneliness, anger, and the desperate need to be understood. The tagline “There’s one in all of us” nails that universal feeling of wrestling with your wild side. The visuals are lush and tactile, making the beasts feel both magical and real, while the quiet score underscores the film’s introspective tone. It’s a film that trusts its audience to sit with discomfort and complexity rather than wrapping everything up neatly.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: the film includes multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, which might be tough to watch. Also, if bugs, spiders, or snakes are on your list, this one makes sure to include those critters in the mix. Those who find scenes of vomiting or emotional manipulation unsettling might want to take caution as well.
emailReview:
Spike Jonze’s *Where the Wild Things Are* is a moody, whimsical journey into childhood’s tangled emotions, with standout performances that bring a bittersweet, reflective edge to a fantasy world both magical and raw.

review:
Candyman is a classic early '90s horror gem that blends urban legend creepiness with social commentary, making it stand out from your typical slasher flick. It’s got that perfect mix of supernatural dread and psychological suspense, anchored by Tony Todd’s unforgettable presence as the titular hook-handed specter. Fans of movies like *Nightmare on Elm Street* or *Urban Legend* will appreciate how *Candyman* uses folklore to explore real-world fears, but it’s elevated by its thoughtful atmosphere and Virginia Madsen’s grounded performance as the skeptic-turned-believer Helen Lyle.

What really sticks with you here is how the film builds its mythos — the tagline, “We dare you to say his name five times,” isn’t just a gimmick but a challenge that ties directly into the story’s tension. Bernard Rose’s direction leans into moody visuals and a haunting score that lingers in the background, making the urban setting feel ominous and alive. The movie isn’t just about scares; it’s probing the power of myth and the way stories can shape reality, which gives it a layer of depth not always found in horror from this era.

Those sensitive to animal deaths should be cautious, as the film includes a notably upsetting scene involving an animal that’s tough to watch. If that’s a big trigger for you, it’s worth keeping in mind before diving into this horror staple.

overview: The story of the Battle of Midway, and the leaders and soldiers who used their instincts, fortitude and bravery to overcome massive odds.
tagline: One battle turned the tide of war.
review:
Midway is Roland Emmerich’s take on the iconic WWII clash that shifted the Pacific theater, and it’s about what you’d expect from a big-budget war movie — all explosions, heroics, and a steady dose of patriotism. If you like your historical epics with plenty of dogfights and military bravado, this one lands squarely in that tradition, though it doesn’t quite reach the emotional heights of classics like *Dunkirk* or *Saving Private Ryan*. It’s more straightforward and less nuanced, but fans of intense aerial combat scenes and star-driven ensemble casts will find plenty to chew on.

What stands out is the film’s commitment to showcasing the key players — Ed Skrein’s Lieutenant Dick Best and Woody Harrelson’s Admiral Nimitz provide solid anchors — and that sense of “one battle turned the tide of war” tagline isn’t just window dressing. The visuals lean heavily into the spectacle of war, with some thrilling dogfight choreography and large-scale naval engagements. The writing keeps it fairly by-the-numbers, but there’s an earnestness in how it portrays the bravery and split-second decisions of these leaders and soldiers that gives it some heart amid the chaos.

Trigger-wise, anyone sensitive to animal harm should be cautious: there’s a surprising amount of animal-related distress here, including multiple deaths of pets and horses, as well as scenes of animal abuse and abandonment. Those who pin the “a dog dies” or “a horse dies” triggers will definitely want to brace themselves. It’s not the usual war movie fare, but the animal content is a significant undercurrent that could catch some viewers off guard.
emailReview:
Midway delivers classic war movie thrills with explosive dogfights and a star-packed cast that brings earnest heroism to a pivotal WWII battle.

review:
The Accountant 2 picks up the puzzle-loving vibe of its predecessor and cranks up the intensity, though it doesn’t quite reinvent the wheel. If you liked the first film’s mix of cerebral crime thriller and action — think a sharper, darker version of Jason Bourne with a math whiz at the center — this sequel will likely satisfy that craving. Ben Affleck returns as Christian Wolff, still navigating a world of shadowy figures and cryptic codes, with Jon Bernthal and J.K. Simmons adding some solid muscle and gravitas to the mix.

What stands out here is Gavin O’Connor’s steady hand behind the camera, keeping the tone gritty while balancing complex action sequences with quieter, character-driven moments. The tagline, “Do you like puzzles?” isn’t just marketing fluff — the story leans into the mental chess game Wolff plays, and the writing by Bill Dubuque keeps the stakes high without getting lost in convoluted twists. Amidst the violence and tension, there’s a strong undercurrent of vulnerability, especially in how Wolff’s relationships are portrayed, giving the film a little more heart than your average thriller.

Heads up for those who are sensitive to darker content: this one includes some body horror sequences and sexual content, plus an animal death that might catch you off guard. These elements add to the film’s gritty realism but could be tough for some viewers. If those triggers are on your radar, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
The Accountant 2 sharpens its cerebral crime thriller edge with gritty action and a surprisingly heartfelt performance from Ben Affleck as a math whiz navigating shadows and puzzles.

Be prepared for: body horror, sexual content, and a sudden animal death.

overview: Over the course of the 1960s, a Midwestern motorcycle club evolves from a gathering place for local outsiders into a more sinister gang, threatening the original group's unique way of life.
review:
The Bikeriders is a moody, slow-burn drama that digs into the dark evolution of a 1960s Midwestern motorcycle club, capturing the uneasy shift from brotherhood to menace. Jeff Nichols directs and writes with a steady hand, crafting a film that feels like a cross between gritty biker lore and a character-driven indie drama—think Easy Rider meets The Outsiders, but with a more somber, reflective tone. The cast, including Austin Butler, Jodie Comer, and Tom Hardy, delivers strong performances that anchor the film’s exploration of loyalty and legacy, even if the pacing sometimes leans toward the deliberately languid.

What stands out here is the film’s attention to atmosphere and period detail, painting a textured picture of a community caught between rebellion and self-destruction. The tagline, “Legacies don’t come easy,” sums up the central tension: as the club grows more dangerous, it threatens the original spirit that brought these outsiders together. Nichols plays with the genre’s familiar tropes but resists turning the story into a straightforward crime saga, instead focusing on the interpersonal fractures and the cost of chasing power. The soundtrack and visuals complement this moodiness, emphasizing a slow unraveling rather than explosive action.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content—there are several distressing moments involving animals, including the death of a dog, a cat, and a horse, as well as instances of animal abuse. Those who pin the jump scares and flashing lights triggers should also be cautious, as the film uses these to heighten tension in a few scenes. If shaky cam is a dealbreaker, be warned it makes an appearance here as well.

The Bikeriders is a moody, slow-burn drama that blends gritty biker lore with indie character study, anchored by powerful performances from Austin Butler, Jodie Comer, and Tom Hardy.

overview: In the future, a strange fungus has changed nearly everyone into thoughtless, flesh-eating monsters. When a scientist and a teacher find a girl who seems to be immune to the fungus, they all begin a journey to save humanity.

review:
The Girl with All the Gifts is a tense and thoughtful twist on the zombie apocalypse genre, blending horror with a surprisingly emotional coming-of-age story. It’s like if 28 Days Later met a dystopian sci-fi fable, with a young protagonist who’s equal parts vulnerable and terrifying. Sennia Nanua’s performance as Melanie anchors the film, lending a complex humanity to a character who could’ve easily been just another monster. The movie stands out not just for its scares, but for its willingness to ask what hope looks like in a world overwritten by decay.

What really sticks is how the film balances bleakness with moments of genuine compassion. The tagline, “Our greatest threat is our only hope,” perfectly captures the moral ambiguity at play here, where survival blurs the lines between monster and savior. The fungus-infected hordes are classic horror fodder, but the story’s heart lies in the relationship between Melanie, the scientist, and the teacher—bringing a fresh emotional depth to the genre. The visuals are grim and atmospheric, and the score quietly supports the building dread without overwhelming the quieter, more reflective scenes.

Be warned: animal lovers should be cautious. The film includes disturbing scenes involving animal harm—specifically a cat being attacked and a dog left abandoned in a dangerous setting. While no explicit animal deaths are shown on-screen, these moments are unsettling enough to warrant a heads-up. So if you’re sensitive to animal distress, you might want to brace yourself or skip those parts.

The Girl with All the Gifts offers a tense, emotionally charged twist on the zombie apocalypse, anchored by Sennia Nanua’s haunting performance that blurs the line between monster and child.

name: The Call of the Wild
overview: Buck is a big-hearted dog whose blissful domestic life is turned upside down when he is suddenly uprooted from his California home and transplanted to the exotic wilds of the Yukon during the Gold Rush of the 1890s. As the newest rookie on a mail delivery dog sled team—and later its leader—Buck experiences the adventure of a lifetime, ultimately finding his true place in the world and becoming his own master.
review:
The Call of the Wild is a sweeping adventure drama that tries to blend a family-friendly tone with the rugged, often brutal world of the Yukon Gold Rush. It’s a bit like Old Yeller meets The Revenant, with Harrison Ford lending his grizzled charm as the loyal John Thornton. While the CGI dog Buck is undeniably impressive and the wilderness backdrop is gorgeous, the movie sometimes struggles to find a consistent rhythm, veering between heartfelt moments and overwrought sentimentality. Fans of animal-led epics will appreciate the earnestness here, but it’s not quite as wild or raw as the original novel’s spirit.

What stands out most is the film’s earnest attempt to capture Buck’s journey from pampered pet to sled dog leader, emphasizing themes of survival, loyalty, and self-discovery. The script leans heavily on classic adventure tropes, but director Chris Sanders sprinkles in some modern visual effects that elevate the story’s scope. Harrison Ford’s warm performance grounds the human side of things, while the supporting cast—including Dan Stevens as the ill-fated Hal—adds some necessary tension. The tagline "Based on the legendary novel" is apt, but this adaptation feels less like a gritty survival tale and more like a glossy family drama with some thrilling sled dog action.

Those who pin the animal death and kidnapping triggers should be cautious, as Buck’s abduction from his home sets the story in motion and there are moments of loss that hit hard. Additionally, the film contains jump scares and some intense, even violent scenes including someone being burned alive, which might surprise viewers expecting a gentler family film. If spiders or flashing lights are on your list, those pop up too. Overall, The Call of the Wild isn’t an easy watch for animal lovers looking for a purely happy tale, but it’s a visually striking adventure with a bittersweet heart.
emailReview:
The Call of the Wild mixes glossy family drama with rugged Yukon adventure, anchored by Harrison Ford’s warm, grizzled presence and impressive CGI that brings the wilderness to life.

Be prepared for: dog kidnapping, animal death, a burning alive scene, jump scares, and spiders.

review:
Love Lies Bleeding is a moody, offbeat blend of crime thriller and romance that feels like a slow burn version of Drive with a lean, muscular twist. Kristen Stewart anchors the film as Lou, a reclusive gym manager whose quiet life is upended by a fiery romance with Katy O’Brian’s Jackie, an ambitious bodybuilder chasing big dreams. The movie doesn’t just lean into the usual star-crossed lovers trope—it drags them into the gritty underworld of Lou’s criminal family, delivering a tense mix of passion and violence that’s as stylish as it is unsettling.

What stands out is Rose Glass’s direction, which brings a sleek, almost hypnotic atmosphere to the story, paired with a sharp script co-written with Weronika Tofilska. The film’s tagline, “Revenge gets ripped,” hits home with the way the narrative flexes its darker muscle, exploring themes of loyalty, ambition, and the messy fallout of love entangled with crime. The supporting cast, including Ed Harris as Lou Sr. and Dave Franco as JJ, add layers of menace and complexity, making the family dynamics feel lived-in and fraught. Visually, the gym scenes and neon-lit nights in Vegas create a striking backdrop for the emotional and physical battles unfolding.

Those sensitive to the death of animal characters should be cautious here, as the film includes a notable moment involving a non-human character. Beyond that, the violence is more implied than gratuitous, but the emotional intensity and undercurrent of danger are constant companions throughout.

Love Lies Bleeding is a sleek, hypnotic thriller that mixes slow-burn romance with tense family crime drama, anchored by Kristen Stewart’s quietly powerful performance and neon-lit gym battles.

name: The Great Outdoors
overview: It's vacation time for outdoorsy Chicago man Chet Ripley, along with his wife, Connie, and their two kids, Buck and Ben. But a serene weekend of fishing at a Wisconsin lakeside cabin gets crashed by Connie's obnoxious brother-in-law, Roman Craig, his wife, Kate, and the couple's two daughters. As the excursion wears on, the Ripleys find themselves at odds with the stuffy Craig family.
tagline: This is no holiday… this is war!
review:
The Great Outdoors is a late-80s family comedy that feels like a John Hughes script got a nature retreat makeover—think Weekend at Bernie’s meets National Lampoon’s Vacation but with more fish guts and less subtlety. The film leans heavily on the clash between Dan Aykroyd’s obnoxious Roman Craig and John Candy’s laid-back Chet Ripley, which sparks plenty of broad, goofy humor. It’s not high art, but it’s charmingly goofy, buoyed by the natural chemistry between Candy and Aykroyd, and it definitely holds up as a feel-good, if somewhat predictable, comedy about family chaos in the great outdoors.

What really stands out is the way the film plays with the classic “fish out of water” trope—except here it’s more “family out of family,” as the two clans butt heads amid fishing lines and campfire mishaps. Howard Deutch’s direction keeps the pace lively, and John Hughes’s script brings that trademark mix of warmth and wit, even if the jokes sometimes rely on tired slapstick. The lakeside cabin setting provides some lovely visuals and a cozy backdrop for the escalating absurdity, with the tagline “This is no holiday… this is war!” capturing the film’s comedic battle-of-the-families vibe perfectly.

review:
It’s What’s Inside is a tense, claustrophobic thriller that feels like a blend of The Invitation and Get Out, mixing pre-wedding party awkwardness with creeping horror and existential dread. Greg Jardin’s direction leans into the unsettling vibe of a gathering gone sideways, and the ensemble cast—featuring James Morosini and Brittany O’Grady—does a solid job navigating the escalating paranoia and bizarre revelations. It’s not a laugh-out-loud horror, but it’s a wild ride that really leans into atmosphere and the slow burn of discomfort rather than cheap scares.

What’s most striking here is how the film uses the mysterious suitcase as a catalyst for unraveling group dynamics and personal traumas, turning a seemingly normal celebration into a nightmare where no one leaves unchanged, as the tagline promises. The writing teases out themes of trust, betrayal, and the grotesque unknown lurking beneath social facades, with some genuinely unsettling body horror moments that catch you off guard. The use of creepy critters like spiders, snakes, and bugs adds to the claustrophobic feeling, making the party setting feel more like a trap. It’s a smart, if unsettling, twist on the “party from hell” trope.

Those sensitive to body horror and creepy crawlies should be warned—this one dives deep into visceral discomfort with spiders, snakes, and bugs playing a disturbing role. Plus, there’s some gaslighting that ups the psychological tension. Animal harm and death, including non-human characters and a dragon, also come up, so if those are on your list, tread carefully.

review:
Phantasm is a cult classic that wedges itself firmly in the weird and eerie corner of late-70s horror, blending supernatural suspense with a surreal, almost dreamlike quality that sets it apart from your average slasher flick. Think of it as a hallucinatory fever dream where a creepy Tall Man with a deadly toolbox haunts a group of kids trying to unravel his mystery. It’s not polished by today’s standards, but that’s part of its charm — fans of offbeat horror like *The Evil Dead* or *Suspiria* will appreciate its unique vibe and low-budget creativity.

What really sticks with you here is the Tall Man himself, played with unnerving calmness by Angus Scrimm, who turns a grave robber into a truly iconic horror villain. The tagline, “If this one doesn’t scare you… you’re already dead!” nails that old-school horror bravado. The film’s mix of eerie atmosphere, bizarre weaponry, and a story that’s as cryptic as it is creepy makes it a fascinating watch. Don Coscarelli’s direction leans into the uncanny, with some genuinely memorable visuals and tension that hold up surprisingly well for such an early horror entry.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to intense horror triggers: Phantasm includes jump scares, blood and gore, and some pretty harrowing deaths, including those of kids and animals. There’s also scenes involving fire, mutilation, and that infamous dog death that has earned its grim reputation. If any of these are on your list, proceed with caution — the film doesn’t shy away from unsettling moments.

name: The Wolverine
overview: Wolverine faces his ultimate nemesis - and tests of his physical, emotional, and mortal limits - in a life-changing voyage to modern-day Japan.
tagline: When he's most vulnerable, he's most dangerous.
review:
The Wolverine is a moody, action-heavy take on the mutant hero that leans into its samurai-inspired setting with a brooding vibe that sets it apart from more colorful Marvel fare. Hugh Jackman’s Logan is at his most vulnerable—physically, emotionally, and existentially—which adds some welcome depth to the usual mutant mayhem. It’s less about flashy superhero antics and more about a gritty, personal journey, so fans expecting nonstop spectacle might want to temper their expectations. Think of it as Logan meets a classic Japanese revenge drama, with a dash of noir.

What really stands out is the film’s atmosphere, from the sleek, rain-soaked streets of modern Japan to the intense, sometimes brutal fight choreography. The tagline, “When he’s most vulnerable, he’s most dangerous,” nails the tone perfectly: this isn’t just another Wolverine punch-fest. The story pushes Logan to confront both physical limits and emotional scars, especially through his interactions with Mariko Yashida and the shadowy Harada clan. Director James Mangold balances these quieter moments with some memorable action set pieces, making the film feel like a character study wrapped in a superhero package.

Heads up for animal lovers: The movie includes several instances of animal death and abuse, including dogs, cats, and horses, which can be pretty tough scenes. There’s also a fair bit of creepy critters—spiders, snakes, bugs—that might unsettle some viewers. So if you’ve got any of those triggers, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
The Wolverine blends gritty samurai atmosphere with Hugh Jackman’s most vulnerable, emotionally charged performance as Logan, creating a brooding and intense take that feels more like a personal revenge drama than a typical superhero flick.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, scenes of animal abuse, unsettling spiders and snakes, and intense, brutal fight violence.

name: In Time
overview: In the not-too-distant future, the aging gene has been switched off. To avoid overpopulation, time has become the currency and the way people pay for luxuries and necessities. The rich can live forever, while the rest struggle to negotiate for their immortality. A poor young man who suddenly comes into a fortune of time finds himself on the run from a corrupt police force known as the "time keepers".

writers: Jonathan Hensleigh, J.J. Abrams, Tony Gilroy, Shane Salerno, Robert Roy Pool
name: Armageddon
overview: When an asteroid threatens to collide with Earth, NASA honcho Dan Truman determines the only way to stop it is to drill into its surface and detonate a nuclear bomb. This leads him to renowned driller Harry Stamper, who agrees to helm the dangerous space mission provided he can bring along his own hotshot crew. Among them is the cocksure A.J. who Harry thinks isn't good enough for his daughter, until the mission proves otherwise.
tagline: For love. For honor. For mankind.
review:
Armageddon is the quintessential late-90s disaster blockbuster, a Michael Bay spectacle that’s equal parts explosive action and heartfelt family drama. It’s got that feel of Armageddon meets The Right Stuff, with Bruce Willis leading a ragtag crew of drillers on a mission to save Earth from total annihilation. While it’s not the most subtle or nuanced sci-fi, it’s undeniably a wild ride with a big heart—plus, Ben Affleck’s cocky A.J. adds just the right dash of tension and charm. Fans of throwback disaster flicks will appreciate the over-the-top stakes and cheesy one-liners, even if it’s not quite as sharp as some of its genre peers.

What stands out are the film’s earnest themes of sacrifice, honor, and love, all wrapped up in its tagline: “For love. For honor. For mankind.” The writing leans hard into classic heroism, and the cast, including Liv Tyler and Steve Buscemi, rounds out a memorable team dynamic. The visuals are pure Michael Bay—big explosions, speedy cuts, and plenty of dramatic close-ups that make the peril feel immediate. The story’s core—a drilling mission on an asteroid paired with nuclear detonation—is as audacious as it is ridiculous, but it somehow nails the emotional stakes, especially in the father-daughter and mentor-protégé relationships.

Heads up for animal lovers: Armageddon doesn’t shy away from some tough content when it comes to animals. Multiple types of animals die on screen, including a dog, a horse, and a cat, among others. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or death, this one deserves a cautious approach—especially since some of the scenes can hit unexpectedly hard amid the space-bound chaos. Spiders, bugs, and snakes also make appearances, so those with bug-related triggers should keep that in mind.
emailReview:
Armageddon is a quintessential late-90s disaster blockbuster with explosive action, heartfelt family drama, and a cast led by Bruce Willis that balances big stakes with cheesy charm.

Be prepared for: on-screen deaths of a dog, horse, and cat, plus unsettling scenes involving spiders, bugs, and snakes.

writers: Michael Brandt, Derek Haas, Chris Morgan, Mark Millar, J.G. Jones
name: Wanted
overview: Doormat Wesley Gibson discovers that his recently murdered father – who Wesley never knew – belonged to a secret guild of assassins. After a leather-clad sexpot drafts Wesley into the society, he hones his innate killing skills and turns avenger.
review:
Wanted is a slick, adrenaline-fueled action flick that rides the wave of early-2000s stylized thrillers—think The Matrix meets a comic book come to life. James McAvoy’s transformation from meek office drone to badass assassin under Angelina Jolie’s leather-clad tutelage feels like the heart of the movie, even if the plot occasionally leans hard into cliché territory. It’s not quite the sharpest or most original of its genre, but the kinetic direction by Timur Bekmambetov and the over-the-top action sequences make it a wild ride that fans of slick violence and revenge tales will appreciate.

What stands out here is how the film embraces its comic-book roots with flair—slow-motion bullet curving, improbably cool kills, and a universe where destiny is both a burden and a weapon. The tagline “Choose your destiny” nails the tone perfectly: it’s all about transformation and empowerment, albeit with a heavy dose of hyper-violence and stylized grit. Morgan Freeman as the mysterious mentor and Terence Stamp’s grizzled assassin add a bit of gravitas, but it’s really McAvoy and Jolie’s chemistry that keeps the story engaging. The movie doesn’t shy away from dark themes or graphic content, which might turn off some, but it’s part of the package for this kind of high-octane fantasy.

Those who pin the animal harm triggers should be heavily warned here—this movie features multiple scenes involving animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, horses, rabbits, and cats. It’s an unfortunate and intense element that’s hard to miss and may be particularly upsetting for sensitive viewers. If you’re triggered by animal suffering, be cautious before diving in.
emailReview:
Wanted is a slick, adrenaline-fueled action flick that feels like a comic book come to life with stylish slow-motion bullet curving and over-the-top kills that keep the energy sky-high.

Be prepared for: multiple scenes of animal deaths including dogs, horses, rabbits, and cats, graphic violence, and intense revenge-driven action.

writers: Jane Goldman, Matthew Vaughn, Mark Millar, Dave Gibbons
name: Kingsman: The Golden Circle
overview: When an attack on the Kingsman headquarters takes place and a new villain rises, Eggsy and Merlin are forced to work together with the American agency known as the Statesman to save the world.

writers: Dan Gilroy, Max Borenstein, Derek Connolly, John Gatins
name: Kong: Skull Island
overview: Explore the mysterious and dangerous home of the king of the apes as a team of explorers ventures deep inside the treacherous, primordial island.
review:
Kong: Skull Island is a loud, pulpy action-adventure that rides the wave of modern monster movies with its heart firmly in the ’70s war flick meets giant ape showdown camp. It’s not aiming for subtlety, and that’s part of the fun—think Apocalypse Now crashes headlong into Jurassic Park, with a dose of King Kong mythology. Tom Hiddleston’s cool, steady presence anchors the chaos, while Samuel L. Jackson’s intense turn as a hotheaded colonel keeps the tension simmering. It’s not Oscar bait, but for fans of big-budget creature features, it’s a wild ride elevated by some surprisingly good practical effects and a killer soundtrack.

What stands out here is the world-building—there’s a real sense of mystery and danger lurking in Skull Island’s primordial jungles, and the film leans into the tribal and monstrous with gusto. The writing leans on familiar genre beats but sprinkles in enough character moments and political commentary to keep things from being just wall-to-wall explosions. Brie Larson’s Mason Weaver adds a thoughtful counterpoint to the military bravado, and the visuals do a solid job of balancing epic scale with intimate human moments. Plus, Toby Kebbell’s dual role as one of the soldiers and Kong’s motion-capture actor is a neat meta touch that fans of behind-the-scenes stuff will appreciate.

Heads up for animal lovers and sensitive viewers: this movie doesn’t shy away from tough scenes involving animals. There are notable deaths of a dog and a horse, and it’s confirmed that animals were harmed during production. If those triggers are on your list, proceed with caution—this one’s not shy about its collateral damage.
emailReview:
Kong: Skull Island delivers a loud, pulpy thrill ride that blends ’70s war movie grit with giant ape spectacle, boosted by strong performances from Tom Hiddleston and Samuel L. Jackson amid stunning practical effects and a killer soundtrack.

Be prepared for: dog death, horse death, animal harm during production, intense jungle violence, and explosive battle scenes.

writers: Glen Morgan, James Wong, Jeffrey Reddick
name: Final Destination
overview: After a teenager has a terrifying vision of him and his friends dying in a plane crash, he prevents the accident only to have Death hunt them down, one by one.
tagline: No accidents. No coincidences. No escapes. You can't cheat death.
review:
Final Destination is a cult classic that helped define early-2000s horror with its inventive take on the “cheating death” trope. Think of it as a high-stakes game of dominoes where every move feels inevitable yet suspenseful—sort of like if Hitchcock met Final Cut meets a particularly grim game of Jenga. It’s not just another slasher flick; it’s elevated by its clever premise and the way it turns everyday objects into instruments of doom. Devon Sawa as Alex Browning anchors the film with enough earnestness to sell the supernatural stakes, while Ali Larter’s Clear Rivers adds a grounded counterbalance to the chaos.

What really sticks with you is how the film builds tension through the unseen force of Death itself, hunting down the survivors one by one. The tagline says it all: “No accidents. No coincidences. No escapes.” The writing cleverly layers in paranoia and inevitability without relying too heavily on gore—though the deaths themselves are memorably elaborate and downright inventive. The film leans into horror conventions like jump scares and creepy visions but twists them into a suspenseful narrative about fate and mortality. The eerie score and the atmospheric direction by James Wong keep the momentum brisk and the chills coming.

Heads-up for those sensitive to jump scares and graphic deaths—this movie doesn’t hold back on creative fatal accidents, some involving gore and body horror elements like finger mutilation and people being burned alive. Also, there are a few emotionally heavy moments involving children and pets dying, which might sting for animal lovers or anyone sensitive to child loss. If spiders and flashing lights set off your alarms, consider yourself warned before diving into this one.
emailReview:
Final Destination turns the “cheating death” trope into a tense, inventive thriller where everyday objects become deadly traps and suspense builds with Hitchcockian precision.

Be prepared for: graphic finger mutilation, people being burned alive, pet deaths, child loss, and jump scares.

Hannibal Smith, Capt. H.M. ‘Howling Mad’ Murdock , Sgt. Bosco ‘B.A.’ Baracus, and Lt. Templeton ‘Faceman’ Peck help out various people they encounter.

name: The Grey
overview: After suffering a violent plane crash, a group of oil drillers is stranded in the most remote wilderness of Alaska, far from any chance of being rescued. Exposed to the icy cold and extreme living conditions, the few survivors, led by Ottway, an experienced hunter, will endure the tireless persecution of a pack of huge wolves.
tagline: Live or Die on This Day.

name: Life
overview: The six-member crew of the International Space Station is tasked with studying a sample from Mars that may be the first proof of extra-terrestrial life, which proves more intelligent than ever expected.
tagline: Be careful what you search for.
review:
Life is a tense sci-fi thriller that rides the familiar wave of space horror but manages to keep you on edge with its slick visuals and a solid cast led by Jake Gyllenhaal and Ryan Reynolds. It’s very much in the vein of Alien or The Thing, where curiosity opens a door to something deadly and unknowable. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it’s a pretty effective blend of claustrophobia and creeping dread — not as iconic as Ridley Scott’s masterpiece, but a worthy late-night watch if you’re into intelligent extraterrestrial threats.

What stands out here is the way the film leans into the tagline “Be careful what you search for.” The story’s about a crew studying a Martian sample that turns out to be way smarter and more dangerous than expected, and the escalating tension feels genuinely earned. The writing from Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick keeps the dialogue tight and the stakes rising, while director Daniel Espinosa’s pacing ensures the dread never lets up. The International Space Station setting offers a claustrophobic playground that ratchets up the suspense, and the creature design nails that slimy, unsettling vibe without overdoing it.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and death, as there are multiple instances involving animals dying, including pets and other creatures. Also, if bugs, spiders, or any squirmy critters make you uneasy, this one’s a no-go — they’re part of the unsettling atmosphere. More seriously, there are scenes involving suicide, self-harm, and torture, so keep those triggers in mind before diving in.
emailReview:
Life is a tense sci-fi thriller that nails claustrophobic dread with slick visuals and a cast led by Jake Gyllenhaal and Ryan Reynolds, delivering a gripping ride into intelligent extraterrestrial terror.

Be prepared for: animal deaths including pets, unsettling bugs and spiders, suicide, self-harm, and torture.

writers: Peter Farrelly, Mike Cerrone, Bobby Farrelly
name: Me, Myself & Irene
overview: Rhode Island State Trooper Charlie Baileygates has a multiple personality disorder. One personality is crazy and aggressive, while the other is more friendly and laid back. Both of these personalities fall in love with the same woman named Irene after Charlie loses his medication.
review:
Me, Myself & Irene is a wild Farrelly Brothers comedy that rides the line between goofy slapstick and surprisingly dark mental health humor. Jim Carrey is in full manic mode, playing a Rhode Island state trooper with a split personality—one part mild-mannered and the other pure unhinged chaos. It’s like Ace Ventura meets Fight Club, but with way more fart jokes and Renée Zellweger as the love interest caught in the middle. The film leans hard into absurdity and crude humor, making it a bit of a time capsule from the early 2000s comedy scene. It’s not high art, but Carrey’s energy keeps it entertaining if you’re in the mood for something loud and raunchy.

What stands out here is how the movie uses Charlie’s dissociative identity disorder as a comedic device, even if it’s not exactly a sensitive or nuanced portrayal by today’s standards. The tagline “From gentle to mental” nails the tone perfectly—shifting between laid-back charm and unpredictable rage. The Farrelly Brothers’ signature blend of physical comedy and offbeat scenarios is on full display, and the supporting cast adds some solid flavor, especially Chris Cooper as the hard-nosed lieutenant. The film’s willingness to get weird with its premise is refreshing, even if some jokes haven’t aged well.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: despite no animals actually dying on screen, there are a few eyebrow-raising moments involving animal harm. A chicken is shoved off-screen into a bad guy’s backside (yeah, really), and two Rottweilers appear tied up in a junkyard, hinting at neglect. Also, there’s a fair bit of bug-related grossness—mainly flies buzzing around Jim Carrey’s face. If you’re wary of animal abuse triggers, this one might be worth approaching with caution.
emailReview:
Jim Carrey delivers manic energy in this wild Farrelly Brothers comedy that mixes absurd slapstick with a surprisingly dark take on split personalities and mental health.

Be prepared for: off-screen chicken assault, tied-up Rottweiler neglect, and plenty of buzzing flies around the lead’s face.

name: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
cleanName: austin powers spy who shagged me

overview:
When diabolical genius Dr. Evil travels back in time to steal superspy Austin Powers's ‘mojo,’ Austin must return to the swingin' '60s himself - with the help of American agent, Felicity Shagwell - to stop the dastardly plan. 

Once there, Austin faces off against Dr. Evil's army of minions to try to save the world in his own unbelievably groovy way.
tagline: First he fought for the Crown. Now he's fighting for the Family Jewels.
review:
Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me is a cheeky, campy sequel that doubles down on the goofy spy spoof formula Mike Myers perfected in the first film. It’s a wild ride through ’60s kitsch and absurd humor, with Myers not only reprising Austin but also slipping into his other iconic roles like Dr. Evil and Fat Bastard. If you liked the original’s blend of silliness and nostalgia, this one delivers more of the same — though it leans into cruder jokes and broader slapstick, so it’s not quite as sharp but definitely bigger and brasher.

What stands out here is the over-the-top premise: Dr. Evil steals Austin’s mojo, forcing him to travel back in time with the help of the delightfully named Felicity Shagwell (Heather Graham). The film thrives on its ridiculous setups and callbacks to spy tropes, with a soundtrack and visual style that revel in retro camp. Verne Troyer as Mini-Me steals a lot of scenes, adding a delightfully weird energy. The tagline, “First he fought for the Crown. Now he’s fighting for the Family Jewels,” perfectly captures the film’s blend of absurdity and self-aware innuendo.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: the film features multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including a dead skunk and some unsettling scenes involving various creatures. If animal harm or death is a hard stop for you, be heavily warned. Also, spiders and bugs make appearances, so those triggers are worth noting as well.
emailReview:
Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me doubles down on the goofy spy spoof with wild ’60s kitsch, outrageous characters, and Verne Troyer’s Mini-Me stealing every scene he’s in.

Be prepared for: dead skunks, animal abuse, creepy spiders, and unsettling insect scenes.

tagline: Matt never saw her coming... but all his friends had!

Though the film is visually modern, the bard's dialogue remains.
tagline: My only love sprung from my only hate.

overview: It's vacation time for Carter as he finds himself alongside Lee in Hong Kong wishing for more excitement. While Carter wants to party and meet the ladies, Lee is out to track down a Triad gang lord who may be responsible for killing two men at the American Embassy. Things get complicated as the pair stumble onto a counterfeiting plot. The boys are soon up to their necks in fist fights and life-threatening situations. A trip back to the U.S. may provide the answers about the bombing, the counterfeiting, and the true allegiance of sexy customs agent Isabella.
tagline: Get ready for a second Rush!

writers: Paul Greengrass, Christopher Rouse, Robert Ludlum

overview: After accidentally crash-landing in 2022, time-traveling fighter pilot Adam Reed teams up with his 12-year-old self on a mission to save the future.

tagline: The party you've only dreamed about.

writers: Jim Wheat, Ken Wheat, David Twohy
name: The Chronicles of Riddick
overview: After years of outrunning ruthless bounty hunters, escaped convict Riddick suddenly finds himself caught between opposing forces in a fight for the future of the human race. Now, waging incredible battles on fantastic and deadly worlds, this lone, reluctant hero will emerge as humanity's champion - and the last hope for a universe on the edge of annihilation.
tagline: All the power in the universe can't change destiny.

writers: Marv Wolfman, Gene Colan, David S. Goyer
name: Blade II
overview: A rare mutation has occurred within the vampire community - The Reaper. A vampire so consumed with an insatiable bloodlust that they prey on vampires as well as humans, transforming victims who are unlucky enough to survive into Reapers themselves. Blade is asked by the Vampire Nation for his help in preventing a nightmare plague that would wipe out both humans and vampires.
review:
Blade II feels like a darker, bloodier upgrade from the original—a vampire action flick that leans hard into Guillermo del Toro’s flair for monstrous design and atmospheric grit. It’s got the stylish edge of a late-90s superhero sequel but with a heavier emphasis on horror and grotesque creature effects. Wesley Snipes returns as the titular half-vampire, half-human Blade, bringing his cool, stoic presence, but it’s really the wild, mutated Reapers and del Toro’s signature visual touches that steal the show. Fans of the first Blade or del Toro’s other genre work will appreciate this as a slick, if somewhat pulpy, dive into vampire lore.

What stands out most is how the film balances its vampire politics with nonstop action and a surprisingly fleshed-out mythology. The tagline "Faster. Sharper. Deadlier." isn’t just marketing fluff — the Reapers are a terrifying new threat that upend the usual vampire hierarchy, making for some inventive fight scenes and creature designs. The cast, including Ron Perlman and Norman Reedus, adds some solid supporting flavor, and Kris Kristofferson’s Whistler continues to provide that grizzled mentor vibe Blade needs. The blend of horror elements with superhero-style combat keeps things moving, though the plot doesn’t stray too far from familiar territory.

Heads up for animal lovers: Blade II is heavy on animal-related triggers, including several instances of animal deaths and abuse. If you’re sensitive to pets or other animals suffering on screen, this one could be rough. Also, the presence of spiders and snakes might unsettle some viewers. So if those are on your list, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Blade II cranks up the gore and creature horror with Guillermo del Toro’s signature flair, turning a vampire action flick into a stylish, monstrous spectacle full of wild Reaper designs and nonstop, brutal fights.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths, scenes of animal abuse, spiders, snakes, and intense creature violence.

name: Twister
overview: TV weatherman Bill Harding is trying to get his tornado-hunter wife, Jo, to sign divorce papers so he can marry his girlfriend Melissa. But Mother Nature, in the form of a series of intense storms sweeping across Oklahoma, has other plans. Soon the three have joined the team of stormchasers as they attempt to insert a revolutionary measuring device into the very heart of several extremely violent tornados.
review:
Twister is the quintessential ’90s disaster flick, blending adrenaline-pumping storm chases with a soap-opera love triangle that somehow works better than you'd expect. It feels like Armageddon meets a weather report, with Helen Hunt and Bill Paxton leading a team chasing tornadoes across Oklahoma. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, the film’s mix of thrilling practical effects and emotional stakes makes it a wild ride that’s still a blast decades later—fans of big-budget natural disaster movies will appreciate its place in that stormy pantheon.

What stands out here is the sheer intensity of the tornado sequences, which remain impressive for their time and grounded by a surprisingly human story. The tagline, “The dark side of nature,” nails the tone—nature is awe-inspiring but merciless, and the storm chasers’ obsession puts them right in its crosshairs. The love triangle adds some tension beyond the weather, with the personal drama occasionally undercutting the action but ultimately giving the characters more to do than just run from flying debris. Plus, Philip Seymour Hoffman’s presence as Dusty hints at the strong supporting cast that rounds out the film.

Heads up for animal lovers: Twister includes multiple scenes involving animal harm and death, including a dog, horse, and cat—all of which might hit hard if those are on your list. Also, if bugs, spiders, or snakes are triggers for you, those appear as well, adding another layer of unease amid the chaos.
emailReview: Twister is a ’90s disaster classic that balances jaw-dropping practical tornado effects with a surprisingly heartfelt love triangle, anchored by standout performances from Helen Hunt and Bill Paxton. Be prepared for: dog, horse, and cat deaths, plus unsettling scenes involving bugs, spiders, and snakes.

name: Safe House
overview: A dangerous CIA renegade resurfaces after a decade on the run. When the safe house he's remanded to is attacked by mercenaries, a rookie operative escapes with him. Now, the unlikely allies must stay alive long enough to uncover who wants them dead.

name: The Tomorrow War
overview: A man is drafted to fight in a future war where the fate of humanity relies on his ability to confront his past.
tagline: The fight for tomorrow begins today.

tagline: Addicted to one-night stands or dependent on one another?

tagline: Someone you pass on the street may already be the love of your life.

writers: Christina Hodson, John Francis Daley, Jonathan Goldstein, Joby Harold, Harry Lampert, Gardner Fox, Robert Kanigher, Carmine Infantino, Jerry Siegel, Joe Shuster, Bob Kane, Bill Finger, William Moulton Marston
name: The Flash
overview: When his attempt to save his family inadvertently alters the future, Barry Allen becomes trapped in a reality in which General Zod has returned and there are no Super Heroes to turn to. In order to save the world that he is in and return to the future that he knows, Barry's only hope is to race for his life. But will making the ultimate sacrifice be enough to reset the universe?

directors: Jeff Schaffer, Alec Berg, David Mandel
writers: Alec Berg, David Mandel, Jeff Schaffer
name: EuroTrip
overview: When Scott learns that his longtime cyber-buddy from Berlin is a gorgeous young woman, he and his friends embark on a trip across Europe.
tagline: No actual Europeans were harmed in the making of this film.

name: Ghostbusters II
overview: Five years after they defeated Gozer, the Ghostbusters are out of business. When Dana begins to have ghost problems again, the boys come out of retirement to aid her and hopefully save New York City from a new paranormal threat.
tagline: Guess who's coming to save the world again?
review:
Ghostbusters II is a solid follow-up that leans into the goofy charm and supernatural hijinks that made the original a cult classic, though it doesn’t quite capture the same lightning in a bottle. Ivan Reitman reunites the original cast for another round of ghostbusting in New York, blending comedy, camp, and a touch of heart. If you liked the first movie’s blend of quirky humor and spooky fun, this one feels like a more polished but slightly less surprising sequel—think Ghostbusters meets a Saturday morning cartoon with a splash of late ’80s sentimentality.

What stands out here is the chemistry among Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, and Harold Ramis, who also co-wrote the script. Their banter keeps the movie buoyant even when the plot stumbles a bit, and Sigourney Weaver’s Dana Barrett returns with her own uncanny troubles that pull the crew back into action. The tagline—“Guess who’s coming to save the world again?”—perfectly sets the tone for a nostalgic, if occasionally uneven, ride through paranormal chaos. The film leans heavily into its spooky visuals and quirky special effects, and while the plot is pretty straightforward, moments like the possessed baby carriage and the slime-powered Statue of Liberty bring a goofy flair that only Ghostbusters could pull off.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this movie features multiple instances where animals die or are otherwise distressed, including pets and non-human creatures. If you’re wary of bugs, snakes, or spiders, those also show up to complicate the ghostly affairs. It’s definitely worth being cautious if those triggers are on your list.
emailReview:
Ghostbusters II delivers a nostalgic blend of goofy charm and supernatural chaos, with standout chemistry from Bill Murray and the gang keeping things lively amid quirky special effects and late ’80s vibes.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths, distressed pets, creepy bugs, snakes, and spiders tangled up in the ghostly hijinks.

writers: Jon Hurwitz, Hayden Schlossberg, Adam Herz
name: American Reunion
overview: The characters we met a little more than a decade ago return to East Great Falls for their high-school reunion. In one long-overdue weekend, they will discover what has changed, who hasn’t, and that time and distance can’t break the bonds of friendship.
tagline: Save the best piece for last.

name: Drag Me to Hell
overview: After denying a woman the extension she needs to keep her home, loan officer Christine Brown sees her once-promising life take a startling turn for the worse. Christine is convinced she's been cursed by a Gypsy, but her boyfriend is skeptical. Her only hope seems to lie in a psychic who claims he can help her lift the curse and keep her soul from being dragged straight to hell.
tagline: Christine Brown has a good job, a great boyfriend, and a bright future. But in three days, she's going to hell.
review:
Sam Raimi’s *Drag Me to Hell* is a gleefully over-the-top horror flick that blends supernatural scares with dark comedy in a way that feels like *The Evil Dead* meets a cautionary urban legend. It’s not just your average curse story — it leans hard into camp and practical effects, giving it a wild, pulpy energy that horror fans craving something both creepy and a little ridiculous will appreciate. Alison Lohman’s performance as Christine grounds the chaos just enough, making you root for her even as things get downright grotesque.

What stands out here is Raimi’s signature style: the frantic camera work, the exaggerated sound design, and a plot that escalates absurdly fast from a simple mortgage denial to a soul-threatening curse. The tagline, “Christine Brown has a good job, a great boyfriend, and a bright future. But in three days, she’s going to hell,” nails the mix of everyday life and supernatural terror perfectly. The psychic angle adds a fun twist, and the movie’s willingness to dive into old-school horror tropes — from creepy bugs to body horror — keeps things unpredictable and entertaining.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and death: this movie does not shy away from some pretty distressing scenes involving pets and other animals, which could hit hard if you’re on the lookout for those triggers. Also, if bugs, spiders, or snakes send you running, the film leans heavily into those creepy crawlies. And, as expected from a Raimi horror, the body horror elements are pretty intense, so be prepared for some gnarly visuals.
emailReview:
Sam Raimi’s *Drag Me to Hell* is a wildly entertaining blend of campy horror and dark comedy, with Alison Lohman’s grounded performance keeping the chaos both creepy and oddly relatable.

Be prepared for: disturbing animal harm and death, swarms of bugs and spiders, intense body horror, and unsettling psychic torment.

writers: Michael Green, Glenn Ficarra, John Requa, John Norville, Josh Goldstein
name: Jungle Cruise
overview: Based on Disneyland's theme park ride where a small riverboat takes a group of travelers through a jungle filled with dangerous animals and reptiles, but with a supernatural element.
tagline: Only one adventure gets this wild.
review:
Jungle Cruise is a loud, colorful adventure romp that feels like Indiana Jones meets Pirates of the Caribbean—if both rides had a baby with a heavy dose of supernatural mumbo jumbo and Dwayne Johnson’s trademark grin. It’s not exactly breaking new ground, but if you’re here for a goofy, action-packed trip through the jungle with Emily Blunt’s determined Dr. Lily Houghton and Johnson’s wisecracking riverboat captain Frank Wolff, you’ll probably have a good time. The chemistry between the leads helps elevate what could’ve been a pretty standard theme-park-movie tie-in.

What stands out is the film’s blend of old-school adventure tropes with modern CGI spectacle. The jungle is lush and dangerous, packed with snakes, spiders, and all the classic jungle peril, but the supernatural elements add a fun twist. Plus, the villainous crew led by Edgar Ramírez injects enough menace to keep things interesting without going too dark. The tagline, “Only one adventure gets this wild,” isn’t lying—the film leans into its wilder, more ridiculous moments with tongue firmly in cheek.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm and death: Jungle Cruise includes the deaths of a dog and a child, which might hit hard for some. There are also jump scares, plenty of creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes, and some harsher moments involving fire and mutilation. If you’re on the lookout for gore, violence, or scenes that might unsettle you with flashing lights or claustrophobic tension, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Jungle Cruise is a loud, colorful adventure romp that blends Indiana Jones charm with Pirates of the Caribbean silliness, all powered by Dwayne Johnson’s grin and Emily Blunt’s determined spirit in a jungle that’s as lush as it is dangerous.

Be prepared for: the deaths of a dog and a child, jump scares, creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes, fire, and scenes of mutilation.

name: Red Sparrow
overview: Prima ballerina, Dominika Egorova faces a bleak and uncertain future after she suffers an injury that ends her career. She soon turns to Sparrow School, a secret intelligence service that trains exceptional young people to use their minds and bodies as weapons. Dominika emerges as the most dangerous Sparrow after completing the sadistic training process. As she comes to terms with her new abilities, she meets a CIA agent who tries to convince her that he is the only person she can trust.

primaryTitle: Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby

name: Talladega Nights: the Ballad of Ricky Bobby
