overview: The fastest man on four wheels, Ricky Bobby is one of the greatest drivers in NASCAR history. A big, hairy American winning machine, Ricky has everything a dimwitted daredevil could want, a luxurious mansion, a smokin' hot wife and all the fast food he can eat. But Ricky's turbo-charged lifestyle hits an unexpected speed bump when he's bested by flamboyant Euro-idiot Jean Girard and reduced to a fear-ridden wreck.
tagline: The story of a man who could only count to #1.
review:
Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby is a wild, absurd comedy that rides the line between outright parody and affectionate tribute to NASCAR culture. Will Ferrell leads as the hilariously dim-witted, all-American speed demon whose life unravels when a flashy French rival (Sacha Baron Cohen) enters the scene. It’s like if Anchorman and Days of Thunder had a baby—loud, ridiculous, and packed with quotable lines. While it’s not the sharpest comedy you’ll see, it’s elevated by Ferrell’s commitment to his character’s ridiculous bravado and the goofy chemistry with John C. Reilly’s sidekick, Cal Naughton, Jr.

What stands out is the film’s unapologetic embrace of over-the-top stereotypes and physical comedy, all under Adam McKay’s direction. The tagline, “The story of a man who could only count to #1,” nails the tone perfectly: it’s about ego, insecurity, and the absurd lengths we go to stay on top. The film leans hard into NASCAR tropes but also pokes fun at them, with a side of ridiculous family drama and even a little existential crisis thrown in for good measure. Plus, you’ll either love or be baffled by the flamboyant Jean Girard, whose presence adds a bizarre but welcome contrast.

Heads-up for those sensitive to animal-related content: this movie features multiple instances where pets and other animals die or are mistreated, which might be surprisingly grim amidst the goofiness. If the idea of animals in distress is a hard pass for you, be cautious here. There’s also some mild gross-out humor (vomiting) and a few moments of gaslighting, but it’s really the animal triggers that stand out most.
emailReview:
Talladega Nights is a loud, ridiculous comedy fueled by Will Ferrell’s over-the-top bravado and a delightfully absurd NASCAR world where ego and ridiculousness collide.

Be prepared for: pet deaths, animal mistreatment, vomiting, and moments of gaslighting.

name: Machete
overview: After being set-up and betrayed by the man who hired him to assassinate a Texas Senator, an ex-Federale launches a brutal rampage of revenge against his former boss.
tagline: They just messed with the wrong Mexican.

name: Event Horizon
overview: In 2047 a group of astronauts are sent to investigate and salvage the starship 'Event Horizon' which disappeared mysteriously 7 years before on its maiden voyage. With its return, the crew of the 'Lewis and Clark' discovers the real truth behind the disappearance of the 'Event Horizon' – and something even more terrifying.
review:
Event Horizon is a 90s sci-fi horror cocktail that’s equal parts cosmic dread and gruesome nightmare—a bit like Alien meets The Shining in space. Directed by Paul W. S. Anderson, it’s got that cult-classic vibe, with a cast led by Laurence Fishburne and Sam Neill delivering some solid performances amid the chaos. The film’s tagline, "Infinite space. Infinite terror," nails it: the story of a rescue mission gone sideways aboard a lost starship taps into deep space paranoia and supernatural horror, making it a wild ride for genre fans, even if it leans heavily into familiar tropes.

What sets Event Horizon apart is its commitment to atmosphere and unsettling visuals. The starship itself feels like a character—dark, labyrinthine, and malevolent. The film blends sci-fi tech with hellish imagery in a way that’s both visually striking and genuinely disturbing. The writing leans into psychological horror, exploring themes of madness and trauma as the crew unravels the ship’s grim secret. While the plot isn’t the most original, the fusion of space exploration with supernatural terror creates a tense, claustrophobic mood that lingers.

Heads up for animal lovers and arachnophobes: Event Horizon features multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, including dogs, cats, horses, and other pets, alongside unsettling bug and spider appearances. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or creepy crawlies, this one’s going to test your nerves.
emailReview:
Event Horizon is a cult-classic blend of cosmic dread and supernatural horror that turns its starship setting into a dark, malevolent character full of unsettling visuals and psychological twists.

Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths including dogs and horses, disturbing spiders and bugs, and intense scenes of trauma and madness.

writers: Tom Wheeler, Brian Lynch, William Davies, Andrew Adamson, Charles Perrault, David H. Steinberg
name: Puss in Boots
overview: Long before he even met Shrek, the notorious fighter, lover and outlaw Puss in Boots becomes a hero when he sets off on an adventure with the tough and street smart Kitty Softpaws and the mastermind Humpty Dumpty to save his town. This is the true story of The Cat, The Myth, The Legend... The Boots.
tagline: Live for danger. Fight for justice. Pray for mercy.

writers: John Glenn, Travis Wright, Hillary Seitz, Dan McDermott
name: Eagle Eye
overview: Jerry Shaw and Rachel Holloman are two strangers whose lives are suddenly thrown into turmoil by a mysterious woman they have never met. Threatening their lives and family, the unseen caller uses everyday technology to control their actions and push them into increasing danger. As events escalate, Jerry and Rachel become the country's most-wanted fugitives and must figure out what is happening to them.

name: Longlegs
overview: FBI Agent Lee Harker is a gifted new recruit assigned to the unsolved case of an elusive serial killer. As the case takes complex turns, unearthing evidence of the occult, Harker discovers a personal connection to the merciless killer and must race against time to stop him before he claims the lives of another innocent family.
review:
Longlegs is a grim, slow-burn horror-thriller that leans heavily into occult serial killer territory, with a strong procedural backbone. Think Silence of the Lambs meets a supernatural twist, with Maika Monroe as the determined FBI agent and a surprisingly eerie Nicolas Cage in the titular role. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, Osgood Perkins crafts a moody, atmospheric experience that fans of dark detective stories will appreciate, even if the pacing occasionally drags.

What stands out here is the way the film ties the killer’s mythos to a personal connection for Agent Lee Harker, giving the usual “hunt the serial killer” plot an emotional hook. The tagline, “Say your prayers,” feels fitting given how much the occult seeps into the story—this isn’t just about catching a bad guy, it’s about confronting something far darker. The supporting cast, including Blair Underwood and Alicia Witt, adds solid weight, but it’s Monroe’s steely focus that keeps the narrative grounded amid the creepier elements.

Be heavily warned if animal harm or death is on your list to avoid—there are multiple instances involving dogs, cats, horses, and other creatures, some of which are quite unsettling. Spiders, snakes, and general bug imagery also contribute to the film’s unsettling vibe. Those sensitive to animal-related content and occult horror should proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Longlegs delivers a moody, atmospheric blend of occult horror and procedural thriller, anchored by Maika Monroe’s steely FBI agent and a chilling Nicolas Cage performance that turns the serial killer mythos into something deeply personal.

Be prepared for: multiple disturbing animal deaths involving dogs, cats, and horses, unsettling spider and snake imagery, and intense occult horror elements.

name: Insidious: Chapter 2
overview: The haunted Lambert family seeks to uncover the mysterious childhood secret that has left them dangerously connected to the spirit world.
tagline: It will take what you love most.
review:
Insidious: Chapter 2 leans hard into the haunted house genre while doubling down on the creepy family secrets that made the first film a hit. Directed by James Wan and co-written with Leigh Whannell, it feels like a slicker, darker sequel that fans of the original will appreciate—think Poltergeist meets The Conjuring’s more tangled family drama. Patrick Wilson and Rose Byrne return as the Lamberts, trying to unravel a sinister childhood mystery that’s got them all dangerously tethered to the spirit world. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but the atmosphere and pacing keep the tension high enough to justify the ride.

What stands out here is the way the film layers its scares with a heavy dose of supernatural mythology, all while managing to keep the emotional stakes grounded in the family’s trauma. Lin Shaye’s Elise Rainier provides a familiar anchor, and the script leans into the idea that what haunts us is often tied to what we love most—a tagline that’s echoed throughout the film’s eerie moments. The visuals are classic Wan: shadowy, unsettling, and inventive with its ghostly apparitions. The score pulses just right, amplifying the dread without overwhelming the scenes.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content—multiple animals meet grim fates here, including dogs, cats, and even a horse, alongside some distressing scenes involving animal abuse and death. The film also doesn’t shy away from body horror, bugs, and unsettling supernatural elements that might unnerve viewers. Plus, there’s some gaslighting and a generally oppressive atmosphere that leans into psychological terror. If any of these hit close to home, be prepared for a rougher watch.
emailReview:
Insidious: Chapter 2 builds on the haunted house vibe with slick direction, chilling family drama, and shadowy ghostly visuals that keep the tension tight and the scares sharp.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and a horse, scenes of animal abuse, unsettling body horror, and intense psychological gaslighting.

writers: Steve Niles, Stuart Beattie, Brian Nelson, Ben Templesmith
name: 30 Days of Night
overview: This is the story of an isolated Alaskan town that is plunged into darkness for a month each year when the sun sinks below the horizon. As the last rays of light fade, the town is attacked by a bloodthirsty gang of vampires bent on an uninterrupted orgy of destruction. Only the small town's husband-and-wife Sheriff team stand between the survivors and certain destruction.

writers: Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, Peter Jackson, Alice Sebold
name: The Lovely Bones
overview: After being brutally murdered, 14-year-old Susie Salmon watches from heaven over her grief-stricken family -- and her killer. As she observes their daily lives, she must balance her thirst for revenge with her desire for her family to heal.
tagline: The story of a life and everything that came after...
review:
Peter Jackson’s *The Lovely Bones* blends supernatural drama with a haunting coming-of-age story, anchored by Saoirse Ronan’s quietly compelling turn as Susie Salmon. It’s a grim, ethereal meditation on loss and grief, sitting somewhere between *Ghost* and *Mystic River*—though it’s more visually stylized than either. The film’s mix of heaven’s pastel dreamscapes and the raw, gritty aftermath of trauma makes for a mood that’s unsettling but strangely beautiful, even if it doesn’t fully escape the weight of its heavy subject matter.

What stands out here is the way Jackson and his co-writers craft that liminal space between life and death, where Susie floats, watching both her grieving family and her killer. The performances from Mark Wahlberg and Rachel Weisz as the Salmon parents bring a grounded emotional core, while Stanley Tucci’s chilling portrayal of George Harvey adds an eerie undercurrent. The film’s tagline, "The story of a life and everything that came after…," really nails its bittersweet tone, capturing that tension between longing for justice and the slow, painful process of healing.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to creepy crawlies—this one features a notable amount of bugs, used symbolically but also enough to unsettle the bug-averse. If little critters get under your skin, be prepared.
emailReview:
Peter Jackson’s *The Lovely Bones* crafts a haunting blend of ethereal dreamscapes and gritty emotional drama, anchored by Saoirse Ronan’s quietly compelling performance and Stanley Tucci’s chilling villainy.

Be prepared for: unsettling bug swarms, ghostly visions, child murder, and tense scenes of stalking.

writers: Jon Hoeber, Erich Hoeber, Warren Ellis, Cully Hamner
name: RED 2
overview: Retired C.I.A. agent Frank Moses reunites his unlikely team of elite operatives for a global quest to track down a missing portable nuclear device.

name: The Heat
overview: Uptight and straight-laced, FBI Special Agent Sarah Ashburn is a methodical investigator with a reputation for excellence--and hyper-arrogance. Shannon Mullins, one of Boston P.D.'s "finest," is foul-mouthed and has a very short fuse, and uses her gut instinct and street smarts to catch the most elusive criminals. Neither has ever had a partner, or a friend for that matter. When these two wildly incompatible law officers join forces to bring down a ruthless drug lord, they become the last thing anyone expected: buddies.
tagline: They're just trying to stay alive long enough to kill each other.

name: Happy Death Day
overview: Caught in a bizarre and terrifying time warp, college student Tree finds herself repeatedly reliving the day of her murder, ultimately realizing that she must identify the killer and the reason for her death before her chances of survival run out.
tagline: Get up. Live your day. Get killed. Again.

writers: Shane Black, Jonathan Lemkin, Alfred Gough, Miles Millar, Channing Gibson
name: Lethal Weapon 4
overview: With personal crises and age weighing in on them, Riggs and Murtaugh must contend with deadly Chinese triads trying to free their former leaders from prison and onto American soil.

writers: Stephen King, Steven E. de Souza
name: The Running Man
overview: By 2017, the global economy has collapsed and U.S. society has become a totalitarian police state, censoring all cultural activity. The government pacifies the populace by broadcasting a number of game shows in which convicted criminals fight for their lives, including the gladiator-style The Running Man, hosted by the ruthless Damon Killian, where “runners” attempt to evade “stalkers” and certain death for a chance to be pardoned and set free.
tagline: It is the year 2019. "The Running Man" is a deadly game no one has ever survived. But... Schwarzenegger has yet to play.
review:
The Running Man is a pulpy, dystopian sci-fi action flick straight out of the ’80s, with Schwarzenegger at his peak as the muscle-bound hero fighting a grim totalitarian future. Think Rollerball meets The Hunger Games before the latter existed—an over-the-top televised death game where criminals run for their lives. It’s not subtle, but it’s got that cheesy charm and relentless pace that keeps you watching, even if the politics and performances sometimes skate on thin ice.

What really stands out is the film's satirical edge, skewering media sensationalism and authoritarian control while delivering plenty of shootouts, stunts, and one-liners. Richard Dawson as the smarmy game show host Damon Killian is a memorable piece of camp, adding a twisted game-show vibe to the brutal gladiator setup. The bleak future is painted with neon-soaked grit, and the plot moves briskly through its “fight for freedom” beats without much filler. If you’re into retro sci-fi with a dose of tongue-in-cheek social commentary, this one’s worth a look.

Heads-up for viewers: this movie doesn’t shy away from animal deaths—dogs, cats, horses—and there’s also a fair share of body horror and brutal violence, including some pretty graphic scenes of characters getting squashed or otherwise maimed. Plus, if bugs, spiders, or claustrophobic moments set off alarms for you, be warned. It’s a wild ride that leans heavily into shock value alongside its dystopian thrills.
emailReview:
The Running Man is a neon-soaked, pulpy sci-fi blast from the ’80s with Schwarzenegger flexing his muscles in a grim televised death game that never takes itself too seriously.

Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths including dogs and horses, unsettling body horror, claustrophobic scenes, and creepy insects.

overview: A film about the tumultuous Gucci family fashion dynasty and the murder of the grandson of founder Guccio Gucci.

overview: 64 years before he becomes the tyrannical president of Panem, Coriolanus Snow sees a chance for a change in fortunes when he mentors Lucy Gray Baird, the female tribute from District 12.

name: Hush
overview: A deaf woman is stalked by a psychotic killer in her secluded home.
review:
Hush is a lean, tense horror-thriller that tightens the usual home invasion setup with a clever twist: the protagonist Maddie is deaf, and that silence is weaponized in chilling ways. Directed by Mike Flanagan and co-written by and starring Kate Siegel, this 2016 film feels like a smarter, scarier take on classics like Wait Until Dark or even a quieter, more claustrophobic version of You're Next. It’s not just another slasher flick—there’s real craft in how it uses sound (and lack thereof) to crank up the suspense.

What stands out is the film’s minimalist approach. Maddie’s isolated home becomes a character itself, and the film plays with perception, forcing viewers to engage beyond auditory cues. John Gallagher Jr. makes a suitably creepy antagonist, “The Man,” whose menace is magnified by Maddie’s vulnerability and resourcefulness. The tagline “Silence can be killer” perfectly sums up the tension: the usual horror beats are elevated by the unique communication barrier and the cat-and-mouse game that ensues. It’s a masterclass in atmosphere, with just enough gore and brutality to satisfy genre fans without going overboard.

Trigger-wise, this one leans heavily into animal harm (including the death of a dog, a cat, and even a horse), plus some unsettling body harm and violence against Maddie. Those sensitive to animal deaths or domestic violence should proceed with caution. There’s also a shower scene and some pretty intense moments involving cutting and self-harm. If you’re squeamish about animals or vulnerable characters in peril, be warned—this one doesn’t pull punches.
emailReview:
Hush is a taut, atmospheric thriller that uses silence as a weapon, with a standout performance by Kate Siegel that turns a home invasion into a nerve-wracking game of survival.

Be prepared for: the death of a dog, a cat, and a horse, violence against a deaf protagonist, cutting, and intense body harm.

writers: Sacha Baron Cohen, Anthony Hines, Dan Swimer, Peter Baynham, Erica Rivinoja, Dan Mazer, Jena Friedman, Lee Kern, Nina Pedrad
name: Borat Subsequent Moviefilm
overview: 14 years after making a film about his journey across the USA, Borat risks life and limb when he returns to the United States with his young daughter, and reveals more about the culture, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the political elections.

name: Man On a Ledge
overview: An ex-cop turned con threatens to jump to his death from a Manhattan hotel rooftop. The NYPD dispatch a female police psychologist to talk him down. However, unbeknownst to the police on the scene, the suicide attempt is a cover for the biggest diamond heist ever pulled.

writers: Michael McDowell, Larry Wilson, Alfred Gough, Miles Millar, Seth Grahame-Smith
name: Beetlejuice Beetlejuice
overview: Thirty-six years after the events of the first film, the Deetz family returns home to Winter River following Charles Deetz's unexpected death. Lydia's life is turned upside down when her rebellious teenage daughter, Astrid, discovers the mysterious model of the town in the attic and the portal to the Afterlife is accidentally opened, releasing Betelgeuse.
tagline: The ghost with the most is back.
review:
Beetlejuice Beetlejuice brings Tim Burton’s signature offbeat gothic charm back to the screen with a sequel that leans into nostalgia while introducing a fresh generation to the macabre fun. It’s a quirky supernatural comedy that feels like Beetlejuice meets Stranger Things, with Jenna Ortega’s rebellious Astrid stepping into the spotlight alongside Winona Ryder’s Lydia and, of course, Michael Keaton’s devilishly entertaining title character. It’s not quite as wildly unpredictable as the original, but there’s enough dark whimsy and chaotic energy here to keep fans of the cult classic intrigued.

What stands out is the way the film explores family grief and legacy through the lens of otherworldly mischief, using the mysterious model town and Afterlife portal as clever plot devices to unravel new mysteries. The cast is a solid mix of returning and new faces, with Catherine O’Hara and Willem Dafoe adding extra layers of eccentricity. The writing leans into classic Burton quirks, blending spooky with silly, and the visuals capture that eerie yet playful vibe perfectly. It’s a fun reminder that sometimes the weirdest stories are the ones worth telling—especially when they come with a ghost who really is the “ghost with the most.”

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this one packs a punch with multiple instances of animal death and harm, including a dog, cat, horse, and other creatures, plus some unsettling scenes involving bugs, spiders, and snakes. If those triggers are on your list, be cautious diving into this quirky but heavy-on-the-creepy sequel.
emailReview:
Beetlejuice Beetlejuice spins Tim Burton’s signature gothic whimsy into a chaotic, offbeat supernatural comedy that blends nostalgic charm with fresh spooky mischief and a standout performance from Jenna Ortega.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, cat, and horse, creepy insects like bugs and spiders, and unsettling snake scenes.

name: Vantage Point
overview: The attempted assassination of the American president is told and re-told from several different perspectives.

writers: Robert Smigel, Adam Sandler, Todd Durham
name: Hotel Transylvania 2
overview: When the old-old-old-fashioned vampire Vlad arrives at the hotel for an impromptu family get-together, Hotel Transylvania is in for a collision of supernatural old-school and modern day cool.
tagline: They're back to raise a little terror.

name: Joy
overview: A Nigerian woman living in America struggles to convince her traditionalist husband not to circumcise their ten-year-old daughter.

name: My Big Fat Greek Wedding
overview: A young Greek woman falls in love with a non-Greek and struggles to get her family to accept him while she comes to terms with her heritage and cultural identity.
tagline: Love is here to stay... so is her family.
review:
My Big Fat Greek Wedding is the kind of rom-com that feels like a warm, chaotic family reunion—equal parts sweet and absurd. Nia Vardalos, who also penned the script, stars as Toula, the young Greek woman caught between tradition and modern love, trying to get her family to accept her non-Greek boyfriend Ian (John Corbett). It’s a cozy, culturally rich comedy that paved the way for a wave of identity-and-love stories, though it’s a bit gentler and more predictable than something like Crazy Rich Asians. Fans of light-hearted, family-centric rom-coms will find plenty to enjoy here.

What stands out is the way the film leans hard into cultural quirks and family dynamics without ever feeling mean-spirited. The Portokalos clan is loud, loving, and a bit overbearing, which leads to plenty of laughs and heartfelt moments. The tagline says it all: “Love is here to stay… so is her family.” Director Joel Zwick keeps the tone breezy and warm, and the standout performances, especially from Lainie Kazan and Michael Constantine as Toula’s parents, bring genuine charm. It’s a film about finding balance between honoring your roots and forging your own path, wrapped in a very approachable, crowd-pleasing package.

Heads up for animal-sensitive viewers: multiple animal deaths are depicted, including a dead lamb shown briefly, and there’s mention of other animals dying or being harmed. Also, if bugs, spiders, or snakes send you running, this one has those too. So while it’s mostly a sweet comedy about love and family, there’s a surprising amount of animal-related content that might catch you off guard.
emailReview:
My Big Fat Greek Wedding is a warm, chaotic rom-com that celebrates loud family love with standout performances and a breezy, culturally rich charm.

Be prepared for: brief animal deaths including a lamb, mentions of snakes, spiders, and other small creatures being harmed.

name: 8MM
overview: A small, seemingly innocuous plastic reel of film leads surveillance specialist Tom Welles down an increasingly dark and frightening path. With the help of the streetwise Max, he relentlessly follows a bizarre trail of evidence to determine the fate of a complete stranger. As his work turns into obsession, he drifts farther and farther away from his wife, family and simple life as a small-town PI.
tagline: You can't prepare for where the truth will take you.

name: The Hunt
overview: Twelve strangers wake up in a clearing. They don't know where they are—or how they got there. In the shadow of a dark internet conspiracy theory, ruthless elitists gather at a remote location to hunt humans for sport. But their master plan is about to be derailed when one of the hunted turns the tables on her pursuers.
tagline: Only designated people may be hunted at the manor.
review:
The Hunt is a slick, darkly satirical thriller that rides the wave of modern conspiracy paranoia and class warfare like a cross between The Purge and Ready or Not. It’s got the twisted game-of-survival setup down pat, but what really distinguishes it is Betty Gilpin’s fierce turn as Crystal, the hunted who flips the script on her privileged hunters. It’s not quite the razor-sharp satire it aims for, but it’s a wild ride elevated by its sharp dialogue and moments of biting humor.

The film leans hard into its premise of an elite group hunting humans for sport, playing with the absurdity of internet-fueled conspiracy theories while delivering plenty of tense, bloody set pieces. The tagline, “Only designated people may be hunted at the manor,” nails the chilling exclusivity that drives the plot, and the remote, claustrophobic setting keeps the stakes high. Damon Lindelof’s writing brings some clever commentary on social divides, even if the movie sometimes sacrifices depth for action.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to animal distress—there’s a particularly upsetting scene involving a pig used as a distraction, which gets graphic and noisy, and meanwhile, a suicide occurs under heavy emotional circumstances, though it’s handled with a strange mix of gravity and dark humor. If animal harm or suicide triggers are high on your list, proceed with caution. The good news: no dogs or other animals are harmed in the making, and the pet dog at the end gets a happy fate.
emailReview:
The Hunt is a slick, darkly satirical thriller that flips the survival game trope with Betty Gilpin’s fierce performance and sharp, biting humor.

Be prepared for: graphic pig distress during a tense distraction, a heavy emotional suicide scene, bloody violence, and intense class warfare tension.

writers: Dick Clement, Ian La Frenais, Christopher Lloyd, Joe Keenan, William Davies, Sam Fell, Peter Lord, David Bowers, Paul Fisher, Robert Nelson Jacobs, Simon Nye, Tim Sullivan
name: Flushed Away
overview: London high-society mouse, Roddy is flushed down the toilet by Sid, a common sewer rat. Hang on for a madcap adventure deep in the sewer bowels of Ratropolis, where Roddy meets the resourceful Rita, the rodent-hating Toad and his faithful thugs, Spike and Whitey.

writers: Danilo Bach, Daniel Petrie Jr., Eddie Murphy, Robert D. Wachs, Larry Ferguson, Warren Skaaren
name: Beverly Hills Cop II
overview: Axel heads for the land of sunshine and palm trees to find out who shot police Captain Andrew Bogomil. Thanks to a couple of old friends, Axel's investigation uncovers a series of robberies masterminded by a heartless weapons kingpin—and the chase is on.
tagline: Axel Foley is back. Back where he doesn't belong.
review:
Beverly Hills Cop II is a slick, 80s action-comedy that leans hard into Eddie Murphy’s wisecracking charm while delivering the kind of over-the-top crime caper that defined the decade. It’s not quite the fresh spark of the original, but it’s got enough punch and flair to keep fans of the series entertained. Think of it as a glossy blend of buddy-cop antics and high-stakes heist thrills, with Tony Scott’s stylish direction adding a bit more polish and edge than your average action sequel.

What really stands out here is the chemistry between Murphy and his sidekicks Judge Reinhold and John Ashton, who provide a grounded foil to the wild goings-on in sunny L.A. The story—Axel Foley chasing down a ruthless weapons kingpin after a shooting—hits familiar beats but gets an extra boost from some heightened set pieces and a sharp, if occasionally goofy, script co-written by Murphy himself. The tagline “Axel Foley is back. Back where he doesn’t belong.” nails the tone perfectly: a fish-out-of-water in a city that’s as flashy as it is dangerous, with humor and heart packed into the chase.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this one includes multiple instances of animals dying or being harmed, including pets, dogs, cats, and even horses. If that’s on your radar, be prepared for a rough ride in that department alongside the usual action violence.
emailReview:
Beverly Hills Cop II brings Eddie Murphy’s quick wit and slick 80s style to a flashy buddy-cop romp that mixes high-energy heists with plenty of humor and heart.

Be prepared for: multiple pet deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, gun violence, and intense shootouts.

name: Outbreak
overview: A deadly airborne virus finds its way into the USA and starts killing off people at an epidemic rate. Col Sam Daniels' job is to stop the virus spreading from a small town, which must be quarantined, and to prevent an over reaction by the White House.
review:
Outbreak is the kind of 90s pandemic thriller that feels both dated and strangely prescient, a tense race-against-time drama anchored by a solid cast including Dustin Hoffman and Morgan Freeman. It’s a classic disaster movie with military overtones, sitting comfortably alongside Contagion and The Andromeda Strain, though it leans more into action and melodrama than subtlety. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it delivers enough suspense and government paranoia to keep you hooked, even if the dialogue occasionally dips into cliché territory.

What stands out here is Wolfgang Petersen’s direction, which balances the clinical terror of a viral outbreak with personal stakes — Hoffman’s Col Sam Daniels is the calm in the storm, trying to keep people safe while navigating political red tape. The tagline, "Try to remain calm," perfectly captures the film’s eerie blend of anxiety and urgency. The quarantine setup and the virus’s rapid spread feel like a grim blueprint for real-world outbreaks, making the film’s tension resonate all the more today. The military showdown and ethical questions about containment and sacrifice give this more heft than your average disaster flick.

Heads up for animal lovers: Outbreak doesn’t shy away from some heavy animal-related content. Multiple animals die, including a dog, a horse, and a cat, and there’s evidence of animal abuse and sad moments involving pets. If you’re sensitive to any of these, plus the unsettling presence of spiders and snakes, be prepared for some tough scenes. It’s a film that reminds you viruses aren’t the only things that can break your heart.
emailReview: Outbreak is a tense 90s pandemic thriller that blends action and melodrama with a hauntingly relevant look at viral chaos, anchored by Dustin Hoffman’s steady performance amid military stakes and government paranoia. Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog, horse, and cat, scenes of animal abuse, and unsettling moments with spiders and snakes.

writers: David Wechter, Bruce Kimmel, Kevin Williamson
name: The Faculty
overview: When some very creepy things start happening around school, the kids at Herrington High make a chilling discovery that confirms their worst suspicions: their teachers really are from another planet!
tagline: These six students are about to discover their teachers really are from another planet.
review:
The Faculty is a late-90s blend of sci-fi horror and teen thriller that feels like a mashup of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and a high school drama. Directed by Robert Rodriguez and featuring a young cast including Josh Hartnett and Elijah Wood, it rides the wave of ’90s paranoia about authority figures but adds a campy, alien twist. It’s not quite as sharp as some of Kevin Williamson’s earlier hits (he’s one of the writers), but it still delivers a fun, if a bit predictable, ride for fans of creepy “teachers gone bad” stories.

What stands out most is the way the film leans into classic body horror tropes with a dash of teen angst. The tagline—“These six students are about to discover their teachers really are from another planet”—perfectly sums up the mix of high school cliques, sci-fi chills, and dark humor. The ensemble cast does a solid job juggling their roles as suspicious students trying to expose a bizarre conspiracy, and Rodriguez’s direction keeps the pace snappy enough to maintain interest even when the plot dips into familiar territory.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal harm triggers—The Faculty is notorious for its unsettling scenes involving animals, including a dog, a cat, and even a horse, with some instances of abuse and death. If those are on your list, proceed carefully. Also, if creepy crawlies like spiders, snakes, and other bugs set off alarms, this one might get under your skin.
emailReview:
The Faculty is a late-90s sci-fi horror with a campy alien twist and a young cast that captures high school paranoia with a fun, body horror edge.

Be prepared for: unsettling animal harm including dog and horse deaths, creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes, and tense scenes of animal abuse.

name: What Lies Beneath
overview: When Claire Spencer starts hearing ghostly voices and seeing spooky images, she wonders if an otherworldly spirit is trying to contact her. All the while, her husband tries to reassure her by telling her it's all in her head. But as Claire investigates, she discovers that the man she loves might know more than he's letting on.
tagline: He was the perfect husband until his one mistake followed them home.
review:
What Lies Beneath is a slow-burn supernatural thriller that leans heavily into psychological unease, with a distinctly early-2000s vibe. Directed by Robert Zemeckis and starring Michelle Pfeiffer and Harrison Ford, it tries to straddle the line between ghost story and domestic suspense, but ultimately feels like a polished but fairly standard entry in its genre. Fans of movies like The Others or The Sixth Sense might appreciate the haunted-house atmosphere, though What Lies Beneath lacks the narrative tightness and genuine scares that elevate those classics.

What stands out here is the strong lead performance from Pfeiffer as Claire Spencer, whose growing paranoia anchors the film’s tension. The tagline—“He was the perfect husband until his one mistake followed them home”—hints at the slow unraveling of trust and secrets beneath the surface, and that slow reveal is the film’s bread and butter. The spooky voices and ghostly images add a layer of eerie suspense, but the movie often leans on familiar tropes rather than subverting expectations. The writing and direction craft an unsettling mood, but the payoff feels a bit muted compared to more daring horror-thrillers.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related content: this one has quite a few distressing incidents involving animals, including multiple pet deaths and abuse. If the idea of spiders, snakes, or bugs crawling around is a no-go, you’ll want to be cautious here too. The film also dips into some body horror and unsettling imagery, so if any of those categories are on your list, proceed carefully.
emailReview:
What Lies Beneath delivers a slow-burning, early-2000s supernatural thriller atmosphere anchored by Michelle Pfeiffer’s tense performance and a creeping sense of domestic paranoia.

Be prepared for: multiple pet deaths, animal abuse, spiders and snakes crawling, and unsettling body horror imagery.

name: The Santa Clause
overview: Scott Calvin is an ordinary man, who accidentally causes Santa Claus to fall from his roof on Christmas Eve and is knocked unconscious. When he and his young son finish Santa's trip and deliveries, they go to the North Pole, where Scott learns he must become the new Santa and convince those he loves that he is indeed, Father Christmas.
tagline: This Christmas, the snow hits the fan.

name: Shanghai Noon
overview: Chon Wang, a clumsy imperial guard trails Princess Pei Pei when she is kidnapped from the Forbidden City and transported to America. Wang follows her captors to Nevada, where he teams up with an unlikely partner, outcast outlaw Roy O'Bannon, and tries to spring the princess from her imprisonment.
tagline: The old west meets the far east.

name: Burnt
overview: Adam Jones is a Chef who destroyed his career with drugs and diva behavior. He cleans up and returns to London, determined to redeem himself by spearheading a top restaurant that can gain three Michelin stars.
tagline: Never underestimate a man with everything to lose.

name: Last Vegas
overview: Three sixty-something friends take a break from their day-to-day lives to throw a bachelor party in Las Vegas for their last remaining single pal.

name: Wild Things
overview: When teen-socialite Kelly Van Ryan and troubled bad girl Suzie Toller accuse guidance counselor Sam Lombardo of rape, he's suspended by the school, rejected by the town, and fighting to get his life back. One cop suspects conspiracy, but nothing is what it seems...
tagline: They're dying to play with you.

writers: Michael Crichton, William Wisher, Warren Lewis
name: The 13th Warrior
overview: A Muslim ambassador exiled from his homeland joins a group of Vikings, initially offended by their behavior but growing to respect them. As they travel together, they learn of a legendary evil closing in and must unite to confront this formidable force.
review:
The 13th Warrior is a brooding historical action-adventure that tries to carve out a niche between Viking saga and supernatural thriller. Antonio Banderas stars as Ahmed, a cultured outsider thrown in with a rough-and-tumble band of Norse warriors, and the film rides that “fish out of water meets monster hunt” vibe with mixed results. It’s not quite the epic clash of cultures you might want, nor the chilling horror flick it hints at, but it’s got a rugged, grimy charm that fans of late-90s sword-and-sandal fare might appreciate. Think Conan the Barbarian meets The Last of the Mohicans—with a dash of eerie folklore.

What stands out here is the uneasy camaraderie between Ahmed and the Vikings, which adds a layer of cultural tension and gradual respect that grounds the otherwise pulpy plot. The tagline “Prey for the living” captures the creeping dread of the legendary evil hunting them, but while the film leans into its mythic themes, it sometimes stumbles under the weight of its own ambition. John McTiernan’s direction keeps the pacing brisk, and the battle sequences have a raw, visceral edge, but the supernatural elements never fully take hold, leaving the movie stuck between genres rather than mastering either.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal harm: The production notoriously involved several incidents of animal cruelty, especially with horses during the battle scenes. This is a major red flag if the “animals were harmed in the making” trigger is on your list, as the footage includes some rough treatment that’s hard to watch knowing what happened behind the scenes. If that’s a concern, proceed with caution.
emailReview:
The 13th Warrior blends gritty Viking action with a hint of supernatural mystery, anchored by Antonio Banderas’s outsider charm and tense cultural clashes that give the film a rugged late-90s adventure vibe.

Be prepared for: graphic horse injuries during battle scenes, intense combat violence, and a persistent undercurrent of animal harm that adds a tough edge behind the camera.

name: Tears of the Sun
overview: Navy SEAL Lieutenant A.K. Waters and his elite squadron of tactical specialists are forced to choose between their duty and their humanity, between following orders by ignoring the conflict that surrounds them, or finding the courage to follow their conscience and protect a group of innocent refugees. When the democratic government of Nigeria collapses and the country is taken over by a ruthless military dictator, Waters, a fiercely loyal and hardened veteran is dispatched on a routine mission to retrieve a Doctors Without Borders physician.
tagline: He was trained to follow orders. He became a hero by defying them.

name: The Pale Blue Eye
overview: A seasoned detective investigates a series of murders at the U.S. Military Academy in West Point in 1830. He is assisted in his investigation by an intelligent and eager young cadet named Edgar Allan Poe.

writers: Stuart Beattie, Baz Luhrmann, Ronald Harwood, Richard Flanagan
name: Australia
overview: Set in northern Australia before World War II, an English aristocrat who inherits a sprawling ranch reluctantly pacts with a stock-man in order to protect her new property from a takeover plot. As the pair drive 2,000 head of cattle over unforgiving landscape, they experience the bombing of Darwin by Japanese forces firsthand.

writers: Linda Woolverton, Noah Harpster, Micah Fitzerman-Blue, Charles Perrault, Milt Banta, Winston Hibler, Bill Peet, Erdman Penner, Joe Rinaldi, Ted Sears, Ralph Wright
name: Maleficent: Mistress of Evil
overview: Maleficent and her goddaughter Aurora begin to question the complex family ties that bind them as they are pulled in different directions by impending nuptials, unexpected allies, and dark new forces at play.
review:
Maleficent: Mistress of Evil leans hard into the fairy tale sequel territory, with all the grandeur and melodrama that entails. It’s a glossy, effects-heavy fantasy that feels like Sleeping Beauty meets Game of Thrones—minus the grit but with plenty of political intrigue and family drama. Angelina Jolie returns with her signature mix of menace and vulnerability, but Michelle Pfeiffer as Queen Ingrith steals several scenes with her sly, scheming queen vibes. It’s not quite as charming or fresh as the original Maleficent, but it’s still a solid, if somewhat predictable, dive into dark fantasy.

The film’s tagline—“Go beyond the fairy tale”—is spot on in terms of theme, though the execution sometimes trips over its ambition. The story juggles impending nuptials, shifting alliances, and a clash between humans and magical creatures, all wrapped in lush visuals and a sweeping score. The chemistry between Jolie’s Maleficent and Elle Fanning’s Aurora anchors the film, exploring complicated family ties and the blurry lines between good and evil. The script occasionally veers into soap opera territory, but the blend of fairy tale spectacle and political machinations keeps it engaging.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this one doesn’t shy away from upsetting moments involving animals, including deaths and abuse—dogs, horses, cats, even a dragon meet grim fates. If you pin animal harm or pet death triggers, be prepared for some tough scenes. There’s also a fair share of creepy crawlies—spiders, snakes, and other bugs—that might set some nerves on edge.
emailReview:
Maleficent: Mistress of Evil dazzles with glossy fantasy spectacle and standout villainy from Michelle Pfeiffer, blending fairy tale magic with Game of Thrones-style political drama.

Be prepared for: animal deaths and abuse involving dogs, horses, cats, and a dragon, plus unsettling scenes with spiders and snakes.

name: The Green Knight
overview: An epic fantasy adventure based on the timeless Arthurian legend, The Green Knight tells the story of Sir Gawain, King Arthur's reckless and headstrong nephew, who embarks on a daring quest to confront the eponymous Green Knight, a gigantic emerald-skinned stranger and tester of men.
review:
The Green Knight is a moody, meditative take on the classic Arthurian legend, blending epic fantasy with a slow-burn arthouse sensibility. If you’ve ever wished Game of Thrones had leaned harder into myth and atmosphere over endless battles, this is your jam. Dev Patel’s Gawain is less swaggering knight and more introspective wanderer, which makes the film feel like a fairy tale told through a foggy dream. It’s not your typical quest flick — expect more symbolism and eerie visuals than sword-swinging action.

David Lowery’s direction leans heavily into tone and texture, with striking green landscapes and slow, deliberate pacing that invites you to sit with the story’s themes of honor and mortality. The tagline, “When honor was everything,” feels like a quiet challenge to modern viewers who might find Gawain’s recklessness frustrating, but it’s also what drives the narrative’s tension. Alicia Vikander’s dual role adds a layer of mystique and ambiguity that keeps you guessing about fate and temptation. The film doesn’t rush to explain itself, which will either enchant or frustrate depending on your patience for symbolic storytelling.

For those sensitive to animal-related content, The Green Knight is fairly gentle. While there are dead animals shown, no animals are harmed on screen, and the horse remains safe throughout the journey. So, if you keep the “animals are abused” or “animal death” triggers in mind, this one’s fairly low-key on that front.
emailReview: The Green Knight is a moody, atmospheric fantasy that trades sword fights for slow-burning symbolism and haunting visuals, anchored by Dev Patel’s introspective take on the classic knight’s quest. Be prepared for: decapitation, mystical body horror, eerie hallucinations, and unsettling themes of mortality and fate.

name: The Invitation
overview: Will and his new girlfriend Kira are invited to a dinner with old friends at the house of Will’s ex Eden and her new partner David. Although the evening appears to be relaxed, Will soon gets a creeping suspicion that their charming host David is up to something.
tagline: There is nothing to be afraid of.

writers: Paul Hogan, Ken Shadie, John Cornell
name: Crocodile Dundee
overview: When a New York reporter plucks crocodile hunter Dundee from the Australian Outback for a visit to the Big Apple, it's a clash of cultures and a recipe for good-natured comedy as naïve Dundee negotiates the concrete jungle. Dundee proves that his instincts are quite useful in the city and adeptly handles everything from wily muggers to high-society snoots without breaking a sweat.
tagline: There's a little of him in all of us.
review:
Crocodile Dundee is a breezy fish-out-of-water comedy that feels like a sunnier cousin to the ’80s wave of culture-clash films. Paul Hogan’s laid-back Aussie charm as Mick “Crocodile” Dundee is the real hook here—he’s equal parts rugged Outback hero and affably clueless city visitor. It’s not highbrow by any means, but it’s got just enough cheek and warmth to stand out among other buddy comedies and urban-rural switcheroos. Fans of lighthearted ’80s fare with a bit of heart will find this one pretty enjoyable.

What’s worth talking about is how the film plays up the contrast between Dundee’s bush savvy and New York’s urban jungle. The tagline, “There’s a little of him in all of us,” hints at the universal appeal of his straightforward, no-nonsense approach to life. The comedy leans on the clash of cultures but never gets mean-spirited, and the script—co-written by Hogan himself—keeps things loose and fun. The city scenes feel like a playground for Dundee’s instincts, from handling muggers to navigating high society, which makes for some memorable fish-out-of-water moments.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to animal-related triggers: this movie is heavy on animal content, including deaths of a dog, cat, horse, and other creatures, as well as scenes of animal abuse and fighting. There are also snakes, bugs, and, naturally, crocodiles in the mix. Animal lovers, especially those who avoid harm to animals in media, should be cautious here.
emailReview:
Crocodile Dundee charms with Paul Hogan’s laid-back Aussie swagger and a sunny ’80s culture-clash vibe that’s equal parts rugged Outback adventure and urban misfit comedy.

Be prepared for: animal deaths involving a dog, cat, and horse, scenes of animal abuse and fighting, plus plenty of snakes, bugs, and crocodiles along the way.

name: Jackass: the Movie
overview: Johnny Knoxville and his crazy friends appear on the big screen for the very first time in Jackass: The Movie. They wander around Japan in panda outfits, wreak havoc on a once civilized golf course, they even do stunts involving LIVE alligators, and so on. While Johnny Knoxvile and his pals put their life at risk, they are entertaining people at the same time. Get ready for Jackass: The Movie!!
tagline: Do not attempt this at home.
review:
Jackass: The Movie is the ultimate no-holds-barred slapstick and stunt spectacle that launched a thousand imitators. If you thought the TV show was wild, the big screen cranks everything up, with Johnny Knoxville and his crew diving headfirst into pain and chaos that feels equal parts reckless and oddly charming. It’s like the lovechild of a daredevil circus and a frat house gone completely off the rails. Fans of absurd physical comedy and cringe-worthy stunts will get exactly what they bargained for, though it’s definitely not for the faint of heart or anyone expecting polish.

What really sticks with you here is the sheer audacity of the stunts—wandering around Japan in panda suits, alligator encounters, and general mayhem on a golf course all make for moments that are as ridiculous as they are jaw-dropping. The tagline “Do not attempt this at home” isn’t just a warning; it’s a mission statement. The film leans fully into its anarchic spirit, using shaky cam and quick cuts to amplify the chaos, while the camaraderie among the cast—Johnny Knoxville, Bam Margera, Steve-O, and the gang—adds a goofy, almost endearing energy that keeps it from descending into pure shock value.

Heads up to those sensitive to animal harm or gore—the stunts do get rough, and there are some genuinely disturbing moments involving animals (including a dog dying), plus the occasional burst of blood and jump scares. If you’re triggered by extreme physical injury or pet harm, tread carefully. This movie is a full-throttle ride into the absurd and painful, so buckle up if you decide to watch.

name: Saw X
overview: Between the events of 'Saw' and 'Saw II', a sick and desperate John Kramer travels to Mexico for a risky and experimental medical procedure in hopes of a miracle cure for his cancer, only to discover the entire operation is a scam to defraud the most vulnerable. Armed with a newfound purpose, the infamous serial killer returns to his work, turning the tables on the con artists in his signature visceral way through devious, deranged, and ingenious traps.
review:
Saw X dives back into the gory, twisted world of Jigsaw with all the signature traps and torment fans expect, but this time with a bit more emotional weight thanks to John Kramer's battle with terminal brain cancer. It’s like Saw meets a medical thriller gone horribly wrong—a scam and a sick man’s desperation fueling the carnage. Tobin Bell’s iconic performance as Kramer anchors the film, giving it a grim gravitas that elevates the usual torture-porn spectacle. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but if you’re here for intricate death traps and moralistic vengeance, this installment delivers with brutal flair.

What really stands out is how the film uses Kramer’s illness as a driving force, setting the stage with hospital scenes and a shady medical procedure in Mexico that spirals into the trademark Saw chaos. The traps are as elaborate and sadistic as ever, pushing characters—and viewers—to the edge of endurance. The writing leans heavily into themes of deception, desperation, and twisted justice, with plenty of flickering lights, jump scares, and intense sound design to keep the tension tight. The movie doesn’t shy away from showing the full, graphic consequence of its traps, including some truly gruesome moments of mutilation and self-harm that fans of the franchise will recognize.

Be heavily warned if you’re sensitive to excessive gore, torture, and graphic violence—this movie pulls no punches in showing broken bones, eye mutilation, and even decapitation. There’s also flashing lights and sudden loud noises throughout, which could be difficult for some. The film includes scenes of kidnapping, restraint, sexual assault, drug use, and claustrophobia, so those triggers are front and center. Plus, the portrayal of terminal illness and mental health struggles is pretty raw, adding another layer of intensity for viewers. This one is definitely not for the faint of heart.
emailReview:
Saw X cranks up the classic Saw formula with Tobin Bell’s chilling return as a terminally ill Jigsaw, blending brutal traps with a medical thriller’s desperate edge and dark emotional weight.

Be prepared for: graphic eye mutilation, decapitation, intense torture scenes, sexual assault, and relentless flashing lights.

overview: A trio of unemployed silent film actors are mistaken for real heroes by a small Mexican village in search of someone to stop a malevolent bandit.
tagline: They're down on their luck and up to their necks in señoritas, margaritas, banditos and bullets!
review:
¡Three Amigos! is a goofy, offbeat comedy that rides the wave of ’80s slapstick but with a distinct Western-meets-Mexican-flavored twist. It’s the kind of film where Chevy Chase, Steve Martin, and Martin Short get to riff off each other as a trio of out-of-work actors who mistake a real bandit situation for a movie gig. If you’re a fan of comedies like *Blazing Saddles* or *The Three Stooges* meets *The Magnificent Seven*, this one’s got that same goofy charm, though it leans more into absurdity than sharp satire. It’s not exactly a laugh riot from start to finish, but it’s got moments that stick thanks to that iconic cast and director John Landis’s knack for broad comedy.

What stands out here is the playful premise—actors caught in a real-life adventure they’ve only ever performed on stage. The tagline promises señoritas, margaritas, banditos, and bullets, and the film delivers on that chaotic mix with a kind of lighthearted swagger. The humor is broad and sometimes goofy, leaning heavily on the trio’s chemistry and the colorful villains they face, especially Alfonso Arau’s El Guapo. The film doesn’t shy away from playing with Western tropes, but it’s less about subverting the genre and more about having fun with it. The writing credits, including Steve Martin himself, ensure a steady stream of witty one-liners and silly antics.

Heads up for animal lovers: this movie is surprisingly heavy on animal-related triggers. There are multiple instances of animals dying or being harmed, including a dog, horse, cat, and other creatures. If you’re sensitive to animal abuse or death, this one might be rough going despite the overall comedic tone. Also, if bugs, spiders, or snakes make you squirm, prepare yourself—there’s no shortage of creepy-crawlies on display. So, while it’s a silly romp on the surface, the animal-related content is definitely a notable undercurrent here.
emailReview:
¡Three Amigos! is a goofy ’80s-style comedy that blends Western flair with offbeat slapstick and the charming chaos of Chevy Chase, Steve Martin, and Martin Short riffing as a hapless trio.

overview: During her Christmas holidays with the royal family at the Sandringham estate in Norfolk, England, Diana decides to leave her marriage to Prince Charles.
review:
One thing is clear after viewing this film: director Pablo Larrain knows how to create environments behind the scenes that allow his lead actors to truly shine in their roles. 

Like his previous film Jackie (2016), this film is both anchored and carried by the strength of its lead. Natalie Portman did some of her best work in Jackie. This time, Kristen Stewart gives a career-best performance, portraying the late Princess Diana. Even if you’re not convinced by a U.S. actor attempting a Welsh accent, you have to admire how well she captures Diana’s one-of-a-kind essence. This is really good work on display, very deserving of all the awards and nominations received.

How much you enjoy the film will probably depend on how well you take to films that use “artistic liberties” when bringing to life the stories of real historical figures. In this case, the film announces right at the beginning with a simple text: 

“A Fable From A True Tragedy.”
emailReview:
Kristen Stewart delivers a career-best performance as Princess Diana in a haunting, artful fable that blurs the lines between history and myth with director Pablo Larrain’s signature atmospheric style.

Be prepared for: intense emotional distress, depictions of a tragic car crash, and moments of raw grief.

overview: An agoraphobic psychologist and a female detective must work together to take down a serial killer who copies serial killers from the past.

review:
Copycat is a ’90s serial killer thriller that leans hard into the procedural side of things, with a psychological twist. Think Silence of the Lambs meets The Bone Collector, with Sigourney Weaver’s agoraphobic psychologist and Holly Hunter’s tough detective teaming up to stop a serial killer who’s basically the ultimate copycat. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but it’s got enough tension and smart character work to keep you hooked, even if the plot plays it a bit safe by genre standards.

What stands out here is the dynamic between the two leads—Weaver’s vulnerable but brilliant Helen Hudson and Hunter’s no-nonsense M.J. Monahan. The interplay between Helen’s trauma-fueled isolation and M.J.’s grit gives the film some emotional grounding amid the grisly murders. Plus, the killer’s modus operandi—copying infamous serial killers from history—adds a chilling meta-layer that keeps the mystery engaging. Jon Amiel’s direction keeps the mood claustrophobic and tense, and the script leans on classic thriller tropes without feeling totally derivative.

Heads up for those who track animal-related triggers: Copycat features several instances of animals dying, including a dog, cat, and horse, as well as some scenes of animal abuse and distress. If you’re sensitive to that, be prepared. There’s also some creepy bug and spider appearances, plus a few heavy themes like suicide attempts and gaslighting that could be rough for some viewers.
emailReview:
Copycat is a tense ’90s thriller that pairs Sigourney Weaver’s vulnerable psychologist with Holly Hunter’s tough detective in a chilling game of serial killer mimicry, wrapped in claustrophobic direction and smart character dynamics.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dog, cat, and horse, scenes of animal abuse, creepy bugs and spiders, plus heavy themes like suicide attempts and gaslighting.
