review:
BASEketball is a goofy sports comedy classic from the late ’90s that feels like a mash-up of Zucker’s signature slapstick with a satirical edge aimed at the corporate sports world. Trey Parker and Matt Stone bring their trademark irreverence as two lovable slackers who invent a hybrid sport, and the film rides that ridiculous premise for all it’s worth. It’s not as sharp as their South Park work, but for fans of absurd humor mixed with underdog sports stories, it’s a pretty wild ride with a cult appeal.

What stands out is the way BASEketball pokes fun at the commercialization of sports leagues—equal pay, no moving teams, and the fight against corporate greed all get a goofy spotlight. The tagline “Two guys invented a game... and turned the sports world upside down!” nails the film’s spirit of anarchic fun. David Zucker’s direction delivers those classic physical comedy bits alongside some surprisingly pointed satire, and the cast—especially Parker and Stone—carry the film’s loose, jokey vibe well. Plus, there’s a solid supporting cast including Ernest Borgnine adding some old-school charm.

Heads-up: this one’s packed with some heavy trigger material. Be especially cautious if the idea of animals dying unsettles you—there’s a distressing scene involving chickens and a shredding machine. Also, deaths (including of kids and pets) and blood/gore show up, along with finger and toe mutilation, amputation, and even someone drowning. There’s sexual content, shower scenes, and some uncomfortable jokes about sensitive topics, plus clowns and spiders for anyone with those phobias. It’s a comedy, but it doesn’t shy away from some dark and graphic moments that might catch you off guard.
emailReview:
BASEketball is a goofy late ’90s sports comedy that blends Zucker-style slapstick with sharp satire on corporate sports culture, carried brilliantly by Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s irreverent charm.

Be prepared for: chickens killed in a shredding machine, finger and toe amputations, child and pet deaths, drowning, and graphic blood and gore.

name: Mowgli: Legend of the Jungle
overview: A human child raised by wolves, must face off against a menacing tiger named Shere Khan, as well as his own origins.

name: Cry Baby
overview: A prim and proper schoolgirl goes against her grandmother's wishes when she dates a motorcycle-riding juvenile delinquent.

primaryTitle: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants
writers: Ann Brashares, Delia Ephron, Elizabeth Chandler
Title_IMDb_Link: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants
name: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants
overview: Four best friends (Tibby, Lena, Carmen & Bridget) who buy a mysterious pair of pants that fits each of them, despite their differing sizes, and makes whoever wears them feel fabulous. When faced with the prospect of spending their first summer apart, the pals decide they'll swap the pants so that each girl in turn can enjoy the magic.

writers: Robert Littell, Ken Nolan, Gary Spinelli
name: The Amateur
overview: After his life is turned upside down when his wife is killed in a London terrorist attack, a brilliant but introverted CIA decoder takes matters into his own hands when his supervisors refuse to take action.
review:
The Amateur is a tense, quiet thriller that leans hard on Rami Malek’s brooding intensity as a CIA decoder turned reluctant avenger. It’s got that “John Wick meets The Imitation Game” vibe—gritty revenge filtered through the lens of a tech-savvy loner pushed too far. While it doesn’t reinvent the spy thriller wheel, it’s elevated by its tight focus on one man’s personal grief colliding with global stakes, making it feel more intimate than your typical action fare.

What stands out most is the way the film uses its London setting and the tagline, “Don’t underestimate him,” to subvert the usual “lone wolf” trope. Instead of flashy shootouts, the story unfolds through careful decoding, bureaucratic stonewalling, and quiet moments of rage. The cast, including Holt McCallany and Rachel Brosnahan, add layers to what could’ve been a straightforward revenge plot, while James Hawes’s direction keeps the pace taut and the tone somber. The writing by Ken Nolan and Gary Spinelli gives the characters enough depth to make the emotional stakes feel real, even when the plot veers into standard thriller territory.

Heads up: this one’s heavy on animal-related triggers—dogs, cats, horses, and other animals die or are abused, and there’s some dog fighting and other unsettling moments involving animals. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or death, this movie will probably hit a raw nerve. There’s also some gaslighting, so keep that on your radar if it’s something you want to avoid.
emailReview:
The Amateur is a brooding, quietly intense thriller that blends Rami Malek’s simmering rage with a tech-driven, emotionally charged revenge story set against London’s rainy streets.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, dog fighting, animal abuse, and gaslighting.

writers: Tim Smith, Arkasha Stevenson, Keith Thomas, Ben Jacoby, David Seltzer
name: The First Omen
overview: When a young American woman is sent to Rome to begin a life of service to the church, she encounters a darkness that causes her to question her own faith and uncovers a terrifying conspiracy that hopes to bring about the birth of evil incarnate.

name: In Her Shoes
overview: Irresponsible party girl, Maggie is kicked out of her father's and stepmother's home—where she lives for free—and is taken in by her hard-working sister, Philadelphia lawyer, Rose. After Maggie's disruptive ways ruin her sister's love life, Rose turns her out as well. But when their grandmother, who they never knew existed, comes into their lives, the sisters face some complicated truths about themselves and their family.

primaryTitle: Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood
writers: Shawn Wayans, Marlon Wayans, Phil Beauman
Title_IMDb_Link: Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood
name: Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood
cleanName: dont be menace south central while drinking your juice hood
cleanNameArticles: dont be a menace to south central while drinking your juice in the hood
overview: When Ashtray (Shawn Wayans) moves to South Central L.A. to live with his father (who appears to be the same age he is) and grandmother (who likes to talk tough and smoke reefer), he falls in with his gang-banging cousin Loc Dog (Marlon Wayans), who along with the requisite pistols and Uzi carries a thermo-nuclear warhead for self-defense. Will Ashtray be able to keep living the straight life?

writers: David Matalon, Sasha Perl-Raver, Jen D'Angelo
name: Totally Killer
overview: The film follows Jamie (Shipka) whose mom, Pam (Bowen) is terrorized by the resurgence of the Sweet Sixteen Killer—a masked maniac that slaughtered a group of teenage girls in the ‘80s. With the help of her friend Amelia (Kelcey Mawema), she travels back in time to 1987 and teams up with the teen version of her mom (Holt) to try and stop the killer.
review:
Totally Killer is a cheeky blend of ‘80s slasher throwback and time-travel comedy that doesn’t take itself too seriously—and that’s exactly what makes it fun. If you’ve ever wanted to see Kiernan Shipka team up with the younger version of her mom (played by Olivia Holt) to stop a masked maniac, this one’s for you. It rides the wave of nostalgic horror-comedies like Freaky but leans heavier into camp and playful banter rather than pure scares, making it a breezy, if somewhat predictable, ride.

What stands out is how the film balances its retro vibe (“Murder is so 1987,” indeed) with sharp, self-aware humor. The dynamic between Jamie, her friend Amelia, and the teen Pam feels fresh enough to carry the plot, even if the killer’s backstory treads familiar ground. Director Nahnatchka Khan keeps the pace brisk, and the soundtrack and neon-lit aesthetics lean fully into the era without feeling like a mere gimmick. It’s not reinventing the slasher wheel, but it’s a solid, entertaining mix of time-travel hijinks and murder mystery with just enough heart to keep you rooting for the trio.

Heads up: this one is heavy on animal harm triggers—dogs, cats, horses, and more meet unfortunate ends, plus some unsettling animal abuse scenes. Anyone sensitive to animal death or cruelty should be cautious here, as those moments are fairly prominent and could be quite distressing. There are also bugs, spiders, and snakes on the list, so if creepy crawlies aren’t your thing, proceed with care.
emailReview:
Totally Killer is a neon-soaked, cheeky time-travel slasher that pairs sharp ‘80s nostalgia with playful banter and a killer soundtrack, making it a fun, if familiar, ride.

Be prepared for: multiple graphic animal deaths including dogs, cats, and horses, scenes of animal abuse, plus creepy bugs, spiders, and snakes.

writers: Lorenzo Semple Jr., Michael Allin, Alex Raymond
name: Flash Gordon
overview: A football player and his friends travel to the planet Mongo and find themselves fighting the tyrant, Ming the Merciless, to save Earth.
tagline: Pathetic earthlings...who can save you now?

name: Titane
overview: A woman with a metal plate in her head from a childhood car accident embarks on a bizarre journey, bringing her into contact with a firefighter who's reunited with his missing son after 10 years.

name: Mousehunt
overview: Down-on-their luck brothers, Lars and Ernie Smuntz, aren't happy with the crumbling old mansion they inherit... until they discover the estate is worth millions. Before they can cash in, they have to rid the house of its single, stubborn occupant: a tiny and tenacious mouse.

name: Novocaine
overview: Nathan Caine was born with the rare disorder CIPA (Congenital Insensitivity to Pain), which means he does not feel physical pain. He grew up a sheltered child, learning to blend his food so he would not unwittingly chew off his own tongue, and he learned to wear a timer to remind himself when to go to the bathroom. But when his bank is robbed and his new love taken hostage, his affliction becomes his greatest strength as he sets out to rescue her.

name: Wet Hot American Summer
overview: The setting is Camp Firewood, the year 1981. It's the last day before everyone goes back to the real world, but there's still a summer's worth of unfinished business to resolve. At the center of the action is camp director Beth, who struggles to keep order while she falls in love with the local astrophysics professor. He is busy trying to save the camp from a deadly piece of NASA's Skylab which is hurtling toward earth. All that, plus: a dangerous waterfall rescue, love triangles, misfits, cool kids, and talking vegetable cans. The questions will all be resolved, of course, at the big talent show at the end of the day.
tagline: High times. Hard bodies. Soft rock.

writers: Ernest Cline, Adam F. Goldberg, Dan Pulick
name: Fanboys
overview: In 1999, Star Wars fanatics take a cross-country trip to George Lucas' Skywalker Ranch so their dying friend can see a screening of The Phantom Menace before its release.

name: The Art of Getting By
overview: George, a lonely and fatalistic teen who's made it all the way to his senior year without ever having done a real day of work, is befriended by Sally, a popular but complicated girl who recognizes in him a kindred spirit.

name: Dangerous Minds
overview: Former Marine Louanne Johnson lands a gig teaching in a pilot program for bright but underachieving teens at a notorious inner-city high school. After having a terrible first day, she decides she must throw decorum to the wind. When Johnson returns to the classroom, she does so armed with a no-nonsense attitude informed by her military training and a fearless determination to better the lives of her students -- no matter what the cost.

writers: Jeffrey Hatcher, Kimberly Simi, Michael Cristofer
name: Casanova
overview: With a reputation for seducing members of the opposite sex, regardless of their marital status, a notorious womanizer discovers a beauty who seems impervious to his charms. However, as he continues to pursue the indifferent lady, he finds himself falling in love.

name: The First Wives Club
overview: After years of helping their hubbies climb the ladder of success, three mid-life Manhattanites have been dumped for a newer, curvier model. But the trio is determined to turn their pain into gain. They come up with a cleverly devious plan to hit their exes where it really hurts - in the wallet!

name: Under the Silver Lake
overview: Young and disenchanted Sam meets a mysterious and beautiful woman who's swimming in his building's pool one night. When she suddenly vanishes the next morning, Sam embarks on a surreal quest across Los Angeles to decode the secret behind her disappearance, leading him into the murkiest depths of mystery, scandal and conspiracy.
review:
Under the Silver Lake is a neon-soaked, cryptic noir thriller that feels like David Lynch taking a bite out of Hollywood conspiracy theories. Andrew Garfield’s disenchanted Sam leads you through the weirdest corners of Los Angeles, chasing a mystery that’s part puzzle, part fever dream. It’s not your typical detective story — more a sprawling, surreal scavenger hunt that fans of cult classics like Mulholland Drive or Inherent Vice might appreciate, though it can get pretty indulgent and obscure at times.

What stands out is the film’s obsession with hidden meanings and secret codes, wrapped in a late-night cityscape drenched in moody, stylized visuals. The tagline “What are they hiding?” perfectly captures its paranoia-tinged vibe, as Sam’s quest reveals a labyrinth of scandals and conspiracies beneath the glossy surface. David Robert Mitchell’s writing leans heavily into atmosphere and cryptic symbolism, which either pulls you deeper or leaves you scratching your head. Riley Keough’s mysterious woman adds a haunting allure that keeps the mystery ticking, even if the plot occasionally meanders.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one is heavy on animal-related triggers, including multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, plus dog fighting. If you’re sensitive to those, be prepared for some tough scenes that might catch you off guard amid the film’s dreamlike haze.
emailReview:
Under the Silver Lake is a neon-drenched, surreal noir that twists Hollywood conspiracy into a fever dream, with Andrew Garfield’s disenchanted lead guiding you through a cityscape thick with cryptic codes and moody paranoia.

Be prepared for: multiple instances of animal deaths and abuse, dog fighting, and unsettling scenes involving animals that break the film’s hypnotic spell.

name: Can't Hardly Wait
overview: It's graduation day at Huntington Hills High, and you know what that means - time to party. And not just any party, either. This one will be a night to remember, as the nerds become studs, the jocks are humiliated, and freshman crushes blossom into grown-up romance.

name: The Final Girls
overview: A young woman grieving the loss of her mother, a famous scream queen from the 1980s, finds herself pulled into the world of her mom's most famous movie. Reunited, the women must fight off the film's maniacal killer.

name: Black Death
overview: As the plague decimates medieval Europe, rumours circulate of a village immune from the plague. There is talk of a necromancer who leads the village and is able to raise the dead. A fearsome knight joined by a cohort of soldiers and a young monk are charged by the church to investigate. Their journey is filled with danger, but it's upon entering the village that their true horror begins.
tagline: In an age of darkness, one man will face the ultimate battle against evil.

name: The Rover
overview: 10 years after a global economic collapse, a hardened loner pursues the men who stole his car through the lawless wasteland of the Australian outback, aided by the brother of one of the thieves.

name: The River Wild
overview: While on a family vacation,  rafting expert Gail takes on a pair of armed killers while navigating a spectacularly violent river.

writers: Michael German, Joe Turner Lin, Daniel Ragussis
name: Imperium
overview: Nate Foster, a young, idealistic FBI agent, goes undercover to take down a radical white supremacy terrorist group. The bright up-and-coming analyst must confront the challenge of sticking to a new identity while maintaining his real principles as he navigates the dangerous underworld of white supremacy. Inspired by real events.
tagline: Defend your nation. Become your enemy.

writers: Remi Weekes, Felicity Evans, Toby Venables
name: His House
overview: A young refugee couple makes a harrowing escape from war-torn South Sudan, but then they struggle to adjust to their new life in a small English town that has an evil lurking beneath the surface.
tagline: When ghosts follow, they never leave.

name: Unsane
overview: A woman is involuntarily committed to a mental institution where she is confronted by her greatest fear.
review:
Steven Soderbergh’s *Unsane* is a claustrophobic psychological thriller that leans hard into paranoia and the unsettling. It’s like *Black Swan* meets *One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest* if both were shot entirely on an iPhone—and that low-fi aesthetic adds an uncomfortably intimate vibe to Sawyer Valentini’s nightmare. Claire Foy carries the film with a tense, deeply anxious performance that keeps you guessing about what’s real and what’s in her head, which fits the tagline perfectly: *Is she or isn’t she?* It’s not reinventing the wheel, but it’s a slick, tight fit in the mental institution thriller subgenre.

What stands out most is how the film toys with perspective and trust. The script by James Greer and Jonathan Bernstein doesn’t waste time, dropping Sawyer straight into the deep end of involuntary commitment where her greatest fears lurk. The score and tight framing amplify the feeling of being trapped, while the supporting cast—including Juno Temple and Joshua Leonard—add layers without stealing the spotlight. If you’re into thrillers that blur reality and mental health in a compact, suffocating package, this one is a neat, if somewhat familiar, addition.

Heads up for animal lovers and sensitive viewers: *Unsane* features multiple distressing scenes involving animals, including the deaths of a dog, horse, cat, and other animals, along with animal abuse. If those triggers are on your list, be heavily warned before stepping into this unsettling world.
emailReview:
Steven Soderbergh’s *Unsane* is a claustrophobic thriller that feels like *Black Swan* shot on an iPhone, with Claire Foy delivering a tense, deeply anxious performance that keeps you guessing what’s real and what’s nightmare.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and horse, animal abuse, and intense scenes of psychological distress.

name: The Runaways
overview: Joan Jett and Cherie Currie, two rebellious teenagers from Southern California, become the frontwomen for the Runaways -- the now-legendary group that paved the way for future generations of female rockers. Under the Svengali-like influence of impresario Kim Fowley, the band becomes a huge success.

writers: Keith Merryman, David A. Newman, Steve Harvey
name: Think Like a Man
overview: The balance of power in four couples’ relationships is upset when the women start using the advice in Steve Harvey’s book, Act Like A Lady, Think Like A Man, to get more of what they want from their men. When the men realize that the women have gotten a hold of their relationship “playbook,” they decide that the best defense is a good offense and come up with a plan to use this information to their advantage.

name: Rules of Engagement
overview: Part war movie, part courtroom thriller, this gripping drama finds a war hero put on trial for a rescue mission gone terribly wrong with only his doubtful friend and fellow marine to represent him.
tagline: A hero should never have to stand alone.

name: Time Lapse
overview: Three friends discover a mysterious machine that takes pictures 24 hours into the future and conspire to use it for personal gain, until disturbing and dangerous images begin to develop.

name: Forever Young
overview: A 1939 test pilot asks his best friend to use him as a guinea pig for a cryogenics experiment. Daniel McCormick wants to be frozen for a year so that he doesn't have to watch his love lying in a coma. The next thing Daniel knows is that he's been awoken in 1992.

name: Possessor
overview: A thriller about an agent who works for a secretive organization that uses brain-implant technology to enable its operatives to inhabit other people's bodies, ultimately driving them to carry out assassinations for high-paying clients.

name: Varsity Blues
overview: In small-town Texas, high school football is a religion, 17-year-old schoolboys carry the hopes of an entire community onto the gridiron every Friday night. When star quarterback Lance Harbor suffers an injury, the Coyotes are forced to regroup under the questionable leadership of John Moxon, a second-string quarterback with a slightly irreverent approach to the game.
review:
Varsity Blues is one of those late-90s teen sports dramas that leans hard into small-town football fanaticism with a dash of rebellious spirit. It’s a familiar setup—high school athletes under pressure, a star quarterback sidelined by injury, and an underdog stepping up—but James Van Der Beek’s John “Mox” Moxon brings enough charm and irreverence to keep things from feeling too formulaic. Think Friday Night Lights meets a teen comedy with just enough bite to remind you that high school can be a battlefield, not just a backdrop for hormonal antics.

What stands out here is the film’s unabashed embrace of Texas football culture as a near-religion, where the stakes feel enormous for these kids and their community. The tagline “Make your own rules” fits Mox’s attitude perfectly—he’s less about fitting in and more about shaking things up. Jon Voight’s Coach Kilmer adds a layer of old-school, tough-love intensity that contrasts nicely with Mox’s laid-back approach, giving the film some real dramatic tension. While it’s not exactly reinventing the teen sports wheel, the mix of drama, humor, and the occasional heartfelt moment keeps it watchable, especially for fans of late-90s nostalgia.

Heads up: Varsity Blues carries a heavy load of tough triggers including the deaths of both a kid and a dog, which could be rough going for sensitive viewers. There’s also some intense bodily harm and jump scares sprinkled in, plus flashing images and scenes of burning that might catch you off guard. If animal harm or sudden shocks are on your radar, tread carefully.
emailReview:
Varsity Blues scores with its mix of late-90s teen sports grit and charismatic performances, capturing the high-stakes world of Texas football with a rebellious edge and plenty of small-town charm.

Be prepared for: dog death, child death, intense bodily harm, jump scares, and scenes of burning.

writers: Peter Jackson, Tony Hiles, Ken Hammon
name: Bad Taste
overview: A team from the intergalactic fast food chain Crumb's Crunchy Delights descends on Earth, planning to make human flesh the newest taste sensation. After they wipe out the New Zealand town Kaihoro, the country’s Astro-Investigation and Defense Service (AIaDS) is called in to deal with the problem. Things are complicated due to Giles, an aid worker who comes to Kaihoro the same day to collect change from the residents. He is captured by the aliens, and AIaDS stages a rescue mission that quickly becomes an all-out assault on the aliens’ headquarters.
tagline: Watch out Aliens... here comes Derek!

name: St. Elmo's Fire
overview: Reluctant to let go of college life, a close-knit team of seven friends--irresponsible saxophone player Billy, young Republican Alec, his girlfriend Leslie, struggling journalist Kevin, drama queen Jules, lovesick waiter Kirby, and Wendy, a social worker with a heart of gold--realise the party is over. And as the burdens of maturity close in on the young dreamers, the complexities of adulthood and the daily struggle of growing up put their sacred friendship to the test. But everyone knows life is not a bed of roses. It won't be easy, but when all is said and done, what will it take for St. Elmo's clique to find its place in the real world?

writers: Joseph Finder, Yuri Zeltser, Grace Cary Bickley
name: High Crimes
overview: A female attorney learns that her husband is really a marine officer awol for fifteen years and accused of murdering fifteen civilians in El Salvador. Believing her husband when he tells her that he's being framed as part of a U.S. Military cover-up, the attorney defends him in a military court.
tagline: Everything you trust. Everything you know. May be a lie...

name: Sleeping with Other People
overview: Can two serial cheaters get a second chance at love? After a one-night stand in college, New Yorkers Lainey and Jake meet by chance twelve years later and discover they each have the same problem: because of their monogamy-challenged ways, neither can maintain a relationship. Determined to stay friends despite their mutual attraction, they make a pact to keep it platonic, a deal that proves easier said than done.
tagline: A romantic comedy with commitment issues.

name: Dog
overview: An army ranger and his dog embark on a road trip along the Pacific Coast Highway to attend a friend's funeral.
tagline: A filthy animal unfit for human company and a... dog.
review:
Dog is a road-trip dramedy that pairs a gruff army ranger (Channing Tatum, who also co-directed) with his equally stubborn canine companion as they journey the Pacific Coast Highway. It’s part buddy movie, part healing story—think *Turner & Hooch* meets a more grounded military dramedy. The tone walks a fine line between heartfelt and slightly rough around the edges, leaning on Tatum’s charm to keep things engaging even when the plot feels a bit familiar.

What stands out here is the chemistry between man and dog, which carries the film through its quieter, more reflective moments. The tagline, “A filthy animal unfit for human company and a... dog,” nails the film’s cheeky spirit. The road trip format allows for a series of episodic encounters that highlight themes of trauma, loyalty, and healing, though it doesn’t stray far from genre conventions. The supporting cast mostly fills out the backdrop, letting Tatum’s Jackson and his dog take center stage in this modest but earnest story.

Heads up: the movie does include animal death, which is a tough spot for many viewers. If you’re sensitive to the death of a dog or animals generally, be heavily warned here.
emailReview:
Dog charms with its rough-edged buddy vibe and the undeniable chemistry between Channing Tatum and his four-legged co-star, making a familiar road trip story feel heartfelt and a little cheeky.

Be prepared for: the death of a dog, other animal deaths, and moments of raw emotional trauma.

name: Blood Work
overview: Still recovering from a heart transplant, a retired FBI profiler returns to service when his own blood analysis offers clues to the identity of a serial killer.

name: Better Watch Out
overview: On a quiet suburban street tucked within a 'safe neighborhood', a babysitter must defend a twelve-year-old boy from strangers breaking into the house, only to discover that this is far from a normal home invasion.
tagline: You might be home but you're not alone.
review:
Better Watch Out is a darkly twisted take on the home invasion thriller that flips your expectations on their head. At first glance, it’s a typical suburban fright fest—babysitter versus intruders—but it quickly veers into a more unsettling, almost gleefully perverse territory. Think Halloween meets a very messed-up coming-of-age story, with Olivia DeJonge’s Ashley caught in a nightmare that’s anything but straightforward. It’s not as polished as some horror-thrillers, but the sharp writing and unpredictable plot twists make it a wild ride that horror fans looking for something offbeat will appreciate.

What really stands out is how the film toys with genre conventions. The “safe neighborhood” tagline feels like a setup for a typical scare, but once the invasion starts, the story peels back layers to reveal a disturbing dynamic between the characters, especially the twelve-year-old Luke. There’s a grim sense of dark humor threaded throughout, and the tension builds in ways that keep you guessing. The performances, especially from DeJonge and Levi Miller, help ground the chaos, making the unsettling moments hit harder. The film’s score and quiet suburban setting only amplify the creeping dread, making you second-guess who’s really in danger.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one is heavy on animal-related triggers, including the deaths of a dog, cat, horse, and other animals, plus some instances of animal abuse. If those are on your watchlist, you’ll definitely want to steer clear or prepare yourself. There are also bugs, spiders, and snakes crawling around, adding an extra layer of discomfort for anyone squeamish. Better Watch Out isn’t shy about pushing buttons—and that extends beyond the human characters.
emailReview: Better Watch Out twists the home invasion thriller into a darkly comic and unsettling coming-of-age nightmare, anchored by sharp writing and standout performances from Olivia DeJonge and Levi Miller. Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dog, cat, and horse, animal abuse, and creepy crawlers like spiders and snakes.

writers: Josh Appelbaum, André Nemec, Harrison Query
name: Heads of State
overview: The UK Prime Minister and US President have a public rivalry that risks their countries' alliance. But when they become targets of a powerful enemy, they're forced to rely on each other as they go on a wild, multinational run. Allied with Noel, a brilliant MI6 agent, they must find a way to thwart a conspiracy that threatens the free world.
tagline: Two heads are better than one.

name: The Good Girl
overview: A discount store clerk strikes up an affair with a stock boy who considers himself the incarnation of Holden Caulfield.

writers: Priscilla Presley, Sandra Harmon, Sofia Coppola
name: Priscilla
overview: When teenage Priscilla Beaulieu meets Elvis Presley at a party, the man who is already a meteoric rock-and-roll superstar becomes someone entirely unexpected in private moments: a thrilling crush, an ally in loneliness, a vulnerable best friend.
tagline: Wife to the king. Icon to the world. Destined for more.

name: The Choice
overview: Travis and Gabby first meet as neighbors in a small coastal town and wind up in a relationship that is tested by life's most defining events.

name: The Inbetweeners 2
overview: Neil, Will and Simon receive an invite from Jay to join him in Australia whilst on his gap year, who promises them it’s ”the sex capital of the world”. With their lives now rather dull compared to their hedonistic school days and legendary lads holiday, it’s an offer they can’t refuse. Once again, they put growing up temporarily on-hold, and embark on a backpacking holiday of a lifetime in an awful car, inspired by Peter Andre’s ‘Mysterious Girl’. Will soon finds himself battling with the lads to do something cultural, whilst they focus their attention on drinking, girls, and annoying fellow travelers.
tagline: Four reasons to get out of Australia.

name: Kill List
overview: Nearly a year after a botched job, a hitman takes a new assignment with the promise of a big payoff for three killings. What starts off as an easy task soon unravels, sending the killer into the heart of darkness.

name: The Good Son
overview: A young boy stays with his aunt and uncle, and befriends his cousin who's the same age. But his cousin begins showing increasing signs of psychotic behavior.

name: Byzantium
overview: Two mysterious women seek refuge in a run-down coastal resort. Clara meets lonely Noel, who provides shelter in his deserted guesthouse, Byzantium. Schoolgirl Eleanor befriends Frank and tells him their lethal secret—they were born 200 years ago and survive on human blood. As knowledge of their secret spreads, their past catches up on them with deathly consequences.

name: It Could Happen to You
overview: Charlie Lang is a simple, kindhearted New York City cop. When he realizes he has no money to tip waitress Yvonne Biasi, Lang offers her half the winnings of his lottery ticket. Amazingly, the ticket happens to be a winner, in the sum of $4 million. True to his word, Lang proceeds to share the prize money with Biasi, which infuriates his greedy wife, Muriel. Not content with the arrangement, Muriel begins scheming to take all the money.

writers: Andy Weiss, Logan Miller, Noah Miller
name: White Boy Rick
overview: The story of a teenager, Richard Wershe Jr., who became an undercover informant for the police during the 1980s and was ultimately arrested for drug-trafficking and sentenced to life in prison.
tagline: In 1980s Detroit, Ricky Wersche Jr. was a street hustler, FBI informant and drug kingpin—all before he turned 16.

name: O2
overview: A woman wakes up inside a cryogenic chamber with no memory of how she got there and must escape before her air runs out.
tagline: No escape. No memory. 90 min to live.

name: Being the Ricardos
overview: A biopic following the lives and marriage of Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz.

name: Roman J. Israel, Esq.
overview: Hard-nosed liberal lawyer Roman J. Israel has been fighting the good fight forever while others take the credit. overview: Six friends hire a medium to hold a séance via Zoom during lockdown — but they get far more than they bargained for as things quickly go wrong.
tagline: Someone new has joined the meeting.
review:
Host is a sharp and claustrophobic horror flick that really nails the “lockdown séance goes wrong” vibe. It’s a found-footage style Zoom horror that feels like Paranormal Activity meets a quarantine-era Black Mirror episode—perfectly capturing isolation anxiety with a digital-age twist. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it stands out by using its limited setting creatively, delivering genuine scares without a big budget or elaborate effects.

What’s most notable about Host is how it leans into the pandemic’s Zoom fatigue and turns it into a conduit for supernatural chaos. The concept of six friends hosting a séance over video calls is simple but effective, and the tension escalates naturally as things spiral out of control. The cast keeps it believable, which is crucial for this format, and the direction by Rob Savage makes the most of everyday tech to build suspense. The tagline, “Someone new has joined the meeting,” perfectly sets up the eerie premise and keeps you on edge.

Those sensitive to animal harm triggers should be cautious, as multiple pets die during the film. There’s also sexual assault, drug use, and a handful of intense psychological and physical terror moments, so be prepared if those are on your list. Bugs, snakes, and spiders make appearances, too, adding an extra layer of creepiness for the arachnophobes and entomophobes out there.

Host is a claustrophobic and clever found-footage horror that turns pandemic Zoom fatigue into supernatural dread with a tense, believable cast and a brilliant low-budget approach.

name: Lord of the Flies
overview: When their plane crashes, 25 schoolboys find themselves trapped on a tropical island, miles from civilization.
tagline: No parents. No teachers. No rules... No mercy.
review:
The 1990 adaptation of *Lord of the Flies* is a grim, unsettling dive into the dark side of human nature, stripped down to a group of schoolboys marooned without adults or rules. This version leans into the raw psychological horror and social breakdown that the story demands, making it feel like *Stand by Me* meets *The Crucible*—but with a much bleaker outlook. While it doesn’t reach the iconic status of the 1963 original, it’s a solid retelling that’s elevated by its intense performances, especially from Balthazar Getty as Ralph and Chris Furrh as the increasingly unhinged Jack Merridew.

What stands out most here is how the film captures the slow, brutal descent from innocence to savagery. The tagline—“No parents. No teachers. No rules... No mercy.”—doesn’t overpromise. The island setting is both idyllic and menacing, underscored by a haunting score that amplifies the tension without overwhelming. The writing keeps the dialogue sharp and often chilling, revealing the fragile dynamics of power, fear, and tribalism among the boys. It’s a grim allegory that feels just as relevant today as when the original novel was published, making the film a worthy if somber exploration of what happens when society’s veneer peels away.

Those who pin the animal harm trigger should be cautious here, as the film includes the deaths of multiple animals, including a dog, horse, and cat. Also be warned if bugs, snakes, or spiders are on your list—they’re present in ways that add to the unsettling atmosphere. It’s a tough watch for those sensitive to cruelty, but that’s part of the point the story makes about the darker impulses lurking beneath the surface.
emailReview:
This grim retelling of *Lord of the Flies* delivers a raw and haunting look at the collapse of innocence, with standout performances that make the story's descent into savagery feel all the more chilling.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and horse, unsettling encounters with snakes and spiders, and a relentless atmosphere of psychological cruelty.

overview: An American girl on holiday in the English countryside with her family finds herself in hiding and fighting for her survival as war breaks out.
review:
How I Live Now is a grim, atmospheric take on the young adult dystopian survival story that leans heavily on its emotional core rather than action set pieces. Think a more intimate, character-driven The Road crossed with the pastoral vulnerability of Atonement, but with the looming threat of war casting a long shadow over the English countryside. Saoirse Ronan gives a quietly fierce performance as Daisy, anchoring the film’s tension and tenderness with a nuanced portrayal that keeps you invested even when the story gets bleak.

What really stands out here is how the film balances its coming-of-age themes with the harsh realities of conflict. The tagline, “Love will lead you home,” isn’t just a romantic line—it’s the emotional thread that pulls Daisy through the chaos, making the personal stakes feel just as urgent as the global ones. The writing doesn’t shy away from the darker aspects of survival, and the sparse, moody visuals underline the isolation and desperation without overdoing it. It’s a slow burn, but one that sticks with you, especially if you appreciate war stories that focus on how ordinary people cope when everything falls apart.

Heads up: this movie is a tough watch if you’re sensitive to animal harm or sexual content, as it includes triggers for a non-human character’s death and bestiality. Those who pin those triggers should definitely be cautious going in.

name: Welcome to Marwen
overview: When a devastating attack shatters Mark Hogancamp and wipes away all memories, no one expected recovery. Putting together pieces from his old and new life, Mark meticulously creates a wondrous town named Marwen where he can heal and be heroic. As he builds an astonishing art installation — a testament to the most powerful women he knows — through his fantasy world, he draws strength to triumph in the real one.
tagline: You can't put this hero in a box.
review:
Welcome to Marwen is a visually striking blend of drama and fantasy that feels like a Robert Zemeckis take on healing through imagination—a bit like Forrest Gump meets a handcrafted dollhouse diorama. Steve Carell’s turn as Mark Hogancamp grounds the film with sincerity, though the tone occasionally wobbles between hopeful and heavy-handed. Fans of stories about trauma and recovery will appreciate its earnestness, even if it never quite escapes the trappings of its genre’s more familiar beats.

What stands out most is the film’s inventive use of Mark’s miniature world, Marwen, as a therapeutic canvas where he reimagines his trauma and the powerful women in his life. The tagline “You can’t put this hero in a box” feels apt, as the movie explores heroism in unexpected forms—both in the real world and through the fantasy battles Mark stages. The art installation element gives the story a unique texture, blending the tactile with the emotional, though some viewers might find the transitions between reality and fantasy a bit jarring.

Those who pin the animal death trigger should be cautious—this one includes multiple instances of pet and animal deaths. There’s also a heavy dose of gun violence and blood/gore that underline the film’s darker moments. Plus, if body dysmorphia or suicide are sensitive topics for you, be warned that they play significant roles in the story’s emotional core.
emailReview:
Welcome to Marwen is a visually inventive drama that blends heartfelt trauma recovery with striking dollhouse fantasy, anchored by Steve Carell’s sincere performance and a tactile, immersive miniature world.

With tongue planted firmly in cheek, the film explores racial identity in 'post-racial' America while weaving a story about forging one's unique path in the world.

writers: David Kirschner, David Casci, Ernie Contreras
name: The Pagemaster
overview: Tyler knows a lot about accidents. So much so, he is scared to do anything that might endanger him, like riding his bike, or climbing into his treehouse. While in an old library, he is mystically transported into the unknown world of books, and he has to try and get home again.
tagline: All the adventure your imagination can hold.

name: The Wolf of Snow Hollow
overview: A stressed-out police officer struggles not to give in to the paranoia that grips his small mountain town as bodies turn up after each full moon.
review:
The Wolf of Snow Hollow is a darkly comic horror-thriller that feels like Twin Peaks meets a werewolf flick — small-town paranoia with a howling twist. Jim Cummings wears multiple hats here as writer, director, and lead actor, and his offbeat tone keeps the story from slipping into typical horror clichés. It’s not the scariest movie you’ll see, but it’s got a weird charm and a dry wit that makes it stand out from the usual monster-movie fare.

What really sticks is the way it balances the absurdity of werewolf lore with the very real stress and dysfunction of a small-town police force. The tagline “Welcome to Snow Hollow” feels like a sly invite to a place where nothing is quite what it seems, and the full moon murders give the town’s paranoia a tangible shape. Robert Forster’s presence adds an unexpected gravitas to the cast, and the mix of quirky characters helps the film land its blend of humor and horror. The visuals lean into the snowy, isolated setting perfectly, creating an atmosphere that’s both cozy and unsettling.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: while no animals dying on screen, there’s a dog death off-screen that’s noted, plus some dead animals shown as roadkill and taxidermy. Also, the film handles some heavier moments involving death of children and parents, and there’s alcohol abuse woven into the story. If those themes hit close to home, it’s worth going in prepared.
emailReview:
The Wolf of Snow Hollow mixes small-town paranoia with a dry-witted werewolf tale that’s equal parts cozy and unsettling, anchored by Jim Cummings’ quirky charm and Robert Forster’s gravitas.

Be prepared for: off-screen dog death, child and parent deaths, roadkill and taxidermy, and alcohol abuse.

name: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones

overview: Following an assassination attempt on Senator Padmé Amidala, Jedi Knights Anakin Skywalker and Obi-Wan Kenobi investigate a mysterious plot into the heart of the Separatist movement and the beginning of the Clone Wars.
tagline: A Jedi shall not know anger. Nor hatred. Nor love.
review:
Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones is a mixed bag that lands somewhere between epic space opera and awkward romance. It leans hard into the prequel trilogy’s signature blend of political intrigue and lightsaber battles, but also can’t quite shake the stilted dialogue and teenage Anakin angst. Fans of the franchise will appreciate the expanding lore and the introduction of the Clone Wars, though the love story feels like it’s stuck in second gear compared to the action set pieces. Think of it as Star Wars meets a somewhat clunky soap opera—ambitious, but uneven.

What stands out here is the world-building—George Lucas doubles down on the galaxy’s political machinations, setting the stage for the eventual fall of the Republic. The ensemble cast, including Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan and Christopher Lee’s Count Dooku, bring gravitas and charm, while Hayden Christensen’s Anakin struggles to sell the darker emotional beats. The tagline, “A Jedi shall not know anger. Nor hatred. Nor love,” perfectly encapsulates the film’s central tension, though the execution is less refined. Visually, it’s a feast of CGI-enhanced battles and exotic locales, even if some effects have aged more than gracefully.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this installment features moments where animals are harmed and even die, which might catch some off guard. If that’s on your list, be prepared for those scenes to make an impact.
emailReview:
Star Wars: Episode II, Attack of the Clones blends grand political intrigue with flashy lightsaber duels, all wrapped in a somewhat awkward teenage love story that never quite takes off.

Be prepared for: animal harm and death, intense battle violence, and emotionally charged moments of anger and loss.

writers: Zak Penn, Stan Lee, Jack Kirby
name: The Incredible Hulk
overview: Scientist Bruce Banner scours the planet for an antidote to the unbridled force of rage within him: the Hulk. But when the military masterminds who dream of exploiting his powers force him back to civilization, he finds himself coming face to face with a new, deadly foe.
tagline: You'll like him when he's angry.
review:
The Incredible Hulk (2008) slots into the Marvel canon as the angriest, greenest, and arguably most brooding entry of its early phase. It’s a solid blend of superhero action and character study, with Edward Norton’s Bruce Banner carrying the film’s emotional weight as he hunts for a cure to his monstrous alter ego. If you’re into the Marvel Cinematic Universe, this one feels like a grittier, moodier cousin to Iron Man, leaning into the sci-fi thriller vibe more than outright comic book spectacle. It’s not quite as flashy or fun as some of the later Marvel outings, but it has its own charm in the way it explores rage and isolation.

What stands out here is the tension between Banner’s scientific quest and the military’s obsession with weaponizing the Hulk, embodied by Tim Roth’s Emil Blonsky, who makes for a compelling foil. The tagline, “You’ll like him when he’s angry,” nails the duality at the heart of the movie—both the character’s curse and his power. Director Louis Leterrier keeps the pace brisk, with some memorable smash scenes that don’t overstay their welcome. The supporting cast, including Liv Tyler and William Hurt, add some grounded human stakes, though the film’s biggest asset remains its willingness to lean into the darker, more conflicted side of its hero.

Triggers to note: this one has a fair share of intense violence, including some graphic military conflict and scenes of people being burned alive. There are also jump scares, flashing lights, and a handful of upsetting deaths, including a kid and a dog, so those sensitive to sudden shocks or loss should be cautious. The film isn’t shy about the darker edges of its story, so if you’re wary of trauma-heavy superhero fare, this Hulk might be a bit much.
emailReview:
The Incredible Hulk (2008) stands out as the moodiest and most brooding Marvel origin story, with Edward Norton’s intense performance anchoring a gritty blend of sci-fi thriller and superhero action.

Be prepared for: graphic military violence, people being burned alive, sudden jump scares, and upsetting deaths of a child and a dog.

writers: Peter Craig, Danny Strong, Suzanne Collins
name: The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1
overview: After surviving the Quarter Quell, Katniss finds herself in the hidden stronghold of District 13, where the rebellion against the Capitol is gaining momentum. Struggling with the weight of becoming the symbol of resistance, she must navigate fragile alliances while trying to protect those she loves. As propaganda battles rage and Panem moves closer to full-scale war, Katniss is forced to confront the true cost of revolution.
tagline: Fire burns brighter in the darkness.
review:
The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 takes a darker, more somber turn in the YA dystopian saga, trading in the survival games for a grim war drama. It feels like The Hunger Games meets a political thriller, with Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen grappling with the crushing weight of becoming a symbol of rebellion. While it lacks the frantic energy of the earlier installments, it’s elevated by its focus on the psychological toll of conflict, offering a moodier, more introspective chapter for fans of the franchise.

What stands out here is how the film leans heavily into the emotional and mental scars borne by its characters. The tagline, “Fire burns brighter in the darkness,” is fitting as the story delves into propaganda battles and the brutal realities of revolution. The visuals often feel stark and claustrophobic, matching Katniss’s internal struggles, while the narrative doesn’t shy away from the horrors of war—death, torture, and betrayal ripple throughout. The performances, especially from Lawrence and a quietly broken Finnick, underscore how trauma shapes these characters, making the spectacle feel more human and harrowing.

Heads up for those sensitive to mental health struggles and violence: this film is thick with PTSD, anxiety attacks, and disturbing depictions of torture and gun violence. There’s also an intense scene involving choking and an unsettling portrayal of mind control that might unsettle viewers. If flashing lights, claustrophobic spaces, or scenes of sexual exploitation—especially involving minors—are on your list, proceed with caution. This installment wears its darkness on its sleeve and doesn’t pull punches when showing the cost of rebellion.
emailReview:
The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 1 shifts the franchise into a darker, more psychological realm where trauma and war take center stage, anchored by Jennifer Lawrence’s powerful, somber performance.

Be prepared for: intense torture scenes, choking, unsettling mind control, sexual exploitation involving minors, and claustrophobic violence.

overview: In the year 2159, two classes of people exist: the very wealthy who live on a pristine man-made space station called Elysium, and the rest, who live on an overpopulated, ruined Earth. That doesn’t stop the people of Earth from trying to get in, by any means they can. When unlucky Max (Matt Damon) is backed into a corner, he agrees to take on a daunting mission that, if successful, will not only save his life, but could bring equality to these polarized worlds.

name: The Da Vinci Code
overview: A murder in Paris’ Louvre Museum and cryptic clues in some of Leonardo da Vinci’s most famous paintings lead to the discovery of a religious mystery. For 2,000 years a secret society closely guards information that — should it come to light — could rock the very foundations of Christianity.

name: The Lost World: Jurassic Park
overview: Four years after Jurassic Park's genetically bred dinosaurs ran amok, multimillionaire John Hammond shocks chaos theorist Ian Malcolm by revealing that he has been breeding more beasties at a secret location. Malcolm, his paleontologist ladylove and a wildlife videographer join an expedition to document the lethal lizards' natural behavior in this action-packed thriller.
review:
The Lost World: Jurassic Park is the slightly darker, twice-as-dinosaur sequel that leans hard into action-thriller territory while still serving up those awe-inspiring prehistoric set pieces Spielberg’s known for. It trades some of the wonder and novelty of the first film for bigger scares and a heightened sense of chaos, making it feel like Jurassic Park meets a survival horror flick. Jeff Goldblum returns with his signature charm as Ian Malcolm, and the ensemble cast adds enough grit and charisma to keep things lively, even if the story occasionally trips over its own ambition.

What really stands out here is the movie’s way of expanding the Jurassic universe—not just with bigger dinos, but by exploring the consequences of Hammond’s hubris in a wilder, more uncontrolled environment. The tagline “Something has survived” isn’t just a tease; it sets the tone for a world where these creatures aren’t just lab experiments but dangerous wildlife. The film’s visuals remain impressive, with tense chase sequences and some genuinely memorable dino encounters. While it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, the mix of a paleontologist, a wildlife videographer, and a macho hunter makes for an interesting dynamic that keeps the narrative from feeling too one-note.

Heads-up for those sensitive to animal-related triggers: this one packs a punch with multiple animal deaths—including a dog, horse, cat, and other creatures—and scenes of animal abuse are present. If you’re on the lookout for triggers involving bugs, spiders, snakes, or any kind of animal harm, be prepared for a fair amount of that here as well. It’s a wild ride, but it’s not shy about showing the cost of playing God with nature.
emailReview:
The Lost World: Jurassic Park ramps up the thrills with bigger dinos, intense chase scenes, and Jeff Goldblum’s signature charm anchoring the chaos of a wilderness where nature fights back hard.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a dog and horse, animal abuse, and unsettling scenes involving bugs, spiders, and snakes.

writers: Daniel Myrick, Eduardo Sánchez, Heather Donahue
name: The Blair Witch Project
overview: In October of 1994 three student filmmakers disappeared in the woods near Burkittsville, Maryland, while shooting a documentary. A year later their footage was found.
review:
The Blair Witch Project is the granddaddy of found-footage horror, and it still holds a special place in the genre thanks to its raw, stripped-down approach. It feels like The Ring meets an amateur documentary, with none of the polish but all the creeping dread. While it’s not exactly a rollercoaster of scares by today’s standards, the film’s commitment to ambiguity and atmosphere makes it a pretty unforgettable slow burn — a movie that thrives on what you don’t see as much as what you do. Fans of minimalist horror or anyone curious about how the genre exploded in the late ’90s will appreciate its pioneering vibe.

What sets this one apart is how it squeezes terror out of the mundane — a shaky camera, the natural sounds of the woods, and the steadily mounting paranoia of three student filmmakers who vanish without a trace. “Everything you’ve heard is true” isn’t just a tagline; it’s the film’s eerie promise, amplified by the “found footage” conceit that blurs the lines between fiction and reality. The lack of a traditional score or special effects means you’re left with just the actors’ reactions and the oppressive forest, which makes the dread feel more personal and less cinematic. It’s a masterclass in restraint, even if the shaky cam can trigger a headache.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this movie includes several instances of animals dying or being abused, including dogs, cats, horses, and other creatures. If you have animal harm on your list, be prepared for some unsettling moments that go beyond just spooky woods and creepy noises. There are also plenty of bugs and spiders crawling around, so entomophobes might want to tread carefully.
emailReview: The Blair Witch Project remains a pioneering found-footage horror that turns everyday woods and shaky cam footage into a creeping, personal nightmare of mounting paranoia and unseen terrors. Be prepared for: multiple instances of animal deaths including dogs and horses, unsettling animal abuse, and plenty of creepy-crawly bugs and spiders.

writers: Michele Alexander, Jeannie Long, Kristen Buckley, Brian Regan, Burr Steers
