Feels like watching a film that was created by a team who really loves Alfred Hitchcock films. A slow-burn mystery, along with some scattered thrills, really amps up the tension long before the credits role. 

Maika Monroe carries the film with a commanding presence, further cementing her status as one of the top mystery/thriller/horror film actors working today. If you ever wanted to see a writer/director combine thematic elements from Lost in Translation and Rear Window, including intentional references to Se7en and Don’t Look Now, this film is worthy of your time.

Just keep in mind some of the notable triggers popping up, particularly the Watched Without Knowing, Stalking, and Blood/Gore categories.
emailReview:
This slow-burn mystery channels classic Hitchcock vibes with Maika Monroe delivering a magnetic performance that keeps the tension simmering long past the opening credits.

Be prepared for: stalking, intense blood and gore, and the unsettling feeling of being watched without knowing.

name: Terrifier 3
overview: Five years after surviving Art the Clown's Halloween massacre, Sienna and Jonathan are still struggling to rebuild their shattered lives. As the holiday season approaches, they try to embrace the Christmas spirit and leave the horrors of the past behind. But just when they think they're safe, Art returns, determined to turn their holiday cheer into a new nightmare. The festive season quickly unravels as Art unleashes his twisted brand of terror, proving that no holiday is safe.
review:
Terrifier 3 picks up the gore-soaked baton and runs with it, delivering exactly what fans of the series—and of ultra-violent slasher flicks in general—have come to expect. If you liked the first two Terrifier films, this one feels like a grim holiday special where Christmas cheer is punched out in favor of Art the Clown’s signature brand of horrifying mayhem. It’s not subtle or highbrow, but it’s a wild ride for those who appreciate practical effects and a relentless killer who turns a festive backdrop into a twisted nightmare.

What stands out here is the way director and writer Damien Leone leans into the holiday setting to ramp up the contrast between the warmth of Christmas and the cold brutality of Art’s return. Lauren LaVera’s Sienna Shaw is still grappling with trauma, which gives the story a slightly more emotional edge beneath the blood and carnage. The film plays with genre conventions without trying to reinvent the wheel—if anything, it’s a celebration of the kind of over-the-top horror splatter that’s become the franchise’s hallmark. The tagline, “Prepare to be terrified again,” really nails the tone: this is a no-holds-barred sequel that doesn’t shy away from making you squirm.

Those sensitive to animal harm should be warned: several animals, including a dog, cat, and horse, meet grim fates. There’s also body horror, scenes of people being burned alive, and an assortment of creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes that might unsettle some viewers. If graphic violence and disturbing animal scenes are on your list, this one’s definitely heavy on those triggers.
emailReview: Terrifier 3 cranks up the gore and holiday horror to deliver a blood-soaked slasher fest that blends festive cheer with Art the Clown’s brutal mayhem and a surprisingly emotional core. Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths including a dog and horse, body horror, people burned alive, and creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes.

writers: Samuel A. Taylor, Billy Wilder, Ernest Lehman, Barbara Benedek, David Rayfiel
name: Sabrina
overview: An ugly duckling having undergone a remarkable change, still harbors feelings for her crush: a carefree playboy, but not before his business-focused brother has something to say about it.
tagline: You are cordially invited to the most surprising merger of the year.
review:
Sabrina is a glossy 90s romantic comedy with a classic makeover-and-misunderstandings plot that feels like a lighter, more polished cousin to old-school screwball romances. Directed by Sydney Pollack and starring Harrison Ford and Julia Ormond, it’s got that refined charm but doesn’t quite reach the spark of the best rom-coms of the era. If you like your love stories with a side of family business drama and a dash of awkward longing, this might hit the spot, though it’s not exactly groundbreaking.

What stands out here is the dynamic between the two brothers—the carefree David and the business-minded Linus—which adds a bit of texture beyond the usual “ugly duckling turned beauty” trope. The tagline, “You are cordially invited to the most surprising merger of the year,” cleverly nods to both the romantic and corporate entanglements at play. The film leans into that old-fashioned charm with elegant visuals and a subtle score, though some of the humor and character beats feel a bit dated by today’s standards.

Be warned if you’re sensitive to animal-related content—there are multiple instances of animal deaths including pets and horses, as well as scenes that might distress animal lovers. The film also touches on heavier topics like sexual assault and suicide, so those triggers are worth noting before tuning in. If you keep an eye out for these, Sabrina works as a somewhat predictable but still pleasant romantic diversion.
emailReview:
Sabrina is a glossy 90s romantic comedy with old-fashioned charm and a quietly compelling sibling rivalry that adds some welcome texture to the classic makeover story.

Be prepared for: multiple pet and horse deaths, sexual assault, and suicide.

name: Synchronic
overview: Two New Orleans paramedics' lives are ripped apart after encountering a series of horrific deaths linked to a designer drug with bizarre, otherworldly effects.
review:
Synchronic is a trippy, darkly philosophical take on the sci-fi thriller, blending body horror with a mind-bending drug-fueled mystery. It rides the wave of recent indie genre fare that mixes grounded human drama with surreal, cosmic ideas — think a more grounded, grimier version of something like *Beyond the Black Rainbow* or *Coherence*. Anthony Mackie anchors the film with a weary, nuanced performance as a paramedic grappling with loss and the surreal consequences of a designer drug that literally warps time itself. It’s not your typical drug thriller, and it leans into weirdness in a way that’s both unsettling and thought-provoking.

The film’s tagline, “Time is an illusion,” sets the tone for a story that unspools with a slow-burn intensity and an eerie atmosphere. The writing leans heavily into existential questions, but it never forgets the human cost, with the paramedics’ lives unraveling amid a series of bizarre and horrific deaths. The New Orleans setting adds a moody, almost haunted vibe to the proceedings, and directors Aaron Moorhead and Justin Benson (known for their work in indie sci-fi) craft some striking, disorienting visuals that mirror the drug’s otherworldly effects. It’s a film that demands patience, rewarding viewers who appreciate puzzles wrapped in grim reality.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this movie includes some tough moments involving animals — there’s abandonment, sadness, and even bestiality flagged among the triggers, as well as a non-human character death. If those are on your list, be prepared for some heavy scenes that might hit hard.
emailReview:
Synchronic is a grimy, mind-bending indie sci-fi thriller anchored by Anthony Mackie’s weary, nuanced performance and soaked in eerie New Orleans atmosphere that warps time and reality with unsettling, surreal visuals.

Be prepared for: animal abandonment, bestiality, non-human character death, and heavy emotional loss.

name: Haunt
overview: On Halloween, a group of friends encounter an extreme haunted house that promises to feed on their darkest fears. The night turns deadly as they come to the horrifying realisation that some nightmares are real.
review:
Haunt is a lean, effective horror flick that taps into the classic “extreme haunted house” trope but cranks up the dread with a palpable sense of real danger. It’s like if you took the DIY terror of Hostel and mixed it with the haunted house fun of something like Truth or Dare, but with a sharper focus on psychological torment. The film doesn’t waste time—this is a tight, tense ride that leans hard into the fear of losing control when your worst nightmares come alive. Katie Stevens leads a solid cast, but it’s really the claustrophobic atmosphere and relentless pacing that stick with you.

What stands out most here is how the movie plays with the idea of fear itself as a predator. The tagline “Some monsters are real” isn’t just a throwaway line—it’s a direct challenge to the audience, blurring the line between staged scares and actual horror. The haunted house concept feels fresh because it promises to exploit each character's deepest fears, which means the scares are personalized and hit with more emotional weight than your average jump-scare fest. Directors Scott Beck and Bryan Woods lean into shadows and silence as much as gore, making the tension simmer before it boils over.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to intense gore and physical violence—there are scenes that get pretty brutal as the nightmare unfolds. While no animals actually die on screen, there’s a brief but potentially unsettling image of a dead spider in a bottle, plus some ambiguous bloody remains that might bother squeamish viewers. If extreme body horror or graphic peril is on your list, be prepared—Haunt doesn’t hold back once the game turns deadly.
emailReview:
Haunt masterfully blends the raw terror of a haunted house with sharp psychological dread, delivering a claustrophobic and relentless thrill ride that keeps you guessing where real danger ends and staged horror begins.

Be prepared for: intense gore, brutal physical violence, a dead spider in a bottle, ambiguous bloody remains, and extreme body horror.

writers: Joe Connelly, Bob Mosher, William Roberts, Richard Alan Simmons, Dean Lorey, Damon Wayans, Gary Rosen
name: Major Payne
overview: Major Benson Winifred Payne is being discharged from the Marines. Payne is a killin' machine, but the wars of the world are no longer fought on the battlefield. A career Marine, he has no idea what to do as a civilian, so his commander finds him a job - commanding officer of a local school's JROTC program, a bunch of ragtag losers with no hope.
tagline: He's looking for a few good men... or a few guys old enough to shave.
review:
Major Payne is a 90s comedy that leans hard into the fish-out-of-water trope with a military twist—think Full Metal Jacket meets Bad News Bears, but way less serious and way more Damon Wayans being loud and obnoxiously hilarious. It’s a pretty standard “tough guy tries to whip a bunch of misfits into shape” story, but Wayans’ over-the-top performance keeps it from feeling stale. If you’re into goofy military comedies with a heart, this one hits the mark without trying to be anything more than a goofy, feel-good romp.

What stands out here is the way the film plays with the contrast between Payne’s brutal Marine mindset and the school’s ragtag JROTC cadets who couldn’t be less prepared for boot camp. The tagline—“He’s looking for a few good men... or a few guys old enough to shave”—perfectly sums up the tone: irreverent and self-aware. The supporting cast, including Karyn Parsons and Michael Ironside, add some solid flavor, but it’s Wayans’ script input and lead performance that really drive the film’s comedic energy. It’s not high art, but it’s got some memorable moments and a goofy charm that’s hard to hate.

Animal lovers, heads up: this one’s heavy on animal-related triggers. There’s dog fighting, a dead animal, rabbit harm, a cat dying, and other distressing animal moments that might catch you off guard if you’re sensitive. If any of those are on your radar, be cautious—Major Payne doesn’t shy away from showing some rough animal stuff, even if it’s not the main focus of the story.
emailReview:
Major Payne is a loud, goofy 90s military comedy where Damon Wayans’ over-the-top performance turns a tired trope into a feel-good romp with plenty of heart and ridiculousness.

Be prepared for: dog fighting, a dead animal, rabbit harm, and a cat dying, all of which add some unexpectedly rough animal moments to this otherwise silly comedy.

name: The Hills Have Eyes
overview: On the way to California, a family has the misfortune to have their car break down in an area closed to the public, and inhabited by violent savages ready to attack.
review:
Wes Craven’s 1977 debut, *The Hills Have Eyes*, is a grimy, relentless slice of backcountry horror that sets the template for many “family trapped in hostile wilderness” thrillers that followed. It’s a rough-and-tumble, grindhouse-tinged nightmare that feels like *Deliverance* meets *The Texas Chain Saw Massacre*, with a heavy dose of 70s grit and paranoia. While it’s not the most polished or subtle, it’s got a raw energy and bleakness that still hits hard, making it a must-watch for horror fans who appreciate the genre’s darker, more savage corners.

The film’s tagline, “The lucky ones died first...,” nails the tone perfectly—there’s no shortage of brutal inevitability here. The setup is straightforward: a family breaks down in a forbidden desert area, only to be hunted by violent, cannibalistic locals. Craven’s direction leans into the claustrophobic terror of isolation and the collapse of civilized order, with some memorable, if rough-edged, character moments that underscore the family’s desperation. The film’s gritty visuals and unsettling atmosphere amplify the dread, and the cast—including Susan Lanier and Dee Wallace—delivers the kind of earnest performances that keep you invested amid the carnage.

Heads up for animal lovers and those sensitive to animal harm: this movie is infamous for its multiple distressing scenes involving animals, including deaths and abuse. Those who pin the “a dog dies,” “a horse dies,” or “animals are abused” triggers should be cautious, as the film doesn’t shy away from showing animal suffering in ways that can be deeply upsetting. If you find those triggers heavy-going, this one will definitely test your limits.
emailReview:
Wes Craven’s *The Hills Have Eyes* is a gritty, unpolished horror classic that mixes 70s grindhouse grit with raw, claustrophobic terror and memorable performances from Susan Lanier and Dee Wallace.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths, animal abuse, intense violence, and a relentless sense of dread in the hostile desert wilderness.

overview: A gang of thugs devise a cruel hoax that goes horribly wrong as Melvin, a nerdy emaciated janitor at the local health club, is cast through a third story window into a vat of hazardous toxic waste.
tagline: He was 98 lbs. of solid nerd until he became...the Toxic Avenger!
review:
The Toxic Avenger is a cult classic that wears its 1980s B-movie heart on its toxic sleeve. Part horror, part comedy, and all-out gross-out spectacle, it’s the kind of low-budget madness that fans of Troma’s brand of schlock will appreciate. If you like your heroes mutated, monstrous, and unapologetically ridiculous, this flick is a wild ride — think The Simpsons’ “Itchy & Scratchy” meets a superhero origin story gone off the rails. It’s not exactly a masterpiece, but it’s undeniably entertaining in its gleeful absurdity.

What stands out here is the film’s unapologetic dive into body horror and camp, with Melvin Junko’s transformation into the Toxic Avenger being equal parts grotesque and oddly endearing. The tagline, “He was 98 lbs. of solid nerd until he became...the Toxic Avenger!” perfectly sums up the goofy underdog charm at play. The writing leans heavily into the trashy, violent, and bizarre, all wrapped in a satirical take on superhero tropes and small-town corruption. The directors, Kaufman and Herz, clearly embrace the goofiness, making the film a pioneer of midnight movie cult status.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content — the film involves multiple instances of animal death, including dogs and horses, and some pretty unsettling scenes involving animals overall. Body horror is another major element, thanks to Melvin’s toxic meltdown. There’s also gaslighting and a fair dose of copaganda lurking, which might catch some viewers off guard. If you’ve got triggers around animal harm or graphic body transformations, this one is definitely a cautionary tale.
emailReview:
The Toxic Avenger is a gloriously gross 1980s B-movie cult classic that blends campy body horror with a goofy superhero origin story, delivering a wild, unapologetic ride full of ridiculous charm.

Be prepared for: graphic body mutations, multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, unsettling animal harm, gaslighting, and intense toxic meltdowns.

overview: In 1989, a misunderstood teenager has a high school crush — who just happens to be a handsome corpse! After a set of playfully horrific circumstances bring him back to life, the two embark on a murderous journey to find love, happiness…and a few missing body parts along the way.
tagline: If you can't meet your perfect boyfriend…make him.
review:
Lisa Frankenstein is a darkly comedic mash-up of teen romance and horror that rides the campy wave of ’80s nostalgia with a Diablo Cody twist. It’s like if *Heathers* crashed headlong into *Frankenstein* — a playfully gruesome tale about a misunderstood girl who literally brings her perfect boyfriend back from the dead. Kathryn Newton’s quirky energy as Lisa Swallows anchors the film, while Cole Sprouse’s Creature adds a brooding charm to this offbeat love story. It’s not quite a horror show, not quite a rom-com, but that in-between vibe is what makes it a delightfully oddball watch.

What really stands out here is the tone — a cheeky blend of gore and heart that never takes itself too seriously. The tagline, “If you can’t meet your perfect boyfriend…make him,” perfectly sums up the film’s irreverent spirit. The storyline’s mix of murderous misadventures and missing body parts leans into classic horror tropes but with a fresh, sarcastic edge from Diablo Cody’s sharp writing. Director Zelda Williams keeps the visuals bright and playful, which helps balance the darker themes and keeps the movie from veering into outright creepiness.

Heads up to viewers sensitive to animal harm and death: this one’s heavy on the unfortunate animal moments, including the deaths of dogs, cats, horses, and more. Plus, if bugs, spiders, or snakes make you uneasy, there’s more than a few creepy-crawlies to watch out for. Those who pin the animal death and abuse triggers should definitely be cautious going in.
emailReview:
Lisa Frankenstein is a cheeky ’80s-flavored horror rom-com that blends campy gore with sharp wit and standout performances from Kathryn Newton and Cole Sprouse.

Be prepared for: multiple dog deaths, cat and horse harm, creepy crawlies like spiders and snakes, and plenty of missing body parts.

name: Dark Star
overview: A low-budget, sci-fi satire that focuses on a group of scientists whose mission is to destroy unstable planets. 20 years into their mission, they have battle their alien mascot, that resembles a beach ball, as well as a "sensitive" and intelligent bombing device that starts to question the meaning of its existence.
tagline: Bombed Out in Space with a Spaced Out Bomb!
review:
Dark Star is a cult classic sci-fi satire that feels like a low-budget cousin to 2001: A Space Odyssey, but with a much more irreverent and goofy tone. Directed by John Carpenter and co-written by Dan O’Bannon, it’s a quirky, offbeat ride about a crew tasked with blowing up unstable planets, only to get sidetracked by their bizarre alien mascot—a beach ball with attitude—and a surprisingly philosophical bomb. Fans of deadpan, absurdist humor in space (think early Carpenter meets the later silliness of Red Dwarf) will appreciate its charm, though it’s definitely an acquired taste rather than a mainstream crowd-pleaser.

What really stands out is how Dark Star manages to weave existential questions about artificial intelligence and purpose into its goofy sci-fi setup. The “sensitive” bomb questioning its own existence is a highlight, blending deadpan comedy with a surprisingly thoughtful undercurrent. The low-budget effects add a layer of camp that’s more endearing than distracting, and the cast—though mostly unknowns—bring a kind of earnestness that sells the absurdity. The tagline, “Bombed Out in Space with a Spaced Out Bomb!” nails the film’s playful tone, which oscillates between slapstick and subtle satire.

Heads up for folks sensitive to animal death and abuse triggers—Dark Star involves the death of several animals, including pets, and there’s a fair bit of unsettling imagery involving bugs and spiders. There’s also a plane crash and a nuclear explosion in the mix, plus a generally gloomy ending that might weigh on viewers looking for a light sci-fi romp. If those are on your no-go list, tread carefully.
emailReview:
Dark Star is a delightfully offbeat sci-fi satire that mixes deadpan humor with surprisingly deep questions about artificial intelligence, all wrapped in charmingly low-budget effects and a quirky cast.

Be prepared for: pet deaths, unsettling bug and spider scenes, a plane crash, and a nuclear explosion.

review:
Becky is a brutal little thriller that leans hard into its dark, chaotic energy—think Home Alone meets a violent hostage nightmare. It’s not subtle, but it’s wildly entertaining if you’re in the mood for a teenage antihero who refuses to play nice when a group of convicts invades her family’s lake house. Lulu Wilson makes for a compelling and surprisingly fierce lead, holding her own against the likes of Kevin James in a rare villainous turn. It doesn’t quite reinvent the genre, but it’s a lean, mean ride that fans of gritty revenge tales will appreciate.

What stands out here is how the film embraces its bloody, grimy tone without apology. The lake house setting adds a claustrophobic vibe that intensifies the escalating violence, while the tagline “There once was a little girl...” hints at a twisted fairy tale gone wrong, which fits the movie’s blend of innocence and savagery. The writing doesn’t shy away from some wild, almost cartoonish brutality that keeps you guessing how far Becky will go—and the supporting cast rounds out a cast of dangerous misfits perfectly. The directors, Cary Murnion and Jonathan Milott, know how to keep the tension taut and the action messy.

If you’re sensitive to animal harm, this one comes with multiple red flags. There are several instances of animal deaths and abuse, including a horse and a cat, plus some unsettling moments involving bugs, spiders, and snakes. The film’s violence extends beyond just people, making it a tough watch for animal lovers. Those who pin the animal harm, pet death, and bug triggers should be cautious going in.
emailReview:
Becky is a chaotic, bloody thriller with a fierce teenage antihero who refuses to back down, anchored by Lulu Wilson’s standout performance and a tense, claustrophobic lake house setting.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including a horse and a cat, graphic bug and spider scenes, and intense hostage violence.

name: Desperately Seeking Susan
overview: Roberta is a bored suburban housewife who is fascinated with a woman, Susan, she only knows about by reading messages to and from her in the personals section of the newspaper. This fascination reaches a peak when an ad with the headline "Desperately Seeking Susan" proposes a rendezvous. Roberta goes too, and in a series of events involving amnesia and mistaken identity, steps into Susan's life.

name: Werewolves Within
overview: Shenanigans ensue when a massive blizzard isolates a small Vermont town, causing simmering resentments to boil over as the oddball townspeople are one by one picked off by a mysterious creature.

writers: Thomas Dixon Jr., D.W. Griffith, Frank E. Woods, Woodrow Wilson, John M. Hay, John G. Nicolay
name: The Birth of a Nation
overview: Two families, abolitionist Northerners the Stonemans and Southern landowners the Camerons, intertwine. When Confederate colonel Ben Cameron is captured in battle, nurse Elsie Stoneman petitions for his pardon. In Reconstruction-era South Carolina, Cameron founds the Ku Klux Klan, battling Elsie's congressman father and his African-American protégé, Silas Lynch.

writers: Julio Rojas, Julio Medem, Katherine Fugate
name: Room in Rome
overview: A hotel room in the center of Rome serves as the setting for Alba and Natasha, two young and recently acquainted women, to have a physical adventure that touches their very souls.
tagline: A night of passion that will change their lives.

name: Out for Justice
overview: Gino Felino (Steven Seagal) is an NYPD detective from Brooklyn who knows everyone and everything in his neighborhood. Killing his Partner was someone's mistake, because he's now Out For Justice.

writers: Phillip Murphy, Christopher Landon, Michael Kennedy
name: Heart Eyes
overview: When the Heart Eyes Killer strikes Seattle, a pair of co-workers pulling overtime on Valentine’s Day are mistaken for a couple by the elusive couple-hunting killer. Now they must spend the most romantic night of the year running for their lives.
review:
Heart Eyes is a slasher-thriller with a Valentine’s Day twist that tries to mix rom-com vibes with genuine chills. It’s a bit like if you combined the tense stalking of Halloween with the holiday-themed setup of a rom-com, but instead of sweet moments, you get a relentless killer hunting couples. Olivia Holt and Mason Gooding make a solid duo as coworkers mistaken for a couple, which adds some nice chemistry and grounded humor amid the chaos. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but it’s a fun, pulpy ride with enough tension to keep you invested.

What stands out here is the way the film leans into its premise—“No couple is safe”—using the Valentine’s Day backdrop to ratchet up the stakes and irony. Josh Ruben’s direction keeps the pace brisk, and the writing team (including Christopher Landon) balances the horror beats with moments of levity without undercutting the suspense. The Seattle setting adds a gloomy, rainy atmosphere that suits the mood perfectly, and the supporting cast, especially Michaela Watkins and Devon Sawa as detectives, add some texture to the story.

Those who pin the “a dog dies” trigger should be cautious, as well as fans sensitive to the presence of spiders and bugs. Animal-related triggers are mostly a non-issue here—there are no real animals harmed or featured beyond some unsettling insect appearances. If you’re skittish about creepy crawlies or the emotional sting of pet loss, keep that in mind going in.
emailReview:
Heart Eyes mixes rom-com charm with slasher chills, anchored by Olivia Holt and Mason Gooding’s engaging chemistry and a moody, rainy Seattle backdrop that amps up the Valentine’s Day tension.

Be prepared for: a dog death, unsettling spiders, creepy bugs, and moments of stalking suspense.

name: It Takes Two
overview: Identical 9-year-olds from very different backgrounds: orphaned Amanda and wealthy Alyssa meet at summer camp and decide to switch places -- and play matchmaker between Alyssa's dad, Roger, and the kind social worker who cares for Amanda.
tagline: Two identical strangers. Two different worlds. One perfect match.

name: Fast Charlie
overview: When his aging mob boss is whacked, Charlie Swift, a loyal friend and hired gun, will stop at nothing to bring down the new crew coming up that took him out. Based on the Edgar Award nominated crime novel, GUN MONKEYS.
tagline: Keep your friends close and your enemies dead.

name: The Dark and the Wicked
overview: On a secluded farm in a nondescript rural town, a man is slowly dying.  His family gathers to mourn, and soon a darkness grows, marked by waking nightmares and a sense that something evil is taking over the family.
tagline: She told you not to come
review:
The Dark and the Wicked is a slow-burn horror that leans hard into dread and family despair, carving out a niche somewhere between psychological thriller and supernatural haunt. Bryan Bertino, who also wrote the film, uses the isolated rural farm setting to build an oppressive atmosphere that fans of films like The Witch or Hereditary will recognize—and appreciate. It’s not a jump-scare fest but more of a creeping malaise that gets under your skin, elevated by Marin Ireland’s quietly powerful performance as Louise, who’s caught in the tightening grip of something truly sinister.

What stands out here is how the film uses its tagline—“She told you not to come”—to frame the entire story as a warning that goes unheeded, setting the tone for the slow unraveling of both family and sanity. The nightmare sequences blend seamlessly with the waking terror, and the sense of an encroaching evil feels tangible and relentless. The score and visuals work in tandem to create a haunting mood that’s less about outright horror and more about the dread of inevitable loss, making this a grim meditation on grief as much as a supernatural thriller.

That said, be heavily warned if animal deaths or animal harm are on your list—The Dark and the Wicked features the deaths of a dog, a horse, and a cat, among other distressing moments involving animals. There’s also body horror and gaslighting woven into the narrative, so those sensitive to these elements should approach with caution. This is not a gentle watch by any means, but if you’re up for a bleak, atmospheric horror that doesn’t shy away from the darker corners of family tragedy, it’s worth the ride.
emailReview:
The Dark and the Wicked creeps in with a slow-burning dread that lingers like a bad omen, anchored by Marin Ireland’s quietly unsettling performance and an atmosphere thick with inevitable grief.

Be prepared for: the deaths of a dog, a horse, and a cat, intense body horror, and relentless gaslighting.

overview: Adrienne is trying to decide whether to stay in her unhappy marriage or not, and her life changes when Paul, a doctor who is travelling to reconcile with his estranged son, checks into an inn where she is staying.

overview: A lawyer puts his family in jeopardy when he captures the last member of a violent clan and tries to forcibly tame her.
tagline: Not every monster lives in the wild.

name: Trapped
overview: When their daughter is kidnapped by experienced nappers (Bacon and Love), the Jennings (Theron and Townsend) turn the tables on this seemingly foolproof plan.

name: All the King's Men
overview: The story of an idealist's rise to power in the world of Louisiana politics and the corruption that leads to his ultimate downfall. Based on the1946 Pulitzer Prize-winning novel written by Robert Penn Warren.

name: Backcountry
overview: A couple on a deep-wilderness hike become hopelessly lost within an aggressive black bear's territory.
review:
Backcountry is a tense survival thriller that leans hard into the primal fear of being lost in the wilderness, only to find yourself in the crosshairs of a hostile black bear. It’s the kind of movie that feels like Deliverance meets The Edge, with a stripped-down cast and a relentless focus on the brutal realities of nature—not your typical creature feature but more of a gritty, slow-burn man vs. wild scenario. Missy Peregrym anchors the film as Jenn, bringing an earnest determination that grounds the story amid the escalating dread.

What really stands out here is the raw, claustrophobic atmosphere Adam MacDonald crafts, using dense forest visuals and natural soundscapes to immerse you fully in the couple’s nightmare. The tagline, “Survive,” isn’t just a slogan—it’s a relentless command that drives the film’s pacing and tension. There’s a quiet desperation as Jenn and Alex navigate not just the terrain but also their fraying relationship under pressure, which adds a subtle emotional undercurrent to the predator-prey dynamic.

Heads up if you’re sensitive to animal-related distress: this one carries a heavy load of triggers involving animals, including deaths of various pets and wildlife, plus some pretty unsettling animal abuse and harm. Bugs, spiders, and snakes also make appearances to raise the skin-crawling factor. If those are on your list, be prepared for a rough ride.
emailReview:
Backcountry grips you with its raw, claustrophobic wilderness tension and Missy Peregrym’s grounded performance as a woman pushed to the edge of survival against a relentless black bear.

Be prepared for: intense animal deaths including pets and wildlife, graphic animal abuse, confrontations with snakes, spiders, and bugs.

overview: 'Sugar' Ray is the owner of an illegal casino and must contend with the pressure of vicious gangsters and corrupt police who want to see him go out of business. In the world of organised crime and police corruption in the 1920s, any dastardly trick is fair.

overview: After the collapse of Earth's ecosystem, Vesper, a 13-year-old girl struggling to survive with her paralyzed Father, meets a mysterious Woman with a secret that forces Vesper to use her wits, strength and bio-hacking abilities to fight for the possibility of a future.

name: Excision
overview: Alienated teen Pauline struggles with the pressures of fitting into high school, pleasing her mother and a burning desire to lose her virginity. With a grotesque curiosity for the darker side of life, Pauline is considered a social outcast by everyone around her. Enticed by flesh, she retreats into her own fantasies and hopes to become a great surgeon - that is, if she doesn't go insane first.

writers: Gerard Johnstone, Akela Cooper, James Wan
name: M3GAN 2.0
overview: Two years after M3GAN's rampage, her creator, Gemma, resorts to resurrecting her infamous creation in order to take down Amelia, the military-grade weapon who was built by a defense contractor who stole M3GAN's underlying tech.
review:
M3GAN 2.0 picks up two years after the original’s chaotic android antics and cranks the sci-fi horror dial up a notch. It’s a slick blend of high-tech thriller and dark comedy that feels like *Ex Machina* meets *Child’s Play*, with Allison Williams returning as the frazzled creator Gemma. While it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, the film leverages its premise to deliver a satisfyingly tense showdown between two killer AIs — M3GAN and a new military-grade weapon — making it a worthy follow-up for fans craving more mechanized mayhem.

What stands out here is the way the movie toys with the idea of technology gone rogue, but with a fresh spin: instead of a lone rogue bot, it’s a battle of programmed beasts. The script by Gerard Johnstone and Akela Cooper smartly balances moments of genuine suspense with sharp, occasionally self-aware humor. Amie Donald’s physical performance as M3GAN remains unsettlingly precise, while Jenna Davis’ voice work adds just the right blend of creep and charm. The tagline, “Miss me?” perfectly captures the film’s cheeky confidence in resurrecting a familiar nightmare to take on a new threat.

Heads up for those sensitive to animal-related triggers — there’s a disturbing number of animal deaths and abuse scattered throughout, including pets and wildlife, which might hit hard. Also, the film doesn’t shy away from body horror elements and some unsettling bug and spider appearances. If you’re wary of gaslighting or misgendering, those themes also pop up here, so keep that in mind before diving into this techno-thriller sequel.
emailReview:
M3GAN 2.0 cranks up the sci-fi horror with a slick, darkly comic showdown between two killer AIs, anchored by Allison Williams’ frazzled creator and Amie Donald’s eerily precise android movements.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths and abuse, unsettling body horror, creepy spiders and bugs, plus gaslighting and misgendering themes.

primaryTitle: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
Title_IMDb_Link: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
name: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace

overview: Anakin Skywalker, a young slave strong with the Force, is discovered on Tatooine. Meanwhile, the evil Sith have returned, enacting their plot for revenge against the Jedi.
review:
Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace is a mixed bag that launched a new chapter in the beloved saga but hasn’t quite aged as gracefully as fans hoped. It’s a sprawling sci-fi adventure with all the trappings of classic Star Wars — Jedi knights, political intrigue, and epic space battles — but it leans heavily into world-building and CGI spectacle, sometimes at the expense of the tight storytelling and character depth that made the original trilogy so memorable. Fans of the broader Star Wars mythos will appreciate the lore expansion and the introduction of young Anakin Skywalker, though the execution can feel clunky and uneven.

What really stands out here is the ambitious scope George Lucas aimed for, especially with the pod-racing sequence and the Duel of the Fates lightsaber battle, which still hold up as some of the franchise’s most thrilling moments. The cast does solid work, with Liam Neeson’s Qui-Gon Jinn bringing a calm gravitas and Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan Kenobi stepping into big shoes with ease. Natalie Portman’s Padmé Amidala brings a regal presence, though some of the political dialogue can feel heavy-handed. The tagline, "Every saga has a beginning," feels fitting — this film is all about setting the stage, even if the script sometimes stumbles under the weight of its own ambition.

Trigger-wise, be heavily warned if animal harm or death is a concern. This episode notably includes multiple instances of animals dying, including a dog, horse, cat, and even a dragon, alongside scenes of animal abuse and dog fighting. Those sensitive to these kinds of triggers will want to proceed with caution.
emailReview:
Star Wars: Episode I, The Phantom Menace dazzles with epic space battles, thrilling pod-racing, and standout performances that anchor a sprawling sci-fi world-building adventure.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dog, horse, cat, and dragon, scenes of animal abuse, and dog fighting.

name: Mr. & Mrs. Smith
overview: After five (or six) years of vanilla-wedded bliss, ordinary suburbanites John and Jane Smith are stuck in a huge rut. Unbeknownst to each other, they are both coolly lethal, highly-paid assassins working for rival organisations. When they discover they're each other's next target, their secret lives collide in a spicy, explosive mix of wicked comedy, pent-up passion, nonstop action and high-tech weaponry.

writers: Craig Mazin, Scot Armstrong, Todd Phillips, Jon Lucas, Scott Moore
name: The Hangover Part II
overview: The Hangover crew heads to Thailand for Stu's wedding. After the disaster of a bachelor party in Las Vegas last year, Stu is playing it safe with a mellow pre-wedding brunch. However, nothing goes as planned and Bangkok is the perfect setting for another adventure with the rowdy group.
review:
The Hangover Part II tries to recapture the chaotic charm of the original but ends up feeling like a more tired, darker remix of its Vegas predecessor. It’s the same Wolfpack formula—rowdy guys, wild misadventures, and a wedding gone completely off the rails—but this time in Bangkok, which amps up the exotic mischief but also leans heavily on shock value rather than fresh jokes. Fans of the first film might appreciate the familiar faces and slapstick antics, but this sequel doesn’t quite hit the same comedic highs and feels a bit like a retread with a grimmer edge.

What stands out here is the setting, which adds a colorful but sometimes unsettling backdrop for the crew’s hijinks. The tagline, "The Wolfpack Is Back," promises the same group chemistry, and you get it—with Bradley Cooper, Ed Helms, and Zach Galifianakis doing their usual thing—but the writing leans more into uncomfortable and occasionally offensive territory. The film plays fast and loose with the boundaries of comedy, pushing into darker themes that don’t always land well, and the visuals are a mixed bag of vibrant Bangkok scenes and grimy underworld vibes. Todd Phillips directs with the same frenetic energy but the tone is less fun, more frantic.

If you’re sensitive to animal harm triggers, be heavily warned here. The film features multiple instances of animals dying or being mistreated, including dogs, cats, horses, and more, which can be upsetting. Those who pin the animal abuse and death triggers should definitely brace themselves before diving in.
emailReview:
The Hangover Part II brings the familiar Wolfpack chaos to the neon-lit streets of Bangkok, mixing wild antics with a darker, more frantic tone that feels both colorful and uncomfortable.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and cats, horse mistreatment, graphic animal abuse, and unsettling scenes of violence.

name: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
overview: After seeking to live a normal life, Logan sets out to avenge the death of his girlfriend by undergoing the mutant Weapon X program and becoming Wolverine.
review:
X-Men Origins: Wolverine tries to carve out a gritty origin story for Hugh Jackman’s beloved mutant but lands somewhere between a by-the-numbers superhero flick and a darker character study. It’s got that early-2000s superhero vibe—think less sleek Marvel Cinematic Universe, more rough-around-the-edges action thriller. Fans of Logan’s gruff charm will appreciate Jackman’s commitment, but the film never quite matches the emotional depth or cool factor of later X-Men entries, feeling a bit like Wolverine’s awkward teenage years before he fully comes into his own.

The action sequences lean heavily on the Weapon X program’s brutal experimentation, and the story hooks onto a revenge plot after the death of Logan’s girlfriend, Kayla. The tagline, “Witness the origin,” promises a deep dive into the character’s past, but the script often defaults to familiar genre tropes rather than fresh storytelling. Liev Schreiber as Victor Creed adds a decent foil dynamic, and the camaraderie with other mutants provides some texture, though it’s mostly overshadowed by the film’s grimmer tone and shaky pacing.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related triggers: this one doesn’t hold back. There are multiple instances involving the death and abuse of animals, including dogs, cats, and horses, plus scenes of dog fighting. If animal harm or death is on your list, be heavily warned here. On the bright side, at least the spiders, snakes, and other critters are just background noise rather than major players.
emailReview:
X-Men Origins: Wolverine delivers a gritty, early-2000s superhero vibe with Hugh Jackman’s gruff charm front and center, though it leans more on familiar genre beats than fresh storytelling.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, graphic scenes of dog fighting, and intense animal abuse that will stick with you.

name: Friends With Benefits
overview: Dylan and Jamie think it's going to be easy to add the simple act of sex to their friendship, despite what Hollywood romantic comedies would have them believe. They soon discover however that getting physical really does always lead to complications.
tagline: Some friends come with a happy ending.

writers: Robert Ben Garant, Thomas Lennon, Milan Trenc
name: Night at the Museum
overview: Chaos reigns at the natural history museum when night watchman Larry Daley accidentally stirs up an ancient curse, awakening Attila the Hun, an army of gladiators, a Tyrannosaurus rex and other exhibits.
review:
Night at the Museum is a zany family-friendly adventure that feels like a mashup of Indiana Jones and Night at the Roxbury — if the latter involved a talking T. rex and an army of gladiators. Ben Stiller leads as Larry Daley, the hapless night watchman suddenly in charge of a museum where history quite literally comes to life. It’s a pretty standard early-2000s comedy in tone, but it stands out thanks to its imaginative premise and the way it blends slapstick with a dash of genuine warmth. Fans of lighthearted fantasy capers will find a lot to enjoy here, even if it’s not breaking any new ground.

What really elevates the chaos is the cast, with Stiller’s everyman charm balanced by Dick Van Dyke’s delightfully quirky turn as the museum’s elderly guard. The film revels in its mashup of history and pop culture, from Attila the Hun’s gruff leadership to the surprisingly adorable T. rex skeleton who basically acts like a loyal dog. The tagline "Where history comes to life" is spot-on, and the movie leans fully into its premise, playing out the mayhem in a way that’s energetic and fun, if a bit predictable. The visuals do a solid job of bringing the exhibits to life without veering into the uncanny valley, and the writing, by Thomas Lennon and Robert Ben Garant, keeps things moving briskly.

Heads up for anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this movie features a variety of animal deaths (including a dog, horse, and cat) and scenes where animals are abused or sad, like the dinosaur who gets a bit down when told no more fetch. There’s also spiders, bugs, snakes, and a general parade of creepy crawlies, so if you’ve got a strong reaction to those, be cautious. The animal-related triggers are definitely the heaviest baggage here, even if it’s all wrapped in a family comedy.
emailReview:
Night at the Museum is a playful early-2000s comedy that mixes slapstick, charm, and a wild cast of historic characters brought to life with surprising warmth and energy.

Be prepared for: animal deaths including a dog and horse, scenes of animal abuse and sadness, plus plenty of spiders, snakes, and creepy crawlies.

name: The Mummy Returns
overview: Rick and Evelyn O’Connell, along with their 8-year-old son Alex, discover the key to the legendary Scorpion King’s might: the fabled Bracelet of Anubis. Unfortunately, a newly resurrected Imhotep has designs on the bracelet as well, and isn’t above kidnapping its new bearer, Alex, to gain control of Anubis’s otherworldly army.
review:
The Mummy Returns is a loud, pulpy adventure sequel that leans hard into the Indiana Jones-meets-ancient-magic vibe. It’s got Brendan Fraser back as Rick O’Connell, this time joined by his family, including an 8-year-old son who gets dragged into the supernatural chaos. It’s not quite as fresh as the first film, but it doubles down on spectacle and scares, making it a solid pick for anyone who likes their action with a heavy dose of cheesy fun and undead baddies. Fans of early 2000s adventure flicks will feel right at home here.

What really stands out is the film’s energy and willingness to embrace the ridiculous. Stephen Sommers directs with a clear love for over-the-top set pieces and pulsing action sequences, from the mystical Bracelet of Anubis to the creeping threat of Imhotep and his undead army. Rachel Weisz’s dual role adds a nice touch of intrigue, while the family dynamic—especially the peril faced by young Alex—raises the stakes just enough to keep things emotionally invested. The tagline “Adventure is reborn” fits perfectly, as the movie tries to outdo itself with bigger creatures, flashier visuals, and more supernatural chaos.

Heads-up for anyone sensitive to intense content: this movie packs in jump scares, some pretty graphic finger and toe mutilation, and a handful of scenes involving burning alive. The kidnap plotline means there’s also kidnapping and the threat of harm to a child, which can be unsettling. Animal lovers should be warned as well—there’s a dog death that might hit hard. So, if spiders, flashing lights, or family peril are on your no-go list, consider this a cautious watch.
emailReview:
The Mummy Returns cranks up the pulpy adventure with Brendan Fraser back in action and a family drama that adds an emotional punch amid the supernatural chaos.

Be prepared for: graphic finger and toe mutilation, burning alive, a dog death, and child kidnapping.

name: Salt
overview: As a CIA officer, Evelyn Salt swore an oath to duty, honor, and country. Her loyalty will be tested when a Russian defector accuses her of being a Russian sleeper spy. She goes on the run, using all her skills and years of experience as a covert operative to elude capture, protect her husband, and stay one step ahead of her colleagues at the CIA. Her efforts to prove her innocence only serve to cast doubt on her motives, as the hunt to uncover the truth behind her identity continues and the question remains: "Who is Salt?"

writers: Dan O'Bannon, Ronald Shusett, Jack Paglen, Michael Green, John Logan, Dante Harper
name: Alien: Covenant
overview: Bound for a remote planet on the far side of the galaxy, the crew of the colony ship 'Covenant' discovers what is thought to be an uncharted paradise, but is actually a dark, dangerous world—which has a sole inhabitant: the 'synthetic', David, survivor of the doomed Prometheus expedition.
tagline: The path to paradise begins in hell.

name: It: Chapter Two
overview: 27 years after overcoming the malevolent supernatural entity Pennywise, the former members of the Losers' Club, who have grown up and moved away from Derry, are brought back together by a devastating phone call.
review:
It: Chapter Two tries to recapture the eerie magic of its predecessor while aging up the Losers’ Club into their adult selves, but it lands somewhere between nostalgic horror and a sprawling, uneven finale. This 2019 horror sequel leans heavily into the supernatural and psychological, blending Stephen King’s sprawling mythology with a typical “grown-up heroes return” trope. Fans of the first film or similar ensemble horror epics like *Stranger Things* might appreciate the callbacks and character arcs, though it doesn’t quite hit the same emotional highs or scares as the original.

The standout here is the cast—Jessica Chastain, James McAvoy, and Bill Hader bring depth and humor to their roles, helping to anchor some of the more unwieldy moments. The film’s tagline, “It ends,” promises a final showdown, and while the climax is ambitious, the pacing sometimes drags under the weight of its long runtime. Director Andy Muschietti keeps the visuals creepy and atmospheric, and Gary Dauberman’s script leans into classic horror beats with a few twists, but the mix of childhood trauma and supernatural terror can feel a bit overstuffed at times.

Heads up for animal lovers and those sensitive to certain darker content: the film includes multiple scenes involving the death of animals (including dogs, cats, and even a horse), as well as general animal abuse and disturbing body horror elements. There’s also gaslighting and some unsettling bug and snake imagery. If those are on your list, proceed with caution—the scares here extend beyond Pennywise.
emailReview:
It: Chapter Two blends nostalgic horror with a grown-up twist, anchored by standout performances from Jessica Chastain and James McAvoy that bring humor and heart to its sprawling supernatural saga.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs, cats, and a horse, unsettling body horror, gaslighting, and creepy bug and snake imagery.

writers: Dr. Seuss, Jeffrey Price, Peter S. Seaman
name: How the Grinch Stole Christmas
overview: Inside a snowflake exists the magical land of Whoville. In Whoville, live the Whos, an almost mutated sort of Munchkin-like people. All the Whos love Christmas, yet just outside of their beloved Whoville lives the Grinch. The Grinch is a nasty creature that hates Christmas, and plots to steal it away from the Whos, whom he equally abhors. Yet a small child, Cindy Lou Who, decides to try befriending the Grinch.
review:
How the Grinch Stole Christmas (2000) is that holiday staple that’s part whimsy, part wild Jim Carrey energy, and all about the clash between festive cheer and cranky curmudgeon vibes. It’s a live-action spin on the classic Dr. Seuss tale that leans into absurdity with its over-the-top makeup and set design, making it feel like a weirdly colorful fever dream version of Whoville. If you like your Christmas movies with a side of slapstick and a dash of heart, this fits right in—though it’s not quite as charming or subtle as the original animated special, Carrey’s manic performance keeps it entertaining.

Where it really sticks out is the world-building: Whoville’s inhabitants are almost cartoonishly exaggerated, which can feel either delightfully quirky or just plain weird depending on your tolerance for heavy prosthetics and goofy accents. Cindy Lou Who’s earnest attempts to crack the Grinch’s icy exterior inject some sweetness, balancing the Grinch’s general nastiness. Ron Howard’s direction keeps the pace brisk, and the film leans into the classic “redemption arc” with a sugary glaze, staying true to the tagline, “You better watch out!” The visuals are a trip, with the sets and costumes leaning into a Dr. Seuss-meets-puppet-show aesthetic, which definitely sets it apart from other holiday fare.

Heads up to anyone sensitive to animal-related content: this version is surprisingly dark in spots, with multiple animal deaths and scenes of animal abuse. It’s not what you expect from a family Christmas movie, so if you’re someone who pins “a dog dies” or “a horse dies,” be prepared. There’s also mentions of self-harm and suicide, which add an unexpected weight. Plus, if bugs and spiders make you squirm, those are in there too. So, while it’s a festive romp on the surface, the triggers lurking beneath might catch some viewers off guard.
emailReview:
Jim Carrey’s wild energy and the film’s bizarre, puppet-show-like Whoville make this holiday retelling a colorful fever dream of festive chaos and quirky charm.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths, scenes of animal abuse, mentions of self-harm and suicide, and creepy bugs and spiders.

writers: Jim Herzfeld, Marc Hyman, John Hamburg, Greg Glienna, Mary Ruth Clarke
name: Meet the Fockers
overview: Hard-to-crack ex-CIA man Jack Byrnes and his wife Dina head for the warmer climes of Florida to meet the parents of their son-in-law-to-be, Greg Focker. Unlike their happily matched offspring, the future in-laws find themselves in a situation of opposites that definitely do not attract.

writers: Allan Loeb, Timothy Dowling, I.A.L. Diamond, Abe Burrows, Pierre Barillet, Jean-Pierre Grédy
name: Just Go With It
overview: A plastic surgeon, romancing a much younger schoolteacher, enlists his loyal assistant to pretend to be his soon to be ex-wife, in order to cover up a careless lie. When more lies backfire, the assistant's kids become involved, and everyone heads off for a weekend in Hawaii that will change all their lives.
tagline: Sometimes you need a girl, to get the girl.

name: Minions
overview: Minions Stuart, Kevin and Bob are recruited by Scarlet Overkill, a super-villain who, alongside her inventor husband Herb, hatches a plot to take over the world.
tagline: Go back to where it all began.

writers: Alex Litvak, Michael Finch, Jim Thomas, John Thomas
name: Predators
overview: A group of cold-blooded killers find themselves trapped on an alien planet to be hunted by extraterrestrial Predators.
tagline: They are the most dangerous killers on the planet. But this is not our planet.
review:
Predators is a sci-fi action throwback that leans hard into the survival-of-the-fittest trope, pitching a ragtag group of killers against the iconic extraterrestrial hunters on their home turf. It’s got that rugged, high-stakes vibe reminiscent of the original Predator but with a 2010s polish and a grittier, more ensemble-driven approach. Fans of tense, creature-feature thrillers will find something to appreciate here, though it doesn’t quite reach the suspense or charm of the classic 1987 film. Adrien Brody’s brooding lead carries the weight, but the movie mostly rides on familiar genre beats rather than reinventing them.

What stands out most is the setting—a hostile alien jungle that feels both claustrophobic and vast, making the hunt feel relentless and inescapable. Nimród Antal’s direction keeps the pace brisk, and the cast’s mix of hardened killers adds some intriguing dynamics, though the script by Alex Litvak and Michael Finch occasionally dips into cliché. The tagline, “They are the most dangerous killers on the planet. But this is not our planet,” perfectly sums up the premise: what happens when predators become prey? The film’s visuals and practical effects do a solid job of selling the brutality of the hunt, even if the story itself doesn’t break much new ground.

Trigger-wise, be heavily warned if animal harm and death are on your list—there’s a distressing number of animals suffering or dying (dogs, cats, horses, and more), and some of it feels uncomfortably graphic. Body horror elements and bugs/spiders also appear, adding a layer of gross-out tension. Plus, those sensitive to vomiting and gaslighting will want to brace themselves. This one leans into its darker, more violent corners, so it’s definitely not for the faint of heart or animal lovers.
emailReview:
Predators is a gritty sci-fi action throwback that traps a tough cast in a claustrophobic alien jungle where survival feels brutal and relentless.

Be prepared for: graphic animal deaths including dogs and horses, unsettling body horror, invasive bugs and spiders, vomiting, and psychological gaslighting.

writers: Len Brown, Woody Gelman, Wally Wood, Bob Powell, Norman Saunders, Jonathan Gems
name: Mars Attacks
overview: 'We come in peace' is not what those green men from Mars mean when they invade our planet, armed with irresistible weapons and a cruel sense of humor.  This star studded cast must play victim to the alien’s fun and games in this comedy homage to science fiction films of the '50s and '60s.
review:
Tim Burton’s *Mars Attacks* is a wild, campy sci-fi comedy that feels like *The Day the Earth Stood Still* meets *Austin Powers*—a gleefully over-the-top send-up of 1950s alien invasion flicks packed with a star-studded cast including Jack Nicholson in a delightfully quirky dual role. It’s not exactly subtle, but that’s the point: it leans hard into absurdity and dark humor, making it a cult favorite for those who enjoy their sci-fi with a big helping of satire and slapstick.

What really stands out here is the film’s unapologetically zany tone and its sharp parody of Cold War era paranoia and cheesy B-movie tropes. The tagline “Nice planet. We’ll take it!” sums up the Martians’ twisted blend of charm and menace perfectly. The chaotic plot and eccentric characters keep things moving, while the special effects and quirky score underscore the film’s campy charm. It’s a blast if you’re in the mood for something that doesn’t take itself seriously and enjoys poking fun at classic sci-fi clichés.

Heads up for animal lovers: this one packs a surprising amount of animal-related carnage, including the deaths of multiple pets and other creatures, plus some scenes of animal abuse and fighting. Those who pin the “animal harm” or “pet death” triggers should definitely be cautious going in. Also, if you’re uneasy about creepy-crawlies, there are spiders, snakes, and other bugs that earn a mention. Definitely a wild ride—just be ready for a few rough spots if you’re sensitive to animal-related content.
emailReview:
Tim Burton’s *Mars Attacks* is a gleefully campy sci-fi comedy that turns 1950s alien invasion tropes into a zany satire full of quirky characters and wild dark humor.

Be prepared for: multiple pet deaths, animal abuse, spider and snake scenes, and chaotic creature chaos.

writers: Justin Haythe, Ted Elliott, Terry Rossio
name: The Lone Ranger
overview: The Texas Rangers chase down a gang of outlaws led by Butch Cavendish, but the gang ambushes the Rangers, seemingly killing them all. One survivor is found, however, by an American Indian named Tonto, who nurses him back to health. The Ranger, donning a mask and riding a white stallion named Silver, teams up with Tonto to bring the unscrupulous gang and others of that ilk to justice.

writers: Steve Franks, Tim Herlihy, Adam Sandler
name: Big Daddy
overview: A lazy law school grad adopts a kid to impress his girlfriend, but everything doesn't go as planned and he becomes the unlikely foster father.
review:
Big Daddy is classic late-90s Adam Sandler comedy with a soft heart, the kind that tries to balance goofball antics with an earnest message about growing up and responsibility. At its core, it’s a “lazy man forced to become a parent” story, with Sandler’s Sonny Koufax adopting a kid to impress a girlfriend—only to get way more than he bargained for. It’s not as sharp or funny as some of Sandler’s best work, but fans of goofy, sentimental comedies like *Mrs. Doubtfire* or *Three Men and a Baby* will find familiar pleasures here. The Sprouse twins as Julian add a surprising sweetness that grounds the zaniness.

What stands out is how the movie leans into its tagline, “Nature called. Look who answered.” There’s a lot of slapstick and dumb humor, but it’s anchored by moments of genuine warmth and growth, especially as Sonny grapples with being an unlikely foster father. The supporting cast, including Leslie Mann and Joey Lauren Adams, round out the quirky ensemble, and Dennis Dugan’s direction keeps the pace light and breezy. It’s very much a product of its time, with some humor and situations that might feel dated or awkward now, but the underlying story about unexpected family bonds holds up.

That said, be warned if you’re sensitive to animal harm or death. The film includes multiple instances where animals die or are mistreated, including dogs, cats, a horse, and birds—yes, quite a lot of sad moments for animal lovers. There’s also child abuse and sexual assault flagged, as well as some unpleasant hate speech and general gross-out moments like spitting. If those are on your radar, you might want to approach with caution.
emailReview:
Big Daddy mixes goofy late-90s Adam Sandler antics with genuine warmth, anchored by the surprising sweetness of the Sprouse twins and a quirky supporting cast.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, child abuse, sexual assault, hate speech, and gross-out moments like spitting.

name: Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls
overview: Summoned from an ashram in Tibet, Ace finds himself on a perilous journey into the jungles of Africa to find Shikaka, the missing sacred animal of the friendly Wachati tribe.
tagline: New animals. New adventures. Same hair.
review:
Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls is a goofy, over-the-top comedy sequel that doubles down on Jim Carrey’s elastic physicality and absurd humor. If you dug the first Ace Ventura for its wild animal antics and Carrey’s unhinged energy, this one feels like more of the same—but cranked up to cartoonish levels. It’s less clever than the original and sometimes leans too hard into slapstick, but there’s a goofy charm to the jungle adventure vibe that fans of 90s comedies will appreciate.

The film’s tagline, “New animals. New adventures. Same hair.” nails the spirit here—Ace is still the same fast-talking, eccentric detective, but now he’s trekking through the African jungle on a quest for the sacred animal Shikaka. Director Steve Oedekerk doesn’t shy away from ridiculous set pieces and physical gags, and the supporting cast adds some flavor without stealing the spotlight from Carrey. The blend of surreal humor and animal hijinks makes it a unique entry in the mid-90s comedy scene, even if it doesn’t hit the same highs as the original.

Heads up for animal-related triggers: this movie features multiple scenes involving animal deaths (including dogs, horses, cats, and more), animal abuse, and some unsettling moments with bugs, spiders, and snakes. If you’re sensitive to animal harm or distress, this one might be tough to sit through.
emailReview:
Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls is a wild, goofy romp that cranks Jim Carrey’s elastic antics and jungle chaos up to cartoonish levels, delivering slapstick and surreal animal hijinks with undeniable 90s charm.

Be prepared for: multiple animal deaths including dogs and horses, animal abuse, unsettling bug and spider scenes, and snake encounters.

writers: Nicole Eastman, Karen McCullah, Kirsten Smith
name: The Ugly Truth
overview: A romantically challenged morning show producer is reluctantly embroiled in a series of outrageous tests by her chauvinistic correspondent to prove his theories on relationships and help her find love. His clever ploys, however, lead to an unexpected result.
tagline: The battle of the sexes is on.

writers: Christopher Markus, Stephen McFeely, Pete Collins
name: Pain & Gain
overview: Daniel Lugo, manager of the Sun Gym in 1990s Miami, decides that there is only one way to achieve his version of the American dream: extortion. To achieve his goal, he recruits musclemen Paul and Adrian as accomplices. After several failed attempts, they abduct rich businessman Victor Kershaw and convince him to sign over all his assets to them. But when Kershaw makes it out alive, authorities are reluctant to believe his story.
tagline: Their American dream is bigger than yours.

name: Leave The World Behind
overview: A husband and wife as head out to a remote corner of Long Island expecting a vacation with their teenage son and daughter. When the owners of the rental return in a panic one night after they say a sudden blackout has swept through the city, the couple aren't sure what to believe. With the TV and internet down and no cell service, the two families are forced into a tense living situation.
tagline: There's no going back to normal.

name: 17 Again
overview: On the brink of a midlife crisis, 30-something Mike O'Donnell wishes he could have a "do-over." And that's exactly what he gets when he wakes up one morning to find he's 17 years old again. With his adult mind stuck inside the body of a teenager, Mike actually has the chance to reverse some decisions he wishes he'd never made. But maybe they weren't so bad after all.
tagline: Who says you're only young once?

writers: Paul W.S. Anderson, Robert Thom, Charles B. Griffith, Ib Melchior
name: Death Race
overview: Terminal Island, New York: 2020. Overcrowding in the US penal system has reached a breaking point. Prisons have been turned over to a monolithic Weyland Corporation, which sees jails full of thugs as an opportunity for televised sport. Adrenalized inmates, a global audience hungry for violence and a spectacular, enclosed arena come together to form the 'Death Race', the biggest, most brutal event.
tagline: Get ready for a killer ride.

name: The Number 23
overview: Walter Sparrow is an animal control officer that becomes obsessed with a mysterious book that seems to be based on his own life. As soon as he opens the book, he notices strange parallels between what he reads and what he's experienced. But now he's worried that a fictional murder might materialize.

writers: Neal Purvis, Robert Wade, Bruce Feirstein, Ian Fleming
name: The World Is Not Enough
overview: Greed, revenge, world dominance and high-tech terrorism – it's all in a day's work for Bond, who's on a mission to protect a beautiful oil heiress from a notorious terrorist. In a race against time that culminates in a dramatic submarine showdown, Bond works to defuse the international power struggle that has the world's oil supply hanging in the balance.
tagline: As the countdown begins for the new millennium there is still one number you can always count on.

name: The Taking of Pelham 123
overview: Armed men hijack a New York City subway train, holding the passengers hostage in return for a ransom, and turning an ordinary day's work for dispatcher Walter Garber into a face-off with the mastermind behind the crime.
tagline: I can't get it out of my head. I'm gonna die today.

writers: George Miller, John Collee, Judy Morris, Warren Coleman
name: Happy Feet
overview: Into the world of the Emperor Penguins, who find their soul mates through song, a penguin is born who cannot sing. But he can tap dance something fierce!

writers: Pierre Christin, Jean-Claude Mézières, Luc Besson

overview: In the 28th century, Valerian and Laureline are special operatives charged with keeping order throughout the human territories. At the center of Alpha is a mysterious dark force which threatens the peaceful existence of the City of a Thousand Planets, and Valerian and Laureline must race to identify the menace and safeguard not just Alpha, but the future of the universe.
tagline: A universe without boundaries needs heroes without limits.

name: The Longest Yard
overview: Pro quarter-back, Paul Crewe and former college champion and coach, Nate Scarboro are doing time in the same prison. Asked to put together a team of inmates to take on the guards, Crewe enlists the help of Scarboro to coach the inmates to victory in a football game 'fixed' to turn out quite another way.

name: The Woman in Black
overview: The story follows a young lawyer, Arthur Kipps, who is ordered to travel to a remote village and sort out a recently deceased client’s papers. As he works alone in the client’s isolated house, Kipps begins to uncover tragic secrets, his unease growing when he glimpses a mysterious woman dressed only in black. Receiving only silence from the locals, Kipps is forced to uncover the true identity of the Woman in Black on his own, leading to a desperate race against time when he discovers her true identity.

writers: Damon Lindelof, Brad Bird, Jeff Jensen
name: Tomorrowland
overview: Bound by a shared destiny, a bright, optimistic teen bursting with scientific curiosity and a former boy-genius inventor jaded by disillusionment embark on a danger-filled mission to unearth the secrets of an enigmatic place somewhere in time and space that exists in their collective memory as "Tomorrowland."
tagline: Imagine a place where nothing is impossible.

writers: Josh Heald, Sean Anders, John Morris
name: Hot Tub Time Machine
overview: A malfunctioning time machine at a ski resort takes a man back to 1986 with his two friends and nephew, where they must relive a fateful night and not change anything to make sure the nephew is born.
tagline: Forget the present. Change the future. Kick some past.

writers: Wes Craven, Alexandre Aja, Grégory Levasseur
name: The Hills Have Eyes
overview: Based on Wes Craven's 1977 suspenseful cult classic, The Hills Have Eyes is the story of a family road trip that goes terrifyingly awry when the travelers become stranded in a government atomic zone. Miles from nowhere, the Carter family soon realizes the seemingly uninhabited wasteland is actually the breeding ground of a blood-thirsty mutant family...and they are the prey.
review:
The Hills Have Eyes (2006) is a brutal, no-holds-barred horror remake that leans hard into body horror and survival terror. Alexandre Aja’s take on Wes Craven’s cult classic amps up the gore and dread, making it feel like The Texas Chainsaw Massacre meets a radioactive nightmare. It’s not subtle, but fans of intense, grimy horror will find it a wild ride—just don’t expect much in the way of nuance or character development beyond sheer desperation.

What stands out is the unapologetic rawness of the film’s atmosphere. The tagline, “The lucky ones die first,” nails the hopeless tone as the Carter family tumbles into a government atomic wasteland inhabited by grotesque mutants. The tension is thick, the violence unflinching, and the mutant family’s menace is as unsettling as ever. Aja’s direction and the gritty visuals work together to make the barren desert feel oppressively hostile, while the cast—including Emilie de Ravin and Ted Levine—keep the emotional stakes alive amid the carnage.

Heads up: this one is heavy on animal harm triggers. Multiple animals die or are abused on-screen, including dogs, cats, and a horse, with disturbing scenes involving bugs, spiders, and snakes adding to the grim tableau. If animal suffering is a dealbreaker for you, be heavily warned before diving into this one.
emailReview:
The Hills Have Eyes (2006) delivers relentless, grimy horror with a radioactive twist, where dread and gore collide in a barren wasteland that never lets up.

Be prepared for: graphic dog, cat, and horse deaths, intense animal abuse, and unsettling bug and snake scenes.

overview: Have you ever wondered why they said they would call but didn't, or why they don't want to sleep with you anymore, or why your relationship isn't going to the next level? Maybe they're just not that into you. Gigi wants a man who says he'll call her - and actually does - while Alex advises her to stop waiting by the phone. Beth wants a proposal after years of a committed relationship with her boyfriend, Neil, who is just fine with the way things are. Janine's not sure if she can trust her husband, Ben, who can't quite trust himself around Anna.
